# Policy decisions

This document records the conversion and product policies of EasyConvert. Each entry gives the reason the policy is right in practice and what it costs, so a later change can weigh the same trade-offs instead of guessing.

The bar for conversion behaviour is the output of mature commercial converters: the same results users already get elsewhere, at the same or better quality and speed. An entry never relies on "another product does this" alone; it states the practical reason behind the common practice.

## Format

Each entry has:

- **Status**: Implemented (with the change that did it), Decided (with the issue that tracks it), or Superseded.
- **Decision**: what the system does.
- **Why**: the practical reason it is right.
- **Trade-offs**: what it costs and who pays.
- **Alternatives rejected**: the options weighed and why they lost.
- **Verified by**: the tests or bench rows that hold it in place.
- **Revisit when**: the facts that would change the decision.

Add an entry, or update one, in the same commit that changes a policy.

## 1. AVIF chroma and bit depth

- **Status**: Implemented (#749, issue #736), decided 2026-10-11. Supersedes the 2026-10-09 policy (graphics 4:4:4, at most 10 bits).
- **Decision**:
  - **Lossy output** is 4:2:0 for all content, photographs and graphics alike.
  - **Lossless output** (quality 100), and pictures with an identity colour matrix, are 4:4:4.
  - **Bit depth**: an 8-bit source is written at 8 bits. A 9- or 10-bit source is written at 10 bits. A source of 11 bits or more, 16-bit included, is written at 12 bits. HDR renditions (PQ or HLG) keep their 10 bits.
  - **Alpha and metadata**: see [22. Image metadata and alpha](#22-image-metadata-and-alpha).
- **Why**: users compare our files with the ones the leading converters give them. Those use 4:2:0 for lossy AVIF and keep high-bit-depth sources at a matching depth. Matching this keeps file sizes comparable for every content class, so a user switching to us does not get files that are suddenly larger. 4:2:0 is also the layout every AVIF decoder handles fastest. Keeping 12 bits for 16-bit sources preserves gradations and editing headroom that a 10-bit cap would throw away.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - At the same quality setting, 4:2:0 softens coloured edges in screenshots, text and line art. 4:4:4 would keep them sharp, at a larger file.
  - 12-bit AVIF needs the AV1 Professional profile. Some hardware decoders, and decoders that implement only the AVIF Baseline profile (AV1 Main), cannot open it, so a 16-bit source can produce a file that does not open on every device.
  - Measured against the reference encoder at the same constraints (BD-rate, 0 is parity, lower is better): the 11 photographs that were 1.6 to 4.9 % behind in SSIM are now between -3.1 and +0.9 %; the 16-bit class is 12 to 13 % ahead in WebP and AVIF PSNR. Photographs stay on the in-process encoder, whose speed is 1.2 to 1.4 times the reference's; the command-line encoder with edge-preserving chroma conversion took the same photographs to +1.3 to +1.7 % SSIM at 0.7 times the speed, which is why the 4:4:4 reference could not be met by encoder tuning alone. On the CI runner after the change the in-process encoder reads 0.95 of the reference's speed on `kodim23` and `photo-b` (the reference now runs at 4:2:0 as well), which #641 tracks.
  - **The bytes of a photograph's AVIF depend on the encoder thread count, and the nightly curve of one photograph sits on the allowance.** The in-process encoder leases 2 threads while the heap is not bounded (`image-threads.ts`), the reference runs on every core, and the AV1 encoder cuts the frame for its threads: for `clic-sergey-zolkin-21232.png` (1542 x 1028) at quality 70 the file is 41,790 bytes on 1 thread, 42,209 on 2 and 42,403 on 4, and the BD-rate against the reference tool of the CI image (`avifenc` 1.0.4 with libaom 3.8.2, installed on the arm64 testbed) is -0.34 % in PSNR and +0.18 % in SSIM on 1 thread, +0.78 and +1.37 on 2, +1.09 and +1.34 on 4. The x86-64 CI runner reads +1.5011 and +1.6045 on 2 threads (the output differs by CPU architecture, in both encoders: ours 42,202 bytes there and 42,209 on arm64, the reference 41,795 and 41,662), against an allowance of 1.5, with the same 16 digits in four nightly runs from 2026-10-17 to 2026-10-19 and on arm64 at the commit that recorded the baseline: the row is deterministic, did not move, and is a gap, not noise. One thread would close it and costs 1.7 times the time (173 ms against 103 ms on the testbed), which would move the speed rows of the photograph AVIF cases (#641); that trade is open, so both rows are tracked in `bench/parity-gaps.json` at the CI value (issue #641) instead of changing the lease or the allowance.
  - The 4:4:4 policy it replaces was the reason for the photo SSIM gap: against a 4:4:4 reference no encoder setting tried (perceptual tuning, edge-preserving conversion, quantiser modulation, a slower speed preset) met both metrics inside the speed gate.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Graphics 4:4:4 with a 10-bit cap** (the previous policy). It gave sharper graphic edges and wider device support, but its file sizes and bit depths diverged from what users expect from converters.
  - **Always 4:4:4.** Larger photographs for no visible gain.
- **Verified by**:
  - `src/lib/conversions/image-encoder-defaults.ts` and its tests.
  - The image parity rows, where the reference encoder runs at the same chroma and bit depth and BD-rate decides.
- **Revisit when**:
  - Users report 12-bit files that do not open.
  - A caller-facing chroma or bit-depth option is added.
  - Decoder support for the Professional profile becomes universal.

## 2. JPEG chroma and encoder tools

- **Status**: Implemented (#716, #719, #722).
- **Decision**:
  - **Chroma**: below quality 90, JPEG uses 4:2:0. At 90 and above it uses 4:4:4, for all content.
  - **Photographs**: baseline scan for colour photographs, progressive scan (without a scan search) for grey photographs, no trellis quantisation.
  - **Graphics**: a quantisation table tuned for structural similarity.
  - **Classification** (#749): a picture with more than 8 bits per sample that shows thousands of tones in its thumbnail is a photograph, whatever the flat share of its background says.
- **Why**:
  - The quality-90 switch is the long-standing default of the common image toolkits, so outputs and sizes match user expectations. Above 90, users ask for fidelity and chroma resolution is visible.
  - Trellis quantisation saves about 8 % of bytes on photographs but adds a large share of the encode time. The reference encoders' defaults do not use it either, so speed parity wins.
- **Trade-offs**: below 90, coloured text in a JPEG is slightly blurred. Photographs are a few per cent larger than the slowest encoder settings would make them. A radiograph (16-bit grey, 44 % flat black) was classified as a graphic and got the graphic table, which zeroes its fine detail: SSIM BD-rate +1.7 % against the reference, -0.7 % with the photograph table. The classifier reads a second, 16-bit thumbnail only for a 16-bit picture the 8-bit one calls graphic, so the encode time did not change (24 ms either way on the 16-bit space photograph).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Always 4:4:4**: noticeably larger files at the same quality setting, with no visible gain on photographs.
  - **Trellis on**: too slow.
- **Verified by**: the JPEG parity rows, quality and speed, on the public picture sets.
- **Revisit when**: CPU budgets change enough that trellis becomes free relative to the reference.

## 3. Lossy audio resampling and sample format

- **Status**: Implemented (#718).
- **Decision**:
  - Audio that needs a rate change goes through the band-limited soxr resampler. Output for a lossy encoder uses 16-bit filter precision.
  - Lossless and PCM outputs, normalised files, and callers who ask for soxr by name keep the full 28-bit precision.
  - 16-bit output is dithered.
  - Opus is the exception: its rate change is left to ffmpeg's own conversion (entry 66).
- **Why**:
  - At 16-bit precision the resampling error sits 83 dB below the signal. The coding noise of Opus at 64 kbit/s, and of AAC and MP3 at their usual rates, sits 25 to 40 dB below it. The resampler is therefore never what a listener hears, and the cheaper filter is built and run faster.
  - Lossless outputs have no coding noise to hide the resampler, so they keep the full precision (97 dB).
  - The default resampler's error is 64 dB below the signal, which is close enough to the coding noise to matter on bright material.
- **Trade-offs**: lossy outputs could carry a measurably, though never audibly, cleaner resample at about 2 ms more per four seconds of stereo audio.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **28-bit precision everywhere**: slower, with no audible gain on lossy outputs.
  - **The default resampler**: faster, but nearer the codec's noise floor.
- **Verified by**: `src/lib/conversions/media-audio-quality.ts` and the audio parity rows. #738 adds a perceptual quality metric.
- **Revisit when**: a perceptual metric shows the precision choice matters at low bit rates.

## 4. Restricted and encrypted PDFs

- **Status**: Implemented (#571 and follow-ups).
- **Decision**:
  - A PDF with an open password needs that password. Without it the request fails with 422.
  - A PDF with owner restrictions only, such as no printing or no editing, is processed after the caller sets `confirmEditRights: true` to confirm they may edit it. Without that confirmation the request fails with 422.
  - An unlock operation removes the restrictions on the same terms.
  - A conversion only reads the file, so owner restrictions never stop it, and an empty open password is not a password: see entry 49.
- **Why**:
  - Owner restrictions are not encryption of the content: any reader can open the file. Commercial PDF tools process such files once the user asserts the right to do so.
  - Refusing them outright blocks routine work, such as compressing a form you filled in, without protecting anyone.
  - An open password does protect content, so it is always required.
- **Trade-offs**: the confirmation relies on the caller's word. The rights responsibility sits with the caller, as it does with every commercial tool.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Refusing all restricted files**: stricter than the market, and it fails users.
  - **Ignoring restrictions silently**: hides a rights question from the user.
- **Verified by**: `src/lib/conversions/pdf-access.ts` and its tests; the pdf-ops parity rows for unlock and decrypt.
- **Revisit when**: legal advice for a target market requires a different flow.

## 5. Document passwords

- **Status**: Decided (#683).
- **Decision**:
  - Callers may supply the password of an encrypted Office or legacy spreadsheet document.
  - The password is used in memory only. It is never logged or stored.
  - A missing or wrong password fails with 422.
- **Why**: encrypted business documents are common, and converters accept their passwords. Refusing them makes a whole class of files unconvertible.
- **Trade-offs**: password handling widens the secret surface. It is contained by never persisting the password, and by redacting it from logs and errors.
- **Alternatives rejected**: refusing encrypted documents.
- **Verified by**: the tests added with #683.
- **Revisit when**: a password must survive a retry. If so, it needs an encrypted, short-lived store.

## 6. External images in HTML

- **Status**: Implemented (#732); the LibreOffice route follows it for every image (#783). What else a page names is entry 51.
- **Decision**:
  - When converting an uploaded HTML page, images it references by public `http`/`https` URL are fetched and embedded, as a browser would show them.
  - The fetch runs in a separate child process with no secrets. That process accepts only public addresses on ports 80 and 443, and pins the resolved address.
  - It re-checks every redirect hop, and caps each image (10 MiB, 10 s) and each document (50 MiB, 100 images, 30 s).
  - The renderer itself stays without network access.
  - Images that fail stay out with a warning. `requireResources: true` turns a failure into 400 instead.
  - Deployments without internet set `HTML_IMAGE_FETCH=off`.
  - The in-process renderer and the staging for LibreOffice use the same loader, so a page gets the same images, warnings and `requireResources` outcome on both. A reference to something that is not an image (a link, style sheet, script, frame) is not fetched on either route; entry 51 says what happens to it.
- **Why**: users expect a converted page to look like the page in a browser. Leaving images out silently produces a visibly broken document. The guards make the fetch safe against server-side request forgery.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - Conversion time depends on remote servers, within the caps.
  - Worker egress must be allowed to public addresses on 80/443.
  - A page on a nonstandard port loses its images, with a warning.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Leaving every external image out with a warning** (the earlier behaviour): safe, but the output is visibly worse than users get elsewhere.
  - **Letting the renderer fetch directly**: it would give a full browser engine network access next to the job's secrets.
- **Verified by**: `tests/html-image-fetch*.test.ts`, `tests/public-address.test.ts`, the end-to-end tests with an independent PDF image reader, and `tests/html-pdf-external-resources.test.ts` (a fetched image next to dropped links on the LibreOffice route, a private-address image, `HTML_IMAGE_FETCH=off`, `requireResources`).
- **Revisit when**: user demand appears for stylesheets, fonts or other ports.

## 7. Characters without a Unicode counterpart

- **Status**: Implemented (#725); extended to every in-process PDF writer (#742), to legacy binary word-processing documents (`.doc`, #726) and, with styles, WP Greek and presentations, in the follow-ups of #760.
- **Decision**:
  - Symbol-font private-use characters are mapped to Unicode with the standard tables for the symbol fonts.
  - A character that no table maps becomes U+FFFD, and a warning names the font and the code.
  - **The PDF writers apply the same rule to any code point no font can draw** (unassigned, private-use, noncharacter, lone surrogate). The code point becomes U+FFFD and the result carries one warning line for each distinct code point. They no longer refuse the document.
  - **Binary word-processing documents (`.doc`) take the font from the formatting of the character**. Each of the ASCII, East Asian and other fonts is the first one set by the run, then by the character style of the run, then by the paragraph style of its paragraph (the Normal style when it has no entry of its own), then by the default character fonts of the style sheet; a style that sets no font hands the choice to the style it is based on. The font of the character is the first of the three that is a symbol font. A Symbol field character (a placeholder in the text plus its own font and code) maps the same way, and in any other font it is the Unicode character it names. A document without a font table or a character whose font index names no font maps nothing, and the warning names no font.
  - **A style chain is followed for at most 32 styles, and a malformed one is refused** (HTTP 400): styles based on each other, a style the sheet does not hold, a style whose size runs outside the table stream, a chain longer than the limit. Each style is resolved once per document.
  - **The WP Greek faces (WordPerfect character set 8) have a table of their own**: the capital and small Greek letters in alphabet order from code 0x21. The slots the set fills with a repeat of another letter and the accented and polytonic letters (their order differs between versions of the set) map to nothing, so they become U+FFFD with a warning like any other unmapped code.
  - **A symbol-font character whose Unicode counterpart no installed font can draw becomes U+FFFD in a PDF**, with a warning that names the font, the code and the counterpart. Text, HTML and the other outputs keep the counterpart. Installing a font that covers the counterpart makes the next conversion draw it. **Binary presentations (`.ppt`) follow the same rule**: the same helper decides what the installed fonts cover, and the warning lines are the same. Presentations in the XML format (`.pptx`) follow it too since entry 169: the symbol typeface of a run (else its Latin one) says which table maps its characters.
- **Why**:
  - The whole document must still convert. Failing it for one glyph is worse than any substitute.
  - A replacement mark is honest.
  - Drawing the code with another font would show a different glyph with no sign of the error, because unknown symbol encodings differ font by font.
  - Word processors keep private-use characters in text on purpose (a bullet or a math symbol typed in a symbol font), so a whole document must not fail for one.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - The reader sees a replacement mark where the original showed a glyph.
  - Plain text, Markdown and HTML to PDF follow the rule too. A file with a stray noncharacter converts, where it used to fail with HTTP 400.
  - A character that is assigned but that no installed font covers still fails, because installing a font fixes it. The exception is a character that came from a symbol-font mapping in a `.doc`: the pictograph and arrow blocks the Wingdings and Webdings tables map to are covered by few fonts, and a bullet or an arrow is not worth a failed document.
  - A symbol-font character that the document stores with the font of an ordinary text style (a check box in the Normal style, whose font is Arial) is not a symbol character to the reader, and it is replaced and reported under that font. The formatting names no symbol font, so any guess would invent a glyph.
  - A PDF made from a presentation shows U+FFFD for an arrow or a pictograph that no installed font covers, where it used to fail the file.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Refusing the document.**
  - **Rendering with a bundled symbol font**: wrong glyphs, silently.
  - **Dropping the character**: the loss would leave no trace in the output.
  - **Refusing a `.doc` whose mapped character has no installed glyph**: the same document converts on a machine with the font and fails on one without, for a decoration.
- **Verified by**: the PPT and `.doc` symbol-font tests (`tests/doc-symbol-fonts.test.ts`, with a document written by the office suite and the PDF text read by a separate PDF reader; `tests/doc-style-fonts.test.ts`, with documents written by hand from the file format; `tests/ppt-text-extraction.test.ts`; and `tests/doc-corpus-symbol-fonts.test.ts` and `tests/ppt-corpus-symbol-fonts.test.ts` on public documents, the Greek letters read against the sentences they stand in), `tests/symbol-font-map.test.ts` (the Greek alphabet in order), `tests/pdf-unicode-text-writers.test.ts` (plain text), `tests/conversion-warnings-scope.test.ts`, and the public document rows (`doc-poi-bug59058.docx` and `doc-poi-41246-2.ppt` convert).
- **Revisit when**: a reliable glyph source for the remaining math fonts appears, or the accented letters of the WP Greek set are confirmed against a real document.

## 8. Empty documents and macros

- **Status**: Implemented (#717).
- **Decision**:
  - An input with no content converts to an empty but valid output, with an `emptyOutput` warning.
  - Macro-enabled Office files have their macros removed before rendering.
- **Why**:
  - An empty input is a legitimate request. A valid empty output, with a warning, lets automated pipelines continue.
  - Macros never affect a static render, and removing them takes untrusted code out of the renderer's reach.
- **Trade-offs**: none for rendered output. Macro-to-macro conversions do not exist.
- **Alternatives rejected**: failing empty inputs, which breaks batch jobs.
- **Verified by**: the office output-check tests, and the real-world corpus gate, which accepts a zero-byte output only for the 39 corpus files that the manifest marks `emptyInput` (six Office and HTML files, 31 legacy Excel workbooks without a cell value, see entry 71, and two PDF pages with no text and no picture, see entry 49), each with the reason read from the file by a tool other than the converter, and never because the conversion declared `emptyOutput` (it does so for any blank text result) (`tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts`).
- **Revisit when**: a format is added whose macros change the rendered result.

## 9. Conversion warnings

- **Status**: Implemented (#725).
- **Decision**:
  - Anything a conversion leaves out or substitutes is reported in `warnings`.
  - That includes dropped streams, omitted images and replaced characters.
  - The warnings appear in the synchronous response body, in the `X-Conversion-Warnings` header, and in the job result and webhook.
- **Why**: a conversion that silently loses content is a quality defect the user cannot see. Reporting it lets callers decide.
- **Trade-offs**: a larger API surface. Warnings are capped at 50 lines plus a count.
- **Alternatives rejected**: logging only, which callers cannot see.
- **Verified by**: `tests/conversion-warnings-api.test.ts` and `tests/media-dropped-streams-api.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: callers need machine-readable warning codes. Add codes beside the text.

## 10. Archive bomb limits

- **Status**: Implemented; the ratio floor changed on 2026-10-17 (issue #783, QA decision: one floor of 32 MiB on every archive path).
- **Decision**:
  - Archive extraction refuses a compression ratio above 100:1 once more than 32 MiB has been decoded. Up to 32 MiB the ratio is not judged. The same floor applies on every path: the native 7-Zip listing and extraction, the gzip, ZIP, 7z and RAR readers, the bzip2, xz, lzip and lzop wrappers, the layers inside a package, and Zstandard. It is one constant (`ARCHIVE_RATIO_FLOOR_BYTES`), and the Zstandard decoder uses the same one.
  - It also refuses archives over the entry-count cap (50,000) and the total-size cap (500 MB). Both are unchanged.
  - Where only the archive's size is known (a stream decoded into a buffer), the output bound is the size cap, or the larger of the floor and 100 times the archive when that is smaller.
- **Why**: a few kilobytes can expand to terabytes, and the ratio cap stops that before disk or memory runs out. But the 500 MB size cap already bounds what any output can cost, and a ratio verdict on a small output only refuses real files: a cabinet of one 14.7 MB file stored in 26.5 KB (553:1), a sparse disk image, a file of one repeated pattern, a log of repeated lines. The earlier floor of 1 MiB was applied by some readers and not by others, so the same file passed one route and failed another; one floor everywhere removes that. Reports of this kind of false refusal are common enough that mature libraries add a grace size to their ratio checks.
- **Trade-offs**: a bomb can now produce up to 32 MiB before the ratio rule judges it. That is still far under the size cap, takes well under a second to decode, and is written to a private directory that is removed afterwards. A legitimate file over 100:1 and larger than 32 MiB is still refused, such as a huge sparse dump.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Size caps only**: a bomb still fills the cap.
  - **No floor**: false alarms on small repetitive files.
  - **A floor per format**: the same file would convert from one container and be refused from another, and each reader would need its own constant to keep in step.
  - **Raising the ratio instead of adding a floor**: it would weaken the check exactly where a bomb is large.
- **Verified by**: `src/lib/conversions/archive-extraction-safety.ts` and its tests (`tests/archive-extraction-safety.test.ts` holds the exact byte: 32 MiB passes at any ratio, one byte more is refused above 100:1), `tests/archive-ratio-floor.test.ts` (a cabinet of 20 MiB of zeros in 36 KB converts to every target; 7z, gzip, bzip2 and xz files of zeros convert at 32 MiB and are refused as ratio bombs at 33 MiB), and the ratio-bomb tests of the ZIP, 7z, gzip, package and encrypted-ZIP routes, whose bombs now decode to 40 MiB.
- **Revisit when**: users report legitimate refusals above the floor. The caps can then become per-plan.

## 11. Open-source engines only, separate programs for copyleft tools

- **Status**: Implemented.
- **Decision**:
  - Every engine is open source and free to run.
  - Copyleft engines, such as the PostScript interpreter and the DWG reader (29), are used only as unmodified separate programs.
  - No paid engine, service or CI runner is adopted.
- **Why**: per-conversion licence costs would make free tiers uneconomic. Using copyleft tools as separate programs keeps their obligations with those programs, and the licence notice lists them (`docs/licensing.md`).
- **Trade-offs**: some formats have no open engine that matches the best paid ones. The gap is measured, not hidden, and tracked as an issue.
- **Alternatives rejected**: paid office or CAD engines.
- **Verified by**: `docs/licensing.md` and the dependency review.
- **Revisit when**: a format has no open engine and real demand.

## 12. Engine choice and version pinning

- **Status**: Decided (#703).
- **Decision**: callers may choose an engine and an engine version for a conversion. Every engine version is pinned in the images, and a pinned version is used until the caller or a release changes it.
- **Why**:
  - Reproducibility: the same input and options give the same output today and next month.
  - Choice: some content renders better in a different engine, and power users need to pick it.
- **Trade-offs**: several engine versions must be kept, with images and tests for each.
- **Alternatives rejected**: always the newest engine, which silently changes outputs between releases.
- **Verified by**: the tests planned with #703.
- **Revisit when**: image size or maintenance cost becomes a constraint. If so, limit the number of retained versions.

## 13. CAD input

- **Status**: Implemented for DXF (#727, #744) and for DWG (#728, see [29](#29-dwg-input)).
- **Decision**:
  - DXF is read in-process. It covers lines, arcs, circles, ellipses, clamped and unclamped B-splines (sampled over their valid Cox-de Boor domain `[knots[degree], knots[control.length]]`), polylines with bulges, blocks with nesting, arrays and negative-Z OCS extrusion, dimensions, and single-line and multi-line text (including horizontal/vertical alignments, `Aligned`/`Fit` baseline orientation and width scaling, `STYLE` width factors, `%%` control codes, and linked multi-column `MTEXT` records wrapped to single-column width). Degenerate block insertions with a zero scale factor are skipped after accounting for their visit budget.
  - Output is one vector page fitted to the drawing extents (both strokes and text boxes), with every text line placed at its true drawing coordinates.
  - Expansion is bounded by one budget for the whole drawing; a drawing over it fails with 422.
  - The CAD parity score reads every output the same way, whatever the renderer draws: ink is any pixel that differs from the page colour, the frame of the drawing is fitted so that the truth strokes (the strokes read from the DXF) lie on ink, and the tolerance is a symmetric 1 % dilation. Ink inside a text box that is on no stroke is taken for glyphs up to a quarter of the box; beyond that it is charged to precision, and ink in a text box never meets a truth stroke that lies outside the text boxes. The score names no colour, line weight or page layout of the product or of the reference tool. B-splines whose knot vector is unclamped are sampled over their valid domain with the reference library's domain sampler, because its path conversion leaves the domain.
  - DWG is converted to DXF by an open-source reader run as a separate program (see [29](#29-dwg-input)).
- **Why**:
  - Fidelity: dropping entity types, misplacing aligned or multi-column text, ignoring negative-Z block extrusion, or extrapolating unclamped B-spline knot vectors outside their domain gives visibly wrong drawings.
  - Fitting the page to the drawing extents matches what CAD exporters produce.
  - The budget stops a small file from expanding into millions of strokes.
  - Scoring: a score that names the product's colours, line weight or page cannot be applied to another renderer, so the same drawing would be judged in a different frame depending on who drew it. Registering the truth strokes onto the picture reads every renderer alike, and the 25 % glyph coverage is above the largest share measured on the corpus renders of both sides (22 % of a text box, median 5 %) while a solid box (100 %) or dense scribbling is not text.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - Drawings beyond the budget are refused. The DWG reader does not handle every vendor version.
  - The fitted frame is optimistic for every renderer, the product and the reference tool alike: it moves to where the truth strokes find ink, so a render that is slightly off reads better than a fixed frame would score it. The product's margin over the reference tool shrinks where the reference was understated before.
  - Each frame edge may move at most 40 % inward and 5 % outward of the box of all ink. A render that leaves out only the outermost outline is over-penalised: the frame cannot grow past 5 %, so it settles on inner strokes and loses precision as well as recall. A render with a page border or a title block is charged for those marks in precision, and the search also starts from the biggest component inside such a border.
  - Text boxes: ink in them that is on no stroke is free up to 25 % of the grown box, so noise below glyph coverage is not charged; that bound is deliberate and the blind spot is at most a quarter of each text box. Text can move the frame when strokes are missing (the miss then shows in precision and extent error), but it never counts as a stroke outside the text boxes.
  - A truth with no strokes, no length, or all strokes on one horizontal or vertical line cannot be registered and scores as nothing drawn for both sides.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - Paid DWG libraries.
  - Adding a title and frame to the page, which users then have to crop.
  - Keying the score on the stroke and text colours of the product, which put the reference tool's black drawings in a different frame and understated them.
  - Using the box of all ink as the frame, which counts text outside the strokes as a scale error.
- **Verified by**: the CAD parity rows, `tests/cad-dxf-*.test.ts` and `tests/bench-cad-ink.test.ts` (the same drawing in several palettes, light on dark included, scores alike; a missing outline costs recall; text or a stray mark outside the strokes does not move the frame; solid or hatched text boxes lower precision; text does not stand in for strokes outside the text boxes; a drawing inside a page border is found).
- **Revisit when**: users hit the budget with real drawings; a renderer draws a page border, a title block or text that the 25 % glyph coverage or the 5 % outward limit misreads; or the corpus gains drawings whose text is denser than the measured 22 %.

## 14. SVG to PDF

- **Status**: Implemented (#727).
- **Decision**: SVG becomes a vector PDF with real text, rendered by a separate SVG renderer in the sandbox from the sanitised SVG. A worker without that renderer falls back to a raster page and records the fallback.
- **Why**: a raster PDF loses text search, selection and sharp printing. A vector page is what users expect.
- **Trade-offs**: one more program in the worker image.
- **Alternatives rejected**: rasterising in process.
- **Verified by**: `tests/svg-native-pdf-route.test.ts` and the vector parity rows.
- **Revisit when**: an in-process vector writer matches the renderer.

## 15. Usage is charged for successful conversions only

- **Status**: Implemented (#690, #948, #954, the #671 rows on reservations, the allowance source and the meter). It holds the QA decisions of 2026-11-02 (only finished conversions are charged, imports and failures charge nothing, and every importer has a daily byte budget of two files at its plan's file size limit) and the QA decision of 2026-11-03, implemented by #954: a caller without an account and a free account each have 10 conversions a day. The 25 of 2026-11-02 rested on a wrong claim about the reference converter and is withdrawn.
- **Decision**:
  - Only a conversion that produces output consumes quota.
  - A conversion that times out (504) or is cancelled by the client (499) is refunded.
  - **A caller without an account has 10 conversions a day on the server** (`ANONYMOUS_DAILY_CONVERSIONS` in `src/lib/plan-limits.ts`; it was 25 from 2026-11-02 to 2026-11-03, and 10 before that). `ANONYMOUS_DAILY_LIMIT` overrides it, and one function reads the override (`getAnonymousDailyLimit`, same file) for the key store, the refusal sentence and the pages. The configuration default (`src/lib/config/schema.ts`) is the constant. A free account has its own constant, `FREE_DAILY_CONVERSIONS` (`TIER_LIMITS.free`), also 10; the anonymous constant is its own literal, equal to it because QA set them equal, so either can change alone. The drop zone states the allowance of the viewer's own plan: the override the server read for a caller without an account, and `TIER_LIMITS` (now in `src/lib/plan-limits.ts`, so the page can read it) for an account, 10 for a free one. The dashboard states the account plan's allowance (`TIER_LIMITS[tier]`) while the usage loads, and shows the used count capped at the limit, so a count made under 25 before the deploy reads 10 / 10 and not 15 / 10. **A refusal states the allowance and the reset only**: "Daily conversion quota exceeded (10 conversions per day). It resets at midnight UTC.", the same for a caller without an account and for an account (`quotaExceeded` in `src/lib/api-keys/guard.ts`, with `dailyConversions` of `src/lib/plan-limits.ts`). It no longer tells a visitor to sign in or use an API key, since a free account has the same 10, nor an account to upgrade, since no plan is on sale. The count is per client address as the proxy reports it (`docs/client-ip-trust.md`). Conversions that run in the browser use no server and have no daily limit.
  - **The pages state the number the server enforces.** The page routes read `getAnonymousDailyLimit()` on the server and pass it to the FAQ, the terms page and the guarantee bar of the converter pages, in both languages, so they name the same number as the 429. The converter and information pages render on request and read the override at run time; the home page and the unit converter page are prerendered (`next build`), so the image passes `ANONYMOUS_DAILY_LIMIT` to the build as a build argument (`Dockerfile.web`, empty by default, which means the constant). **The repository variable `ANONYMOUS_DAILY_LIMIT` is the one source of the allowance.** The deploy workflow passes it to the image build and to the deploy step (`.github/workflows/deploy-oci.yml`); `deploy/oci/deploy.sh` writes it into the env file of the release, which Compose passes to every application service, and refuses a web image whose label `easyconvert.anonymous-daily-limit` (the build argument, `Dockerfile.web`) names another value, before anything starts. The env secret cannot set it: the allowlist leaves it out, so `filter-env` drops such a line. The variable is unset today, so the build and the servers use the constant. The status page says that conversions in the browser have no daily limit; it does not name the number.
  - **A link import (`/api/fetch-url`) is never charged a conversion.** It reserves no unit and commits none, so a file brought by link and converted costs one conversion, not two. It still answers 429 with the quota problem type before it fetches anything when the caller has no conversion left (`requireUnitLeft`, a check of the remaining count that reserves nothing, inside the guard's zero-unit check; it cannot be combined with reserving units). Three bounds take the place of the conversion count:
    - **a daily byte budget for every caller**, in the record store of the anonymous upload budget (entry 137). Its size is two files at the plan's file size limit (`dailyBudgetBytes` in `src/lib/api-keys/anonymous-upload-budget.ts`, the rule entry 137 gave the anonymous budget: "two files at the limit"): 2 GiB for an anonymous address bucket, where it is shared with uploads, 2 GiB for a free account, 10 GiB for Pro and 20 GiB for Enterprise, each from `PLAN_MAX_FILE_BYTES` in `src/lib/plan-limits.ts`. An account's budget is keyed by its user id and counts only its link imports. A spent budget answers 429 with the `upload-budget-exceeded` problem type (`refusal: "daily-bytes"`, `limitBytes`, and `plan` for an account), worded in both languages;
    - **a meter on the bytes an import receives**, following how byte quotas are kept in practice by the traffic quotas of proxies and the per-user network quotas of file hosts: the running total of the bytes actually transferred, per user and day, decides; a new transfer is refused once the total is over the cap; and a transfer in flight may pass it by what it reads before the next check. The rule is the transfer cap of a file sync tool: a transfer starts while the running total is under the limit, and one in flight stops once the total passes it, checked before and after each read. `/api/fetch-url` and the graph node both run through one helper (`withLinkImportMeter` in `src/lib/api-keys/anonymous-upload-budget.ts`). Before it fetches, an import is refused as `daily-bytes` when the day has no bytes left, counting the bytes received and those open uploads reserved. While it reads, it charges the day atomically (a compare-and-set of the day's record) once at least 4 MiB are not charged yet (`LINK_IMPORT_METER_BATCH_BYTES`), and once more when it ends, however it ends. **Each charge writes the import's running total under its import id** (`chargeImport`), so a write that landed but lost its reply, written again, adds only what is new, as a retried request with the same idempotency key has one effect; a charge that fails is made good by the next one, and the last charge is written once more when the import ended without it or it failed. The record keeps an import's total until the import's deadline plus five minutes (`LINK_IMPORT_CHARGE_GRACE_MS`; the deadline of the synchronous route, or the job's for a graph node), as an idempotency key keeps its result after the request ended, so the last charge written again adds nothing as well. An import that received no byte writes nothing. The meter answers one verdict after each count and at the end, `ok`, `too-large` or `day-reached`, the read limit first as for a declared length, so the route and the graph node stop a body for the same reason. Admission reads the record without writing it. The sync tool checks its total, kept in memory, on every 1 MiB read; this total is a record in a shared store, so it is written once per batch. When a charge takes the day past its budget, the import stops reading and is refused as `daily-bytes`, final for the day, with a sentence that says the day's limit was reached while the file was read (`dailyLimitReachedDetail`). The last batch is checked the same way when the body ends, so whether a file fits does not depend on where its batches fall. **A running import takes its day past the budget by at most one batch**, so imports that run at once pass it by at most one batch each. **A declared length is used only for a body sent as it is** (`declaredBodyBytes`): with no `Content-Encoding`, or `identity`, its `Content-Length` is parsed strictly (decimal digits, a safe integer), once, for both callers. The fetch client decodes a compressed body while its `Content-Length` keeps the compressed size (it keeps the header list as received and pipes the body through its decoders, as the Fetch standard leaves open, https://github.com/whatwg/fetch/issues/1524), so the length of a compressed body is never compared with the bytes read, never caps the stream and never lowers anything. A declared length past the import limit is too large (413); past what the day has left, it is refused before a byte is read with the budget's 429, `refusal: "larger-than-left"` and `leftBytes` (`declaredOverflow`). The read limit is per file and independent of the day: `URL_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES` (100 MiB) for `/api/fetch-url`, refused as too large (413). Each sentence of these refusals has one source (`budgetRefusalDetail`, `largerThanLeftDetail`, `dailyLimitReachedDetail`), read by the route and the graph node alike. A body without a usable declared length that passes the day is refused as `daily-bytes`. Bytes read after the deadline count too, and a last charge that fails is logged with the bytes it may leave unpaid and never replaces the answer. An import whose process died stays charged with what it charged before it died, at most one batch less than it read;
    - **the shared identity of visitors no proxy attributes is refused** with the 503 an upload gets (`unattributedTransferRefusal`, the same sentence for both): every visitor would share one budget;
    - **a conversion slot**, taken like a synchronous conversion (`acquireSyncSlot`, 5 for an anonymous or free caller) and released however the import ends;
    - **one deadline for the whole import**, headers and body, the synchronous deadline (`SYNC_DEADLINE_MAX_MS`, 120 s by default, through `runUnderDeadline`). A remote that is still sending at the deadline is cut off and the import answers 504 with the code `fetch_timeout`. Each hop still has 12 s to send its headers.
  - **A graph `import.url` node takes the same budget** (`importUrlWithinBudget` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-url-import.ts`), through the same `withLinkImportMeter`, keyed by the graph's owner and sized by the owner's plan. Its read limit is per file: the smaller of the node's limit (`GRAPH_URL_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`, 5 GiB) and the plan's file size limit (`PLAN_MAX_FILE_BYTES`, 1 GiB for anonymous and free), past which it fails as too large. Imports of one owner run at once and keep nothing from each other, so two nodes of a free account with one file of its day left both complete. A node whose owner's day has no bytes left, whose file declares more than is left, or whose reading takes the day past its budget fails at once with the refusal code `import_budget_exceeded` (`ImportBudgetExceededError`, 429, final, worded in both languages), so under `fail_fast` its graph fails and charges nothing. The node keeps the error that stopped its stream and throws it once the storage backend rejects, so a remote backend that wraps the stream's error in its own `StorageServiceError` cannot hide `import_budget_exceeded` or the too-large failure. `classifyJobFailure` reads whether a failure may be retried from the error (`retryable` on `ConversionFailedError`, true for `EngineMissingError`), not from its class. **A retried attempt reads the file again and is charged again for what it reads.** That is the cost of metering the bytes received: only a reservation made before reading could be handed from one attempt to the next. A node job without an owner cannot be charged to a budget and fails closed; every node the API queues has one.
  - **A request ends with its unit given back unless it was charged.** `withReservedUnit` in `src/lib/api-keys/guard.ts` holds a reservation while a request runs and gives it back when the request ends, by an answer or a throw, unless the request committed it or handed it to queued work (a job or a graph), which then commits it or gives it back when it ends. `/api/convert`, `/api/convert/batch`, `/api/v1/convert`, `/api/queue/jobs` and `/api/v1/jobs` use it, and all five take the reservation through `reserveConversionUnit`, which exempts the shared identity of unattributed visitors. The guard returns why it refused as data (`ConversionRefusal`), and one route-layer function answers it for every route (`conversionRefusalResponse` in `src/lib/api/conversion-refusal-response.ts`): 503 when the quota store is offline, else 429 with the `quota-exceeded` problem type, the day's count in the rate limit headers, and `dailyLimit`, `remaining` and `requiredUnits` beside a detail that names both numbers, so a graph that needs three conversions with two left is told it needs 3 and has 2. The early checks of `/api/v1/convert` and `/api/v1/jobs` (no conversion left at all) answer through the same function. The two `/api/v1` routes admit no anonymous caller (401), so that exemption never applies there.
  - **A queued graph is charged only by its scheduler, for the conversions it ran.** One table in `src/lib/jobs/graph-operations.ts` holds the rule of every operation (`CHARGE_RULES`, typed over every operation so a new one cannot be added without a rule), read by `graphNodeCharge` when a node completes and by `graphReservationUnits` when a graph is submitted; an operation it does not know is an error, never free. The test of each operation is its loop in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-executor.ts`: an operation that runs once for each input and makes one output of it charges one unit for each output, as a batch charges each file. That is `convert`, `ocr`, `thumbnail`, `media.package`, `watermark`, `pdf.watermark`, `pdf.protect`, `pdf.unlock`, `pdf.split-pages` (one ZIP of parts for each input PDF), `pdf.extract-pages`, `pdf.delete-pages`, `pdf.reorder-pages` and `pdf.rotate-pages`; `optimize` charges only the outputs it made smaller. Each input's output is stored under its own key, `intermediate/{graphId}/{nodeId}/{index}/{name}` (and `results/{graphId}/{nodeId}/{index}/{name}` for `export.internal`), built by one helper for every intermediate and result key (`nodeOutputKey` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-jobs.ts`; a node that makes one file of all its inputs, such as `merge`, `metadata`, `archive.create` and `import.url`, uses index 0), so two inputs whose outputs share a name (two `scores.csv` files converted, or a thumbnail of each picture), or two `export.internal` nodes whose results share one, are files of their own that keep their readable names, and a node is charged for its distinct outputs; the scheduler answers each output key once. An operation that does one job over all its inputs charges one unit when it produced an output: `merge`, `metadata` (of the first input), `archive.create` and `archive.extract` (one archive, its split volumes stitched into one). A node that produced nothing is free, an optimize node with no input included, and so is an optimize node that made nothing smaller. Imports and exports (`import.upload`, `import.url`, `export.url`, `export.internal`) only move files and charge nothing, as the reference service charges processing tasks only. `/api/v1/jobs` reserves by the same rule when the graph is submitted: one unit for each input a node charged per output declares and one for each one-job node, so a graph is refused up front when the caller has fewer units left than it needs, and a single conversion through the `tasks` pipeline costs one unit, as on `/api/v1/convert`. **A node charged per output whose inputs hold more files than it declares** (an unpacked archive) first extends the graph's reservation by the difference (`holdUnitsForInputs` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-reservation.ts`, through `extendQuota` of the key store: one script in Redis, `EXTEND_QUOTA_LUA_SCRIPT`, and the same check in the process), in one step and only when the units fit under the owner's daily limit. When they do not, the node fails with `quota_exceeded` (`NodeQuotaExceededError`, 429, final, worded in both languages) before any work, naming the conversions left, so under `fail_fast` its graph charges nothing. Only units that do not fit fail the node. A reservation that ended, or whose day's count expired at midnight, is reported apart (`no-reservation`: the script checks both keys with `EXISTS`, as the settle and the rollback do, and never writes a count; the key store of a process without Redis makes the same check of its count of the reservation's day), and the node runs on without extending (see Trade-offs). The extension is keyed by the node and holds what the node needs in all, so a retry holds the same units instead of adding them, and it is counted in the reservation, so the settle or the rollback ends it. The charge of a graph therefore never passes the day's limit. **A graph without a conversion is refused** with 422 and the problem type `graph-without-conversion` (worded in both languages, listed in the OpenAPI document) before anything is reserved or fetched: it would cost nothing while it fetched and stored files. A graph holds that one reservation for all its nodes. Its node jobs carry no reservation id (`GraphNodeJobMetadata` cannot hold one), so the lifecycle listeners of the worker, which commit or give back the reservation of any job that carries one, leave it alone. The scheduler (in Redis and in the process) settles it to the units its nodes charged once the graph completes, whether its last node completed or failed under `continue`, and refunds the rest; that is nothing when no conversion produced a result. It gives the reservation back once the graph fails or is cancelled. **Every end of a node job reaches the scheduler**: the node runs its whole body, from opening its sealed options on, inside one `try`, so a failure before its work starts (a password that cannot be unsealed, the page limit of its owner, its start record) fails the node like any other, and the job listeners report every end the node never sees itself: the worker's `failed` event, raised once for the last attempt and for a job the stalled sweep fails, and the queue's `cancelled` event (`reportGraphNodeEnded` in `src/lib/queue/conversion-queue.ts`). The cancel listener is attached to the default queue only, which receives the `cancelled` events of the resource queues, so a cancel is reported, refunded and released once. The scheduler ignores a second report of a node that already ended, the Lua scripts in Redis and the same check in the process. **One node job cannot be cancelled on its own**: `DELETE /api/queue/jobs/{id}` and `DELETE /api/v1/jobs/{id}` answer 409 for a `{graphId}:{nodeId}` id and name the graph in `graphId`, because a graph is run, charged and cancelled as one job. Routing the cancel to the whole graph was rejected: it would stop sibling nodes the caller did not name. **A graph's end always reaches its reservation.** The one call that records the end (the Lua transition in Redis, `recordEnd` in the process, before any await) ends the reservation before anything else, for both schedulers (`finishGraph` in `src/lib/queue/graph/graph-end.ts`): the terminal scripts return the reservation id and the units with the transition, so draining the outbox, reading the ready nodes, cancelling the other node jobs or reading the graph state can fail only after the settle or the rollback. Both schedulers end a graph through one function, `finishGraph(graph, end, between)`, which the call that recorded the end calls once with the end as one value (`{ outcome, reservation: settle(units) | rollback }`): it settles or rolls back first, then runs the steps between (cancelling the other node jobs, draining the outbox), then tells the webhook and removes the files, so a storage fault delays the cleanup but never the charge or the notice. A failure of a step between is logged and the announcement still runs, so the webhook and the cleanup are not lost once the end is recorded; a completion that did not end its graph still fails when its drain fails, so its node is tried again. The state is read once after the settle, with one more read when it fails, and handed to the steps between, so the cancels of the other node jobs use that read and not one of their own; a read that finds no state is logged and not repeated. Without the state the webhook cannot be addressed, which is logged, and the holds on the input files still end and the intermediate files are still removed, from the input keys the end transition returned (`EndedGraph.inputKeys`). `finishGraph` answers what the steps between returned (the stopped nodes, the completion), so no scheduler keeps a variable for it; when they failed, the answer is what the transition recorded. Each node job a step between cancels is cancelled on its own and a cancel that fails is logged (`cancelGraphNodeJobOrLog` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-jobs.ts`), in both schedulers, so one node job that cannot be cancelled never leaves the others running; the scheduler in the process lists only the cancels that did not fail. Each failure of these steps is logged with the graph id and the reservation id, including a settle or rollback the key store did not apply (`{success:false}`) and a webhook it did not deliver. A count of units the Redis scheduler cannot read as a strict integer gives the reservation back and is logged, instead of charging a guessed count or leaving the reservation open. A retried attempt of a resource-queue job that a worker took through the default queue is retried by the queue that holds it, so a node job is never lost between attempts. The `tasks` pipeline of `/api/v1/jobs` builds its graph with `fail_fast`, the scheduler's policy that ends the job as failed when a task fails, as the reference service does and as the public schema's `failurePolicy` values (`fail_fast`, `continue`) say.
  - **`/api/v1/convert` charges a synchronous conversion as its last step.** The result is stored, recorded and its answer built before the unit is committed. Recording the answer under the `Idempotency-Key` comes after the commit, and a store that fails there is logged and the success is answered, so a client is never told a charged conversion failed and charged again on a retry; the key's lock then stays until it expires, so a repeat in that minute is turned away instead of converted again.
  - **A batch reserves and is charged for the files it will convert.** A file of an unknown format is skipped; it reserves nothing, so it cannot use up the last conversion. A file that fails ends the batch, so a batch that answers converted every file it reserved for and commits them.
  - **A reservation is a lease that its holder renews**, as a lock service leases a lock to the process that holds it. `reserveQuota` leases the units for 90 s (`RESERVATION_LEASE.provisionalMs` in `src/lib/api-keys/reservation-ledger.ts`), and `withReservedUnit` renews the lease every 30 s while its request runs, a third of the lease, as a lease client sends its keep-alive at a third of the lease's time to live, so one missed renewal does not end it. The unit of a process that dies before it commits or hands off comes back within 90 s. Handing the reservation to queued work (a job or a graph) first renews the 90 s lease. That renewal is the proof that the reservation still counts, as a fencing token proves a lock still held at a hand-off: when it finds the reservation gone (its lease ended while the request ran), nothing is queued, and the request is refused with a 503 and `Retry-After`; the units are already back, so nothing is given back. A renewal that throws is refused the same way, and the request gives the units back as it ends. The job is sealed and given its deadline before the hand-off, and a graph is sealed there too, so a refusal there gives the units back at once and only the queue write can have an unknown outcome. A sealed graph carries the id it was sealed for, as a signature names its key, and both schedulers refuse a graph that is not sealed for the id it is stored under (`assertSealedFor` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-jobs.ts`), so no graph is stored with its secrets open or sealed where its node jobs cannot open them. The reservation keeps the 90 s lease through that write, and moves to 24 h (`handedOffMs`, a day, at least an hour past `JOB_DEADLINE_CEILING_MS`, the bound of every deadline setting, which the ledger module checks when it loads) only once the write returned or the lookup after it found the work, as a lease holder extends its lease once the work it covers is confirmed. The queue reports every end of that work, and the long lease is only the backstop for an end that is never reported. The work renews it as well when it takes the reservation, as a queue consumer extends its hold on the job it takes: a worker that takes a job with a reservation, and a graph start after its last step, once it queued its first nodes and read its state back, so a start that throws on any step leaves the 90 s lease (`leaseToHandedOffWork` in `src/lib/api-keys/hand-off.ts`). One helper renews every lease (`renewLease`), so a store that fails is logged the same way on every path. A renewal to the long lease that throws once the work is stored is tried once more at once and then logged, since the work runs either way; one that finds no live lease (work that committed fast, or a graph that already settled) is logged as a warning. **The clock of a lease is the clock of the Redis server**: every script reads `TIME`, and callers pass durations, never times, so a process whose clock runs ahead never ends the live lease of another, the failure the analyses of lease-based locks warn of; the ledger of a store without Redis reads its own clock, the only one its reservations are seen by. Every step first gives back the units of each lease that ended, one Lua script per step in Redis (per owner and day, a sorted set of the leases by their end and a hash of the units each holds, `src/lib/api-keys/quota-lua-scripts.ts`) and the same step in the process (`MemoryReservationLedger`), so no step acts on a lease that ended and a read of the day's count never counts one. Both stores implement one interface (`ReservationLedger`), and the key store chooses one.
  - **A reservation is charged on the day it was made**, as a request is billed to the period it arrived in. `reserveQuota` reads the date once for the count, the reservation id and its lease. The id names the owner and the day (`res_<encoded user id>_<YYYY-MM-DD>_<ms>_<random>`), from which any process finds the keys of that day, and the keys of a day live until its midnight or the end of its longest lease, whichever is later. A job or a graph that ends after midnight therefore commits, settles, extends or gives back its units on its own day.
  - **Commit, settle and rollback act once, and only on what is there.** They act only on a live lease, so one after a commit, a rollback or the end of the lease changes nothing, and they change the count only while its key exists, so no step writes a count without a lifetime. In Redis mode a script that fails is logged and reported as not done; the counts the process keeps for a store without Redis are never touched.
  - **An enqueue that fails after it stored its work leaves the unit to the work.** A route chooses the job id (or the graph id) before it queues (`handOffConversionJob` in `src/lib/queue/enqueue.ts`), and when queueing throws it looks the work up by that id (`HandOff.recover`): work that was stored is answered as queued and owns the reservation, and when the lookup finds nothing or fails, the reservation stays on the 90 s provisional lease it held through the write, with no write to the store that just failed, so work whose write lands late still finds it live, and the lease gives the unit back when none does. The id plays the part of an idempotency key, so a write that landed but lost its reply has one effect. The input of a job is held across the enqueue and the lookup, so a job found after a failed enqueue keeps its hold. Any other failure gives the hold up, since the submitter does not hold resources for work that may never exist, and a worker takes the hold of a job when it picks the job up (`takeInputHold` in `src/lib/storage/retention-service.ts`, from `processNodeJob`; an `import.upload` node takes it for its graph), as a queue consumer takes its own lease on a message it receives: a job stored late holds its input from the moment it runs, and one whose input was deleted in between fails as a missing input. Keeping the hold of a hand-off that could not tell was rejected: holders are capped at 32 (`MAX_HOLDS`), so 32 refused submissions of one upload made it answer as not found for the rest of its day. **A graph whose start stored its state and then failed is started or cancelled, never left waiting**: the graph's lookup (`recoverStart`) drains the outbox that the start wrote with the state, as an outbox relay drains its table until it is empty (enqueue is idempotent by job id, so a node queued before the failure is not queued twice), and answers the graph as started; when the outbox still cannot be drained, it cancels the graph, which gives its units back, and the route answers 503. Only a failed start cancels a graph whose id its client was never given, so a cancel refused because the graph is already cancelled with the reason of a failed start (`START_FAILED_REASON`) met an earlier try of that cancel whose reply was lost. The end steps that try may have skipped run again (`endCancelledStart` in `src/lib/queue/graph/node-jobs.ts`, through `finishGraph`): the reservation is given back, the stopped node jobs are cancelled, and the input holds and intermediate files end. Each step does nothing the second time, and the start is answered as not started, so the route answers 503 with the unit already back. A graph that refuses the cancel because it completed, failed or was cancelled for another reason, or that still runs, is answered as started with the state read after the cancel, and the route answers it rather than a 503 a retry would submit again. A cancel that throws is tried three times, 100 ms and 200 ms apart (`GRAPH_START_CANCEL_ATTEMPTS`), as an idempotency record is written again; after the third the recovery is unknown. The request's own input is stored only once the submission passed every check and holds its units, so a refused request stores nothing.
- **Why**:
  - Users should not pay for failures they did not cause. Charging only success also gives the service an incentive to fail less.
  - A link import is a step toward a conversion, not a conversion; charging both made the common path of the web interface cost two units from an allowance of ten. QA decided an import is not charged; that decision does not make imports unbounded, so they get the bounds of the bytes they bring in: the byte budget that already bounds uploads, a slot and a deadline.
  - **The import shares the upload budget rather than having its own** because both bring a file onto the server for a conversion, and one number a day for that is the one users can be told. A second budget of the same size would let a bucket bring in twice as much by mixing the two ways. Sharing it also reuses the record, its store and its day rollover unchanged.
  - **A short lease renewed by the request, and a long one for queued work**, because only the request has a process that can die between reserving and handing off, and it is the one place that already wraps every reservation (`withReservedUnit`). Queued work needs no renewer while it runs: the queue reports each of its ends, whatever process runs it, so it renews once, when it takes the reservation. The day's keys living as long as its leases keep the charging day right by construction: no step meets a count that is gone while a lease of it lives.
  - **The 10 conversions are the allowance QA set on 2026-11-03**, equal to the published free plan of the converter the product is measured against: its pricing page, read live on 2026-11-03, says "Start free with 10 conversions per day" and gives 10 credits a day. A free account has the same 10, so signing in does not raise the count; what an account adds is its history, files and API keys.
  - **The match is by count, not by credit.** On the reference a credit is about one minute of conversion time, every conversion costs at least one, office to PDF two and PDF to office four, and a longer conversion costs more (the same page, read 2026-11-03). Its 10 credits are therefore at most 10 short conversions. Here every successful conversion counts one, whatever its kind or length up to the plan's processing limit, so 10 here is never fewer conversions than the reference's 10 credits give.
  - **The 25 of 2026-11-02 is withdrawn.** It rested on the claim that the reference allowed 25 a day. That claim was wrong: the published free plan allows 10. The product states only facts the reference states, so the number follows the published fact and not the earlier reading of it.
  - **It matches practice** as far as one reference shows: the converter the product is measured against caps its free plan at 10 a day (read on 2026-11-03), and a count that small bounds the compute one address can spend. No second service was read for this change.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Stricter for users, lighter for the servers (2026-11-03).** A visitor or a free account that converted 11 to 25 files a day is refused from the 11th, and a batch of more than 10 files cannot run in one day. The compute one address can spend on the server falls to 10 conversions a day from 25, 2.5 times less (arithmetic on the cap, not a measured load). Conversions that run in the browser stay unlimited. A paid plan keeps its 500 and 10,000, but none is on sale (`PAID_PLANS_ON_SALE`).
  - Repeated failing requests cost compute without consuming quota. Processing-time caps, concurrency caps and rate limits bound that cost.
  - **A day can pass its budget by one batch for each import running**: an import charges in batches of at most 4 MiB, so it learns that its day is spent only at the batch that passed it.
  - **A crash retry of a graph import is charged again** for the bytes it reads again, as the graph bullet says.
  - **A node over an unpacked archive fails when its files do not fit in the day**, after the unpacking ran, because the count of files is known only then.
  - **A change of the allowance takes a build and a deploy.** The variable reaches the pages through the build, so a deploy of an image built before the change is refused until the new build exists.
  - **A unit reserved by a request whose process dies counts for up to 90 s**, and one whose request cannot renew its lease for 90 s (Redis unreachable, an event loop blocked that long) is given back while the request runs, so that conversion is not charged.
  - **Work whose end is never reported keeps its unit for 24 h**, counted on its own day, which is over by then for most of it.
  - **Work stored after a failed enqueue whose lookup found nothing is charged only when a worker takes it within 90 s**: its reservation stays on the provisional lease until the worker renews it. A job that waits longer in the queue finds no reservation when it is taken, runs free, and its renewal and commit are logged. A job that was never stored keeps its unit for those 90 s.
  - **A graph whose cancel throws on every try after a failed start may stay running with ready nodes nobody queues**: the request answers 503, the unit comes back when the 90 s lease ends, and the graph stays listed as running until it is cancelled.
  - **A day's count outlives midnight while a lease of it lives**, so a node over more files than its graph reserved still extends against its own day after midnight. A count that is gone anyway (removed by hand) is reported as `no-reservation`, and the node runs on without extending.
  - **`/api/v1/jobs` answers 500 when the idempotency store fails after its job was queued**; the job keeps the unit and a retry queues a second job. Row of #671.
  - **The deploy that brings leases overlaps the release before it only briefly, and a rollback leaves the open leases counted until midnight.** A deploy recreates each service in the one Compose project, stopping its old container before it starts the new one, and an old worker stops taking jobs when it is told to stop and finishes those it took within its 120 s grace. Work a new web queued reaches an old worker only in the time between the start of the new web and the stop of the old worker: that release finds no key of its form, so such work is not charged when it succeeds and is given back only when its lease ends when it fails. Rolling back to the release before leases leaves the reservations open at that moment counted until midnight, since that release neither reads nor ends a lease; its own reservations are kept as before.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - Charging on submission.
  - Charging a link import and refunding it when the conversion is charged: the remaining count would show a unit that is not spent, and an import that never reaches a conversion would stay charged.
  - Keeping 25 (the decision of 2026-11-02): it states a number the reference does not publish for its free plan, and each conversion above 10 costs compute the reference does not give away.
  - 10 for a caller without an account and 25 for a free account: the reference's free plan is 10, so an account would get more than the reference gives and the page would have to explain two numbers. Either constant can still change alone (`FREE_DAILY_CONVERSIONS`, `ANONYMOUS_DAILY_CONVERSIONS`).
  - A rollback in each early return: six of them were missing, and the next route would miss one again.
  - A separate byte budget for imports: see Why.
  - A reservation that lives until its day ends: a process that died kept its unit until midnight, and work that ended after midnight found no reservation to charge, settle or extend.
  - Renewing the reservation from the worker heartbeat: a queued job has no worker until it runs, and the queue already reports its end.
  - Giving the unit back whenever an enqueue throws: a job stored before the throw ran without being charged.
  - Leaving the unit to the work for 24 h when the lookup after a failed enqueue finds nothing or fails: a job that was never stored held a conversion of its owner for a day.
  - Moving the lease to 24 h before the queue write, and back to 90 s after an unknown outcome: the move back is a write to the store that just failed, and when it failed the unit stayed a day.
  - Answering every failure of a start as unknown: sealing and deadline errors are thrown before anything is written, so a refused request held its unit for 90 s.
  - Answering a graph found after a failed start as queued: its root nodes were never queued, so it stayed running, its unit held for a day, and no webhook came.
  - Lease ends computed by each process from its own clock: a process whose clock ran two minutes ahead gave back the live leases of the others.
  - Zeroing a batch before its charge and restoring it when the charge fails: a charge that landed but lost its reply would be charged twice.
  - Cancelling the whole graph when one of its node jobs is cancelled by id: it stops sibling nodes the caller did not name, and the caller already has the graph id to cancel it.
  - A side-effect block in each scheduler for each way a graph ends: six copies drifted apart (one ran the cleanup before the settle, so a storage fault skipped the charge and the webhook).
  - Holding every byte left in the day for a graph import: two imports of one graph, or the retry of one, refused each other with a message that said the day was spent.
  - **A hold taken before reading**: an import held one file or the rest of the day before it read, and read no more than it held. Each fix to it opened the next defect: a hold of the whole day refused sibling imports, a short hold needed a cause (`held`), a held import was retried and charged again for what it had read, waits pinned worker slots, a hold lowered to a declared length broke every compressed body, and its typed errors were wrapped by remote storage. Metering the bytes received needs none of these and is how byte quotas are kept in practice. A reservation of the file's size up front is the cautious mode of the reference implementation (pending bytes plus the source size in `checkLimits`), which an import cannot use, since most remotes declare no length it can trust.
  - Ending the reservation after the graph state is read: a failed read left the graph ended and its reservation charged in full.
  - Charging a node that makes one output of each input once: a thumbnail node over 100 images cost what one conversion costs, while a convert node over the same images cost 100.
  - Checking the daily limit only when a graph is submitted: a conversion after an unpacked archive was charged past the day's limit without bound.
  - Rendering the home page and the unit converter page on request so they read the override at run time: it costs a render of the two most visited pages on every request, for a number that changes with a deploy.
  - A byte budget for accounts sized from the daily conversions (10 × 100 MiB for free, 500 × 100 MiB for Pro): it gives a paid plan hundreds of gigabytes a day. Two files at the file size limit is the rule the anonymous budget already follows.
- **Verified by**:
  - `tests/graph-node-charge.test.ts`: the charge rule of each operation, and the units a graph reserves by its declared inputs.
  - `tests/helpers/graph-charge-cases.ts`, in the process (`tests/quota-graph-charge.test.ts`) and on Redis (`tests/quota-accounting-redis.test.ts`), through real workers: a graph is charged only the conversions it ran and nothing when it fails or is cancelled, a node over more files than reserved extends its reservation or fails with `quota_exceeded`, and an `import.url` node is charged its bytes and refused with `import_budget_exceeded`.
  - `tests/helpers/graph-start-recovery-cases.ts`, on both schedulers: a stored start is started or cancelled, a cancel that landed but lost its reply answers 503 with the unit back at once and ends the node jobs and input holds, a graph its owner cancelled first is answered as started, and a cancel that throws three times is unknown.
  - `tests/job-input-deletion.test.ts`: a late job whose earlier output was deleted fails as a missing input, and an upload node takes the hold its graph start gave up. `tests/graph-scheduler.test.ts`, on both schedulers: a graph that is unsealed or sealed for another id is refused and nothing is stored.
  - `tests/helpers/reservation-lease-cases.ts`, on both ledgers: a lease that is not renewed gives its units back after 90 s, a handed-off reservation ends on its own day, and stored work keeps its unit past the provisional lease, also when its first extension throws.
  - `tests/reservation-lease.test.ts`: the fence before a hand-off, an unknown start left on the provisional lease, the input hold of a stored job, a hold given up by a hand-off that could not tell and taken by the late job when it runs, a good submission after 40 refused ones, and a job or graph whose secret cannot be sealed answering 503 with the unit back.
  - `tests/quota-accounting-routes.test.ts` and `tests/quota-accounting-redis.test.ts`: the allowance, free and metered link imports, refusals that leave the count alone, and a Redis graph start that cannot read its state after its drain left on the provisional lease.
  - `tests/link-import-meter.test.ts`: how an import is metered. `tests/oci-deploy.test.ts` and `tests/prerendered-allowance.test.ts`: the allowance the image is built with and the deploy passes, and the worker `main` tag.
  - **The allowance of 10 (2026-11-03).** `tests/quota-accounting-routes.test.ts` pins `FREE_DAILY_CONVERSIONS`, `ANONYMOUS_DAILY_CONVERSIONS` and `TIER_LIMITS`; `tests/prerendered-allowance.test.ts`, `tests/redesign-verification.test.ts`, `tests/plan-file-limit-client.test.ts` and `tests/i18n-api-errors.test.ts` pin the number the pages, the drop zone and the Korean refusal state. Thirty tests failed on the old 25 before the constant changed (red), and passed after. `next build` with the origin set prerenders the English and Korean home pages with 10 and no 25. The allowance label check of `deploy/oci/deploy.sh` needed no change: the repository variable is unset, so the build argument, the image label and the value the deploy passes are all empty and agree, and the web image and the worker image of one release come from one commit (the pair check on `org.opencontainers.image.base.name`). Its smoke conversion did need one, which the first version of #954 missed: it posted a PPM to `/api/convert` and was charged to the anonymous allowance of the bridge gateway on every deploy, rollback and reconcile, so the 11th start of a UTC day would have been refused with 429 and a rollback after it could fail as well. It now runs through the fixed-input probe of entry 122. `tests/deploy-smoke-probe.test.ts` holds it: twelve smokes after the allowance is spent all answer a one-pixel PNG and charge nothing, a public caller with forged headers gets no conversion of its own from the probe and is still refused by `/api/convert`, and `tests/quota-accounting-routes.test.ts` pins both refusal sentences.
- **Revisit when**: abuse through deliberately failing jobs appears in metrics, link imports are used for bulk download, accounts reach their daily import budget often, requests are seen to lose their lease while they run, the reference converter's published free allowance changes, or the metrics show visitors leaving at the 10th conversion in numbers the product cannot accept.

## 16. Free and anonymous limits

- **Status**: Decided (#693). The processing and concurrency caps are implemented (#690). The absence of a page limit is implemented (#693): no request is refused because of the page count the caller's plan allows.
- **Decision**:
  - **Free and anonymous callers**:
    - files up to 1 GB;
    - no page limit;
    - up to 5 minutes of processing per conversion;
    - at most 5 concurrent conversions;
    - **a caller without an account and a free account each have 10 conversions a day on the server** (entry 15).
  - **Output files**: deleted ten minutes after their first complete download or an hour after they were stored, whichever comes first (entry 125), with immediate deletion on request.
  - **Page counts**:
    - the plan of the caller never refuses a request for its page count; the per-plan table (50, 500 and 2,000 pages) is removed, and a page range (`page`, `pages`) is checked for syntax and against the page count of the document only;
    - a page specification is at most `MAX_PAGE_SPEC_CHARS` = 8,192 characters (the limit the PDF page operations already had, now in the shared parser of `page-range.ts`), and its ranges are sorted and joined where they overlap or touch (the pass of Chromium's `printing::PageRange::Normalize`, `printing/page_range.cc`), so reading it costs its tokens and the pages it selects, never the product of the two;
    - a range past the end of the document is refused when the document is read, which for a queued job is in the worker, not at submission: the job is accepted and then fails with the typed range error, since the page count of a document is not known before it is opened;
    - the work of a request is bounded by its job deadline: 5 minutes for free and anonymous callers, and the maximum of the tier for every caller. A document (the `document` family of `src/lib/queue/job-deadline.ts`: document, presentation, spreadsheet and ebook sources) gets that maximum whatever its size, because its pages are known only once it is converted; the per-page allowance (`JOB_DEADLINE_PER_PAGE_MS`) had no caller that knew a page count, so it is removed with its setting. The other work keeps its base and per-MiB or per-media-second scaling;
