A `clip-path` that is not the page (entry 42 drops the page clip) is measured against what is drawn under it: every vertex of the flattened device-space geometry the writer writes (the vertices of strokes and of the outlines of fills, and the corners and origin of a bitmap-font character that becomes TEXT) is tested against the clip region, and so is every segment between two of them, and the clip is dropped when no point is more than 1 pt outside it, which is `PAGE_CLIP_TOLERANCE_PIXELS` (96/72 device pixels, the same point the page clip uses). Under two or more clips at once the drawing must be inside each of them, with no tolerance: a point a little outside each of two clips can be far outside their intersection, which can even be empty (clips at y < 100 and y > 100.8 around a line at y = 100.4), and the intersection is not measured. Otherwise the page is refused with the reach in the message. "Outside by at most 1 pt" is the Euclidean distance of a vertex to the region, so a vertex 1 pixel off a corner in both axes is 1.41 pixels away.
  - **The region** is the union of the shapes of the `<clipPath>` that are drawn with straight edges (`path` without arc or Bézier commands, `rect` without corner radii, `polygon`), in the user space of the clipped element (its `transform` included), each shape moved by its own `transform` and the `<clipPath>`'s, and filled by its own `clip-rule`. `clip-rule` and `visibility` are inherited properties, and a clip shape inherits them from the ancestors of its `<clipPath>`, not from the element the clip is on (SVG 1.1 section 14.3.5): the shape's own keyword, else its parent's value up to the root, else nonzero and visible; `inherit` and any other value take the parent's. A point is inside by cairo's winding count (nonzero, or evenodd) and a point on an edge is inside. The distance of a point is its distance to the nearest edge, which is its distance to the region because every edge borders it (the counts on its two sides differ by one); a shape with two edges that lie on one another (a spike of no width, a path drawn twice under evenodd), whose edges may border nothing, is refused, and a polygon whose points are all on one line fills nothing and is left out. A segment between two vertices is not measured against a convex clip (the distance to a convex region is convex along a segment, so the ends hold its largest value). Against any other clip a segment is cut where it crosses the clip's edges; each piece is inside or outside as a whole, since no edge crosses it, and an outside piece of length L whose ends are d0 and d1 away holds no point farther than (d0 + d1 + L) / 2, because the distance changes by at most the distance moved. A piece is halved, its middle measured, until that bound is within the tolerance or a middle is past it. A clip that is empty, hidden (`display`, `visibility`), or of no area hides everything and refuses the first shape drawn under it.
  - **Refused as before, with a reason**: `clipPathUnits="objectBoundingBox"` (the box of the clipped element is not exact on flattened geometry), a clip on the `<clipPath>` or on one of its shapes, a `<text>`, `<use>`, `<g>` or any other shape element in it, a curve in it (`circle`, `ellipse`, a rounded `rect`, a `path` with arcs or Béziers: its flattened outline is off the curve by more than the path reader's 0.25 user units, since its Bézier test stops at 8 halvings and reads the distance to the chord's line, arcs take steps of a sixteenth of a turn and circles 36 sides, and that error grows with the scale of the clipped element, 3 pixels for a circle of radius 2 under `scale(20)`), two edges of a shape on one another, an id that is missing or is not a `<clipPath>`, a value that is not a `url(#id)` reference, and a `clip-path` on the root element. A value in a refusal is cut to 40 characters.
  - **Clip limits** (this reader's own, neither reference has any): 8 clips active under one element (`MAX_ACTIVE_CLIPS`), 1,024 edges in one clip (`MAX_CLIP_EDGES`), coordinates of a clip and of what is drawn under it within 10^9 device pixels (`MAX_CLIP_COORDINATE`: 50,000 times the largest PDF page, 14,400 points or 19,200 pixels a side by ISO 32000-1 Annex C.2, and far enough below 1e154, where a squared distance overflows and the distance became NaN, which passed the old test) and 8,388,608 edge tests in a page (`MAX_CLIP_WORK`, 2^23, counted as vertices times the edges of each clip they are tested against, plus each segment's crossing test and each halving of a piece, plus every point of a clip placed under an element, plus the pairs of edges of each clip shape tested for lying on one another). **The figure is 3.5 times what the heaviest real page used.** The same counter, left running past a clip refusal so that each page is counted whole (a page that another element refuses stops there), read the page SVG of 4,452 pages that hold a clip, in 651 of the 1,328 PostScript and PDF files of the real-world and regression corpora in the local cache (the first 40 pages of each file; `006137` and `001048` whole): the median page used 30 edge tests, 99% of them under 53,110, and the most was 2,396,264 (page 22 of `govdocs1-001503.pdf`: 1,111 clips of 5 to 134 edges, 41,000 path commands); the next two were 2,189,772 and 633,716, and the 607 clips of `006137` and `001048` took at most 26,776 a page. The first limit, 2^26, was chosen without that measurement and was 28 times the heaviest page: a page built to spend all of it (1,023-edge clips against 400,000 vertices, or 80,000 placements of a clip under a matrix that leaves it no edge) cost 1.0 to 1.5 s at about 22 ns an edge test on the Linux VM (Ubuntu 24.04, 4 vCPU) and 3.0 to 3.6 s on the CI runner, past the 3 s the hostile-input tests allow. At 2^23 the same pages cost 0.15 to 0.35 s on the VM, and a test writes a page that spends 2,421,179, the heaviest real page's figure, so a later cut of the limit under the real need fails. A clip is parsed once per id, charged to the 500,000-vertex budget once, and placed under each element that names it, so 30,000 references cost 30,000 placements; each vertex is tested once against each active clip. A clip over the limits is a refusal.
  - **Refused as before**: a picture (entry 42), a mask, a negative, non-numeric, relative or unit-bearing dash length, `paint-order`, `vector-effect` and `mix-blend-mode` away from their neutral values.
- **Why**:
  - **The reference writers drop these attributes.** Inkscape's `share/extensions/dxf_outlines.py` (GPL, read for behaviour only) takes the stroke colour and the transformed path in `process_shape` (lines 265 to 301) and reads no dash array, width, opacity or clip. pstoedit 4.02 (GPL, behaviour only) writes the dash pattern only as a line type in its version 14 driver, and as one of five stock names (`CONTINUOUS`, `DASHED`, `DOT`, `DASHDOT`, `DIVIDE`) chosen by `guess_linetype` from the number of entries (`src/drvbase.cpp` lines 812 to 866, `src/drvdxf.cpp` lines 960 to 969, `src/dxfacad.h` lines 237 to 325); its version 9 driver writes none, and its dash offset is parsed and never used (`src/drvbase.cpp` line 779 reads it, `guess_linetype` at lines 812 to 866 never does). It writes no width in version 9 (`src/drvdxf.cpp` line 6).
  - **The line type is the faithful option and costs little.** ezdxf (MIT) writes an R12 line type as groups 72, 73, 40 and 49 (`entities/ltype.py` `export_r12_dxf`), reads one into the pattern it draws (`compile_line_pattern`, which also moves a leading gap to the end), draws the pattern along a whole polyline (`addons/drawing/pipeline.py` `draw_path`, `LineTypeRenderer`) and scales it by `$LTSCALE` and the entity's scale. The stock names of pstoedit lose the pattern, and solid, as Inkscape writes it, loses the dash. A line type keeps the pattern in the file where a reader can change it, and a page of 29,000 dashed segments adds a few line types, where cutting the dashes into entities adds a polyline per dash.
  - **Bit 128 is needed for a polyline.** ezdxf names it `POLYLINE_GENERATE_LINETYPE_PATTERN` (`lldxf/const.py` line 277; `entities/polyline.py` line 63: "linetype pattern is generated continuously around the vertices"). A flattened curve is many short segments, each shorter than a dash, which a reader that starts the pattern again at each vertex draws as a solid line.
  - **The limit of 12 lengths** is the one in the AutoCAD customization guide ("up to 12 dash-length specifications per linetype"); LibreOffice's reader keeps 32 and silently drops the rest (`vcl/source/filter/idxf/dxftblrd.hxx` `DXF_MAX_DASH_COUNT`, `dxftblrd.cxx` lines 57 to 61), so a writer that follows the stricter limit is read by both. The 256 patterns are this writer's own bound; the real files need at most 5 on a page.
  - **The files** (macOS host, Poppler 26.09, Ghostscript 10.07.1, ezdxf 1.4.5). Of the nine files that entry 77 left refused, four convert, every page, and the other five stay refused for something else:

    | File | Result | Pages | Dashed pages (line types) | ezdxf audit errors | Ink IoU of all content, mean of pages, no / 2 pixel tolerance |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | `govdocs1-000730.ps` | converts | 2 | none; page 2 strokes 1,120 elements under a 1.93 to 1 scale | 0 | 0.44 / 0.87 |
    | `govdocs1-002433.ps` | converts | 5 | 3 (1 line type) | 0 | 0.39 / 0.86 |
    | `govdocs1-005434.ps` | converts | 22 | 12 to 15 (3 to 5 line types a page) | 0 | 0.33 / 0.84 |
    | `govdocs1-006955.ps` | converts | 8 | 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 (1 to 3 line types; page 8 has 2,480 dotted strokes on 1) | 0 | 0.33 / 0.81 |
    | `govdocs1-001048.ps` | refused | 15 | page 11 clips two paths and the farthest vertex is 13.18 pt past the clip with Poppler 26 and 9.88 with Poppler 24 (clip rule below) | | |
    | `govdocs1-002956.ps` | refused | 33 | page 28: the text layer reads its 13 bitmap-font characters as spaces | | |
    | `govdocs1-003229.ps` | refused | 20 | pages 17 and 18: SVG of 8.1 and 7.1 MB past the 5 MiB limit | | |
    | `govdocs1-004087.ps` | refused | 5 | pages 2 and 3 hold pictures (entry 42) | | |
    | `govdocs1-006137.ps` | refused | 66 | 16 pages clip to a region that is not the page; 12 of them are dropped by the clip rule, page 43 is refused with either Poppler release, and 20, 50 and 60 are written with Poppler 24 and refused with 26 (clip rule below) | | |

    The ink IoU is the overlap of the ink of the ezdxf drawing add-on's render (matplotlib, 100 dpi, black on white, line types honoured) and of Ghostscript's render of the PostScript page (100 dpi, ink below luminance 160), over all 37 pages. It is low at no tolerance because a DXF here holds outlines: filled shapes (the markers and error bands of the plots) are drawn as outlines, and the text is a stock font. Without the text, over the dashed pages, the no-tolerance IoU of the line type against a solid line is 0.55 against 0.56 on page 3 of `002433` (the one page where the solid line is higher), 0.35 / 0.53 / 0.61 / 0.47 against 0.33 / 0.52 / 0.60 / 0.47 on pages 2, 3, 5 and 7 of `006955`, 0.47 against 0.38 on its page 8, and 0.40, 0.35, 0.37 and 0.36 against 0.33, 0.31, 0.31 and 0.31 on pages 12 to 15 of `005434`; with a 2-pixel tolerance the two are within 0.03 of each other but on page 8 of `006955`, where the dotted curves that Ghostscript draws as separate dots are dense enough for a solid line to overlap them (0.76 against 0.85). Seen side by side, the render of the line types shows the dotted curves of the PostScript and the solid line shows dense black bands.
  - **The clips of the two files that clip** (flattened vertices of the page SVG, in points, with Poppler 26.09 on the macOS host and Poppler 24.02 on the Ubuntu 24.04 VM that the CI image matches; the SVG differs between the releases, so the distance of a page near the line does too; Poppler writes every clip as `<clipPath><path clip-rule="nonzero" d="M x y L x y L x y L x y Z M x y"/></clipPath>` on a `<g clip-path>` with no transform, 607 clips in the two files, none nested, none of another shape):

    | `govdocs1-006137.ps` pages | Farthest vertex past its clip (pt), Poppler 26 | Written | Poppler 24 | Written |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | 30, 32, 35, 36, 46, 52, 53, 62 | 0 (everything inside) | yes | 0 | yes |
    | 49 | 0.004 | yes | 0.003 | yes |
    | 56, 57 | 0.19 | yes | 0.144 | yes |
    | 21 | 0.76 | yes | 0.571 | yes |
    | 20 | 1.145 | no | 0.858 | yes |
    | 50 | 1.205 | no | 0.904 | yes |
    | 60 | 1.275 | no | 0.956 | yes |
    | 43 | 19.43 | no | 14.57 | no |

    With Poppler 26, 12 of 16 pages are written and 4 are not, so the file stays refused, with page 20 first; with Poppler 24, 15 are written and page 43 alone is refused, and the file stays refused. The test therefore holds the rule and not one release's figures: a page is refused with a reach above one point or written, a page that reaches far past its clip (43 of `006137`, 11 of `001048`) is refused with both, and the pages 20, 50 and 60 may go either way. 
    12 of 16 pages are written and 4 are not, so the file stays refused, with page 20 first. Page 11 of `govdocs1-001048.ps` reaches 13.18 pt past its clip with Poppler 26 and 9.88 with Poppler 24 (its other 14 pages hold no clip). The measurement on the boxes of the control points that an earlier draft of this entry reported (9 pages inside, 6 at most 1.14 past, page 43 at 19.4) is the same data at lower resolution: with the vertices of every clipped path of the page, pages 50 and 60 reach 1.205 and 1.275 pt, so 12 pages and not 15 clear one point. An independent reading of the SVG (a script that takes each clip's rectangle and each path's flattened vertices, without the reader's code for the region and the distance) gives the same distance for every page and the same pass and refusal for all 16; a limit of 1.3 pt would write pages 20, 50 and 60 too with Poppler 26 and leave only page 43, which is the result Poppler 24 gives at one point (QA's call, not made here). The 12 pages that are written, converted by the real pipeline with the other pages left out (`pages` option) and read by ezdxf: 0 audit errors on each. The ink of the ezdxf drawing add-on's render (matplotlib, 100 dpi, black on white) against Ghostscript's render of the same PostScript page (100 dpi, ink below luminance 160): within 2 pixels, 0.967 to 0.997 of the DXF ink lies on Ghostscript's ink (so the dropped clips add no ink outside the page's own), 0.836 to 0.974 of Ghostscript's ink is within 2 pixels of DXF ink (a DXF holds the outlines of filled shapes, and the text is a stock font), and the overlap of the two is 0.370 to 0.696 with no tolerance and 0.899 to 0.984 with 2 pixels.
  - **Opacity** is `1` on every element of the nine files, so none depends on this entry.
  - **Dashed strokes are almost always uniform.** The largest ratio of the two axis scales of a dashed stroke is 1.0024 in `006955`, 1.011 in `002956` and 1.32 in `006137` (18 strokes); every other dashed stroke of the nine files is under an exactly uniform transform or under one within 1 part in 10,000.
  - **Cost.** Nothing is written for a page without dashes: the zip of `000097`, `000773` and `006007` (the files of entry 77) is byte for byte what the base writes. A dashed shape adds one group-6 pair and, for a polyline, the flag; the line types of a page are a few hundred bytes. The vector and cad families of the reference parity run give the same 39 and 97 rows on the base and the head (`vector/shapes.svg->wmf/ssim` fails on both). The clip rule changes none of them either: with the base at origin/main and the head with the clip rule, the 39 vector rows and the 97 cad rows read identically (`--parity --quality-only --quick`, ezdxf on the path). A page without a clip pays nothing for the rule (no clip is entered); a page with 1,508 vertices under 68 clips costs 4 edge tests for each vertex. After the review of the clip rule (nested clips, pieces of segments, inheritance, curves, edges on one another, the coordinate bound and the plain decimals) the same holds: the vector and cad rows read identically on the head before and after it, every DXF entry of the zips of `000097`, `000773`, `006007`, the four files above and the 12 pages of `006137` is byte for byte the same, and the 16 clipped pages of `006137` keep their result and reach (none of their clips has a curve or is nested), each read in 5 to 46 ms on both.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A dash under an unequal scale or a skew has one length for every direction**, so its period is off by up to the square root of the ratio of the scales (15 % at the 1.32 of `006137`, 0.12 % at the 1.0024 of `006955`); the centre line is exact.
  - **The phase of a dash is lost.** A line that the PostScript starts half way through a dash starts at the beginning of one (16.1 pt offset of a 32.2 pt dash on page 7 of `006955`).
  - **Dropped opacity draws a transparent element as an opaque one**, and a fully transparent element appears as lines; the references do the same.
  - **A dashed outline in a reader that ignores line types** (some viewers and importers) is solid, which is what the reference that writes no line type gives.
  - **Five of the nine files stay refused**, for content this entry does not change: the clips past one point, the picture policy, the SVG size limit and a text layer without text.
  - **A dropped clip draws up to one point of what it hid** (0.76 pt on page 21 of `006137`), the same one point the page clip allows; nothing beyond it is drawn, because the page is refused instead.
  - **A drawn curve is measured on its flattened line, so a curve whose control points lie outside the clip but whose flattened line does not is not counted, and a stroke's width is not counted**: the writer writes neither (centre line only).
  - **Under nested clips nothing may reach outside, where one clip allows a point.** None of the files nests clips; a drawing that touches the edge of two clips at once by a fraction of a point is refused.
  - **A clip drawn with a curve is refused**, where its flattened outline would hold a drawing on most scales; Poppler writes every clip with straight edges (all 607 clips of the files).
  - **Two edges on one another refuse the clip** even where they are inside it (two polygons of one path that share a side); the files have none.
  - **A clip on a large number of edges, or deeper than 8, is a refusal**, where a reader without limits would measure it.
  - **`objectBoundingBox` clips and a clip on a clip stay refused**, where an exact box and an intersection of regions could be measured; neither appears in the files and both have a simple fail-closed answer.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Solid lines for dashes (Inkscape).** It drops the pattern that a line type keeps for the price of a table entry.
  - **The five stock line types of pstoedit.** They keep the number of entries and lose the lengths.
  - **Cutting each dash into its own polyline.** It is exact under any transform and needs no table, and it multiplies the entities (the 32,435 dashed elements of the nine files, each cut at its length over its period) against the 500,000-vertex budget; it also leaves a reader no pattern to change.
  - **Writing the dash offset as a rotated pattern.** A line type cannot start in a gap, and a pattern that starts inside a dash has an odd number of elements, which ezdxf's reader drops the last of (`pipeline.py` `_create_pattern`), so the rotated pattern would be drawn wrong where the plain one is only out of phase.
  - **Refusing a dash under a skew above some ratio.** None of the files that convert has one, and the bound would be this project's own; the period error is bounded by the square root of the ratio.
  - **Dropping every clip, as both references do.** Entry 42 refuses a clip that hides geometry because dropping it draws what it hides; the rule above keeps that refusal for any clip that hides more than a point, and drops the rest.
  - **Measuring the boxes of the control points instead of the vertices.** It is a bound that is never lower than the flattened path and needs no region; it is not exact for a clip that is not a rectangle, and the exact measure costs a few lines more (the vertices and the region are already in device space).
  - **Cutting the drawing at the clip.** The clip is geometry too, and a DXF writer that cuts outlines at a region needs a polygon clipper for strokes and fills; it would convert page 43 of `006137` and page 11 of `001048` and change the drawing, which no reference exporter does.
  - **A wider tolerance.** The one point is QA's decision and the page clip's own; three pages of `006137` reach between 1.1 and 1.3 pt.
  - **The tolerance under nested clips, with each clip measured on its own.** The distance to an intersection has no bound from the distances to each clip. Measuring the intersection needs a polygon clipper, for files that nest no clips.
  - **Holding one clip to the tolerance and the others to zero.** It is not sound either: a point inside one clip and within a point of the other can be far from their intersection, or the intersection can be empty.
  - **Measuring the middle of each piece of a segment outside a non-convex clip.** The middle is not the farthest point: a needle of the clip that ends half a pixel from it let a line through of which 160 pixels are hidden.
  - **Refusing every outside piece longer than twice the tolerance.** A piece between two crossings is then within the tolerance, but a piece that ends at a vertex already a point away is not, so it holds only with the bound of the ends, which the halving uses anyway.
  - **Flattening the curves of a clip at 0.25 device pixels over the scale, or adding the flattening error to the distance.** The path reader's tolerance is not a bound on the error of its outline (8 halvings at most, a test against the chord's line and not its segment, arcs and circles cut in fixed steps), so either needs a curve flattener with a proven bound, for clips that no file has.
  - **EMF and WMF with the same rules.** A metafile pen can carry a dash style and a skewed pen, but it is a different encoder (extended pens), so they keep entry 42's refusals.
- **Verified by**: `tests/dxf-pen-attributes.test.ts`, red before the change (30 of 50 tests): the line type, its pattern and its scale, odd lists, separators, inheritance and cancellation by `none`, equal patterns defined once, bit 128 on a polyline, solid cases, dots and butt caps, the phase left out, strokes under `scale(2 1)`, `skewX(45)` and a stretching viewBox written at their transformed points, opacity dropped on a shape and on a group, what is still refused; hostile arrays (13 lengths, a repeated odd list past 12, a million lengths and 4 million separators refused by their length, negative, NaN, Infinity, `1e999`, percentages, units, hexadecimal, empty entries, a length that is not finite on the page, a pattern below the written precision, 257 distinct patterns, 30,000 uses of a dashed shape) each inside 3 s; an independent read by ezdxf of the line types and their compiled patterns with 0 audit errors. `tests/postscript-real-file-refusals.test.ts`, red before the change (all three tests of each of `000730` and `002433`, the two files tried against the old writer): the four files convert, every page with TEXT, word recall and agreement as in entry 77, ezdxf audits every page with no error and no entity naming an unknown line type, the dashed pages are exactly the ones listed and name a defined line type; the five others match their row of `known-refusals.json`. `tests/svg-metafile-geometry.test.ts` (EMF, WMF and CGM still refuse dashes, opacity and skewed strokes) passes unchanged. The clip rule: `tests/dxf-clip-region.test.ts`, red before the change (34 of 42 tests), covering the distance (to the region, not the sides: the corner case), the tolerance on both sides of one point, a clip on the shape itself and in a style, the clipped element's transform and the `<clipPath>`'s and the shape's, a rotated rectangle, a concave path (a vertex in the notch and a segment that leaves between two vertices inside), `clip-rule` (nonzero, evenodd, a reversed hole, from the shape, its style, the `<clipPath>`), the union of shapes, a polygon, nested clips (each holds, a clip ends with its element, the depth limit), every refusal that carries a reason, a clip that hides everything and one that has nothing under it, a bitmap-font character under a clip, and the hostile cases (a clip of a million vertices, one of 1,025 edges, a clip named by 30,000 elements, the most edges against the most vertices, NaN, Infinity and overflowing coordinates and matrices, a zero matrix) each inside 3 s. The review of the clip rule, each red before its fix: the reviewer's clips at y < 100 and y > 100.8 around a line between them (nested clips hold to their intersection), a frame with a needle half a pixel from the middle of a hidden line (the farthest point of a piece), `clip-rule="evenodd"` on the root and on `<defs>`, `inherit`, a hidden `<defs>` and a shape visible again (inheritance from the ancestors), a NaN distance from a clip of `1e200` and coordinates past 10^9, `stroke-dasharray="1e308 1e308"` and a coordinate of `1e22` (plain decimals), a spike of no width, a path drawn twice under evenodd and a bow tie of no area that cuts a rectangle (edges that border nothing), a 3 MB dash array used 2,000 times (60.9 s before, refused at its first use after) and the 1,024-character bound, a circle, an ellipse, a rounded rectangle, cubic, quadratic and arc paths and a round hole flattened 3 pixels off under `scale(20)` (curves), and 80,000 placements of a clip of 1,023 points under a singular matrix and a refusal of a 100,000-character id (the work of a placement and the length of a message). `tests/svg-page-clip.test.ts` (a clip that clips something is still refused by the DXF writer when it hides more than a point). `tests/postscript-real-file-refusals.test.ts`, red before the change on the same two files: the 12 pages of `006137` write and ezdxf audits them without errors, and the four pages of `006137` and page 11 of `001048` are refused with a reach past one point, converted by the real pipeline one page at a time.
- **Revisit when**: QA widens or narrows the one point of the clip rule (a limit of 1.3 pt leaves only page 43 of `006137`); a real page needs more than the 2^23 edge tests of the clip work limit; a file draws under a clip that is not a rectangle, a clip with a curve, nested clips, an `objectBoundingBox` unit or a clip on a clip; the metafile encoders write extended pens (then EMF and WMF can hold dashes); a reader is found that needs the dash offset; or a file draws dashes under a skew of a ratio where a period error shows.

## 80. Text in annotation appearances: widget captions, field values, free text and stamps, read from the pdf.js operator list

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, `pdfjs-sechandler.pdf` row), decided 2026-10-23 (QA request in issue #783: the PDF text path reads the text that annotation appearance streams draw, the way the reference readers do).
- **Decision**:
  - **The text of an annotation's appearance stream is part of the page's text.** The in-process PDF reader (entries 49 and 70) adds it after the page's own items, as items with a position, so the layout analysis, the density test that decides whether a page needs OCR, the word geometry for hOCR and ALTO, and every text output see it like any other text. A page whose only text is a push button caption or a field value is a page with a text layer.
  - **Which annotations: the ones pdf.js draws.** The operator list pdf.js builds for the page holds each annotation it may draw between `beginAnnotation` and `endAnnotation`; the reader walks those stretches. That leaves out an annotation with the Hidden bit or the NoView bit, and, for a non-widget, the Invisible bit; it includes every subtype that has an appearance (Widget of every field type, FreeText, Stamp, Square, Line and the rest) and the appearance pdf.js builds for a text field when the form sets NeedAppearances. A check box or radio button draws the state `/AS` selects. A link and a popup draw nothing. The Print bit is not required (the page is read as on screen).
  - **Where the text goes.** It is positioned by its own matrices (the annotation's rectangle, the appearance's /Matrix and /BBox, then the text state), so it falls in reading order where it lies on the page, as with Poppler's layout; in the item list it follows the page's own items in the operator list's order (non-widgets in the order of /Annots, then widgets, then popups).
  - **Text state.** The walk follows `Tc`, `Tw`, `Tz`, `TL`, `Ts`, `Tm`, `Td`, `TD`, `T*`, `q`/`Q`, `cm` and the matrix of a form XObject drawn inside the appearance, and a Type 3 font's own glyph scale. A gap in a TJ array of more than 0.102 em adds a space and one of more than 0.6 em (or a move back of more than 0.2 em) starts a new item, the constants of pdf.js's text extraction. The run's string goes through pdf.js's own `normalizeUnicode`.
  - **Left out.** A run with right-to-left letters (pdf.js reorders it with a bidirectional pass that pdfjs-dist does not expose, so it would come out in drawing order) and a run in a vertical font; a page too busy for its operator list (more than 20,000 text items, the reader's existing rule) reads no annotation text; optional content is not evaluated (an annotation in a hidden layer is read).
  - **Bounds.** Annotation items count against the limits of the page's own items, because they are items: 100,000 items and 2,097,152 characters a page, 1,048,576 characters in one item, 500,000 items and 16,777,216 characters in a document, 2,000 pages, the 60 s deadline, the 4,096 fonts, the operator-list cap of 2,000,000 per page, the 256 levels of graphics-state nesting. The stream guard (`pdf-stream-guard.ts`) now also decodes the normal appearance stream of every annotation pdf.js builds, and the forms they draw, under the budgets of the page content, for every job that reads a page: the text and layout jobs, and also the density test of OCR and the word-geometry job, which take the page content as pdf.js gives it but have pdf.js build the annotations. The annotations are those of /Annots as pdf.js reads it, the page's own or else the nearest one up the /Parent chain (`getInheritableProperty`; a chain longer than the 64 levels a page tree may have is refused), and of a state dictionary it decodes every stream whatever its /Subtype, since pdf.js draws the one /AS names without looking at it. Each stream is counted as it is reached. The budgets: 64 MiB for a stream, 256 MiB for the document counted once per annotation that draws a stream (so 7 annotations sharing a 40 MiB appearance are refused), 200,000 content streams, 100,000 form invocations, 16 levels of forms, no form that draws itself. A document whose pages list more than 50,000 annotations in all (each listing counts, so pages that share one /Annots array count it once each), a page that lists one annotation twice, and an annotation with more than 64 appearance states are refused with a 400 before pdf.js builds any annotation. An appearance whose data is damaged is left out and the rest of the page is read, as pdf.js does.
- **Why**:
  - **pdf.js draws these annotations and its text API does not reach them.** `Page.getOperatorList` adds the operator list of every annotation for which `mustBeViewed` holds and logs and skips one that fails (`pdf.worker.mjs` in pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, lines 59711 `_isViewable`, 60455 widget `mustBeViewed`, 65859 to 65866). The text API, `Annotation.extractTextContent` (59976), runs only for an annotation whose `hasTextContent` holds, which is a text field with an appearance and no NeedAppearances (61012) and FreeText (61993); it is `false` for the rest (59973). So a push button caption, a choice field, a check mark or a stamp never arrive as text, and `pdfjs-sechandler.pdf` has exactly that: the page is empty and the text sits in the caption of a push button widget. The operator list has all of them, with a Unicode value in every glyph, and its annotation stretch is placed by the matrices of `CanvasGraphics.beginAnnotation` (`pdf.mjs` line 19283).
  - **Poppler prints the same annotations** (master of 2026-10-23; GPL, read for behaviour only). `Page::displaySlice` draws every annotation (`poppler/Page.cc` lines 627 to 637), `Annot::isVisible` leaves out Hidden and, on screen, NoView (`poppler/Annot.cc` 2009 to 2016), and `pdftotext` shows pages on screen (`utils/pdftotext.cc` line 418). It differs from pdf.js in three places: it draws the Invisible bit's annotations, it builds the appearance of a field that has none (`AnnotWidget::draw`, `Annot.cc` 5889 to 5903) and with NeedAppearances it rebuilds every field's appearance (a button without a caption then draws nothing).
  - **Reuse order.** (1) pdfjs-dist as it is: `getAnnotations()` gives `textContent` for the two kinds above only, which does not read the file this was filed for. (2) An installed tool: `qpdf --flatten-annotations` turns appearances into page content that pdf.js reads as text, but it skips every widget when the form sets NeedAppearances (`libqpdf/QPDFPageDocumentHelper.cc` lines 59 to 65 and 88 to 106, qpdf 12.2.0), `screen` forbids only NoView so Hidden annotations are included (`libqpdf/QPDFJob_config.cc` lines 197 to 206), and it needs a process and a rewritten file for every page with an annotation; Poppler's `pdftotext` cannot tell annotation words from page words. (3) New code over the pdf.js operator list: about 350 lines that only follow the text state, written after `evaluator.js` `getTextContent` and `canvas.js` as listed above; everything that decides what is drawn (flags, states, generated field appearances, damaged streams) stays pdf.js's.
  - **The caps.** Neither reference has one for annotations: pdf.js builds every operator list at once and Poppler draws each. The reader's thread has a 1 GiB heap, and pdf.js keeps what it built for the annotations of each page until the document closes, so the cost is the document's and not the page's. It read 10,000 annotations of one page in 0.6 s, 30,000 in 1.3 s and 60,000 in 2.2 s (1.5 GB resident); 99,998 widgets that draw a caption, on two pages sharing one list, in 2.8 s for the text and 3.0 s for the density test; and it ran out of memory at 149,997 on three pages, for either job (Square annotations without an appearance cost less: 499,990 were read and 1,249,975 ran it out of memory). The cap for the document is 50,000, half of what was read. Of the 1,256 real-world PDFs qpdf reads, the most annotations one lists is 891 (166 on one page); none lists an annotation twice, on one page or on two, and none puts /Annots on a /Pages node; their 23 states dictionaries hold one or two states, as a check box and a radio button have (Off and the on state, ISO 32000-1 section 12.7.4.2.3), and pdf.js draws at most three (/AS, the on state and Off, `Annotation.setAppearance`, `_processCheckBox`, `_processRadioButton`), so the state cap of 64 is far from any real form. A repeated annotation is refused instead of counted because pdf.js builds every entry anew: 3,000 references to one widget with 100,000 states (1.5 MB) ended in V8's `Invalid array length` before the guard counted anything, and 20 references to one highlight of 50,000 quadrilaterals took 4.1 s and 1.43 GB in the density test. The stream budgets are the ones the page content has; an annotation's appearance was decoded by pdf.js with none before (a 128 MiB Flate bomb and 100,000 nested `q` in an appearance were accepted, the second after 60 s).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Where pdf.js and Poppler differ, the text follows pdf.js.** A text field with a value and no appearance in a form without NeedAppearances is blank (Poppler prints the value). A page that draws a word itself and also in a button caption a point away has both (`pdf-pypdf-pdflatex-forms.pdf`: Poppler prints `Submit` once, the page has it twice, and the layout joins the two copies, which are 1.3 pt apart where it merges copies within 0.6 pt, into `SubmitSubmit`).
  - **Annotation text in a right-to-left or vertical run is not read**; it was not before either.
  - **Rules in an annotation** (a field's border) are still placed by the page's transformation matrix, not the annotation's (the walk for rules does not know `beginAnnotation`); this is unchanged and out of this entry's scope.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **`getAnnotations()` text alone**: it misses the push button of the file this was filed for, choice fields, stamps and generated field appearances.
  - **`qpdf --flatten-annotations`, then read the page**: see above; NeedAppearances forms and Hidden annotations come out wrong, and every page with a link would pay a process.
  - **`pdftotext -bbox-layout` words merged into the pdf.js items**: no way to tell which words an annotation drew.
  - **A cap on annotation items of its own**: the item and character limits of the page already bound them.
  - **A cap per page as well as the one for the document**: pdf.js keeps every page's annotations, so one page is bounded by the document's cap.
  - **Skipping annotation text in the density test when a page lists too many**: pdf.js would still build the annotations it asks for, and the streams they draw would not be checked.
  - **Decoding only the state /AS names**: pdf.js also draws the on state and Off of a button, which it picks with rules that read the field's value, so every state is decoded and their number is capped.
  - **/Annots inherited down the /Kids of the page tree, as the reader carries /Resources**: pdf.js follows /Parent, which a damaged file can point outside the tree.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-annotation-text.test.ts` (red on origin/main, 16 of 18: `pdfjs-sechandler.pdf` through the reader, pdf to rtf, pdf to docx and pdf to pdf, which stopped at OCR; word recall against `pdftotext` on six files with form fields, free text and stamps; hand-written pages for the subtypes, the Hidden and NoView bits against Poppler, reading position, NeedAppearances, a check box's states and a damaged appearance), `tests/pdf-annotation-text-walk.test.ts` (the walk on hand-written operator lists, positions worked out from ISO 32000-1) and `tests/pdf-annotation-text-hostile.test.ts` (6 of 11 red before the guard, the others are the positive controls and the item limits that already held: 50,001 annotations; forms nested to the limit and past it; an appearance that draws itself; 100,000 nested `q`; a 128 MiB bomb; a 40 MiB appearance shared by 7 annotations; 100,001 runs, a 1 MiB item and 540,000 runs over six pages). Over the 1,266 cached real-world PDFs, 28 outputs changed and 1,238 are byte for byte the same (the hash of the text), no file changed from read to refused or back, and the word recall against `pdftotext` rose on 27 of the 28 (for example `pdf-pdfbox-annotations.pdf` 0.075 to 0.950, `pdfjs-sechandler.pdf` 0 to 1, `pdf-pdfjs-annotation-choice-widget.pdf` 0.487 to 1, `govdocs1-003896.pdf` 0.947 to 0.989), and fell on one (`pdf-pypdf-pdflatex-forms.pdf` 1 to 0.75, above). `--parity --quality-only --quick` on the families `document` (27 rows, none failing) and `pdf-ops` (101 rows, none failing) on the development Mac; epubcheck, `python3-olefile` and `python3-xlrd` are not installed there, so 80 `document` rows were not evaluated and CI evaluates them. Reading time of four files (one without annotations, one of 126 pages with 102 links, one form with 11 fields, one of 46 pages with a line annotation), median of 5 alternating runs of 15 reads on the development Mac under a load average of 4 to 6, base against head: 18.8 and 19.1 ms, 850.5 and 852.6 ms, 124.3 and 125.0 ms, 106.4 and 108.5 ms, with overlapping ranges: no measurable difference. A first version that asked every page for its annotations read the 126-page file in 996 ms against 848 ms (+17 %, 1.2 ms a page for the links), so a job that reads the operator list anyway goes straight to it and any other job asks the page first. The review's probes are in `tests/pdf-annotation-text-hostile.test.ts`, red before the bounds (14 of 27): a check box state that is a 128 MiB bomb marked `/Subtype /Image`; a bomb and 50,001 annotations listed on the /Pages node, and a bomb listed on a /Parent outside the page tree; an annotation listed twice, 3,000 references to one widget with 100,000 states, and 20 references to one highlight of 50,000 quadrilaterals in the density test; 65 states; a bomb in the density test and in the word-geometry job and 50,001 annotations in the density test; three pages sharing one list of 16,667 annotations. Each is refused with its typed error within 15 s while the process grows by less than 512 MB; 64 states, an annotation listed on the /Pages node, a widget caption in the density test, and 4,000 annotations sharing 64 states (refused at 200,000 content streams) are the controls. After the bounds the 1,266 texts hash the same as before them, and the guard for annotations alone refuses two files, the two every target already refuses (`pdf-qpdf-deep-pages.pdf`, `qpdf-issue-146.pdf`). The guard costs the density test 0.1 to 8.4 ms on six files whose test takes 28 to 529 ms (median of 7, load average 5 to 12). pdf.js caches a page's operator list, so reading it for the annotations and again for the content builds it once (the second call returns the same promise in 0.01 ms).
- **Revisit when**: a real file shows right-to-left or vertical annotation text, a corpus file has a field value that Poppler prints and pdf.js does not draw (then NeedAppearances handling would follow Poppler), pdfjs-dist exposes its bidirectional pass or a text-extraction call for a single appearance stream, or a cap of this entry (50,000 annotations in a document, 64 states, one listing an annotation) turns away a real file.

## 81. Pictures of a PDF in HTML and Markdown: the reader waits for pdf.js to deliver each picture

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, row "the in-process Markdown and HTML routes embed a picture or not from run to run"), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **A picture the PDF paints is in the HTML, Markdown and Word result, on every run.** The text reader (entries 49, 70 and 80) finds the pictures a page paints in its pdf.js operator list. For each one that is not a plain JPEG it takes the pixels pdf.js decoded, and it now waits until pdf.js has delivered them. pdf.js decodes a picture in a task of its own and posts it to the page after the operator list has already resolved, so the old code, which looked the picture up the moment the list resolved, found it on some runs and not on others and left it out silently.
  - **Which table to ask.** A picture that several pages paint is kept in the table shared by the document, under an id that starts with `g_`; every other picture is in the page's own table. The reader asks the one the id names.
  - **A picture pdf.js cannot decode arrives as null** and is left out, the same on every run. A document whose picture never arrives ends at the 60 s deadline of the text thread, which is the typed error it already was.
  - **A picture is encoded once per pdf.js object id, and every placement of it shares those bytes.** The reader keeps the encoded result of an id (a PNG of the decoded pixels, or the PDF's own JPEG stream) and gives the same bytes to every later placement, on the page and on other pages. Markdown and HTML still write one data URI per placement, so the output holds one copy at each place the PDF paints the picture; Word, ODF and EPUB write the picture once, because the layout gives placements that share bytes one entry of the document's picture table (the same rule the other readers apply by content).
  - **The limits:** 256 pictures a page, **32,768 picture placements a document**, the 128 MiB of picture bytes a document, 50 million pixels a picture, the pixel cap of `assertInputPixels`, the operator-list cap, and the thread's deadline and heap. A document that places more than 32,768 pictures, or whose placements hold more than 128 MiB, is refused with a typed 413 (`PayloadLimitError`), the same way for every run; the placements are counted, not the distinct pictures, because the Markdown and HTML output grows with the placements. No wall-clock decision is made about a picture: the wait ends when pdf.js delivers it.
  - **Each page is cleaned up once it is read.** pdf.js keeps the pixels it decoded for a page in the page's object table, typed arrays outside the V8 heap and so outside the heap limit of the text thread, until `page.cleanup()` clears it. The reader calls it after the text, the operator list and the geometry of the page are read. It clears the page's operator lists and its own table and nothing else: the document's shared table (`g_` ids) and the fonts stay, so a picture a later page shares is delivered to it again.
- **Why**:
  - **The repeats and the cap come from the references' behaviour, with a bound added.** pdf.js decodes a picture once per object for all the draws of a page (`LocalImageCache`, `pdf.worker.mjs` of pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, line 31918) and once for all the pages that paint it (`GlobalImageCache`, line 32044: a picture is shared after `NUM_PAGES_THRESHOLD` = 2 pages, and the cache stops growing at `MAX_BYTE_SIZE` = 50,000,000 bytes once it holds `MIN_IMAGES_TO_CACHE` = 10 pictures); the reader encodes by the same key. Poppler (26.07.0) writes one image per draw and has no limit: `pdftohtml` names a file or data URL for every draw (`HtmlOutputDev.cc`, `drawImage`, `createImageFileName`), and `pdfimages` writes or lists one per draw (`ImageOutputDev.cc`, `++imgNum` in `listImage` and `writeImage`; the `ref` is passed but never used to skip a repeat). So Markdown and HTML, which have no way to name a picture twice in a data URI, keep one copy per placement, as the reference does. The bound is ours: without one, an 83 KB PDF that draws a 1x1 picture 256 times on each of its pages made 23,296 pictures in 20 s, about 238 times its size as Markdown, and a PDF of 129 such pages ran a test process out of memory. 32,768 is 2.6 times the largest document of the two samples (12,544 placements in `gd-547959.pdf`; the real-world maximum is 5,482 in `govdocs1-000282.pdf`) and a power of two like the other limits here. The byte budget could not do this work: the largest document of the samples holds 93.5 MiB of pictures (`govdocs1-003066.pdf`, 40 placements), so a tighter byte limit would refuse real files, and a document of small pictures never reaches 128 MiB.
  - **The cleanup is what pdf.js does.** Its viewer cleans a page when it leaves the screen (`PDFPageProxy.cleanup`, `pdf.mjs` line 16071). Without it, 60 pages of one 3000 x 3000 picture each reached 1.87 GiB resident in a child process, and 40 pages of 4000 x 4000 pictures 2.22 GiB; with it the resident set stays at about 650 MiB however many pages there are.
  - **pdf.js itself waits.** Its renderer stops at the operator list's `dependency` operator until `objsPool.get(id, callback)` has the object, and takes an id that starts with `g_` from the shared table (`pdf.mjs` of pdfjs-dist 6.3.289, `executeOperatorList`, lines 17495 to 17503). The worker posts the picture from a `PDFImage.buildImage(...).then(...)` that nothing awaits (`pdf.worker.mjs`, `buildPaintImageXObject`, lines 40664 to 40716), on success and on failure (null).
  - **The loss was large and had nothing to do with load.** Two runs of the code before the change on the 1,261 real-world PDFs differ in the pictures of 16 files (21 in the earlier measurement) and on the 625 regression PDFs in 18 (19 in the earlier one), with no load of ours on the machine; with twelve busy loops running, 24 of 34 of those files changed over ten runs (five to Markdown and five to HTML). The race was lost for most pictures: 31,805 pictures in the Markdown of the real-world files before and 50,836 after (556 files with a picture before, 616 after), 10,859 before and 36,850 after on the regression sample. Where no document limit applies the count is the one Poppler's `pdfimages -list` gives: 1,271 and 1,271 (`cc-2400138.pdf`), 1,526 and 1,526 (`cc-0600046.pdf`), 48 and 48, 28 and 28, 7 and 7, and 2 and 2.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The results hold more pictures, so they are bigger and take longer**: all 1,261 real-world files take 449 s instead of 414 s in one process (8 % more); a PDF with 12,544 pictures (`gd-547959.pdf`) takes 10.9 s where the old code, which dropped most of them, took 0.6 s. The 128 MiB budget turns a document with more picture bytes than that into a typed 413 on every run, where the old code lost the pictures and converted; no file of the two samples reaches it.
  - **A document that places more than 32,768 pictures is refused** where the code before the change converted it, with most of its pictures. No file of the two samples is near it. A caller that needs such a document gets the typed 413 and can ask for a format that does not repeat a picture (Word, ODF or EPUB are bounded by the same count).
  - **The same picture can still be written twice in Word.** pdf.js gives a picture that two or more pages paint the id of the shared table from the second page on, and the first page's draws carry the page's own id, so the picture is encoded once for each of the two ids and appears twice in a Word file; the repeats on a page and the pages after the second share one.
  - **A document whose pictures pass a limit keeps the pictures up to it** (for example 1,043 of 11,353 in `gd-085248.pdf`); the limits are the old ones.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A fixed delay or a retry loop**: a wall-clock bound decides by the speed of the machine, which is the defect.
  - **Awaiting the decode promises inside the worker's own thread**: pdf.js does not expose them; the object table is its interface.
  - **Reading every picture again with another decoder**: pdf.js already decoded it; a second decoder would differ from it in colour handling.
  - **Leaving the old behaviour and recording a warning**: the pictures are the document's content.
  - **One reference-style definition for a repeated picture in Markdown** (`![][1]` and `[1]: data:...`): the Markdown, HTML and Word results are built from the same document model, HTML needs the data URI in each `img` anyway, and no reference output (pdftohtml, pdfimages) shares a picture between draws.
  - **Dropping the placements past the limit with a warning**: the result would hold a prefix of the pictures chosen by page order, which is not what the PDF shows; the document's other limits (pages, text items, picture bytes) refuse instead.
  - **A limit on the size of the output** like the 16 MiB of rendered Markdown (`MAX_MARKDOWN_OUTPUT_CHARS`): real files exceed it (the Markdown of `govdocs1-003066.pdf` is 125 MiB, and 64 of the 1,875 files of the samples that convert have a Markdown result over 16 MiB), so it would refuse them.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-picture-determinism.test.ts` (red on the code before the change, 6 of 6: a page table that delivers late, the shared table, a picture pdf.js cannot decode, `pdfjs-issue9972-2.pdf` and `pdfjs-issue9972-3.pdf`, 12 runs each to Markdown or HTML, and a hand-made PDF with six pictures and every core busy for 12 runs of each), and two runs of the code after the change over the 1,261 real-world and the 625 regression PDFs to Markdown (every picture hashed, the warnings and the errors compared) that are identical, with the same nine refusals as before, and ten runs (five to Markdown, five to HTML) of the 34 files that changed between runs, with and without twelve busy loops, with 0 of 34 changing (24 of 34 before, under load).
- **Verified by (repeats and cleanup)**: `tests/pdf-picture-repeats.test.ts` (red before the change, 5 of 5: 256 placements of one object share no bytes, a document is not refused past the placement limit, 256 placements on a page write 256 media files in Word, a PDF of 129 pages of 256 placements ran the test process out of memory, and 300 pages that share a picture did not finish in 65 s; after the change the file runs in 5 s) and `tests/pdf-picture-memory.test.ts` (red before the cleanup: 60 pages of 3000 x 3000 pictures peak at 1,871 MiB in a child process against a 1,000 MiB limit, 636 to 718 MiB after; a picture shared by 8 pages is found on every page with the cleanup in place). Corpus: Markdown of the 1,261 real-world and the 625 regression PDFs on the code before and after the change, every picture hashed, the output size, the warnings and the errors compared: 0 differences in 1,886 files, and 0 between two runs of the code after (87,686 placements, 45,253 distinct pictures); the largest document is 12,544 placements (`gd-547959.pdf`) and the largest in bytes 93.5 MiB (`govdocs1-003066.pdf`), so no file reaches a limit. `gd-547959.pdf` takes 11.0 to 14.5 s before and 1.0 to 1.3 s after (four alternating runs each, same output of 12,055,158 characters, 339 distinct pictures in 12,544 placements).
- **Revisit when**: a document has more picture bytes than the budget and a caller needs the pictures it has, or pdf.js starts to await the decode before it resolves the operator list.

## 82. Headings of a Markdown file: the ids of github-slugger, so that links to a heading work in every target

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, rows "in-process Markdown to pdf writes no heading ids" and the Markdown to HTML, Word and EPUB heading ids), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **A heading of a Markdown file gets the id a Markdown view on a code host gives it**, and `[text](#id)` is a link to it in the PDF written in-process and in the page handed to the office suite. The id is made as `github-slugger` 2.0.0 (ISC licence, which follows the table-of-contents filter that site renders Markdown with) makes it: the text of the heading (the words it shows, without the marks of emphasis, code and links), lower case, every character of its table removed, spaces to hyphens, and a heading whose id was given before is numbered `-1`, `-2` in document order. A heading whose id is empty (`# !!!`) has none, and the next such heading is numbered.
  - **The character table is the original's, byte for byte** (`src/lib/markdown/github-slug.ts`, with its notice). It is not `\p{L}\p{M}\p{N}\p{Pc}`: that class keeps superscripts and fractions the site removes and removes code points the table of the original keeps, 15,847 code points in all (Node 24, Unicode 17). The 78 test vectors of the original (`tests/fixtures/github-slugger`) give the same ids.
  - **The markdown-it path gives the same ids** (`markdown.ts`, which writes the HTML, Word, ODF and EPUB results). A core rule after the parse puts an `id` on every heading (`h1` to `h6`, also inside a quotation or a list), before the policy pass, which allows `id` on headings and nowhere else. The title is read as markdown-it-anchor 9.2.0 reads it (`getTokensText`: the `text` and `code_inline` tokens of the heading's inline content), and the id is the one above, numbered in document order. markdown-it-anchor's own default slug (`encodeURIComponent` of the lower-cased title) is not used, because it keeps punctuation; its numbering of repeats (`-1`, `-2`) is the same as the slugger's (identical on 200,000 random sequences of titles such as `a`, `a-1`, `A` and `a 1`). The writers already made a bookmark, an `id` or an anchor of every heading id (entry 55), so nothing else changed: HTML `<h2 id>`; Word a bookmark around the heading and a `w:hyperlink w:anchor` for each link (the writer's own name rule, for example `_second_part2`, applies); EPUB an `<a id>` in the heading and a link to the chapter that holds it (`chapter2.xhtml#second-part`); ODF a bookmark and a link. This follows pandoc's writers (behaviour only, GPL; 3.6.4): `Writers/Docx/OpenXML.hs` 379 to 413 and 1092 to 1098 (the heading's identifier as a bookmark around its contents), 908 to 912 (`w:hyperlink w:anchor` for a `#` link), 1100 to 1108 (a bookmark name of at most 40 characters that starts with a letter, else a hash); `Writers/HTML.hs` 983 (the identifier is the heading's `id`); `Chunks.hs` about 118 (a `#id` link in a chunked EPUB points to the chunk file that holds the id).
  - **Links to a place in the document are kept** (`#` followed by a name). One to an id that no heading has stays text, as every internal link of the in-process renderer does (entry 55). Links to the web and mail addresses are as before, and nothing else is linked.
- **Why**:
  - **Markdown files are written for that site.** A link such as `[usage](#command-line-usage)` or `[Über](#über-café)` names the id it gives, so the ids must be the same ones, including for letters outside ASCII and for the punctuation it removes (`C++ & Rust` is `c--rust`).
  - **The reference renderers agree on the result.** The office suite, given the staged page, writes a link annotation with an `/XYZ` destination for each of two internal links (qpdf), and a browser follows `#id` to the element with that id (HTML Living Standard, "the indicated part of the document"); the in-process renderer already does it for every id (entry 55). Only the ids were missing.
  - **No writer of ours had a rule to follow.** The Markdown reader of `markdown.ts` (markdown-it, CommonMark) gave headings no id either, so a link to one went nowhere in the HTML and was text in the Word, ODF and EPUB results; `github-slugger` is the maintained implementation of the rule. It is ported (a table and ten lines, ISC, notice in the file) and not added as a dependency, because this is its only use.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A link to an id that no heading has** is text in the in-process PDF, Word, ODF and EPUB, and stays a link to nothing in the HTML (markdown-it writes it as it is, and a browser does nothing with it).
  - **An underlined (setext) heading is not a heading to the in-process PDF renderer** (unchanged), so it has no id there; markdown-it reads it, so it has one in the other targets.
  - **The ids are new attributes in the HTML result.** A page that styles or scripts `h2` by position is not affected; one that already wrote its own `id` on a heading cannot, because raw HTML is escaped (`html: false`).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **The default of markdown-it-anchor** (`encodeURIComponent` of the lower-cased text with spaces turned into hyphens): it keeps punctuation (`hello%2C-world!`), which the site's ids do not.
  - **Pandoc's rule** (`auto_identifiers`): it drops digits and punctuation at the start and joins words differently, and Markdown files for this audience are written for the site above.
  - **A Unicode category class for the table**: see above, 15,847 code points differ.
  - **Linking every `#name` whether a heading has it or not**: a link that goes nowhere is worse than text.
- **Verified by**: `tests/github-slug.test.ts` (the 78 vectors of the original in order, plus the numbering of repeated and numbered ids and `__proto__`) and `tests/markdown-pdf-heading-links.test.ts` (red on the code before the change, 3 of 4: qpdf for the link annotations, rectangles, name tree and `qpdf --check`, pdftotext for the words under each rectangle and at each destination, over links in both directions, punctuation, emphasis and code in a heading, Korean, German and accented letters, repeated headings, a link to a heading that is not there, and a link to the web), and `tests/markdown-heading-ids.test.ts` for the markdown-it path (red on the code before the change, 7 of 7 at the time: the fragment, an empty slug, headings in a quotation and a list, and each of HTML (ids and link fragments read by parse5), Word (bookmarks and `w:hyperlink` anchors by saxes, every link has a bookmark), EPUB (`epubAnchors`: every link has an id in its chapter, no duplicate, every id a valid name) and ODF; a heading longer than a bookmark name is linked in Word and EPUB), and the staged page converted by the office suite (two links with destinations). `tests/markdown-commonmark-spec.test.ts` takes the heading ids off before it compares with the specification, and two tests that wrote the old heading markup (`conversions.test.ts`, `advanced-conversions-boost.test.ts`) expect the ids. The quality rows of the document family are the same for the code before and after (27 measured on the Mac, 92 on the Linux VM; the 12 EPUBCheck rows are not measured, the tool is not installed on either). The ported function and the original give the same slug for `a`, one code point and ` B`, for every code point of Unicode.
- **Revisit when**: a Markdown file of the corpus links by the id of another dialect, or a caller needs the markdown-it path to leave the heading ids out.

## 83. An img without a source: its alt text in line, or nothing, and never a refusal

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, row "in-process HTML to pdf refuses `<img>` without `src`"), decided 2026-10-24 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **An `<img>` with no `src`, or an empty one, converts.** Its request is broken (HTML Living Standard, "update the image data": a selected source of null), so it represents the text of its `alt` when that is not empty and nothing otherwise, and the in-process renderer draws that text in line with the words around it, or nothing (rendering, "Embedded content": an `img` that represents some text is a non-replaced phrasing element with that text, one that represents nothing has natural dimensions of 0). A browser prints the same page the same way; the text of a probe page with five such images came out the same in the browser and here.
  - **The size of the element is ignored**: a one-pixel `<img src="" width=1 height=1>` draws nothing, as a tracking pixel does.
  - **A source that names something is as before**: an image that cannot be loaded is left out and reported, and a reference that is not absolute http or https is refused when the caller asks for resources.
- **Why**:
  - **Two real pages were refused** with "HTML <img> has no src attribute" (a typed 400): `govdocs1-000449.html` and `govdocs1-001121.html`, each by a one-pixel `<img src="">`. The pages hold 7,173 and 4,578 characters of text, which is what a reader wants.
  - **The office suite draws nothing for these elements**, with or without `alt`; the browser and the standard draw the alt text. The in-process renderer follows the standard, which keeps the words an author wrote for a reader who cannot see the image.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The office suite route and the in-process route differ on the alt text of an image with no source**: the first leaves it out, the second keeps it. It is the same difference they have for any image that does not load, where both leave the image out and neither draws its alt text.
  - **No icon for a missing image** is drawn, which the standard allows ("optionally").
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping the refusal**: the page has text and no image to lose.
  - **Always drawing nothing**: the standard says to draw the alt text, and a browser does.
  - **A warning for each such image**: pages carry many (spacers and counters); the conversion report is for content that is lost.
- **Verified by**: `tests/html-image-without-source.test.ts` (red on the code before the change, 5 of 5: the exact text of pages with an empty `src` and an absent one with and without `alt`, in a paragraph, a heading, a table cell and a link; the two pages above against the same pages with the element deleted, with the images of the page not fetched) and a probe page printed by a browser and by this renderer with the same text.
- **Revisit when**: the office suite route draws the alt text of an image that cannot be loaded, or a caller needs a warning for images left out.

## 84. sharp's libvips from its own release build, with libwebp, mozjpeg and libpng at -O3 and every download pinned

- **Status**: Implemented (epic #759, rows "the prebuilt sharp-libvips builds libwebp and mozjpeg with -Os" and "the image rows' reference gets an ffmpeg-re-encoded PNG"), decided 2026-10-23 (QA decision: add a SHA-pinned build stage once the x64 CI experiment passed; it passed in run 39984292745).
- **Decision**:
  - **The worker image ships a libvips-cpp.so of its own build** (`Dockerfile.worker`, stages `sharplibvips-build` and `sharplibvips`; scripts and pins in `docker/sharp-libvips/`). It is the upstream sharp-libvips release that `package-lock.json` installs (v1.3.4, commit `ebb95f8`, the build of `build/posix.sh`), run in that release's own build container (Rocky Linux 8 at the digest of the multi-architecture index the upstream release run resolved, gcc-toolset-15 15.2.1-7.1, glibc 2.28), with one change: mozjpeg, libpng and libwebp are compiled at `-O3` (`option-f.patch`). Every other library keeps the upstream flags, except aom on x64, which entry 121 builds as a Release at `-O3`. Only `libvips-cpp.so.8.18.7` replaces the copy of the npm package; the addon, the versions and the notices of the package stay as they are, since the library versions are the release's own (`versions.properties`).
  - **One stage serves both architectures.** The stage takes the platform of the build, as every stage does (`docker compose build` on the host, so arm64 on the Ampere A1 host and amd64 in CI), and `docker/sharp-libvips/env.sh` picks the settings of the upstream `platforms/linux-x64` or `platforms/linux-arm64v8` Dockerfile by `uname -m`.
  - **Every download the build script makes with curl is pinned, and its other ways to fetch are closed.** The upstream archive by SHA-256; each of the 32 files `posix.sh` downloads for Linux (27 source archives and 5 patches; it asks for the freetype archive twice) by the SHA-256 of its bytes (`sources.sha256`), served through `fetch-pinned.sh`, which stands in for `curl` while the script runs and downloads over HTTPS only, redirects included (`--proto-redir '=https'`); the notices file from the pinned archive instead of the upstream `main` branch (`pinned-notices.patch`); `rustup-init` by SHA-256 and the Rust nightly by date (`nightly-2026-10-23`); cargo-c by version with its lock file; meson and ninja by wheel digest; gcc-toolset-15 by release. A download that is not pinned, or whose bytes differ, fails the build, and so does a pin the build no longer asks for. The tarballs the script unpacks carry Meson wrap files that clone from the network when a dependency is missing (the `wrap-git` files of pango 1.58.2 for glib, harfbuzz, cairo, fribidi and fontconfig name a branch, not a commit, and fontconfig's `freetype2.wrap` does too), and the toolchain installs `git`, as the upstream build container does; every `meson setup` therefore runs with `--wrap-mode=nodownload` (`MESON` in `env.sh`), which lets a wrap use only a subproject that is already unpacked, and `git-local-only.sh` stands in for `git` while the script runs. `posix.sh` never calls git, and leaving the program out fails the build (libxml2's `meson.build` requires it). The sources ask it for three versions, `git --version` (CMake's `find_package(Git)`), `git describe` (libxml2) and `git --git-dir=<dir>/.git describe --match=v[0-9]*` (aom), which read no network and find no repository in an unpacked archive; the stand-in passes exactly those to the real git and refuses every other call, such as a clone, and records it in the file `build.sh` checks after the script, so a tool that swallows the error still stops the build. A stand-in that refuses every call fails the build on those three queries (the first build of this change did).
  - **The build fails when the pins no longer describe it**: the upstream platform Dockerfile is not the one `toolchain.sh` mirrors (by digest), `versions.properties` names another libvips than 8.18.7, the lock file or the installed `@img/sharp-libvips-linux-<arch>` is not 1.3.4 (a sharp upgrade that brings another release), or sharp does not encode with libvips 8.18.7 mapped from the package's own `lib` directory, from a file with the SHA-256 the stage wrote beside the library (`check-sharp.sh`, run by `use-libvips.sh` in the runtime stage and in CI).
  - **CI runs on the same library.** `.github/workflows/sharp-libvips.yml` builds the `sharplibvips` stage for linux/amd64 when its key (`cache-key.sh`: the stage's lines and the files they copy) is not in the Actions cache, and saves it. The stage hands over exactly two files, `libvips-cpp.so.8.18.7` and its `.sha256`, and `check-build-output.sh` fails unless a directory holds those and nothing else, both regular files and no symlink, with the digest of the library in the second. The workflow runs it before it saves the cache entry, the `container` job before the image build mounts the restored directory, and `use-libvips.sh` before it copies anything, in CI and in the runtime stage of the image, which mounts the stage whole instead of copying a directory into `node_modules`, so a swapped `.node` file or a link in the cache would not reach `node_modules`. The jobs that convert pictures put it into `node_modules` after `npm ci` (`.github/actions/sharp-libvips`, which runs `use-libvips.sh`): `tests`, `conformance`, `parity-quality` and `parity-speed` in `ci.yml`, and `perf`, `bench`, both parity jobs, `bench-ab-speed` and `realworld` in `nightly.yml`. The `container` job builds the image with the cached stage as the `sharplibvips` build context, so the stage is built once per key. The base of a speed comparison runs on its own library (`scripts/ab-base-dependencies.sh`): it shares the head's `node_modules` only when the lock file and the key are both the same.
  - **Cache key, main and pull requests.** A key in the cache costs a lookup (the job runs on every event and the converting jobs wait for it). A missing key is built in the job, about 18 minutes on a 4-core runner. On `main` the first run after a change of the build saves it, and every pull request restores it from `main`'s scope; a pull request that changes the build builds and saves it in its own scope, so its own jobs test the library it builds and no other pull request waits for it or reads it. There is no restore key: a stale library is never used.
  - **The image speed rows time both sides on the same bytes** (`bench/families/image.ts`). A PNG source cannot be given to the reference as it is (it would apply the file's gAMA chunk, entry 22 and `bench/png-metadata.ts`), so ours is timed on the file the reference reads, the decoded pixels with the EXIF, XMP and ICC blocks; a JPEG source is read by both as it is. The quality rows still encode ours from the original.
- **Why**:
  - **Upstream builds these codecs for size.** `posix.sh` sets `-Os` for every library (lines 44 to 46, "Default optimisation level is for binary size (-Os) / Overridden to performance (-O3) for select dependencies that benefit") and overrides it for zlib-ng, lcms, libheif, libimagequant, highway, cgif, libultrahdr and libvips, but not for mozjpeg (`MinSizeRel`, line 205), libpng (line 212) or libwebp (line 225), which do the encode work of the WebP and JPEG rows.
  - **Measured on the x64 runner** (run 39984292745; base time over head time in alternating pairs of the speed rows, the prebuilt library against this build):

    | Row | Base/head | Ours against the reference, prebuilt then this build |
    |---|---|---|
    | `wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` | 1.144 | 0.936, 1.070 |
    | `screenshot.png->webp` | 1.182 | 0.960, 1.133 |
    | `wm-screen-history.png->jpg` | 1.217 | 0.882, 1.088 |
    | `lineart.png->webp` | 1.105 | 0.877, 0.971 |

    The other WebP and JPEG rows are 1.06 to 1.31 and the AVIF rows 0.99 to 1.01 (aom is unchanged). A rebuild of the same release without the patch measured 0.99 to 1.01 on every row, so the gain is the flags, not the newer toolchain.
  - **The output does not change.** 247 outputs (77 samples to WebP, AVIF and JPEG, and four quality points of the timed samples) are byte-identical to the prebuilt library's, for the rebuild without the patch and for this build; the strict quality gate of the image family passed (823 rows, none failing). On the arm64 VM the same build was byte-identical on 12 image rows and 7 to 21% faster.
  - **Pinned downloads.** The upstream script fetches its sources with `curl | tar` and five patches with `curl | patch`, with no checksum, and one file from a moving branch; the worker image pins its other downloads by SHA-256 (the 7-Zip and LibreDWG stages). The GNOME and cairo archives of the list match the checksum files those projects publish.
  - **Same bytes in the speed rows.** `wm-alpha-graph.png` is 58,819 bytes and the file the reference reads 44,013, and sharp decodes them in 2.57 and 0.86 ms; timing ours on the original charged it a decode the reference did not pay. On the 4-core arm64 VM (the npm package's library, the old and the new harness in the same pairs, 24 to 96 pairs a row) ours times 1.01 to 1.18 faster on the WebP rows of PNG sources (`wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` 0.901 to 0.974 of the reference), 0.99 to 1.01 on the AVIF rows and 0.98 to 1.00 on the JPEG rows; `photo-a.jpg` now gives the reference its JPEG too (`->webp` 1.072 to 1.223, `->avif` 1.784 to 1.807, `->jpg` 1.144 to 1.149).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Build time.** A worker image built without its layer cache spends about 18 minutes more on a 4-core x64 runner (container 433 s, libvips 637 s in the experiment) and builds the stage natively on the arm64 host. Building arm64 on an amd64 machine under emulation would take hours; the image is not built that way.
  - **Image size.** The library is 19,550,624 bytes on x64 against 18,699,288 for the prebuilt (4.6% more), and the copy of the npm package stays in its lower layer, so the image grows by about 19.6 MB.
  - **Vulnerabilities.** A fix in libwebp, libpng, mozjpeg or any library of the build reaches the image when sharp-libvips releases it and the pins move with the sharp upgrade, as before; a fix that cannot wait can be one more patch in `docker/sharp-libvips/`.
  - **Every sharp upgrade that brings another sharp-libvips release** moves the pins in one change: `env.sh` (commit, archive digest, versions, the two platform Dockerfile digests after `toolchain.sh` is compared with the new Dockerfiles), `sources.sha256` (from the new `versions.properties`), and the two patches if their context moved. The build fails until it is done.
  - **Generated archives can change bytes.** Eleven source archives, three patches and the upstream archive are files GitHub or GitLab generate from a tag, a commit or a pull request; if a host regenerates one differently, the build fails until its digest is checked and moved.
  - **What is not pinned by digest.** The Rocky Linux packages other than the compiler (`dnf update`, signed by the distribution), the crates of librsvg (from the lock file of its release archive, with the checksums the lock file holds, through cargo's own client), and whatever a program fetches with its own client without going through `curl` on `PATH` or Meson's wraps: the build container has no network restriction, and `/usr/bin/curl` called by an absolute path would not be seen.
  - **A cache entry is trusted by its key.** The restored directory is checked for its two files and the digest of the library, but a digest file written next to a swapped library by whoever saved the entry matches it, and nothing compares it with a build of the stage. Anything that can write to the Actions cache in `main`'s scope under this key before the job that builds it (some jobs of the workflows hold `issues: write`, `pull-requests: write` or `packages: write`) would have its library loaded by the later jobs. This is the shape of the `ab-base-modules` and `bench-ref` caches, whose `node_modules` and reference build are trusted the same way. Accepted, as for those caches.
  - **CI.** One more job (a lookup when the key is cached), the 18-minute build on `main` after a change of the build and on the pull request that makes it, about 7 MB of Actions cache per key, and a copy of `node_modules` for the base of a speed comparison whose library differs. A nightly comparison with a commit whose build is no longer cached fails at its restore step.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **The distribution's libvips** (Debian 13 ships 8.16.1, built at `-O2`): sharp 0.35.5 requires libvips 8.18.7 or newer (`src/common.h` lines 20 to 23), so sharp cannot be built against it.
  - **A sharp release old enough for libvips 8.16**: gives up the fixes of every sharp release since, to change a compiler flag.
  - **The distribution's codec libraries under the upstream libvips** (libjpeg-turbo for mozjpeg, Debian's libwebp): the JPEG bytes change, and every image row would move with them.
  - **A native addon of our own around the encoders**: a C++ surface to maintain and to secure, for the same libraries.
  - **`-O3` for every library, aom included**: the AVIF rows did not move with the three codecs changed, and nothing was measured for the others.
  - **`set -o pipefail` in the upstream script instead of the refusal file**: its `readelf ... | grep -q` checks (lines 444 and 446) would then fail when `grep` exits before `readelf` has written everything.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts` (the download check serves only pinned bytes over HTTPS and records every refusal; `MESON` carries `--wrap-mode=nodownload`; `git-local-only.sh` passes only the three version queries and refuses and records the rest; the build output check fails on an extra file, a directory, a hidden file, a symlink and a changed library or digest file, and `use-libvips.sh` leaves `node_modules` untouched when it fails; `check-sharp.sh` fails on a library whose digest is not the build's; the cache key moves with the stage and its files and not with other stages; the base of a speed comparison shares, copies or installs its dependencies as above; every converting job uses the build before it converts; the container job uses the cached stage), the updated `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts`, `tests/container-ci-job.test.ts`, `tests/ci-parity-workflow.test.ts`, `tests/runtime-baseline.test.ts` and `tests/phase-4-security-and-sandbox-hardening.test.ts`, the build of the stage itself (every download checked, `use-libvips.sh` and `check-sharp.sh` in the runtime stage), and the experiment above. A build of the stage for linux/amd64 in a VM (2026-10-24) gave the experiment's library byte for byte (SHA-256 `7f74bee5fbfc7d12c4234415fa9d07c829629564996d294f4aaac027b4062a3c`), and the image built on it encodes WebP with that file mapped. The build for linux/arm64 in a VM (2026-10-24), before and after `--wrap-mode=nodownload`, `git-local-only.sh`, HTTPS-only redirects and the two-file output, gave the same library byte for byte (SHA-256 `49031d3edff79be6e5cc73821ac6d5ccbf222d589ec4f6a896d80c098f2fc450`, 18,848,888 bytes); the amd64 build is the first run of the workflow on the pull request. A stage mounted as a build context (`RUN --mount=type=bind,from=sharplibvips`, as the runtime stage does) overrides a stage of the same name, passes `check-build-output.sh` with the two files and fails it with a third.
- **Revisit when**: upstream changes the flags of these libraries (then the patch goes), sharp is upgraded (the pins move, and the speed rows are measured again), a host regenerates a pinned archive, sharp-libvips starts publishing checksums of its sources, or the arm64 host builds the image so slowly that a prebuilt stage from CI is worth publishing.

## 85. PDF text: code 0 of a nonsymbolic simple font with no glyph name is the .notdef glyph, which has no text
