- **Verified by**: `tests/server-only-option-paths.test.ts`: the batch route answers 400 and writes no file for `outputPath` set to a file outside the job directory; `/api/convert`, `/api/queue/jobs`, `/api/v1/convert` and `/api/v1/jobs` (multipart and JSON) refuse it the same way; task and graph node options are refused; each listed key is refused by name; the engine toggles still pass; `subtitles.input` is refused for an absolute path, a `../` path and another user's key; `masterPlaylistName` values `../x.m3u8`, `a/b.m3u8`, an absolute path, a backslash, the wrong extension and 129 characters are refused by the schema and by the builder; the escape table for `'`, `:`, `\`, `,`, `;`, `[`, `]`, `=` and trailing whitespace, each read back whole by a model of `av_get_token`; and FFmpeg itself opening a file named with all of these through the escaped value (`movie=filename=...` in a lavfi graph). The embedded-stream burn in `tests/media-stream-mapping.test.ts` runs the new `subtitles=filename=...:si=0` form with libass on the Lima VM. Every new test failed before the change, and each fix was taken out by hand to show its tests fail. The prototype rule: every route above refuses options whose own `__proto__` holds `outputPath`, and writes no file (before the change `/api/convert`, `/api/convert/batch` and `/api/v1/convert` wrote the file and the queue routes answered 200 and 202); task and graph node options are refused the same way; a `__proto__` nested in `subtitles` or an array, and a `constructor` holding a `prototype`, are refused by name, while a plain `constructor` passes; a nesting of 50,000 levels is scanned without overflowing the stack. `tests/job-deadline-review-fixes.test.ts`: `bindJobLimits` and `stripEngineControls` given parsed JSON with an own `__proto__` return a copy with no inherited `outputPath` and the ordinary prototype. The cast-read test failed while `fontPath` was read and passes with the reads removed.
- **Revisit when**: a staged subtitle upload is built (then `subtitles.input` can return as a caller-owned key staged under a fixed name), the worker's internal callers stop passing `outputPath` through options, or QA decides to make the options object closed (`additionalProperties: false`). Also when one of the four undeclared keys the cast-read test lists is declared in the schema or removed (then it leaves the test's list), or when request bodies are parsed by a parser that already refuses prototype keys.

## 108. SFTP storage: a path, the user and the host are checked before they reach the sftp client, every argument is quoted as the client reads it, and each call keeps its key in a directory of its own and gives the client none of the server's environment

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #761, the SFTP row of "External review of `abcdf793`"), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request); the review of the first version added the batch mode, the checked address, the pinned host key and the output bounds below. The OpenSSH source cited below is openssh-portable at the tag V_9_9_P2.
- **Decision**:
  - **The batch script is built from fixed verbs and quoted arguments.** The adapter writes its commands (`get`, `put`, `ls -l`, `rm`, then `quit`) to the standard input of `sftp`. A command is a verb the adapter chose followed by arguments, each in double quotes with `\` and `"` escaped by a backslash. That is the whole quoting rule of the client's `makeargv` (`sftp.c` 1196 to 1337): inside double quotes it unescapes `\"` (1246 to 1250), keeps `\\` for the glob step that follows to undo (1264 to 1268), takes whitespace and `#` literally, and escapes `?`, `[` and `*` itself (1325 to 1332). A verb is never caller data, so the `!` that starts a local shell command (`parse_args`, `sftp.c` 1391), the `-` that turns off error handling and the `@` that silences the echo (1358 to 1369) cannot stand in command position.
  - **A path or base path with a control character is refused.** Any character of the Unicode class Cc (which holds the line feed, the carriage return, the tab, NUL, DEL and the C1 range), the line and paragraph separators U+2028 and U+2029, and a lone surrogate, in a remote path or in `basePath`. A remote path is a 400 (`StorageInvalidKeyError`), a base path or other credential field a 400 (`StorageInputError`), and no `sftp` process starts.
  - **One batch line is at most 2046 bytes.** The client reads a line with `fgets` into `char cmd[2048]` (`sftp.c` 2212 and 2310), so a longer line is cut and its tail runs as the next command. A path that would make a longer line is refused as an invalid key. The check runs before an upload is read from its stream.
  - **A key cannot leave the base path.** The base path is normalised with POSIX rules (`path.posix.normalize`), refused when it climbs out of the login directory, and a key is normalised the same way and refused when it is empty, names the base path itself, starts with `..` (also under a server root, where the join would otherwise clamp it to a different file) or does not start with the base path followed by `/`. A relative result is written with a `./` prefix, because `get`, `put` and `ls` read their arguments with `getopt` (`sftp.c` 407 and 490), which would take a path that starts with `-` for an option.
  - **The destination is checked, and follows `--`.** The user name must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9_.@-]{0,99}$` (the rule of the user name of AWS Transfer Family `CreateUser`, `[\w][\w@.-]{2,99}`, with its three character minimum dropped so a one or two character name still works). The host must be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address without a zone, or a name of RFC 1123 labels (at most 63 characters each, 253 in all) with no `:`, `/`, `@`, space or leading `-`. The port must be a whole number from 1 to 65535. The client is started with `... -- user@host`: its `getopt` loop (`sftp.c` 2470) ends at `--`, and it hands the host to `ssh` after another `--` (`sftp.c` 2655). An IPv6 address goes in brackets, the form `hpdelim2` and `cleanhostname` read (`misc.c` 747 and 796), because `parse_user_host_path` (`misc.c` 838) would otherwise take the first `:` for the start of a path. The adapter checks them when it is built, so an adapter with a bad field never exists.
  - **The key is a file in a directory of one call.** `mkdtemp` makes the directory (mode 0700) and the key is written into it with `wx` and mode 0600. The directory is removed in a `finally` whatever happens: success, a non-zero exit, a spawn failure (also one thrown at once) and a kill by the timeout. The download and upload spool directories are removed on every failure path as well; the download spool was left behind when `sftp` failed.
  - **The client has a minimal environment and a time limit.** `env` is exactly `PATH` (`/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`), `HOME` (the directory of the call) and `LANG` (`C.UTF-8`), where `...process.env` carried every secret of the server to the child. `spawn` is given `timeout` of 15 minutes, after which the child gets `SIGTERM`; before, a stuck connection kept the process and the key for ever. A write error on the standard input of a child that never started is caught instead of ending the server.
  - **A failed command ends the call with an error.** The client is started with `-b -`, which reads the batch from standard input and stops at the first failed command with exit status 1 (`-b` is `sftp.c` 2521 to 2531, the batch mode is passed as `err_abort` to `parse_dispatch_command` at 2344, a non-zero result leaves the loop at 2345, and the exit is `exit(err == 0 ? 0 : 1)` at 2699). Without it the client only prints the failure and exits 0: a `put` into a missing directory, an `rm` of a missing file and an `ls -l` of a missing file all exited 0 (observed with OpenSSH 10.3p1), so an upload reported success for nothing uploaded, a delete always returned true and a head returned size 0. Now an upload whose `put` failed rejects, a delete whose `rm` failed returns false, and a head whose `ls -l` failed returns null. An exit of 255, which `fatal()` gives for no connection, a refused host key or no authentication (`sshconnect2.c` 479 and 542), is never read as a missing file: it rejects, as `StorageAuthenticationError` when the message is `Permission denied` or `Authentication failed` and as `StorageAdapterError` otherwise. A missing file is told from other failures of exit 1 by the client's own `not found` and `No such file` text, read for exit 1 only and only for a download.
  - **The client connects to the address that passed the SSRF check.** The adapter resolves the name once, refuses it when any answer is restricted, and puts the first answer (the order the resolver returned) in the destination (`user@93.184.216.34`, an IPv6 address in brackets) with `-o HostKeyAlias=<name>`, so the host key is still looked up under the name. A name that gives a public address to the first lookup and a link-local, private or loopback address to a second one is never asked a second time. The test makes the second answer `169.254.169.254` and requires that the resolver is called once and that the address is not in the arguments.
  - **Host keys.** A credential may carry `hostKey`, a `known_hosts` line or a public key of type `ssh-ed25519`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp384`, `ecdsa-sha2-nistp521` or `ssh-rsa`. It is read when the adapter is built (one line of printable ASCII, no `@cert-authority` or `@revoked` marker, base64 key data of at most 8192 characters whose own type string equals the type on the line, the check `sshkey_read` makes at `sshkey.c` 1314 to 1383) and refused as a 400 otherwise. The call writes `* <type> <key>` to `known_hosts` in its own directory and runs `ssh` with `StrictHostKeyChecking=yes`, `UserKnownHostsFile=<that file>` and `GlobalKnownHostsFile=/dev/null`, so only that key is trusted and a host that shows another key is refused with exit 255 (`hostkeys_foreach_file`, `hostfile.c` 760 to 860, reads the host field as a pattern list, so `*` matches the name, an address and any port form). Observed against a local `sshd`: the pinned key connects, another key is refused with `Host key verification failed`. A fingerprint is not accepted, because `ssh` has no option that pins one. When the credential has no `hostKey`, `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new` is kept, and its risk stays: `ssh` does not read `$HOME` for its files (it takes the home directory from the password database, `ssh.c` 710 and 1434; observed with `HOME` set to another directory), so the known hosts file is `~/.ssh/known_hosts` of the user the worker runs as, `/home/easyconvert` in `Dockerfile.worker`, which `docker-compose.yml` mounts as a tmpfs. A key accepted on first use is kept until that container restarts and is checked on every connection until then; after a restart it is trusted again on first use, and a key shown by someone on the path at the first connection is accepted. The field is stored with the rest of the credential JSON, so no schema changed.
  - **What the client prints is bounded and read by line.** At most 64 KiB of standard output and 64 KiB of standard error are kept; the first byte past either stops the client with `SIGTERM` and rejects, so a server that streams without end costs 64 KiB of memory and not the 15 minutes of the time limit. Standard error goes into an error message cut to 512 characters, and a missing download is reported as `Remote object not found: "<key>"` with the key and not the batch. A `get` writes a spool file whose size the server decides: it is measured every 100 ms and the client is stopped when it passes 10 GiB, the largest object the object store stages to scratch disk (`REMOTE_STAGED_OBJECT_MAX_BYTES`), so a file may pass the cap by what one interval writes. `head` reads the size from the first listing line after the echoed command (`sftp> ls -l "<path>"`, `sftp.c` 1573), anchored to the whole line and to the format of `ls_file` (`sftp-common.c` 217, where the link count of a remote file is always `?`), so a key that spells a listing inside the echo cannot set the size and a reply with no listing line is an error and not size 0.
- **Why**: the paths were written inside double quotes into the script, so a line feed followed by `!cmd` ran a local shell command in the worker (the OpenSSH `sftp` runs a `!` line read from its standard input, which the tests show against the real client) and a `"` ended the quotes; the user name and host were one argument, so `-oProxyCommand=...` was an `ssh` option; the key was written to a guessable name in the shared temp directory and never removed; and the child inherited every secret of the server.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Some user names are refused**: one that holds a character outside letters, digits, `_`, `.`, `@` and `-`, begins with anything but a letter, digit or `_`, or is longer than 100. A directory service that issues names such as `DOMAIN\user` needs this rule widened.
  - **A host with an underscore or a non-ASCII name is refused**; an internationalised name has to be given in its `xn--` form. A private or internal name was already refused by the SSRF check.
  - **A relative base path stays relative to the login directory** and is written with `./`, which the server reads as the same file.
  - **A key that climbs above its base path is refused, not clamped.** A client that sent `../x` under the server root got `/x` before and now gets a 400.
  - **The 15 minute limit also ends a transfer that is still moving.** It is a cap for the whole process, not a stall timer, so a file that needs longer than that over the link fails.
  - **Without a `hostKey` the key is trusted on the first connection of each container life.** An attacker who sits on the path at that moment is accepted. The field closes it for a credential that carries it; making it required, and a screen that shows the fingerprint to copy, are left to a decision.
  - **The address is chosen once and the first answer is used.** If it is down while another answer of the name is up, the call fails and does not try the next one; a retry gets the same order from the resolver. The address checks of the other adapters resolve a second time and have the gap this closes.
  - **A server that sends more than 64 KiB of listing is an error.** A `head` of a directory with a very long listing rejects instead of reading its first line, and a `head` of an empty directory, which prints no listing line, rejects as well; the key of an object is a file.
  - **A `delete` and a `head` now raise on a refused login, a lost connection and a killed client** where they returned false and null.
  - **A pinned `hostKey` that the server rotates fails every call until the credential is updated.** That is the point of pinning, and the error is the client's `Host key verification failed`.
  - **`password` and `passphrase` credentials are not passed on** (`BatchMode=yes` forbids a prompt), as before; this change does not alter that.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Only removing line feeds and quotes from the path**: a blacklist; the client reads other characters (for example `\` before a quote) and the length limit by its own rules, and the quoting rule above is the client's own.
  - **A library that speaks SSH in process (`ssh2`, MIT, maintained)**: it is not a dependency of the repository, it would put a second SSH stack and its host key handling inside the server process, and the change would replace the transfer path, which this fix does not need to do. It is the way to pin a host key to a credential and to remove the child process, and is left for that decision.
  - **`-o User=` with the host alone as the operand**: it would also keep a user name out of the operand, but the user name still needs the check, and `--` with a checked pair is the form the client's own usage line shows.
  - **Passing the key with `ssh-agent` or a file descriptor**: `sftp -i` takes a path only.
  - **Removing the key in an `exit` handler of the process**: a crash between the write and the handler leaves it; a directory of one call removed in `finally` does not depend on the process surviving.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sftp-adapter-injection.test.ts`. The hostile remote paths `a\n!touch /tmp/pwned`, `a"\n!id`, a carriage return, NUL, U+0085, U+2028, a tab, a lone surrogate and a path of 2100 bytes in the four operations, with no `sftp` process started; `../../etc/passwd`, `../x`, `a/../../x`, `/../etc/passwd`, `..`, the empty key and the base path itself, under a base path and under the server root; the user names `-oProxyCommand=touch /tmp/x` and others, and the hosts with a leading `-`, a space, a colon, an `@`, a zone and an empty label, refused when the adapter is built; the operand after exactly one `--`, with an IPv6 address in brackets; the key file at 0600 in a 0700 directory of its own, absent after success, a non-zero exit, a spawn error, a spawn that throws and a kill by the timeout, and no leftover `easyconvert-sftp-*` directory; the child `env` holding only `PATH`, `HOME` and `LANG` while the test process had `ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` set. The quoting is held against the real client, not a copy of its rules: `/usr/bin/sftp -D <sftp-server>` puts, lists, gets and removes files named with spaces, quotes, backslashes (also a trailing one), `*`, `?`, `[`, `#`, `$`, a backtick, `!`, a leading `-` and non-ASCII characters, by exactly those names and with `!touch injected` running nothing, and a control test shows that the old unquoted script does run a local command in the same client. Each fix was taken out by hand (no control-character check, no escaping, no length cap, no containment check, no `./` prefix, no user name, host or port check, no base path checks, `...process.env`, no `--`, the directory not removed, a 0644 key file, no timeout, no handler on the child's standard input) and the tests failed each time.
  - **Added by the review of the first version** (`tests/sftp-adapter-injection.test.ts`). The `-b -` argument before `--`; against the real client a `put` into a missing directory, an `rm`, a `get` and an `ls -l` of a missing file exit 1 and stop the batch, and a control row shows the same four exit 0 without `-b`; an upload that rejects, a delete that returns false and a head that returns null for a failed command, and a refused login, an exit 1 with no command text and a kill by the timeout that do not become false or null; the resolver stubbed to give a public address once and `169.254.169.254` after, with one call to it and the checked address, `HostKeyAlias` and no other mention of the name in the arguments, the first of several answers, an IPv6 answer in brackets and one restricted answer refusing the call; the pinned key written as `* <type> <key>` for a bare key, a comment, a `known_hosts` line, a port form and an address list, with the strict options and no `accept-new`, and 14 values refused when the adapter is built (empty, a fingerprint, two lines, a line break, `@cert-authority`, `@revoked`, `ssh-dss`, a type that differs from the key data, bad base64, no key data, a non-ASCII character, 9000 characters of key data); the listing parsed from the real client's output for files named with spaces, quotes, `*`, `?` and `[a]`, a crafted key that spells a listing inside the echo with size 999 ignored, and a reply with no listing line rejected; a client that streams standard output or standard error without end stopped within the cap plus two chunks; a spool made 10 GiB plus one byte long stopped and removed; and a `get` of a missing file answered with the key and none of the batch. Every real-client row of an awkward name now sits beside the decoy siblings `a.txt`, `*`, `?` and `[a]` and asserts that only the named file is created, listed, read and removed, with the decoys still holding their content. Each of these fixes was taken out by hand and the tests failed.
- **Revisit when**: a credential must carry a host key (to make the field required) or a fingerprint is wanted (it needs an in-process SSH library), the worker image ships a different SFTP client or the transfer moves to an in-process SSH library, a customer needs a user name outside the rule above, or a transfer legitimately runs longer than 15 minutes.

## 109. MP3 and Ogg sources need FFmpeg: no in-process decoder stands in for it, and the switch that routes a source around FFmpeg is server-only

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #761, the last launch-blocking row of "External review of `abcdf793`"), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **MP3, AAC and Ogg (Vorbis, Opus) sources are decoded by FFmpeg or refused.** With no native engine (FFmpeg not installed, or the in-process path chosen by server code), a source in one of them is refused with `EngineUnavailableError('ffmpeg', ...)`, which the API answers with 503, before any byte of it is read. `decodeAudioBuffer` does this for the hints `mp3`, `ogg`, `oga`, `opus` and `vorbis`, for an MPEG audio sync word, for an `OggS` page header and for an ID3v2 tag that is not followed by ADTS or FLAC data, as it already did for AAC. One function, `refuseWithoutFfmpeg(codec)`, serves all three codecs.
  - **The in-process MP3 decoder is deleted.** `decodeMp3` read the frame header, took the bytes after the side information as 576 pairs of (magnitude, sign) values, raised the magnitude to the power 4/3, and ran an inverse MDCT with a sine window over them. It had no side information, no bit reservoir, no scalefactors, no Huffman decoding, no stereo processing, no alias reduction and no polyphase synthesis filterbank (ISO/IEC 11172-3), so its output for any real MP3 was noise at the right length, and `mp3 -> wav` and `mp3 -> flac` answered 200 with it. It also built the sample list as a JavaScript array, one number per sample.
  - **The in-process Ogg decoder is deleted.** `decodeOgg` parsed the pages, read the codec from the first packet and then either returned zero samples (a stream with no audio packet, which became an empty WAV or FLAC with a 200) or threw a bare `Error`; the code after that branch, which read each packet as 16-bit PCM, could not be reached. A broken Ogg stream is now a 503 for the missing engine, not a 200 with no audio and not a 500.
  - **`disableNativeEngine` is server-only.** It is in `SERVER_ONLY_OPTION_KEYS` (policy 107) and out of the public options schema, so a request that carries it is refused by name with the reason `server_only_option` on every route (400 on the legacy routes, 422 on `/api/v1`). The option still exists on the `ConversionOptions` type, for server code and tests that need the in-process path. Evidence for the choice: the only code that reads it is `convertMedia` (`media.ts`); no other source file sets it (the web app, the worker, the queue and the edge pipeline do not; the edge pipeline lists it among the options it ignores); every other use is a test that forces the host-without-FFmpeg path (12 test files before this change); and what it opens for a public caller is only a worse path, the in-process WAV and FLAC pipeline, which decodes untrusted bytes in the process that runs `convertMedia` instead of in FFmpeg and refuses most of what FFmpeg converts.
  - **The library index no longer exports `decodeMp3` or `decodeOgg`.**
  - **The other in-process audio code does not synthesise output.** `decodeWav` (PCM, float and AIFF) and `decodeFlac` read the samples the file holds; `encodeFlacStream` and the WAV writer write the samples they are given; the resampler is a Kaiser-windowed sinc filter with TPDF dither at the 16-bit output; `renderMidiToWav` is a synthesiser, which is what a MIDI source needs; `encodeOggContainer` and `encodeOpusContainer` only wrap packets a caller supplies and refuse raw samples. The memory the WAV and FLAC decoders need for a large file is a separate row of #761 and is not changed here.
- **Why**: a converter that cannot decode a format must say so. A 200 with made-up samples is worse than any error, because the caller keeps the file and believes it is the song. FFmpeg decodes MP3, Vorbis and Opus faithfully, trims the encoder delay and padding the Xing or LAME header records, and is the engine the reference converter lists for these formats; the worker image already carries FFmpeg 9.0.2 (policy 105) for every other lossy path.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A host without FFmpeg cannot convert an MP3, Ogg, Opus or AAC file to WAV or FLAC.** Before, it got noise for MP3 and an error for the rest. The worker image has FFmpeg, so the production path is unchanged; only a developer machine without it sees the 503.
  - **A truncated or damaged Ogg or MP3 is a 503, not a 400 or 422, when FFmpeg is missing**, because without the engine nothing can tell a damaged file from a good one. With FFmpeg present its own verdict decides, as before.
  - **A library or test that called `decodeMp3` or `decodeOgg` directly breaks.** None in the application did; the tests that did are changed (see below).
  - **A client that sent `disableNativeEngine`** now gets a 400 or 422 naming the key where the request used to succeed.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Porting a real MP3 decoder to TypeScript** (the Huffman tables, requantisation, stereo, IMDCT and polyphase synthesis of ISO/IEC 11172-3, as in FFmpeg's `mpegaudiodec_template.c`, minimp3 (CC0) or mpg123): the engine that every other lossy path needs is already required, a port is a second decoder of untrusted bytes in the server process that has to match FFmpeg sample for sample, including the delay trimming, and Vorbis and Opus would still need their own.
  - **Keeping `decodeMp3` as a decoder of frame headers that returns silence of the right length**: that is the same lie with less noise.
  - **Keeping `disableNativeEngine` public and refusing only MP3 and Ogg sources**: the option would still send a caller down a path that FFmpeg does not take for no benefit a caller can name.
  - **Keeping `decodeOgg` to validate headers and return a typed error**: the page parser had no other use once the decoder returned nothing, so it would be a validator without a decoder behind it; the refusal is typed already.
- **Verified by**: `tests/media-no-fake-audio-decoders.test.ts` (an MPEG-1 Layer III stream, the same behind an ID3v2 tag, Ogg Vorbis and Opus with audio packets, with headers only, with a short identification packet, cut off mid-page, and bytes named as Ogg, each to WAV and FLAC with `disableNativeEngine` and with `FFMPEG_PATH` pointing at nothing: a 503 naming `ffmpeg` and no output; `decodeAudioBuffer` by hint, by sync word, by `OggS` and behind an ID3v2 tag; the index exports neither function), `tests/server-only-option-paths.test.ts` (the schema and all six routes refuse `disableNativeEngine` by name; every server-only key is refused), and `tests/phase-2-sota-precision.test.ts` (an MP3 written by the reference encoder converts to WAV through FFmpeg with the sample count of an independent FFmpeg decode, and is refused in process). The new tests failed on the code before the change, and each fix was taken out by hand to show its tests fail. Tests changed: the Ogg decode assertions in `tests/phase-1-archive-and-media-fidelity.test.ts` and `tests/phase-3-pure-codecs-parity.test.ts` called the deleted `decodeOgg` on streams it answered with empty PCM or `Unsupported audio format`; they keep the container assertions and the refusal is now tested once, in the new file. The old `decodeMp3` oracle test compared only the length of its output with FFmpeg's and that the samples were not all zero, which noise also satisfies.
- **Revisit when**: QA wants the media tools to work on a host without FFmpeg (then a decoder is taken from a maintained permissively licensed library, with the reference decoder's output as the oracle, not written here), or an audio format that FFmpeg decodes is added to the in-process WAV and FLAC pipeline.

## 110. CI runners are pinned to Ubuntu 24.04 until the jobs are moved to the next image on purpose

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: keep the nightly and CI gates working). The pin fixes the label, not the image build, and this change does not claim a green nightly. The nightly stays red from other causes: the cold apt cache after an image rotation (a row of issue 763), the AVIF speed rows of issue 641 and `realworld-gate`. `realworld-gate` reported bad-output 1 on 10-25, 10-26, 10-27 (crash 1 as well) and 10-29; on 10-28 it had 9 of 10 shard reports, because `realworld (2)` hit the apt limit.
- **Decision**:
  - Every job in `.github/workflows/` that names a runner uses `ubuntu-24.04` instead of `ubuntu-latest`, 28 jobs in nine workflows. The four jobs that call a reusable workflow with `uses:` name no runner.
  - `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts` holds four rules for every job of every workflow file:
    - A job has exactly one of `runs-on` and `uses`.
    - `runs-on` is exactly `ubuntu-24.04`.
    - `uses` names only a local file under `./.github/workflows/`.
    - Every local `uses`, of a job or of a step, names a file or action folder that exists.
    The counts (32 jobs, 28 with `runs-on`, 4 with `uses`) are checked as well.
  - `pytz` is pinned in `.github/actions/ci-setup/pip-packages.txt` (2026.5), and `install-tools.sh` checks `python3 -I -c 'import pytz'` in `verify_bench_python_modules`, which runs after `verify_cad_tools`.
  - The pin is `pytz==2026.5` and not 2026.6. Version 2026.6 was uploaded on 2026-10-29, the day it would have been pinned, while 2026.5 had been out since 2026-10-04 and meets the same need.
  - The label moves to `ubuntu-26.04` in one change of its own, made when the jobs have been run on that image and pass.
- **Why**:
  - The hosted runners move `ubuntu-latest` from Ubuntu 24.04 to 26.04 gradually, between 2026-10-19 and 2026-11-19. The image changes per run, not within one: the nightlies of 2026-10-26, 10-27 and 10-28 ran 24 of 24 jobs on `ubuntu-24.04`, and the nightly of 2026-10-29 (run 40845395326) ran 24 of 24 on `ubuntu-26.04`.
  - On 26.04 the benchmark step failed in `data.check` of `bench/reference-server.py`: DuckDB imports `pytz` when it returns a TIMESTAMPTZ value to Python, and `pytz` was in neither `pip-packages.txt` nor `apt-packages.txt`. It was an undeclared dependency that 24.04 happened to carry, and this change declares it. In a clean virtual environment with the pinned list, reading a TIMESTAMPTZ Parquet column through `read_parquet_duckdb` fails with `Required module 'pytz' failed to import` and returns the row once `pytz==2026.5` is installed.
  - The two apt failures of the same night (`bench-parity-quality (image)` and `(video)`) are not an image defect. Both are `task apt exceeded its limit of 300s` with an empty `APT_CACHE_HIT`: the package cache is keyed on the image version, so the first run on a new image build downloads everything inside the limit. `realworld (2)` on 24.04 failed the same way on 2026-10-28. This change does not fix it, and a row for it is in issue 763.
  - A gate whose image changes under it measures the image, not the change. The speed rows compare runs over CI history, and the quality rows depend on the tool versions the image installs.
  - Pinning the image version is the documented way to opt out of the move until a workflow is ready.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - The pin fixes the label but not the image build. The runner provider still rebuilds the `ubuntu-24.04` image weekly, and each new build changes the image version that keys the caches, so the apt cache starts cold after every rotation.
  - The jobs stay on an older image until the move is made, and miss the newer preinstalled tool versions it carries.
  - The move becomes a task of its own: the tool setup, the reference tools and the speed history all have to be checked on the new image.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keep `ubuntu-latest` and fix the setup for 26.04 now.** That would change the image under every gate in the same window as the conversion work. Speed history before and after the move could not be told apart.
  - **Pin only the failing jobs.** One rule and one label are easier to hold than a list of exceptions: with a single label, a test can assert it for every job, and a job added later cannot start on another image unnoticed.
- **Verified by**: `tests/ci-install-apt-tools.test.ts`, `tests/ci-setup-tasks.test.ts` (`verify_bench_python_modules` returns 1 and prints the `::error::` line when `python3` cannot import `pytz`, and returns 0 when it can; red with `return 1` changed to `return 0`; `main` stops at the first failing step and runs every step when none fails, red with `|| return 1` removed after `run_tasks` or `verify_cad_tools`), `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts` (the group "the runner image of every workflow job" reads every file under `.github/workflows/`; red with one job set back to `ubuntu-latest`, where it names the file, the job and the label, and green with the 28 jobs on `ubuntu-24.04`), and `grep -rh "runs-on:" .github/workflows`, which lists 28 jobs, all on `ubuntu-24.04`. The CI run of this change and the next nightly report `Image: ubuntu-24.04` in their runner set-up logs.
- **Revisit when**: the hosted runners announce the end of support for `ubuntu-24.04`, or the jobs have been run on `ubuntu-26.04` with tool setup, quality and speed rows passing. The move is then one change that switches the label, fixes the setup (the apt cold-cache limit included) and restarts the speed history.

## 111. CRC-32 is the runtime's zlib routine alone, a converted tar is written over its unpacked bytes when the entries keep their places, and the floor of the Silesia xz row

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #685 and two flake and follow-up rows of epic #759), decided 2026-10-25 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **`crc32` is `zlib.crc32` and nothing else.** The slicing-by-8 table routine that stood behind it (`crc32Slicing8`, built for a runtime without `zlib.crc32`) is deleted with its tests, and so is `crc32.ts`; its 17 importers in `src` call `zlib.crc32` directly. The worker image pins `node:24.20.0` (`Dockerfile.worker`) and CI runs `node-version: 24`; `zlib.crc32` has been in Node.js since 22.2 and is the CRC-32 of the bundled zlib with its vector paths, so the fallback could not run in either. `engines` (`>=24.0.0`) is advisory to npm and is not what guards this.
    - **The `crc32` alternative of the `compression` rule in `bench/family-map.json` (line 153) stays for now.** The parity gate maps the deleted path and fails on a path that no rule covers, so the alternative goes in the next change that touches the compression family (the "Found by #897" row of the checklist of #759).
    - **The CRC-32 tests are deleted with the fallback.** The 5x timing test timed Node's zlib against a byte loop that lives in the test, and the published check values, the lengths and alignments against the byte loop, the running checksum and the gzip trailer check ran Node's own routine against its specification, so no change to the project could fail them. The value is held where the project uses it: the readers compare the stored CRC-32 with one computed over the data (`archive-zip-reader.ts` 644, `xz-format.ts` 173, 297 and 359), so a wrong CRC-32 written by the ZIP, xz or other writers fails the extraction tests that read back an archive the project wrote. The phase-3 ZIP test reads a ZIP that `createZipArchive` wrote back through `extractZipArchive` and compares the files with the originals byte for byte; a probe that flipped the stored CRC-32 of `nested/doc1.txt` in both headers was refused with "does not match its CRC-32".
  - **The tar that a gzip, bzip2 or xz stream is turned into is written over the unpacked bytes when every entry keeps its place** (`consumeUnpackedAsVettedTar`, `archive-stream.ts`, called by the gzip route and by the 7-Zip route of xz and bzip2).
    - **How it is written.** `tarFromEntries` builds the canonical headers, padding and end blocks from the vetted entries. The rewrite is two passes. The first only compares each body that lies in `unpacked` (`isOldBody`, a test of byte range containment, not of the identity of the `ArrayBuffer`, so a pooled buffer that the new headers share keeps the path) with its place in the joined tar. The second writes the new headers, padding and end blocks over the old ones and leaves the bodies where they are. The result is `unpacked` itself, cut at the end of the second end-of-archive block, so the 5 MB payload is not copied again to join the segments.
    - **When it applies.** Every body is at the offset the joined tar gives it, and what follows the rewritten tar in `unpacked` is at most one tar record (20 blocks, 10,240 bytes: what GNU tar and Python's `tarfile` pad a tar to). A longer tail is data an attacker chose (a gzip of a 2-byte file and 30 MiB of zeros decodes to 31 MB), and a view of `unpacked` would keep all of it alive behind a 2 KB result.
    - **What is returned otherwise.** The segments of `tarFromEntries`, as they are, with no copy, and nothing is written over `unpacked` (the writes come after the whole check and after the check of the tail). This covers a layout change, a longer tail and a tar without end blocks. The bodies in the segments are views of `unpacked`, so the caller must not reuse it on these paths either. A tar whose entries are all dropped (`./` only, or links only under `skipLinks`) returns the segments of its own 1,024 bytes of end blocks.
    - **The layouts that change** are a repeated name that drops an entry, a link that is left out (a hard link between two entries moves every later body up a block; one that is the last entry only shortens the tar and keeps the path), an entry dropped for a name that sanitises to nothing (`./` from `tar -cf x.tar .`), a pax `x` record that the canonical output does not write (sub-second `mtime`, `atime`, `ctime`, from GNU tar `--format=posix` and Python `tarfile`), a long-name `L` or `x` record whose canonical `path` record takes another number of blocks, and a vendor typeflag (`A` to `Z`) that is skipped. A tar without end blocks keeps its bodies in place but is shorter than the rewritten tar. Either way the bytes are exactly the segments joined.
  - **Every tar writer returns zeros of its own, never a shared buffer.** The end block and the padding are new zeros in every tar that returns several segments (`pushEndOfArchive`: `Buffer.alloc(1024)`; `pushPadding`: a zeroed slice of the Node.js allocation pool, `Buffer.allocUnsafe(n).fill(0)`). What a segment may alias, who owns the input and what the caller does with a result is one rule, stated once on `StreamedArchive` (`archive-stream.ts`); this entry does not restate it.
  - **The file route writes the segments with one `fs.writevSync` call** (`writeOutputSegments`, `src/worker/worker-output.ts`). The layouts above hand the segments on with a header, a body and a padding for each member, so a tar of 2,000 members is 6,001 ranges. libuv splits a vector into system calls of `IOV_MAX` buffers (1,024 on Linux and macOS) itself, so the call takes any number of ranges. The call returns the bytes it wrote, which may stop inside a range, so the loop continues with what is left (the call that follows retries what is left and raises if the failure persists, and a count that stops inside a range continues inside it). A call that returns 0 while bytes are pending is an error, not a retry, and so is a count above the bytes pending. The buffer route is `streamedArchiveResult` in `src/worker/engines.ts`: it joins several segments with `Buffer.concat` and keeps a single one as a view.
  - **Limits and vetting are unchanged**: the listing, the extraction policy, the entry and size caps, the collision rule, and the reading of every header by the in-process reader run before the function, on the same buffer, and the bytes of an untrusted archive are still only ever the headers `tarFromEntries` wrote and the bodies the reader returned. `writeOutputSegments` had and has no size cap of its own; the caps are the ones the streaming routes apply before they return segments.
  - **The xz, 7z and tar to 7z rows keep the floor entry 50 measured**; the measurements below add the x64 figures and the split of the call.
  - **The page ZIPs of multi-page vector outputs need no change.** Entry 78 already moved them to the platform zlib and the project's `ZipWriter`. A CPU profile of `govdocs1-000773.ps` to DXF on the base (3.4 s a conversion, 195.9 MB of DXF, ZIP of 22,498,460 bytes) has no `longest_match`, `deflate_slow` or JavaScript CRC-32 frame; the main thread is bound by the DXF writer (35% of the CPU), the SVG geometry reader and the wait for `pdftocairo`.
- **Why**:
  - **CRC-32 flake.** `tests/archive-bitlevel-throughput.perf.test.ts` timed the table routine against the byte loop and read 1.41 to 1.43 on the CI runner (x64, cold). On the arm64 VM the same routine is 2.69 times faster than the loop once warm (medians of 22 alternating runs); `zlib.crc32` is 0.559 ms [0.549, 0.589] for 4 MiB, 13.3 times the loop and 7.5 GB/s. Nothing in the product called the table routine, so the test measured dead code against a loop that exists only in the test. Deleting both is subtract before add; no ratio was loosened.
  - **Where the xz call goes** (`silesia-xml` as a tar, 5.36 MB, xz level 6, one stream and one block, 4-core arm64 VM, Node 24.22, pinned 7-Zip 26.01, `xz` 5.4.5; medians of 41 to 100 alternating calls). The reference command (`xz -d -c file`) takes 24.2 to 25.5 ms. The pinned 7-Zip decoding the same stream with its output on a pipe takes 17.2 to 19.1 ms, and its options change nothing outside the noise (`-mmt1`, `-bso0 -bsp0 -bse0`, the archive as a file argument, standard output redirected to a file); the decode is one serial LZMA2 block. Our call, through the dispatcher, takes 22.3 to 22.7 ms (1.055 to 1.074 of the reference). The split of the 5 ms above the bare 7-Zip run, from a CPU profile of 200 calls and `--trace-gc`: starting the child through `unshare` 1.8 ms, the copy of the chunks into the buffer that has room for a tar header 0.7 ms, the copy that joins the tar 0.77 ms, mark-compact pauses 1.6 ms (caused by about 16 MB of buffers allocated per call), reading, vetting and writing the 21 headers 0.1 ms. On the x64 CI runner (nightly of 2026-10-24, run 40074698318) `silesia-xml.xz->tar` is 122.1 MB/s against 135.4 for the reference (ratio 0.935 [0.877, 1.005]) and `silesia-xml.7z->tar` is 127.0 against 116.6 (1.098); there the same 5 ms is the gap, and each millisecond removed is worth about 2.3 points of the ratio.
  - **Why the tar is written over the unpacked bytes.** It removes the join copy and its 5 MB allocation from every gzip, bzip2 and xz to tar call of a tar payload. Base and head alternating in one process (outputs compared byte for byte every call): head against base of the median 1.071, 1.060 and 1.040 for xz (head 20.4 to 20.7 ms, base 21.2 to 22.2), 1.120, 1.055 and 1.068 for gzip (3.5 ms against 3.7), 1.025, 1.013 and 1.011 for bzip2 (57 against 58 ms, where the 52 ms block sort is the limiter): the head is ahead in all 12 runs. The parity harness cannot resolve a change this size on a call that starts a child process (its head against base read 0.84 to 1.15 on a route this change does not touch, and 1.03 with the base code on both sides); none of its runs reports a regression and the quality rows are unchanged.
  - **Why the end block and the padding are new in every tar.** A module buffer handed out as a segment is shared by every result and by whoever writes to one. Each version that kept a shared constant and copied it on the branches that could return it alone moved the hazard to another branch, because the constant was handed out at all. The new end block and padding cost nothing measurable on the Silesia tar (base against head of the median 0.990 to 1.024 over xz, gzip and bzip2, with and without a tail) and 0.05 to 0.37 ms on a tar of 2,000 members (see the alternatives for why the padding is a pooled slice).
  - **Which producers keep the layout** (measured 2026-10-25 on the arm64 VM with GNU tar 1.35, bsdtar 3.7.2 on libarchive 3.7.2, Python 3.12.3 `tarfile` and 7-Zip 23.01 `-ttar`; a sample tree of 8 entries in three forms, with fresh files (sub-second mtimes), with whole-second mtimes and with a 130-character name without a slash added, each archived by naming the top-level entries and by `.`; every output equal to the joined segments of `tarFromEntries`): named top-level entries, in all three forms, take the in-place path with GNU tar `--format=gnu` (the default; the long name as an `L` record), bsdtar (default pax restricted; the long name as a path-only `x` record) and 7-Zip. GNU tar `--format=posix` and the Python `tarfile` default (pax) take the segments path in all six archives, since every member has an `x` record with `mtime` that the output does not write. With `.` as the root, 7-Zip stays on the in-place path, and GNU tar and bsdtar write a `./` member that sanitises to nothing, so they take the segments path. A tarball made with `tar czf x.tgz dir` (GNU default) or `bsdtar` takes the in-place path, and one from `--format=posix` or Python does not.
  - **Why the file route writes with `writev`.** On the segments path every member is three ranges, and one `writeSync` for each is one system call for each. On the arm64 VM, 6,001 ranges (5,584,384 bytes, the shape of a tar of 2,000 members), one process, per-segment `writeSync` and batched `writevSync` alternating for 41 rounds, three runs: per-segment 3.11, 3.55 and 3.25 ms against 1.16, 1.51 and 1.31 ms (2.35 to 2.67 times; the output compared by SHA-256 every round, no short write seen). `strace -c` counts 6,001 `write` calls and 6 `writev` calls for a run. The `writev` run is bound by the copy of 5.6 MB into the page cache (4.8 GB/s); the per-segment run adds about 0.33 microseconds for each range. A single call for the whole list against batches of 1,024 ranges (Node.js 24.22, 6,001 ranges, 3,822,712 bytes, 61 alternating rounds, four runs): one call took 1.41 to 1.98 ms and the batches 1.52 to 2.15 ms (batches over one call 1.02 to 1.10), and one `writevSync` with all 6,001 buffers returned 3,822,712 and wrote a file with the SHA-256 of the joined buffers. `strace -c` shows 6 `writev` system calls for each file either way (738 for 123 files), so the batch saved no system call and cost an array for each batch. Through the dispatcher (`convertWithNative7z` with an input path and an output path, gzip of a 2,000-member tar with 20 KiB of zeros behind it, base `039c89da` and head alternating in one process for 61 rounds, outputs equal every round) the whole conversion is 12.33 ms against 9.94 ms (median; 1.24 times).
  - **Why not more.** The decode is 76% of the xz call on the VM and cannot be split (one block, strictly serial). The pieces left are each under 2 ms and one of them, the child start through `unshare`, is the isolation of entry 50. A prototype that wrote 7-Zip's output to a file and read it back saved 0.5 to 1.3 ms of 18 in a bare loop and moves the whole output through the disk of the worker.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **`unpacked` is changed, and what is returned aliases it.** The function writes into the buffer the stream was unpacked into when the result is a view of it. The two routes own that buffer (the output of the child, or of `zlib.gunzip`) and nothing reads it after the tar is returned. On the segments path the segments hold views of its bodies and `unpacked` is not written. A caller must not reuse the buffer after the call on any path. The module has other functions that hold a caller's bytes (`vetTarSource`, `stageTarForSevenZip`), so the contract is that the argument is a buffer the caller owns, which the two call sites satisfy.
  - **Results may alias the input** (the rule of `StreamedArchive`), and a write through one is a write to the input. No consumer writes through a result; copying every such payload would cost one copy of the data for a case that does not occur. A consumer that must write copies first.
  - **A tail of up to one record keeps the buffer the tar lies in alive.** The in-place result is a view, so it pins the backing store of `unpacked`: on the gzip route the zlib output chunk (at least 64 KiB, `INFLATE_CHUNK_MIN_BYTES`, `inflateChunkHint`), on the xz and bzip2 routes the 7-Zip frame (the output with room for one header before it and 1,535 bytes after it). The tail the check lets through is at most 10,240 bytes, so what a hostile archive can make the result hold is bounded by that and by the chunk or the frame, not by the input. A longer tail is not held by the result: the segments are joined into a buffer of the tar's size or written to the file.
  - **A runtime older than Node.js 22.2 fails at the first checksum** (`zlib.crc32 is not a function`) where the old code fell back. The image pin and the CI version keep that from happening in this project; a self-hosted run on an older Node.js outside them is not supported.
  - **After a short write the file route allocates one array for the rest of the list**, and a failed write leaves the partial output file where it was written (as before). A write that returns 0 for a non-empty range throws where the `writeSync` loop before it, and `fs.writeFileSync`, would loop; a regular file reports an error rather than 0, so this guards a destination that does not behave like one.
  - **The xz row stays at the measured floor.** The nightly row is tracked in `bench/parity-gaps.json` (issue #685) with its history; this change moves the CI ratio by an expected 0.02 to 0.04 and does not take the row to a clear pass by itself.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A looser or repeated-median floor for the table routine's test**: it would keep a test of code nothing calls.
  - **Keeping the table routine for runtimes without `zlib.crc32`**: there is none that the image pin or CI allow.
  - **Keeping the CRC-32 tests as a pin on the runtime**: they would fail only on a Node.js whose zlib is wrong, which the image pin and CI version already exclude, and not on any change to the project; the readers' CRC-32 checks cover the project's use.
  - **A shared end-of-archive constant with a copy on the branches that could return it alone**, and **copying a long tail out after the rewrite**: each handed the constant out on another branch or added a full-size copy beside the live `unpacked` on the file route.
  - **`Buffer.alloc` for each padding**: a new `ArrayBuffer` per member. On a 2,000-member tar (4,485,120 bytes, 1,995 of the 2,000 members padded) gzip to tar read 0.970 to 0.987 of the median against the pooled slice in 10 runs of 60 alternating calls, and 2,000 such allocations take 0.8 to 1.1 ms in a bare loop against 0.24 to 0.33 ms for the pooled slice. One zero buffer per tar carved into the paddings would close the rest but needs the total padding before the first member or a size passed through every tar writer.
  - **Copying every payload that a result views**: it would make every result private to its caller, at the cost of one copy of the data on routes that are bound by it, to guard against a write that nothing makes.
  - **A JavaScript batch of 1,024 ranges for each `writevSync`** (the first version of this change): libuv already splits the vector per system call, so it saved no system call and measured 1.02 to 1.10 times slower than one call.
  - **One `writeSync` for each range** (the file route before this change): 6,001 system calls for a tar of 2,000 members, 2.0 ms of 12.3.
  - **Rewriting the headers in place without checking the layout**: a dropped entry or a longer header moves every later body, and the result would not be the vetted tar.
  - **Standard output of 7-Zip to a file**, **a warm 7-Zip process** (entry 50) and **a decoder in the process** (entry 50: 1.3 to 1.5 times `xz`).
- **Verified by**:
  - **`tests/archive-stream-tar-in-place.test.ts`** shows that the gzip and xz routes write the tar over the unpacked bytes only where the layout allows it, never write onto a body or into the rooms around the frame through the write methods the test observes (index assignment, `write*` and `DataView` setters are not observed), return segments equal to the reference tar everywhere else, and do not keep a long tail alive behind the worker result.
  - **`tests/archive-tar-writers-no-sharing.test.ts`** shows that every tar writer pads and ends with zeros of its own, and that a write through one result reaches a second result of the same input only where a result views the input.
  - **`tests/worker-output-segments.test.ts`** shows that the file route writes the ranges joined, in one `writevSync`, continues after a short write, and throws on a failure, on a call that accepts no bytes and on a count of exactly one byte above the bytes pending.
  - **Byte identity** against the previous head: the output of the gzip, xz and bzip2 routes for the 5,355,520-byte tar of the Silesia `xml` file, plain and with 1 MiB of zeros appended, through the buffer route and the file route, is 5,346,816 bytes with sha256 `926c14ca49179051b47853dd039752f3b6b5bb39b2a0e0e6f2c31aba545c32f6` before and after.
  - **The existing stream, native, in-process, POSIX tar and RAR tests on the Linux VM with 7-Zip, `xz` and Python, with `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1`**, the phase-3 tests and `tests/ci-test-shards.test.ts`. The 13 tests of `archive-native-bzip2` that need `lbzip2` are skipped without the strict mode and fail on its missing tool with it, on the base as well.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image or the runner changes the 7-Zip build or the isolation wrapper (then the 5 ms are measured again), a stream route needs the unpacked buffer after the tar is returned, a consumer needs to write to a result or to the input it was made from (then the stored payloads are copied at that consumer or in the writers), `fs.writevSync` changes how it splits or continues a vector, or the nightly row sits clear of 0.97 for ten nights (remove it from `bench/parity-gaps.json`).

## 112. Wall-clock assertions of the unit tests: counts, forced states, CPU time and bounds sized from measured spread

- **Status**: Implemented (flake rows of issue #692, epic #763), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request).
- **Decision**:
  - **A claim about work done is asserted on a count of that work.** The hostile RocketBook chunk-table cases count the calls to the inflater (none before a page over the chunk limit is refused, and a control that reads a page at the limit shows the counter sees calls). Their wall-clock guard is the 10 s hang guard of `tests/helpers/timing.ts`, and each of those cases names a test timeout of 20 s: the runner's default of 5 s is shorter than the guard and would end a hanging case first.
  - **A claim about growth is a comparison of two sizes in CPU time.** The author line of white space compares 16,250 and 65,000 spaces, interleaved, best pass (`expectLinearOnInputs`, bound 8 for 4 times the input). A fixed wall-clock bound on one size cannot tell a linear split from a quadratic one on a host of unknown speed.
  - **A state the test needs is forced, not waited for.** The zombie fixture kills its sleeper only after the line it sent through `cat` came back (so the shell has been replaced by a process that never waits), then polls with `waitUntilStopped` for the zombie. Its two waits end after 10 s with their own message under a test timeout of 30 s, and the shell and its sleeper form one process group that the `finally` signals, so a stalled case leaves no sleeper behind. The job-pool cases that need a job to be slower than a 1 ms deadline read their input from a named pipe, so the job cannot answer before the test writes to it; the case of a job given its own deadline writes the file 100 ms after the job server opens it. A pool that ignores the deadline is given an answer by a timer 5 s after the case starts, so it fails on the verdict within seconds and the `finally` runs.
  - **A growth ratio is not taken from a baseline of a few tenths of a millisecond.** The four MOBI cases of unclosed constructs compare a 400 KB hostile book with a 400 KB book whose constructs are closed (CPU time, interleaved, best pass); the hostile book may cost at most as much as the plain one, the plain book must be read to the end, and its sample must be above the timer floor. The case whose cost is bounded work per entry (4,096 characters looked on for a closing tag) keeps its comparison of 100 KB and 400 KB, which sits at tens of milliseconds.
  - **Time that is a claim about the work is CPU time, and memory is read after a collection.** The 1.92 megapixel palette case reads the CPU time of the fresh process (best of five runs), calls the collector before the baseline and between runs, and bounds the memory a run adds at 40 MiB. The two block sort cases that compare speeds or sizes (the speedup over prefix doubling and the scaling of 4 times the block) read CPU time as well.
  - **A child that measures memory runs with the heap bound of the service, read from the file that sets it.** The peak-memory case and the palette case take `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` from the worker service of `docker-compose.yml` (`tests/helpers/service-heap.ts`), so the value cannot drift from the service. The peak-memory case builds its noise from a seeded generator.
  - **A speedup bound sits between the spread of the current code and the readings of the code it replaced.** The block sort must be 1.55 times faster than prefix doubling in CPU time (ratio 0.645), not 2 times (0.5).
  - **The event-loop case of the level-19 zstd encode is unchanged.** It already measures the CPU time of the loop thread between ticks (entry 63).
- **Why**:
  - **Rocketbook.** The case timed a page of 65,536 of the smallest zlib streams, the control that is read in full and inflates all of them, against 1,000 ms: it took 1,514 to 1,902 ms in 20 of 20 runs beside 36 busy processes on the 4-vCPU test VM, and 0 of 20 beside 12; the runner read 1,005, 1,032 and 1,099 ms. After the change 20 of 20 pass beside 36. The author line of white space ran under the same default guard after that change, and a splitter without the look-behind of `AUTHOR_SEPARATOR` took 2,020 ms for it, as the review of this change measured (0.32 ms with it) and still passed. The comparison of 16,250 and 65,000 spaces reads 2.9 to 3.3 times idle (12 runs) and 2.7 to 3.4 times beside 24 busy processes (12 runs) against the bound of 8; without the look-behind it reads 18.4 times (133 ms to 2,451 ms) and the case fails.
  - **Zombie.** The old fixture raced a shell that exits its sleeper before it is replaced against the time the shell needs to be replaced. It did not fail in 300 runs beside 24 busy processes (6 at a time), nor in 40 runs of the case beside 12 and 36; the new fixture also gave 300 of 300 and cannot depend on the order, since the kill follows the proof that the parent never waits. A shell that never echoes (`exec sleep 100` in place of `cat`) ends the case after 10 s with "2 lines did not arrive within 10000 ms" and leaves no process behind.
  - **Job pool.** A job on a real file races a 1 ms deadline against a conversion in a warm child. The reorder of entry 63 left the race with a cold child, which was not seen to lose in 40 runs beside 12 and 36 busy processes. The named pipe makes the order certain: a pool that ignores the deadline of a job (the timer of the pool lengthened by an hour) fails the two pool cases on the verdict after 6.0 s and 5.6 s; without the release timer a case waits for the pipe until its 240 s timeout.
  - **MOBI.** The case did not fail in 40 runs of the old test (20 beside 12 busy processes, 20 beside 36). What was measured is the baseline: the same 100 KB book of unclosed links took 0.38 to 1.61 ms in six rounds of one process on a quiet machine, and at 1 MB the ratio for 4 times the input read 3.2 to 8.6 against the bound of 8, so a pass or a fail rests on a sample that the compiler tier and the collector move by a factor of three. The same-size ratio of hostile to plain book reads 0.03 to 0.27 idle (15 runs per case) and 0.03 to 0.29 beside 12 busy processes (15 runs per case), because the plain book is the more expensive to read (about 55 ms against 2 to 14 ms). The bound is 1. A reader whose picture-tag or MOBI-tag pattern lost the `<` from `[^<>]*` and so scanned to the end of the book for each unclosed tag read 190 and 182 times the plain book (about 12 s against 63 and 65 ms) and failed the two cases whose construct it scans. The case of contents links that never close ends at the 256-level nesting limit of the HTML reader (the hostile book costs 2 ms, the plain one 56 ms), and lifting that limit moves it to 11.5 ms against 70 ms, so it did not fail either; the same holds for the case of link tags with a position, whose `filepos` pattern the reader reaches only for a book that has a contents page (read in `tocPage`), which the markup of that case does not have. Those two cases state that unclosed links do not make the reader slower than a closed book, and nothing more.
  - **Palette.** The failure the issue lists (75 MiB against 60) was memory; the case also holds a wall-clock bound that failed in 20 of 20 runs beside 36 busy processes (2.35 to 2.67 s against 1.5 s). The process uses 314 to 327 ms of CPU time idle and 328 to 345 ms beside 12 busy processes, so the CPU bound of 1.5 s leaves 4 times the cost. Memory added read 28 to 43 MiB idle (10 runs) and 29 to 33 MiB beside 12 busy processes before the change. With the collector called before the baseline and between runs, and the child run with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` as the service runs, it reads 11 to 18 MiB idle (10 runs) and 7 to 17 MiB beside 24 busy processes (10 runs); without the arena bound 15 to 25 MiB (5 runs beside 24). The 75 MiB did not reproduce, and a high-water mark that includes uncollected garbage is the one cause the host's load can change. The bound of 60 MiB was left unchanged by that first change and no longer matched the readings: a quantizer that keeps 8 bytes per pixel more (15 MiB) read 52 MiB, which 60 MiB lets through and 40 MiB fails, and one that keeps 6 bytes per pixel more passes. After the change 20 of 20 pass beside 12 busy processes.
  - **Peak memory.** The same 2000x2000 x 6 frame animation to GIF added 504 to 541 MiB without the service's heap bound (8 runs, 12 busy processes), 320 to 372 MiB with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1` and 363 to 416 MiB with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`; to WebP 436 to 521 MiB and 291 to 340 MiB. Without the bound, oriented 2000x2000 animations peaked at 471 MiB (6 frames), 482 (7), 518 (8), 565 (10 noisy frames to GIF), 591 (11) and 617 (14), and 3000x3000 x 5 frames reached 685 MiB. The `tests` job does not set the variable and the service does, so the bound of 576 MiB (the 512 MiB budget plus a 64 MiB margin, unchanged by this entry) was held at a figure the service never reaches, with 35 MiB to spare at the largest run; the child that has the service's bound leaves 160 MiB under it. The spread of one input stays at 49 to 52 MiB. The case did not fail in 5 runs of the old test beside 12 busy processes.
  - **Block sort.** The ratio of the sorter to prefix doubling was 0.44 to 0.50 in wall-clock time over 22 runs (idle and beside 24 busy processes; the median of 9 alternating runs reads 0.446 to 0.490, no tighter than the best pass the helper keeps), and the old bound of 0.5 failed 1 run in 20 beside 12 busy processes (0.508) and 1 in 20 beside 36 (0.558), after the helper's 12 passes. In CPU time the same case reads 0.447 to 0.595 idle (20 runs), 0.425 to 0.570 beside 12 busy processes (20 runs) and 0.456 to 0.585 beside 24 (20 runs); CPU time reads wider than wall-clock time here, and the cause was not isolated. The previous sorter reads 0.74 to 0.81 in CPU time on the test VM (10 runs) and read 0.65 to 0.66 in wall-clock time on the runner (entry 64), so the bound of 0.645 sits above every reading of the current sorter (8% over the largest) and under both. Put back in place of the current sorter, the previous one fails the case (ratio 0.82). The scaling case of the same file (4 times the block, bound 8) read 8.0 to 9.0 times in 7 of 20 runs of the file beside 12 busy processes in wall-clock time (11.5 ms to 91.8 to 103.9 ms); it reads CPU time now, and 3 of 3 idle runs of the file pass.
  - **Event loop.** The loop thread held the loop for 1.6 to 3.6 ms in 5 runs of the level-19 encode beside 36 busy processes, against a bound of 105 ms, and the synchronous control for 458 to 525 ms; the old case of the issue (112.26 ms) read the lateness of a timer, which entry 63 replaced. 40 of 40 runs of the unchanged case pass beside 12 and 36.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The block sort may lose up to 30% of its speedup unseen** (2.2 times to 1.55 times); a regression to the previous sorter (1.2 to 1.4 times) or to prefix doubling still fails. The runner has not read the CPU-time ratio of the current sorter yet; the bound rests on the test VM and on the wall-clock reading of the runner.
  - **The memory of the palette case may grow by about 20 MiB unseen** (readings reach 18 MiB, the bound is 40); the bound was 60 MiB before and hid 42 MiB.
  - **A same-size comparison does not see work that grows with the input and is the same for a plain book.** The scaling of plain books is not the claim of these cases; the one case that keeps a scaling comparison is the one whose hostile book is slow by design. The cases of contents links and of link tags with a position catch nothing that a pattern change can do; they are kept as the statement above.
  - **A child with the service's heap bound sees less memory than a child without it.** A change that only raises the memory of a process with many arenas is not seen; the service is not such a process.
  - **A pipe-fed job needs `mkfifo` on the path**, which every runner and the test VM have.
  - **The CPU-time bound of the palette case says nothing of the wait for a core.** A slow host does not fail it; a slower algorithm does.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Raising the 1,000 ms, 1.5 s or 60 MiB bounds**: it hides a run that is slow for another reason and still fails when the host is busier than the sample.
  - **Retrying a failed case**: the failure is the information, and a retry of a wall-clock comparison passes whenever the host is quieter than the first time.
  - **A work counter inside the MOBI reader**: the reader is production code and the issue is limited to tests; the same-size comparison needs none.
  - **The median of alternating runs for the block sort**: it read as wide as the best pass (0.446 to 0.490 against 0.44 to 0.50).
  - **Calling the collector in the child of the peak-memory case**: one conversion runs in the child and the collector cannot be called inside it; the heap bound is what the service does.
- **Verified by**: `tests/rocketbook-reader.test.ts` (a reader that inflates one stream before each refusal fails three cases; a splitter without the look-behind fails the white-space case), `tests/process-state.test.ts`, `tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts` (a pool that ignores a job's deadline fails), `tests/mobi-book-structure.test.ts` (a reader that scans to the end for each unclosed picture or MOBI tag fails two cases), `tests/palette-quantizer-quality.test.ts`, `tests/image-peak-memory.test.ts` and `tests/bzip2-bwt.perf.test.ts`, the first five of them 20 of 20 on the Linux test VM in strict mode beside 12 busy processes (the base rows are in the pull request).
- **Revisit when**: a runner measures the block sort above 0.6 in CPU time or the peak memory within 100 MiB of the bound, a plain case of a file here fails on a count it did not change, or the `tests` job sets `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` (then the case sets nothing of its own).

## 113. An `.xls` is the office suite's BIFF8 export of a typed XLSX workbook, XLSX cells keep their types, and a table that is not well formed or does not fit a sheet is refused

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #444, epic #760), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: write real workbooks before launch instead of withdrawing the target).
- **Decision**:
  - **Every `.xls` output is a BIFF8 workbook in a Compound File, written by the office suite's `MS Excel 97` export** (`soffice --convert-to xls`, the filter the suite picks for the extension). Every source reaches the export as an XLSX workbook that was checked against the BIFF8 sheet (`convertXlsTarget`, `src/worker/office-suite-route.ts`): an XLSX or XLSM source is checked as it is and exported in one pass; ODS and Numbers are first written as XLSX by the suite itself, which holds what the suite loaded, and that workbook is checked and exported; a table the in-process engine reads (CSV, TSV, JSON, Parquet, Kingsoft workbooks) is written as an XLSX workbook by the engine (`writeTransientWorkbook`), checked and exported. A PDF is read as in 120. The workbook never goes to the output path of the request. With no office suite the answer is `EngineUnavailableError('soffice')` (503): the in-process engine has no BIFF8 writer, and the pairs are in `NATIVE_ENGINE_ONLY_PAIRS`.
  - **The SpreadsheetML 2003 writer (`generateXlsXmlFromData`) is deleted**, and with it the XML that was served under an `.xls` name. The reader of that XML (an `.xls` upload that is SpreadsheetML) stays. The branch that returned an `.xls` input unchanged for the `.xls` target is deleted too; the registry never offered the pair, and the engine now answers it as an unsupported target.
  - **Pages to `.xls` is withdrawn from the registry.** The `.pages` bytes were read as CSV text and the XML around that text was served as a workbook; the office suite has no export of a text document to a spreadsheet filter.
  - **XLSX cells are typed** (`src/lib/conversions/xlsx-writer.ts`, ECMA-376 Part 1, 18.3). A number is a number with no `t`, a boolean `t="b"`, text goes through `sharedStrings.xml` (`t="s"`, once for a repeated value), a date is a serial number under a date format. The shared-string layout follows xlsxwriter (BSD-2-Clause, `sharedstrings.py`): the `_xHHHH_` escape of control characters, `_x005F_` in front of a literal that reads like one, `xml:space="preserve"` around outer whitespace, `count` and `uniqueCount`. The package has `styles.xml` with one date format, and the sheet declares its `dimension`.
  - **A text field is a number only when its sheet shows the same text.** The pattern is `-?(0|[1-9]\d*)(\.\d*[1-9])?` with at most 15 significant digits (the digits a double keeps, `DBL_DIG`) and `String(Number(text)) === text`. A figure with zeros after its last digit (`20.00`, `5.50`, `0.0`) is the number it spells under a `0.00`-style format with as many decimals (custom ids from 165), when `toFixed` gives the text back and it has at most 15 decimals: a spreadsheet's CSV import stores such a field as a number (LibreOffice `ScColumn::ParseString`, `sc/source/core/data/column3.cxx` lines 2290 to 2313 at master 9f554658c082, sets a value cell for a plain decimal), and the format keeps the zeros on view, so SUM and pivots see every cell of a money column. `00004`, `007.50`, `+5`, `1e4`, `1,250`, a 16-digit identifier, `-0` and `-0.00` stay text. A field is a date only when it is an ISO calendar day (`YYYY-MM-DD`, a real day, 1900-03-01 to 9999-12-31, which avoids the days Excel numbers twice). JSON and Parquet keep the types they have: a finite number is written as the shortest text that reads back as the same double (`37.77490123456789`, `0.30000000000000004`, `1e-7`), a boolean a boolean, a string is text whatever it spells, `null` is an empty cell, an integer past the safe range and a nested value are text. A JSON array of objects takes its header from the keys of every record in the order they first appear (`fieldsInFirstSeenOrder`, the data engine's own table builder), and an item that is not an object is a `DataParseError` (400). Parquet goes to the data engine's reader for a spreadsheet target, never to the delimited reader.
  - **The date format is `yyyy\-mm\-dd` (custom id 164), not the built-in id 14.** Id 14 is the short date of the viewer's locale, so the same workbook reads `03/05/2024` in one office suite and `2024. 3. 5.` in another, and an export to CSV would not give back the field it came from.
  - **Delimited text that is not well formed is refused.** The sheet is read with `parseDelimitedRows` (`delimited-detect.ts`, the reader of the data engine): any quote error (an unterminated quote, a quote that closes inside a field) is a `DataParseError` (400) with the row. The fallback that split each line on the delimiter, and with it the one-cell sheet, is deleted, for the XLSX, ODS and XLS targets alike. `tab` sources are split on TAB, a BOM is dropped. JSON that does not parse was refused already (`parseJsonTableCells`).
  - **Nothing is cut to fit a sheet; the refusal is a 413** (`SheetLimitError`, a `PayloadLimitError`, so every route answers its `status`; `DataLimitExceededError` keeps its 400 for the YAML, XML, nesting and output caps). The bounds are in `src/lib/conversions/office/sheet-bounds.ts`: 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns for XLSX ("Excel specifications and limits"; LibreOffice `MAXROWCOUNT` and `MAXCOLCOUNT`, `sc/inc/address.hxx`), 65,536 rows and 256 columns for BIFF8 (the same page for Excel 97-2003; a `Rw` is 16 bits and a `Col` 8 bits in [MS-XLS]), 32,767 characters in a cell (the same page; xlsxwriter cuts at this length, here the table is refused). The XLSX bounds are checked on the last cell that holds something, so empty fields at the end of a row are no cells. The BIFF8 bounds are checked on the workbook before the export, because the export cuts without a word (measured with LibreOffice 24.2: a sheet of 70,001 rows came back with 65,536, and one of 300 columns with 256). `xls-limits.ts` streams every part an office suite may open as a worksheet, because the suite is what cuts the rows: the sheets the workbook lists (`discoverXlsxSheets`: the workbook is the part the root `_rels/.rels` names as the office document, else `xl/workbook.xml`; every `sheet` with a relationship id counts whatever its name, with none or an empty one, and whatever the prefix of its `id` attribute; its part is the relationship's target resolved against the workbook's directory with `resolveZipPath`, so `../xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` and `/xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml` are found; a part is listed once), the parts under `xl/worksheets/`, and the parts that `[Content_Types].xml` types as a worksheet (measured with LibreOffice 26.8: a 65,537-row sheet reached through each of the first five shapes was exported cut to 65,536 rows). A tall part that nothing references is therefore refused too, a false 413 that no real producer causes and the safe side of a check that must not miss a sheet the suite opens. A workbook that lists a sheet whose part is not in the package is refused (400), never passed. The reader keeps its own rule for the name of a sheet (one without a name is skipped), and now reads a part that several sheets list once, at its first sheet, where it read the part again under each name; where it looks changes too. A package with no worksheet to check is refused with the reader's own message (400), as the reader refuses it, instead of passing the check. The count is of the cells that hold a value, a formula or an inline string, a `row` or `c` without `r` following the one before, as SheetJS does (xlsx 0.18.5, `parse_ws_xml_data`, xlsx.js lines 14851, 14854, 14880 to 14881 and 14924); the declared `dimension` is not read. The parts are charged to one decoded-byte budget for the workbook (`InflateBudget`, the 256 MiB the XLSX reader gives its sheets). A package that is not a ZIP, a part that does not inflate, a cell reference that is not A1 and a source file past the 256 MiB the check reads are refused, never passed on unchecked.
  - **The lists beside the cells of a worksheet are streamed into their final shape and bounded, never ended silently at the scanner's 50,000 and never held as element objects.** Sheets of a workbook: 10,000 (`MAXTABCOUNT`, LibreOffice `sc/inc/address.hxx` line 64, the most Calc opens), listed once each by part; the sheet past it is refused (413) at that element, so a package of millions costs the time of the bound. Merged ranges and hyperlinks together, over the whole workbook: 1,048,576, one for each row of a worksheet; neither Excel nor LibreOffice documents a bound for merged ranges, so it is taken from memory: a range is four numbers and took 66 bytes of heap (measured with Node 24, 1,048,576 in an array: 66 MiB), and a count per sheet alone would leave sheets times that. Past it the lists stop growing and the conversion goes on without the rest, which is deliberate: CSV, TSV and JSON do not use merges or links, and refusing them for lists they ignore would refuse a file that converts today. The elements counted are the ones the scan took, so the scan costs the time of the bound (3 million `mergeCell`s in a package of 177 KB: 2.0 s of CPU and 0.74 GB peak resident with the sheet read whole and checked for well-formedness, 1,048,576 kept). There is no bound per worksheet. 65,530 is what Excel lets an author add to a sheet, not what a file can hold: LibreOffice 26.8 writes 70,000 `hyperlink` elements and 70,000 relationships for a column of 70,000 URLs, and a per-sheet cap of 65,530 refused that file for every target, though most targets do not use links at all. A sheet's relationships part is read once, under the decoded-byte budget of the workbook (the 256 MiB its sheets share), and keeps only the ids that the sheet's links name, plus its drawings, so the map follows the number of links and not the size of the part. The relationship elements scanned over one read of a package are counted against an allowance of 2,097,152 (2^21: a relationship for each of the 1,048,576 links the workbook may hold, and as many again for the sheets, the drawings and the root), and the element past it is refused (413). A part is scanned in full whatever ids are asked for, and the cost is by element and not by byte, which the budget does not bound: measured, 2.1 million short `Relationship` elements cost 0.3 s of CPU, and 70 sheets of 30,001 of them in a 110 KB package are refused after the same scan as 280 sheets. `Override` elements of the content types: 100,000, the 10,000 sheets with room for the other parts. The sheet itself stays under the 256 MiB workbook budget, whatever the lists hold. The helpers that read relationships and stream elements are not specific to workbooks and live in `src/lib/conversions/office/opc-parts.ts`. The XML scanner ends a scan at an opening whose same-name nest is deeper than its bound (64 levels), where it went on to the next opening and walked the nest again: 4,000 openings of one tag took 3.8 s, 16,000 over a minute, and now cost one walk. Two other shapes cost a walk to the end of the input at every step and are linear now: one open tag with many self-closing children of its name (80,000 took 13.7 s, now 3.5 ms), and many openings after a stray closing tag of the same name (64,000 took 7.8 s, now 5.8 ms), because the search for the next opening and the next closing of a tag keeps its last answer and a miss, which hold for every later position of the scan (CPU time on this host, Node 24, `tests/safe-xml-scanner-depth.test.ts`; 36,000 random documents, well formed and not, return the same elements as the scanner before the change). Elements found before the nest are still returned; a nest this deep is not found in any real file, and the answer for one is none of its elements.
