Where the tables of some pages are found and the others hold only text, only the tables are written, as Camelot and tabula-java return only tables, and the conversion warns which pages lost their text (`Left out the text outside the tables of pages ...`, as `reportLeftOut` reports pages it leaves out).
  - **A page without a text layer is read as it is for a document** (`readPdfContentForOffice`, the code that `readPdfForOffice` calls) and the other pages keep their layout: with OCR on, the tables of the pages that have a text layer are still found, and each page OCR read is a sheet `Page N`, a recognized line for a row. A page OCR read as empty text is not a page it read: it keeps its text layer, and so its tables, in the sheets and its own text in the document. With `ocrMode` `force` or `redo` every page is read by OCR, so its tables are not detected; this is the document outputs' behaviour too. A document with no text layer at all is the same case with no tables. No OCR is added for this output; the tables of a scan are not detected.
  - **A workbook holds at most 10,000 sheets** (`WORKBOOK_MAX_SHEETS`), the tabs LibreOffice Calc holds (`MAXTABCOUNT`, sc/inc/address.hxx); Excel states no count ("Excel specifications and limits": limited by available memory). Past it the answer is a typed 413 (`SheetLimitError`) and nothing is cut. The writer holds the count and the sheet names to account (`writeXlsxWorkbook`): at least one sheet (ECMA-376 Part 1, 18.2.20: `sheets` holds one or more `sheet`), a name of 1 to 31 characters, none of `[ ] : * ? / \`, and different from the others without regard to case, or the writer throws. The other bounds are the existing ones: the layout budget of a page (60,000,000 steps, `PdfLayoutLimitError`, 400), 20,000 cells and 400 grid lines for a table (`pdf-layout/limits.ts`), 2,000 pages for the text read (`PDF_TEXT_MAX_PAGES`), and the worksheet bounds of 113 (1,048,576 rows, 16,384 columns, 32,767 characters a cell; 65,536 rows and 256 columns for `.xls`).
  - **The XLSX writer writes more than one sheet** (`writeXlsxWorkbook`): the sheets share one string table and one set of cell formats, as the package of any spreadsheet writer has them (xlsxwriter, `workbook.py`), and `writeXlsx` is its one-sheet case, `Sheet1`.
- **Why**: a PDF table that comes out as a spreadsheet is the thing a person converts a PDF to a workbook for, and the refusal of 113 gave them nothing. Table extractors of record agree on the method (ruling lines where there are lines, aligned text where there are none, snap and join tolerances: pdfplumber's `find_tables` with its "lines" and "text" strategies, Camelot's lattice and stream flavours, tabula-java's `SpreadsheetExtractionAlgorithm` and `BasicExtractionAlgorithm`), and the repository already has both detectors with budgets and tests, so the work is a thin layer from tables to a workbook.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Aligned text can be read as a table where there is none** (prose set in short columns that do not flow into each other) **and a table without lines or with uneven gaps can be missed**; the same rules as the DOCX and HTML outputs decide, so a fix to them fixes all three. A table that is missed is written as a sheet of text lines when the document has no other table, and left out, with a warning, when it has.
  - **A page with a table and a page with only text give a workbook of the table alone**, and the conversion warns which pages lost their text. The text is in the DOCX and the TXT conversions of the file.
  - **A scan gives the text OCR read, never a table**, and needs the OCR engine, as the document conversion does.
  - **The pieces of a text line that sit apart are one cell.** The layout pass joins a row's segments into a line before it reads paragraphs, so a line of two columns that is not a table gives `Total 42` in one cell, not two. A text sheet is a reading of the page, not a grid.
  - **The layout is analysed once.** The second pass that the first version ran for the tables is gone: on a 1,929-page text PDF with no table it cost 22.9 s of the 47.4 s of the conversion, all in one synchronous call.
  - **A table whose header is bold in one page and plain in the next, or whose columns shift by more than 4 points, is two sheets.** The join rule is that of the document output (`TABLE_WIDTH_TOLERANCE`).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A Python sidecar running pdfplumber or Camelot**: the worker image has no Python and would need a second runtime, its packages and their updates in the sandbox, for tables the repository's own analysis already finds.
  - **A new detector for this output**: a second set of rules that disagrees with the document output about what a table is, to be fixed twice.
  - **Refusing a PDF with no table**: it keeps the 400 of 113 for the case where a person most expects text.
  - **All tables of a document concatenated in one sheet, as tabula-java's command line writes CSV**: a workbook has sheets for this, and the concatenation loses where one table ends and the next begins.
  - **Cutting the sheets at 255**: an old limit of spreadsheet programs that no current one has; a 300-page text PDF would be refused for nothing. The bound is the one of the program that reads the workbook.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-tables-to-sheets.test.ts` (a ruled table, a table with merged cells and a table of aligned text from the structure corpus, `tests/fixtures/pdf-structure`, with the truth of what each was written from; a 90-row table over three pages written by the Markdown to PDF writer; pages with no table, a page of vertical Japanese against its truth, a page of angled text only, and blank pages; a table page beside a scanned page with OCR on, with the recognition stubbed and with Tesseract, and with an empty recognition of the table page under `force` and `redo`; the warning that names the pages left out, and the running footer that is neither a row nor left-out text nor a warning; the first and last line of a one-page letter and the per-page invoice number kept as rows; a PDF of one line at the top of each page converted; the lines of a wrapped cell; pages written out by hand for the running header, the numbering of two tables in a page; a count of the layout budgets, one for each page; the sheets of one workbook, the 413 for a merge past the grid and for 10,001 sheets, a workbook of no sheet, and the sheet names the writer refuses; `tests/pdf-text-hostile-input.perf.test.ts` (2,000 pages that are each one open paragraph under a running footer lay out in time linear in the page count); `.xls` read back by the office suite and by the record walker of `tests/helpers/biff8-records.ts`), `tests/xlsx-typed-cells.test.ts` and `tests/xls-real-binary-output.test.ts` (the one-sheet package unchanged), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` (the PDF pairs have an engine path and are no longer expected to be refused), and the touched tests on Ubuntu 24.04 with LibreOffice 24.2 and Tesseract under `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1`. No benchmark family has a PDF to spreadsheet row, so there is no parity row for this output yet.
- **Revisit when**: a nightly or user file shows a table missed or split (then the rule is fixed in `pdf-layout/tables.ts` for every output), QA wants the text of pages without a table written beside the tables, tables of scans are wanted (then the recognized words are laid out with the same detector), or a benchmark row for PDF to spreadsheet exists to compare the cells against a reference.

## 121. aom is built as a Release at -O3 in the x64 libvips of the worker image, as libaom's own build type and the other encoders of entry 84

- **Status**: Proposed (issue #641, row "Found by the 2026-10-25 nightly"), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request). It becomes Implemented when the x64 speed run of the pull request shows the four photograph AVIF rows at or above 0.90 and the strict quality gate of the image family passes; the arm64 VM cannot show either, see Why.
- **Decision**:
  - **On linux-x64, `docker/sharp-libvips/aom-release-x64.patch` configures aom with `CFLAGS="${CFLAGS} -O3"` and `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`** (upstream: `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel` over the `-Os` of `posix.sh` lines 44 to 46). `build.sh` applies it with `--fuzz=0` only when `PLATFORM` is `linux-x64`. No other option of the aom build moves (NASM, high bit depth, no decoder tools). The `CFLAGS` prefix is redundant with Release's own `-O3` and is kept for the same shape as the mozjpeg hunk of entry 84.
  - **arm64 keeps the upstream aom (entry 130 gave arm64 the patch after the comparison below was done).** The arm64 rows already pass on the VM (1.02 to 1.16 of the reference), `-march=armv8-a` has fused multiply-add in its baseline and libaom does not set `-ffp-contract`, so different inlining at `-O3` may fuse different floating-point operations of its rate decisions and change bytes. Nothing builds or compares the arm64 stage in CI, so the change waits for that comparison.
  - **Nothing else changes.** The one-tile encode, the thread lease (`imageThreadsFor`), the effort, the quality and the tune of entries 93 and 86 stay. The speed jobs already ran with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2` since #768 (entry 93 added it to the quality jobs only), so the arena bound is not part of this change.
- **Why**:
  - **What moved the rows.** The four rows fell on the first nightly after #878 and nothing else in #878 reaches a photograph's speed: the one-tile encode of entry 93 (the `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX` line #878 added is in the quality jobs; the speed jobs have had it since #768, `cbaf0962`). Measured on the arm64 VM (4 cores, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, `bench:quality -- --parity --speed-only --family image --base-root`, head the worker's one-tile library and base the library with auto-tiles on, 24 interleaved pairs a row): head against base `photo-a.jpg->avif` 0.645, `photo-b.png->avif` 0.815, `kodim23.png->avif` 0.586 and `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png->avif` 0.693; every other image row 0.98 to 1.03 (the WebP row of `photo-a.jpg` 0.878 over 240 pairs of a noisy run, upper bound 0.99). The same factor holds on the x64 nightlies: `photo-a.jpg->avif` fell from 1.288 to 0.903 of the reference (a factor of 0.70). Toggling the two #878 changes on the VM with the reference in the same pairs (15 pairs, the reference's command-line encoder at `-q 70 -s 6 -j all`; reference time / ours, above 1 is faster than the reference):

    | Row | Auto-tiles on, arena unset | Auto-tiles on, arena 2 | One tile, arena unset | One tile, arena 2 |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | `photo-a.jpg` | 1.234 | 1.750 | 1.078 | 1.146 |
    | `kodim23.png` | 1.196 | 1.851 | 1.035 | 1.101 |
    | `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png` | 0.860 | 1.456 | 0.826 | 1.007 |
    | `photo-b.png` | 0.950 | 1.365 | 0.817 | 1.114 |

    The bound on the arena lets the encode lease four threads instead of two, so it helps (1.06 to 1.69 times); the tiles are what the rows lost.
  - **Why one tile cannot be given its parallelism back.** The tiles were the parallel work (entry 93), and a tiled file moves with the thread count and costs 0.7 to 2 % BD-rate against the reference, which the quality rows stop. A thread-count sweep of the one-tile encode (768 x 512, 2 to 8 threads) is flat (47.6, 47.1, 47.7, 48.1 and 47.5 ms), and a sampling of the runnable threads of an encode shows one thread for the first 5 to 10 ms (decode, conversion), two to three in the wavefront of the encode and one for the last 8 to 10 ms (bitstream packing); the reference has the same shape (`avifenc -j 1` 82.3 ms against 50.4 ms on 4 threads, ours 73.7 ms against 45.8 ms), so no thread or lease setting in our hands changes the ratio. The dispatcher adds 0.7 ms (768 x 512 PNG) to 2.2 ms (768 x 512 JPEG) to the library call.
  - **Why the arm64 VM does not show the failure.** On the VM the head reads 1.155, 1.125, 1.105 and 1.017 of the reference in the harness (`photo-a.jpg`, `photo-b.png`, `kodim23.png`, `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png`), so the rows pass there; avifenc's start-up (about 10 ms of its 82 ms on one thread) is an advantage of our in-process encode that the one-tile loss does not remove. On x64 the base read 1.29 to 1.42 of the reference where the VM's base reads 1.79 for `photo-a.jpg`, so the library is about 0.72 times as fast against the reference on x64 as on arm64, whatever the tiles. This is the difference this entry addresses and it is inferred, not profiled.
  - **What the x64 gap is taken to be.** The library's aom, the encoder that does most of a photograph's AVIF work, is built differently from the reference's (libheif, libvips and the JPEG decoder differ too, but none of them is size-optimised against a speed-optimised reference build). The upstream release builds every library for size and overrides it "for select dependencies that benefit" (`posix.sh` lines 44 to 46); aom is not among them (`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel`, line 182), while libaom's own default build type is Release (`CMakeLists.txt` of 3.15.1, lines 34 to 39), and entry 84 measured the same switch on libwebp, mozjpeg and libpng at 1.10 to 1.22 times on x64 with identical bytes. Entry 84 rejected "-O3 for every library, aom included" because the AVIF rows did not move with the three codecs and nothing was measured for aom; this entry measures it in the way entry 84 did, on the x64 runner.
  - **Not measured here.** The VM has no CMake or NASM and may not build software, so the library with aom at -O3 was not built, and neither the speed gain nor the identity of the bytes was observed. On x64, bytes are expected to be identical: `-march=nehalem` has no fused multiply-add, and entry 84 found 247 outputs identical for three codecs. The strict quality gate of the image family is a tolerance check, not a byte comparison, so a byte comparison against the base on the CI build is recorded in the pull request when it is available.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Build time and size.** The aom compile is slower at -O3 and the library larger; entry 84 measured +4.6 % size for the three codecs; the growth for aom, the largest codec of the library, is not measured. The stage's cache key moves with the patch, so the first run on `main` after the merge builds the stage once (about 18 minutes on a 4-core runner).
  - **If the x64 run shows no gain**, the entry is withdrawn and the four rows stay below 0.90 until a different lever is found (a libheif conversion that is vectorised for the x64 baseline `-march=nehalem` is the next candidate); nothing else here depends on it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Tiles back for photographs** (`auto-tiles` on, or tile columns by size): the rows return to 1.3 to 1.8 of the reference on the VM, but the file moves with the thread count and the quality rows fail (entry 93).
  - **The command-line encoder for photographs**: it changes every photograph's bytes and tune, and makes the rows slower than the base on the VM (the process start and the PNG hand-off cost about 10 ms of 46).
  - **More encoder threads** (8 on 4 cores): the sweep above is flat.
  - **`-O3` for every library**: the libraries that do not encode a measured row stay as upstream builds them.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts` (the aom patch changes the build type and nothing else, `build.sh` applies it on linux-x64 only, and `option-f.patch` keeps the three `-O3` hunks of entry 84), the build of the stage in CI (applied with `--fuzz=0`, so a hunk whose context moved fails it), and, to be read from the pull request, the x64 speed run (head against base and against the reference on the four rows) and the strict quality gate of the image family.
- **Revisit when**: sharp is upgraded (the pins move and the hunk's context with them), the x64 run settles the gain, an arm64 build of the stage can be compared with the base byte for byte or by the quality rows (then arm64 takes the patch too), or the launch is past and the pass line of entry 114 goes back toward 0.97.

## 122. Shared OCI host: one stack inside a hard budget of 3.5 cpus and 20 GiB, local storage on a capped mount, and deploys from a runner of its own

- **Status**: Implemented (part of issue #900; the configuration check it relies on is issue #564), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: launch on the existing OCI A1 instance, add no billable resource, keep every file off cloud storage, and leave room to grow; QA chose the domain `convert.aquilaxk.site` and approved an AppArmor profile of the stack's own). On the host, the deploy user, `/opt/easyconvert`, the scratch mount, the runner, the environment with its secret, and the fork approval setting were set up on 2026-10-30. DNS, the origin certificate, the nginx site and the AppArmor profile remain for QA (`docs/deploy-oci.md`, first-time setup). #954 moved the smoke conversion to a probe that charges no allowance and that the nginx site does not forward; a host that installed the site file before it installs it again. #671 added to that smoke a check of the convert route that charges nothing, a positive control for the public check, the label read before anything starts, and a verdict that keeps its place until its conversion ends.
- **Decision**:
  - **One host, no new billable resource.** The stack runs on the instance that already exists in ap-seoul-1 (VM.Standard.A1.Flex, arm64, 4 OCPU and 24 GB), on its 50 GB data volume (where the container runtime keeps its data), behind the host's nginx and the CDN's free plan. Nothing is resized, added or migrated: no instance, no block volume, no object storage, no load balancer, no paid monitoring.
  - **The budget is 3.5 OCPU and 20 GiB for the whole stack, from two numbers in the env secret** (`EASYCONVERT_BUDGET_CPUS`, `EASYCONVERT_BUDGET_MEMORY_GB`). `deploy/oci/deploy.sh budget` derives the services from them: Redis 0.2 cpu and 512 MiB, the web 23% of the cpus and 27.5% of the memory (0.8 cpu and 5632 MiB), the worker the rest (2.5 cpus and 14336 MiB), and one worker job per 3.4 GiB and at most two per cpu (4 jobs). A value in the env secret for one service wins over the derived one. `docker-compose.prod.yml` carries the same values as defaults.
  - **Limits are hard and the weight is soft.** Every container has `cpus`, `mem_limit` and an equal `memswap_limit`, so neither stack can take the host; every container has `cpu_shares: 512` against the default 1024 of the other service, so under contention the other service wins and otherwise this stack uses idle cores. Every container has `oom_score_adj: 500`, which ranks it ahead of Guaranteed pods (-997) and of Burstable pods that request more than half of the host's memory, and behind BestEffort pods (1000) and Burstable pods that request less than half, if the other service runs as Kubernetes pods; the score only orders victims in a host-wide shortage, and the hard limits are what protect the other service. Processes are capped per container by `pids_limit`; the per-uid `nproc` is 4096, because it counts every process of uid 10001 on the host and the web and every worker share that uid.
  - **The application containers run under an AppArmor profile of their own** (`deploy/oci/apparmor-easyconvert`, named `easyconvert`): Docker's default rules (moby's `apparmor/template.go`) with ABI 4.0, `userns` and `unix`. Ubuntu 24.04 sets `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`, which refuses the user namespace that every native conversion is started in (`unshare -r -n`) to a program under a profile that does not grant it. On the shared host both `docker-default` (ABI 3.0, which does not mediate that namespace) and `easyconvert` allow it, measured in a container on 2026-10-30. The profile pins the behaviour against a later Docker or host change, and the deploy checks it instead of assuming it: it stops when `/etc/apparmor.d/easyconvert` differs from the file of the checkout, reads the profile of the web and worker containers with `docker inspect --format '{{.AppArmorProfile}}'` (it must print `easyconvert`), converts a one-pixel PPM to PNG through the smoke probe `/api/health/conversion` (ImageMagick in the sandbox), checks the convert route and runs `unshare -r -n` in the worker, all before it moves the links, and returns to the previous release when one fails. With `STRICT_SANDBOX=true` a host that refused the namespace would fail every native conversion while `/api/health` stays green, which is why the smoke is the gate.
  - **Storage is local and capped.** `STORAGE_DRIVER` defaults to `local`. Uploads, results and every `/tmp` are directories of one mounted loop file system of a fixed size (default 12 GiB, `noexec,nosuid,nodev`) on the data volume, so a full scratch gives ENOSPC to this stack and not to the host. `deploy.sh guard` refuses to run when the directory is not a mount point or the data volume has less than 15 GiB free, and warns at 85% use.
  - **Redis persists, in a small append-only file.** Users, API keys, quota counters and the queue live in Redis (`src/lib/auth/redis-user-store.ts`, `src/lib/api-keys/redis-key-store.ts`, `src/lib/queue/bullmq-engine.ts`), so a restart without persistence would sign everyone out and forget keys. `appendonly yes`, `everysec`, rewrite at 16 MB, `maxmemory 256mb` with `noeviction`: at most a second of writes is lost, a full Redis refuses writes instead of dropping queued jobs, and the file stays in the megabytes. Redis is on an internal network, has a password, and publishes no port.
  - **The web port is `127.0.0.1:8090`**, a port that is not among those the host already uses. nginx is the only way in (`deploy/oci/nginx-easyconvert.conf`); the origin certificate is a CDN origin certificate installed by hand, because port 80 is closed and DNS-01 needs an API token on the host.
  - **Images and deploys.** The worker image is built for arm64 on the arm runner and the web image is that digest plus the Next.js build (`Dockerfile.web`), because the synchronous convert route runs the engines in the web process. A deploy is started by hand, from `main`, on a runner registered with `easyconvert-production` as its only label, in the environment `easyconvert-production` that QA approves. It accepts only the refs `main` and `sha-<40 hex>`, pins both images by digest, refuses a web image whose recorded base (`org.opencontainers.image.base.name`) is not the worker image it pinned (read from the pinned web digest, not from the tag), starts them with `docker compose up -d --wait`, checks the AppArmor profile of the containers, `/api/health`, the smoke (the probe and the check of the convert route) and the worker's namespaces, then the canonical host of the pages and the public block of the smoke probe, and returns to the previous release when any of them fails or the job is cancelled. The workflow `exec`s `deploy.sh`, which runs every long command in the background and waits for it with `wait`, so that a cancel ends the running command and restarts the previous release at once; `deploy.sh reconcile` starts the current release again from its pinned `images.env`, and `deploy`, `rollback` and `reconcile` hold a lock. The job log is public and carries line numbers, digests and an HTTP status, never a line of the secret or an answer body. Pull requests from outside contributors' forks wait for approval before any workflow runs, because any workflow file can name the runner's label. Only the current and the previous release and their images are kept; images are removed one by one by digest and only from the two repositories of this stack, never with a prune.
  - **One version per production deploy, never one per pull request.** Beta releases are `0.y.z`: `y` is raised for a planned deploy batch and `z` for an urgent hotfix deploy, the first beta is `v0.1.0` and is published as a pre-release, and `1.0.0` comes when every conversion feature and the frontend are complete (QA decision 2026-10-30). The numbers follow Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html), which fits a public API and an SDK that others pin; a build is identified by its image tag `sha-<commit>`, and a version names the deploy of one build. `CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 (keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/): an `Unreleased` section grouped as Added, Changed, Fixed and Security, moved under the version at the deploy. The notes of a release are written by hand from `.github/RELEASE_TEMPLATE.md` (Highlights, Security, Added, Changed, Fixed, Removed / Deprecated, Known limitations, Operations, Full changelog).
  - **Scale-out is kept possible.** The web and the workers share only Redis (`REDIS_URL`) and the storage driver's root; `REDIS_URL` in the env secret replaces the Redis of the stack; `STORAGE_DRIVER` can be `s3` or `oci`; `--profile split` runs a worker per resource class, each with its own replica count and limits; the web port is per host.
  - **The jobs of the deploy workflow run on `ubuntu-24.04-arm` and on the self-hosted runner, the two exceptions to entry 110**: the images are built natively for arm64, and the deploy runs on the host itself.
  - **The deploy's smoke probe takes no file and charges nothing (#954).** `deploy.sh` asks for `GET /api/health/conversion` on the loopback port of the web service. The route converts a one-pixel PPM of its own to PNG through `dispatchConversion`, the dispatcher of `/api/convert`, so ImageMagick still runs in the sandboxed child that every native conversion starts in. It reads nothing of the request, so it reserves and charges no unit, and every start of a day passes it. The host nginx answers 404 for every path under `/api/health/` (`location ^~ /api/health/`), so the public port never forwards it; the readiness answer `/api/health` stays public. Until #954 the smoke posted the PPM to `/api/convert`, where it was an anonymous conversion of the address the framework fills in for a request without forwarding header (the bridge gateway), so under the allowance of 10 (entry 15) the 11th start of a UTC day would have been refused with 429, and an automatic rollback after it as well.
  - **Each release is smoked the way its own image says.** A rollback and a reconcile start an older release with the newest `deploy.sh`, so the smoke cannot be a property of the script. The web image names its smoke in the label `easyconvert.smoke-probe` (`Dockerfile.web`), and `deploy.sh` reads it with `docker image inspect` from the web image that the `images.env` of the release being started pins, as it reads the allowance label. A release whose label is the probe path gets the probe and then the check of the convert route (next paragraph). An image with no label at all, built before #954, gets the upload of the PPM to `/api/convert` it was deployed with, which spends one unit of the anonymous allowance of the bridge gateway, so a deploy or a rollback to such a release on a day whose 10 units are spent is refused with 429 as before. A reconcile does not smoke such a release: the hourly reconcile of a host whose `current` is unlabelled (after a deploy of an older `sha-` ref, or a rollback past #954) would spend the whole allowance by itself, and the release passed its smoke when it was deployed; the worker's namespaces are still checked. An absent label is told from an empty one, and an empty label, a label `deploy.sh` does not know and one it cannot read are all refused, so a new release whose probe fails is never smoked another way. `deploy()` reads the label of the new image together with the other checks of the pulled images, before the release directory is made and before `compose up`, so a refused label leaves the running stack alone. The legacy upload arm goes once the current and the previous release both declare the probe, which is when no rollback can reach an unlabelled image (`CONVERT_SMOKE_URL` stays for the route check). Label values the job log shows (this one, the allowance and the recorded base image) are written shell-quoted, since the log is public and a value can hold a line break.
  - **The convert route is checked without a conversion, and so without a charge (#671).** After the probe, `deploy.sh` posts a valid multipart upload (the one-pixel PPM, `targetFormat=png`) whose `options` field is `not-json`, to `/api/convert` on the loopback port, and requires 400 with the code `invalid_options`. The route reads the caller and applies the burst limit, reserves a unit, takes a concurrency slot, parses the form and checks the file, the target and the pair before it parses the options, and refuses them before it reads the file's bytes or starts an engine. The refused request gives the reservation back, and only a conversion that succeeded is charged (entry 15), so the check spends none of the allowance, and the route has no exemption, header or secret for it: it is an ordinary request that a public caller can send as well, and it is metered like one. What it proves is the guard and its key store, the reservation and its rollback, `acquireSyncSlot`, the multipart parser and the request wrappers; what it leaves to the probe is the engine and the sandbox, and what it leaves to the test suites is the spoof check and the answer of a successful conversion. Any other status, or another code, fails the start and is logged by its status only. It runs for the releases that declare the probe, on every start path, so the hourly reconcile also tells that the stack could not reach its key store.
  - **Every deploy checks the public block.** After the canonical host check it asks the public site through the nginx of the host, `curl --resolve <host>:443:127.0.0.1 https://<host>/api/health` for the host of the release's origin and requires 200 (the positive control: a site that is down, or answers every path with 404, proves nothing about the probe), then asks `https://<host>/api/health/conversion` through the same resolve and moves the links only on a 404. Any other answer fails the deploy and rolls back, so a host whose site file predates the block, or whose nginx does not answer, fails closed; the log says which of the two failed, and tells a forwarded probe (200, reinstall the site file) from another answer. The origin certificate is trusted by the CDN only, so the request does not check its chain; it reads the status of the local nginx and nothing else.
- **Why**:
  - **Measured load of the shared instance over 7 days** (hourly aggregates from OCI monitoring, read-only): CPU hourly mean 4.7% (maximum 5.4%); CPU hourly maximum 13% on average, 23% at the 95th percentile and 47% at most; memory hourly maximum 15.7% on average, 16.1% at the 95th percentile and 19.5% at most. On 4 OCPU and 24 GB that is about 0.2 OCPU on average with peaks near 1.9 OCPU, and at most about 4.7 GB.
  - **The other service is still in development at EasyConvert's launch**, so it needs little. 3.5 OCPU and 20 GiB leave 0.5 OCPU and 4 GiB for it and the operating system, and its measured peak of 4.7 GB is why the memory limits are hard.
  - **The worker's 14 GiB follows the repository's own sizing.** The input limits are sized for about 3.4 GiB per job (`src/lib/conversions/office/spreadsheet-limits.ts`, `src/lib/conversions/image-input-limit-config.ts`: 10 GiB shared by 3 jobs), and `docker-compose.yml` gives a memory-class worker 14 GiB. 4 jobs in 14 GiB keep each job at 3.5 GiB, so the heaviest office, video and raster jobs fit.
  - **One worker for every queue at launch, not one per resource class.** Each worker repeats the baseline memory of its engines, and one worker with four slots uses a budget this size without that. The class workers stay in the file behind a profile for later.
  - **A scratch directory without its own file system has no cap** on a volume the other service shares, and a tmpfs would be counted against the memory limit.
  - **A profile of the program's own is Ubuntu's documented way to grant a user namespace under the restriction** (the AppArmor `userns` rule of ABI 4.0); it changes nothing for the other service, while the sysctl is host-wide. Measured on an Ubuntu 24.04.5 VM with the restriction on and AppArmor 4.0.1: `unshare -r -n` fails unconfined and under Docker's default rules rendered on ABI 4.0 (`userns_create` denied), and succeeds under this profile with only a loopback interface in the new namespace; unix sockets still work, and AF_ALG and `mount` stay denied. On the production host, in a container, `docker-default` allows it too, because it is written for ABI 3.0; so the profile is not what makes conversions work today. It pins that behaviour against a later Docker or host change, and the smoke conversion is what decides.
  - **ABI 4.0 mediates more than 3.0** (`/etc/apparmor.d/abi/3.0` against `abi/4.0` of AppArmor 4.0.1, Ubuntu 24.04.5): user namespace creation (granted by the profile), POSIX message queues (no rule, so denied; no engine of the stack is known to use them), the capability `checkpoint_restore` and the network family `mctp` (both covered by `capability,` and `network,`, and the capabilities are dropped anyway), and policy-format features.
  - **Deploy checks and synthetic probes stay off the metered paths and off the public listener.** Kubernetes sends its probes from the kubelet to the container directly, or runs them as a command inside it, never through the ingress. A widely used Java application framework moves its management endpoints to a port of their own and, bound to 127.0.0.1, allows no remote connection. A self-hosted code forge lets only an allowlist of addresses (localhost by default) reach its readiness and liveness checks and exempts them from its request throttling. A managed cloud load balancer sends its target health checks straight to each target, on a health check port and path that can differ from the traffic's. All four keep the check out of the user's meter and off the public path, and none gives the checker a way to do a user's work. Here the probe is a path the reverse proxy does not forward, and it does no user work at all.
  - **The web process cannot see the socket peer, so the exemption is not an address check.** `next start` serves the App Router, whose handlers get a Web `Request` without its socket. The framework writes the peer into `X-Forwarded-For` only when the request carries none (`req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] ??= socket.remoteAddress` in `next/dist/server/base-server.js` of 15.5), so a direct caller names the address it wants, and a request from the host and one through nginx both arrive from the bridge gateway. A listener of its own would need a custom server, or a second server process in the web container's 5.6 GiB. A probe with a fixed input needs neither, and holds no exemption a caller could use, because it converts nothing the caller sends.
  - **nginx matches the normalized URI.** It decodes `%XX`, resolves `.` and `..` and merges slashes before it picks a location, and a `^~` prefix stops the regular expressions (the `location` directive of `ngx_http_core_module`). Run with the nginx 1.24.0 package of Ubuntu 24.04 in front of an upstream that records each request, none of nine spellings of the probe reached the upstream (`/api/%68ealth/conversion`, `/api/health%2Fconversion`, `//api//health/conversion`, `/api/x/../health/conversion`, forged `X-Forwarded-For`, `CF-Connecting-IP`, `X-Real-IP` and `Forwarded` among them) while `/api/health` did; with the previous site file all nine reached it.
  - **Versions per deploy and not per pull request**, because the deploy is what a user, a status page and a rollback can name; the merged pull requests between two deploys are one batch. SemVer rather than CalVer because the public API and the SDK need a compatibility signal, which a date does not give, and beta `0.y.z` keeps that signal honest while the interfaces still change.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A large file waits in the queue instead of being given more capacity.** Four heavy jobs at once can together pass the worker's 14 GiB; the kernel then kills the largest process of the container and that job fails, while `WORKER_MAX_RSS_MB` (4096) recycles a worker that grows past it between jobs. Raising the budget is the remedy.
  - **How long a result stays is set by the retention policy**, entry 125 (issue #665), through `RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS` (3600) and `RESULT_DELIVERED_GRACE_SECONDS` (600) in the env secret, and the disk it may use by `RESULT_DISK_HIGH_PERCENT` (85), `RESULT_DISK_LOW_PERCENT` (80) and `RESULT_DISK_REFUSE_PERCENT` (95). The compose file passes all five through and sets no default; the application's schema holds them, and the application reads them since PR #919 (the retention policy). The scratch cap bounds the worst case.
  - **A sync conversion that takes more than 100 seconds fails at the CDN's free plan (HTTP 524)**, although the application allows 120 seconds; such a conversion is started as a job and polled.
  - **The scratch cap is shared** by uploads, results and temporary files of both services; one runaway job can fill it and fail the others with ENOSPC.
  - **The free-caller concurrency limit is counted per web process** (issue #691), so a second web host would allow up to the limit on each.
  - **The AppArmor profile is installed by hand on the host** and must be loaded before a deploy; a container that names a profile that is not loaded does not start, and the deploy then returns to the previous release. Membership of the `docker` group, which the runner's user needs, is root-equivalent on the host, so the runner must take no job but the deploy: it has one label, and fork pull requests wait for approval. That is still trust and not a barrier: anyone who can push a workflow file to the repository, or approve a fork's run, can run code as root-equivalent on the shared host. Today that is the owner alone; narrowing the runner to a `sudoers` rule for `deploy.sh deploy|rollback|reconcile` is a row of the hardening backlog (#761).
  - **The failure dump of a deploy is public.** A failed release prints the last 80 lines of the web and worker logs into a public job log. The services are not meant to log a secret value, but nothing proves it for every error path. The nginx edge log follows the distribution's rotation, which has no size limit.
  - **The check of the convert route stops at the options.** It does not read the file's bytes, run the spoof check or convert, so a fault in those steps is held by the test suites and, for the engine, by the probe. It needs the key store and the queue: a route that cannot reserve answers 503 and fails the start, which is the point of the check. It passes the guard like any anonymous caller, so a start on a day when the bridge gateway's allowance is spent (only the unlabelled upload spends it) is refused with 429 at the reservation, as that upload is.
  - **Whatever reaches the web container's port directly can run the probe**: processes on the host and containers on the stack's networks. It converts one pixel and answers the same PNG every time. Callers at once share one conversion and its outcome, a failure included, is reused for 5 seconds, as the readiness verdict is (`HEALTH_CACHE_TTL_MS`), so calling it more often adds no conversion: at most one runs at a time, and the next starts 5 seconds after its verdict, and not before its conversion has ended (a conversion that ignores the abort at its 30-second deadline keeps the place, and callers meanwhile get the 504 it gave). The readiness verdict and this one share one helper (`src/lib/health/verdict-memo.ts`) with a reset hook for tests. The edge middleware's per-address limit does not bound it, because a direct caller names its own `X-Forwarded-For`; that rotation on the loopback port predates #954 and is a #671 row.
  - **A cancelled deploy is restarted on the previous release without waiting**, because the runner kills the job seconds after the cancel; a cut-short restart is repaired by `deploy.sh reconcile` (by hand, or the hourly cron line), which starts the current release from its pinned images. Deploying the current ref again would not repair a release of the ref `main`.
  - **The size of the other service's data on the data volume was not measured**; the 15 GiB free-space gate and the 12 GiB scratch cap are set so that a deploy stops instead of filling it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A second instance, a bigger instance or another volume**: adds cost; QA ruled it out for launch.
  - **A bucket for uploads and results**: a paid-tier dependency and files outside our disk; the retention settings of entry 125 with a lifecycle rule as a backstop are the scale-out plan instead.
  - **tmpfs for the scratch**: counted against the memory limits, and a large video or archive would need the memory twice.
  - **Redis without persistence**: loses accounts and keys at every restart.
  - **A prune of images and containers on the host**: it would reach the other service's images.
  - **CalVer** (a date as the version): says when and not whether an interface broke, which a public API and an SDK need.
  - **A version for every merged pull request**: floods the release list, and a version no one deployed can be neither rolled back to nor named in an incident.
  - **Turning `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns` off**, as the CI runners do: it lifts the restriction for every program of the shared host, the other service included.
  - **`apparmor=unconfined` for the containers**: drops Docker's deny rules for `/proc`, `/sys` and `mount` along with the restriction.
  - **A logrotate stanza for the edge log**: the distribution's `/etc/logrotate.d/nginx` already covers `/var/log/nginx/*.log`, and logrotate skips a log that two stanzas name.
  - **Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 or DNS-01**: port 80 is closed, and DNS-01 stores a token with DNS write access on the host.
  - **A separate web image with its own engines**: duplicates several gigabytes; the web image is one layer on the worker image.
  - **An exemption in the guard for a header or an address the smoke sends**: a header is written by the client, and the address a route sees is the one a direct caller writes into `X-Forwarded-For`.
  - **A shared secret the smoke sends and the guard checks**: it puts an unmetered path into the guard behind a value that lives in the env file and the container; a leak makes it public. The fixed-input probe and the refused upload have nothing to leak.
  - **A deploy-only header, or a setting, that makes `/api/convert` skip the charge for the route check** (the first design #954's review offered): the check would run a real conversion through the guard with a bypass in it, a new secret in the env file and a branch that production never takes otherwise. A request that is refused after the reservation reaches the same code and charges nothing by the rule that already exists.
  - **The route check as `compose exec` into the web container** (also offered in review): it needs no label, but the request still comes from the container's own address and is charged to it like any upload, and it runs the check where the host's proxy and port mapping are not.
  - **An account or API key for the smoke with a large allowance**: still metered, and a fresh host has no such account until someone creates it.
  - **`allow 127.0.0.1; deny all;` instead of `return 404`**: `allow` reads the client address after the real-IP module, which takes it from `CF-Connecting-IP`, so the rule would rest on a header.
  - **Standalone Next.js output**: `next.config.mjs` turns file tracing off, and the worker image already holds the production modules with the library build it pins.
- **Verified by**: `tests/oci-deploy.test.ts` (loopback-only ports, no published Redis, the hardening keys with the AppArmor profile, `oom_score_adj` and an `nproc` above the sum of every `pids_limit`, the profile's ABI, `userns`, `unix` and Docker's deny rules, the limits and their sum, the scale-out shape, the nginx site, the workflow's single runner label, the `exec` of its deploy steps and its build trigger evaluated path by path with a matcher that does not skip dot files (the workflow files and `.dockerignore` build, `CHANGELOG.md` and the release template do not), the allowlist with the two retention keys, and `deploy.sh` run against stand-ins: a dropped env line logged by number only, also an upper-case fragment such as a base64 padding, refs other than `main` and `sha-<40 hex>` refused before any call, an unusable budget, a web image built on another worker checked on the pinned digest, a profile file that differs from the loaded one, a container under another profile, a worker that cannot create its namespaces, the smoke asked of `/api/health/conversion` with no form, followed by one upload to `/api/convert` whose options are `not-json` that must be refused 400 `invalid_options` (another status or another code rolls the release back), with only the HTTP status logged on a failed or non-PNG answer, the upload to `/api/convert` without that field for a release whose web image has no `easyconvert.smoke-probe` label (a deploy of such a ref, the automatic rollback and the manual rollback to one), a reconcile of an unlabelled `current` that sends ## 123. Speed parity runs nightly on main, and a pull request runs its checks once per head commit

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #649, epic #763), decided 2026-10-30 (QA decision: the project is in development, not in operation). It supersedes the speed checks of a pull request in entry 17 and the label rule restated in entry 47. Extended on 2026-10-31 (QA request) with the rule for absolute time bounds in the pull request suites.
- **Decision**:
  - **Speed parity is not a pull request check.** The `parity-speed` job leaves `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `verify` no longer reads the `automerge` label, and the label only arms auto-merge. The nightly `bench-parity-speed` job measures every family on `main` and judges each row against its recorded history and the reference, as it already did. A failing night opens or updates the `nightly-regression` issue (`report-failure.yml`), which now lists the commits since the last successful run of the same workflow on the same branch, newest first, at most 50, with the compare view for the rest. Those commits are the suspects: the regression is fixed or the commit reverted after the merge.
  - **A speed comparison before the merge is on request.** `gh workflow run nightly.yml --ref <branch> -f ab_base_ref=main` measures the speed rows of the branch against `main` in the same pairs (`bench-ab-speed`, one shard per family), with the acknowledged slowdowns of entry 92. Nothing requires it.
  - **The pull request workflow starts on `opened`, `synchronize` and `reopened` only.** It used to start on `labeled` and `unlabeled` too, so adding the `automerge` label cancelled the run and started all 37 jobs again. Now each head commit runs once: the change filter, the static checks and build, six test shards, the conformance gate in four parts (was ten), the integration and container jobs, quality parity for the changed families, and `verify`. That is 17 jobs, under the 20 standard jobs the account can run at once.
  - **The changed families are read against the first parent of the merge commit under test.** The event's base sha can be another commit of `main` than the one the merge was made with, and a diff against it counted the commits between the two as changes of the pull request: run 41045586315 measured all 13 families for a change of four. The other base reads of the workflow already used the first parent.
  - **The duration tables of the shards were refreshed from that run's recordings** (`.github/ci/test-durations.json`, `.github/ci/conformance-durations.json`, with the `--update` commands of `scripts/ci-test-shards.mjs` and `scripts/ci-conformance-parts.mjs`). The conformance table had not been refreshed since #639: its parts planned 223 s each and ran from 70 s to 281 s. The registry-wide checks that only part 1 runs now record 1.7 s, not 89 s.
  - **The `security` label is read when parity quality runs.** A change of that label takes effect with the next push.
  - **The speed shard check of the `changes` job is removed** (`scripts/ci-parity-shards.mjs`). It made sure a pull request that edits a speed gap entry had a speed shard to back it. The nightly run measures every family and backs every entry.
  - **A time bound in a file the pull request gate runs is a hang guard, and a guard sits 20 times above the time the work takes on a fast core.** A shared x64 runner under shard load measured about 5 times slower than an Apple-silicon laptop, so a bound within a small factor of the local time fails without a regression: the merged-range case of `tests/xlsx-element-bounds.test.ts` read 10,630 and 12,211 ms of CPU against 10 s (the test takes 2.4 s on the laptop, 1.7 s of it CPU in the reader), a first request through the convert route timed out at the 5 s default of a test, and a timer floor of 7 ms read 6.977. A claim that needs a tighter bound (the cost of reading a sheet that lists three million ranges, the CPU time of the quantizer at 1.92 megapixels) lives in a `.perf.test.ts` file and runs in the nightly workflow, which is where a timing claim belongs: behavioural assertions (the count of kept ranges, the refusal and its status) stay in the pull request suite.
  - **`expectWithinHangGuard` makes the author state the time and refuses a guard under 20 times it.** `tests/helpers/timing.ts` takes `{ guardMs, expectedLocalMs }` and throws before it compares anything when `guardMs < 20 * expectedLocalMs`, whatever this machine measured, so the check cannot flake. The cases of `tests/dxf-clip-region.test.ts`, `dxf-pen-attributes`, `pdf-object-stream-leading-white`, `pdf-text-partial-tounicode` and `font-type1-reader` that had a bound 11 to 17 times above their local time use it with the 10 s guard of the file (20 s for the map-copy cases of 0.7 s); the refusal each case expects is what pins the limit, and the guard only stops a hang.
  - **Rule G7 of the anti-cheat guard refuses any other absolute bound on a measured time in a pull request suite.** It reads `expect(<time read from a clock, or named ms, elapsed, cpuMs, heldMs>).toBeLessThan(OrEqual)(<bound>)` in every `*.test.ts` file that is not a `.perf.test.ts` file, and passes the bound only when it is a constant named `..._HANG_GUARD_MS`, a point in time (`Date.now() + ...`) or, for anything that reads CPU time, never: CPU time is a claim about the work and goes through `expectWithinHangGuard`. Rule G7b refuses a `..._HANG_GUARD_MS` constant under 10 s. The existing bounds are in the ratchet baseline (`scripts/anti-cheat-baseline.json`, 126 entries in 57 files, each with the margin measured on 2026-10-31, and 14 read and not measured): 69 of them sit 50 or more times above the local time, 15 sit 20 to 50 times above, and 28 sit under 20 times: 23 are waits the test sets (a deadline or a kill timeout, which a slow runner does not stretch), 3 are bounds computed from a reference measured in the same run, and 2 are the event-loop CPU time against the product budget of 100 ms. The baseline can only shrink.
  - **A merged range past the bound costs the decoding of the file and nothing more, and the column definitions and rows are looked for where the schema puts them.** The reader already ended the scan for `mergeCell` and `hyperlink` at the bound. The scans for `cols` and for the rows walked the whole sheet part, millions of `mergeCell` elements after the cell data included; the sheet is now split at `sheetData` (ECMA-376 Part 1, 18.3.1.99) as SheetJS splits it (xlsx 0.18.5, `parse_ws_xml`, xlsx.js lines 14527 to 14532, with `cols` read from the part before the cell data at lines 14552 to 14556). On the 3 million range sheet the best CPU time of 6 runs falls from 1,694 to 1,381 ms; a sheet that lists 1,048,576 ranges falls from 1,046 to 902 ms. What is left is the work of keeping a million ranges and the check that the part is well formed XML (policy entry 113), which both need the whole part.
  - **A test that starts an engine names the timeout that only stops a hang.** A malformed legacy document is handed to the office suite when one is installed (`src/worker/libreoffice-pool.ts`), which starts a process: 1.1 s on the laptop and 2.3 s for the first request of a process, over the 5 s default of a test on a loaded runner. The case that answers 400 for a malformed file has its own test and the 60 s engine timeout of the suite; the case that answers 422 for an encrypted file does not start an engine and keeps the default. The first request of the routing classifier of the conformance gate loads the readers it dispatches to (0.9 s) and is made in a `beforeAll` with its own timeout.
  - **A timer floor has room for the clock that reads it.** The stub of `tests/bench-ab-host.test.ts` sleeps 8 ms and the timed call read 6.977; the floor is half the sleep. The pool case that two tasks run on two threads compares the start and end each task reports (each starts before the other ends) and no longer a total of 550 ms for two 300 ms spins.
- **Why it is right in practice**:
  - **Development stage.** No user depends on the speed of a deployed build yet. A regression found the next morning costs a revert or a fix, not an incident.
  - **Post-merge performance tracking is the usual practice for large projects.** Browser engines, compilers and language runtimes run their performance suites on the main branch per commit or per night, and bisect a regression to a commit range afterwards. Per-change timing gates are rare because shared runners are noisy and timing runs are long.
  - **Queue cost.** One conversion change used to run the whole workflow twice (on the push and again when the label was added), up to 37 jobs each time. Jobs above 20 queue, and with two or three pull requests open every run waited for runners. The measured wall time of one uncontested run was about 17 minutes; time to merge was 30 to 60 minutes.
  - **Timing assertions are noisy on shared runners, so established projects keep them out of the blocking path.** Timing checks that are tied to the speed of a core run on a quiet machine after the merge or in a non-blocking job, a bound that stays in the blocking path is sized as a ceiling that only a hang reaches, and a failed timing check is not retried until it passes, since a retry hides the information a flaky bound gives. This repository already works that way (entry 112 and `tests/helpers/timing.ts`); the incidents were bounds that did not.
  - **The audit.** 255 test files with a time bound or a timing helper were run once on the laptop with the matchers recorded (7,413 numeric comparisons, 190 of the 216 lines of the static search reached); the cases whose tools or samples are not installed on the laptop (the qpdf runner, the DWG fuzz, the OCCT samples, the native bzip2 and deflate children) were read and not measured and are marked so in the baseline.
- **Benefits and trade-offs**:
  - A pull request merges about 10 minutes after its last push (the longest job: quality parity at about 10 minutes, the test shards at about 9), estimated from the step times of run 41045586315 with no queueing. Runner time per conversion change falls from about 320 to about 110 minutes.
  - The cost: a speed regression merges, and `main` is slower until the nightly run finds it and someone fixes or reverts the change. The nightly run of a quiet day measures it within 24 hours; the report names the commits to look at.
  - The cost: a speed gap entry a pull request adds to `bench/parity-gaps.json` is no longer backed by a run of that pull request. The nightly run judges it against the history, and review must read it.
  - Four conformance parts run about 8 minutes each instead of 4; they still end before the test shards.
  - The cost of the 20 times rule: a hang guard of 10 s no longer fails a quadratic reader that takes 3 s. The refusals, counts and statuses the cases assert catch a reader that lost its limit; the growth of the cost is the claim of the nightly ratio suites.
  - The cost of the baseline: 126 absolute bounds stay until they are moved or sized by the rule, and the 28 under 20 times (listed with their margin) are read again when one of them fails on a runner.
  - The two event-loop cases that sit at 14 and 15 times (7.3 and 6.8 ms against the 100 ms budget of the product) are kept: the budget is the claim and cannot be widened.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A separate speed workflow started by the `automerge` label, with its own required check**: keeps the merge gate, but still costs up to 16 jobs and about 11 minutes per merge, for a number the nightly run measures anyway at this stage.
  - **An opt-in `speed-check` label workflow**: the hand-started nightly comparison above already measures a branch against `main`, so a second workflow would duplicate it.
  - **Fewer test shards**: the test shards are the longest jobs after quality parity; fewer would lengthen every run.
  - **Conformance of the changed families only**: the conformance gate has no map from a registry pair to a benchmark family yet; it stays whole until one exists.
  - **Retries of a failed timing case (`retry` in the vitest configuration)**: it passes whenever the runner is quieter the second time, so the bound keeps its fault and the pull request loses the signal.
  - **Raising the 10 s of the merged-range case, or the 5 s default of every test**: the first hides a reader that costs a second of CPU for nothing, the second lets every hang wait longer for no case that needs it.
  - **A guard that compares the measurement with the margin at run time**: it fails on the slow runner it is meant to protect against; the margin is checked on the numbers the author states.
- **Verified by**: `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts` (the triggers, the four conformance parts, the job count of every workflow, and the report script run against a stand-in client: the suspects newest first, the cap of 50, no earlier good run, a good run on the same commit), `tests/ci-parity-workflow.test.ts` (no label event and no speed run in the pull request workflow, the `verify` gate against result sets, and the family mapping run against real git repositories: a later `main` named by the event no longer adds families), `tests/ci-conformance-parts.test.ts`, `tests/container-ci-job.test.ts`, `tests/sharp-libvips-build.test.ts`, `actionlint` on every workflow, and the run of this pull request, `tests/timing-helpers.test.ts` (a guard under 20 times the stated time is refused before the measurement is read), `tests/guard-anti-cheat-rules.test.ts` (rules G7 and G7b, among them the CPU time of the work against a hang-guard constant, which is the form of the merged-range case), `tests/xlsx-element-bounds.test.ts` (a sheet with prefixed elements still gives its columns and rows) and `tests/xlsx-element-bounds.perf.test.ts` (a reader that takes every range reads 2.64 times the cost of a sheet just past the bound against the limit of 2).
- **Revisit when**: the service is in operation and a user depends on its speed (then speed parity returns to the merge gate, as a label-started workflow with its own required check), the nightly run misses a regression for more than one night, or runner concurrency rises above the jobs two pull requests start together; a runner measures a pull request case that the baseline lists above 10 times its bound (then it is moved or sized by the rule); or the baseline has not shrunk in a quarter.

## 124. Rows of the nightly refusals of 2026-10-30: an Outlook message is read, a PDF becomes an EPUB from its blocks, an encrypted package is named as encrypted, and binary sources are never text

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, rows of the real-world run of 2026-10-30: 508 of 18,797 jobs refused), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: triage the refusals, fix the gaps).
- **Decision**:
  - **An Outlook message (`.msg`) is read as [MS-OXMSG] lays it out and written as text**: `From`, `To`, `Cc`, `Bcc`, `Date` and `Subject` lines, a blank line, the body, and a list of the attachments by name and size. Before, the bytes of the compound file were decoded as UTF-8 and written as the "text": a `.txt`, an HTML page and a ZIP of 29 KB of mojibake, and a PDF that failed on the first glyph no font has (`U+0871`, the compound file's signature). The body is the plain-text property; when it is empty the HTML property (read with the page's own encoding rules), then the compressed RTF property ([MS-OXRTFCP]: the 207-byte dictionary, the checksum of the specification, the raw size limited to 64 MiB). A string stored as 8-bit text is decoded in the code page the message states (`PR_INTERNET_CPID`, else `PR_MESSAGE_CODEPAGE`, else Windows-1252; a value of 0 or below is unset and the next property stands). The code pages read are the Windows ones (1250 to 1258, 874, 932, 936, 949, 950, 10000), 20127, 20866, 28591 to 28605, 65001, and the Unicode and East Asian ones of mail: 1200 (UTF-16LE), 50220 (ISO-2022-JP), 51932 and 20932 (EUC-JP) and 54936 (GB18030); a code page the decoder does not know is refused with a typed 400. An RTF body that holds no text is the normal shape of a message that only carries attachments, so it gives an empty body (the headers and the attachment list are written); an RTF body that cannot be read (a checksum or size that does not match, a code page or bytes the RTF reader refuses) is left out with a conversion warning, not a refusal of the message. A recipient is taken from its recipient storage (SMTP address first), else from the display lists; an Exchange address (`EX`), of a sender or a recipient, is left out unless the message carries the SMTP one (one rule for both). At most 10,000 recipients and attachments are listed. A compound file with no message property stream is refused (typed 400).
  - **A source with no reader is refused, never written as text.** The fallback of the text writers (`toString('utf-8')`), in the document and the office routes alike, now runs the guard the other office sources already had (`assertReadableAsText`), after the one source that has a reader of its own (`.msg`) and the text sources that declare UTF-16 (below): a compound file, ZIP or 7z container, or a file with a null byte in its first 4 KiB, is refused with the typed "fail-closed against mojibake" answer. DjVu (`.djvu`, `.djv`) was the second source that fell through to it (471,000 characters of mojibake for a 0.5 MB book to `txt`); it is now a typed refusal until a reader exists (see Revisit when). A text source (`txt`, `text`, `md`, `log`, `rst`, `man`) that starts with a UTF-16 byte order mark is decoded with `decodeTextInput` before the guard, for every target; a source with no reader that merely starts with the same two bytes is still binary and still refused.
  - **A PDF becomes an EPUB from the block model the PDF reader built**, as it already became a DOCX. The EPUB used to be written from the structured text of the document, parsed again as Markdown with the limits of a user's Markdown (1 MiB of source, 100,000 blocks, 20 levels of nesting). A row of numbers (`50. 50. 108. 45. ...` in a table of station assignments) opened one nested list per number and was refused as "nesting exceeds the 20 level limit", and the 345-page and 357-page books of the sample hit the size and block limits. calibre writes MOBI, AZW3, PDB, LRF and OEB from this EPUB (entry 118), so seven refused jobs and the EPUB of three files are fixed together. The Markdown limits stand for Markdown a caller sends.
  - **A password-protected `.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx` (and their macro, template and slide-show variants) is refused as encrypted (typed 422)**, not as a spoofed extension, on `POST /api/v1/jobs`, `POST /api/v1/convert` and `POST /api/convert` alike (the jobs route answered a 400 "Stored object is unavailable" and the two convert routes a 400 until their spoof catches asked `isUnprocessableInputError`). Office writes the encrypted package into a compound file with the entries `EncryptionInfo` and `EncryptedPackage` ([MS-OFFCRYPTO] 2.1); the signature rules took that for a forged upload ("initial magic bytes indicate application/x-cfbf"). The names are read from the directory of the file where it lies, for a buffer, a file on disk (at the offsets of the directory sectors) and an object in a store (by range requests), through the reader the compound-only formats already use (entry 103). A compound file without both entries, and any other extension, is still refused as a spoof.
  - **An EOT font reads its header flags.** A font compressed with MicroType Express (flag 0x4) is refused by that name (it was refused as a font "with no glyph outlines"); font data XOR-encrypted with 0x50 (flag 0x10000000) is decoded; font data that is no sfnt, or that the header declares larger than the file, is refused where the reader used to make a font of the raw bytes of the file.
  - **A PDF page that holds only its number converts to hOCR and ALTO.** A page below the density threshold is recognized instead of read; when recognition finds nothing on it, the page now takes its word boxes from its own text layer (the way the pages above the threshold do), where the document used to be refused with "hOCR/ALTO need word geometry: page 2 has text but no recognized lines".
- **Refusals that stand** (each checked with an independent reader; the table is in the pull request): 31 workbooks, documents and slide shows that print more than 500 pages to page images (entry 44); the corrupt, truncated or fuzzed Office files that LibreOffice 26.8 and `7z` refuse as well; the password-protected legacy files LibreOffice cannot open either; the videos that `ffprobe` shows no audio stream in; the PDFs `qpdf --check` cannot repair; the classic HFS volumes, the tokenizing ZIP method and the damaged disk image that 7-Zip refuses; the `.doc` files that LibreOffice 24.2 refuses and 26.8 reads (an engine version, recorded in entry 97, not worked around).
- **Why**:
  - **References.** [MS-OXMSG] 2.1 to 2.4 for the streams and the property table; Apache POI HSMF `MAPIMessage` and Apache Tika `OutlookExtractor` for the fallback order of the body and the recipients (both Apache License 2.0, behaviour followed, no code copied); [MS-OXRTFCP] 2.1 for the compressed RTF, checked on the real messages (the raw sizes their headers declare, and the words of one RTF found in its plain body); [MS-OFFCRYPTO] 2.1 for the encrypted package; libeot `eot2ttf` and the EOT member submission for the header flags. The EPUB follows the DOCX route of the same reader. The text of the two real messages is checked against the streams that `7z x` extracts from them (the body streams are pinned by SHA-256 in the tests).
  - **A refusal is worth more than a file nobody can read.** The `.msg`, `.djvu` and `.djv` outputs were counted as good by the corpus run, which checks the type of an output and not its content, so the garbage was invisible until the PDF path failed on it.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **An attachment of a message is listed, not extracted.** The list gives the name and the size; the attachments are not packed into the ZIP target, which holds the text of the message as the other text sources do.
  - **A `.txt` that really holds NUL bytes (UTF-16 text without a byte order mark) is refused by the guard** where the writers used to produce text with NUL characters; a UTF-16 file with a byte order mark is read as text for `txt`, `text`, `md`, `log`, `rst` and `man` (any target). A UTF-16LE mark (`FF FE`) is still turned away earlier, by the signature rules, which take those two bytes for an MPEG audio frame; that refusal is older than this entry and unchanged.
  - **A `.msg` is offered as `pdf`, `html`, `txt` and `zip` only.** The office text extractor reads a message too (so a later target needs no second reader), but the registry does not advertise `docx`, `odt` or `epub` for it.
  - **The EPUB of a PDF no longer carries the Markdown renderer's escaping**: its text is the text of the model, as in the DOCX.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Raising the Markdown limits for PDF text**: the limits are a safety boundary for Markdown a caller sends, and the nesting fault is text read as markup, which no limit repairs.
  - **Escaping the first marker of every paragraph of the structured text**: the structured text is also the text of other writers that show it as it is.
  - **Keeping the spoof answer for an encrypted package**: the file is what its extension says, and the caller can act on "encrypted" (remove the password), not on "spoofed".
  - **Reading a `.msg` through the office suite**: LibreOffice imports it as plain text (the same mojibake).
- **Verified by**: `tests/outlook-message.test.ts` (a body of 50,000 and 200,000 spaces then a letter in CPU time linear in the length (red before: 15.8 times for 4 times the input), an attachment-only message with an empty RTF body, a damaged RTF body that warns, the new code pages, a code page of 0 or below, code pages no decoder reads (typed 400), Exchange addresses of recipients and the office text of a message; the three real messages to text, HTML, PDF and ZIP, headers and attachment counts pinned and the body streams of `7z x` pinned by SHA-256; messages built from the properties: recipients by kind, the date, an Exchange sender, an 8-bit string in code page 1251, the HTML and compressed RTF bodies; the checksum, size and cut-off refusals of the RTF decompressor; a Word document named `.msg`, bytes that are no compound file, and a DjVu header refused to `txt` and `pdf`), `tests/pdf-to-epub-model.test.ts` (red on the base: a row of numbers and the three real PDFs, 71 to 357 pages), `tests/encrypted-ooxml-package.test.ts` (buffer, file on disk and object in a store, six extensions, the real files with the typed error), `tests/encrypted-document-routes.test.ts` (the jobs route and both convert routes answer 422 for an encrypted package and 400 for a Word document named `.xlsx`), `tests/text-source-utf16.test.ts` (UTF-16 text sources of both byte orders, and the binary sources that start with the same bytes), `tests/office-html-text-linear.test.ts` (the blanks before a line break cut in one pass: red with the old pattern, which took 42.9 s for 300,000 tabs), `tests/font-eot-flags.test.ts` (the XOR flag round trip, the compressed flag, a lying size, the two real IBM Plex EOT files), `tests/pdf-hocr-sparse-page.test.ts` (red on the base: a page with a text layer and no recognizable ink, and the real 32-page report).
- **Revisit when**: a DjVu reader is added (the reference service's `ddjvu` and `djvutxt` from djvulibre, or a decoder of IW44 and JB2); an Outlook attachment should be extracted into the ZIP target; MicroType Express decompression is added (libeot, MPL 2.0, decodes it); a UTF-16 text source without a byte order mark must be read (then `decodeTextInput` for it).

## 125. Results are deleted after delivery: a result goes ten minutes after its first complete download or an hour after it was stored, and an upload goes ten minutes after the last job that reads it ends

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #665, row "file retention and deletion"), decided 2026-10-30 (QA request: the service keeps no user files; input and output are deleted right after the result is delivered, and an undelivered result expires soon).
- **Decision**:
  - **A result lives until the first of two times.** `RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS` (default 3600, 60 to 86400) after it was stored, when nobody downloaded it completely. `RESULT_DELIVERED_GRACE_SECONDS` (default 600, 1 to 3600) after its **first complete delivery**. The grace period never extends the first time. After either, the object is deleted from storage and the download answers **410 Gone** to its owner (404 to anyone else, as before) for a further day, then 404.
  - **Delivered means the server handed every byte to the connection.** One 200 response whose body was handed over to its end, or responses whose handed-over bytes together cover byte 0 to the last byte (the ranges are merged and kept per result, at most 32 pieces; a client that needs more is never counted and the result expires after the undelivered time). The body is read from storage only when the connection asks for more (`src/lib/api/delivery-stream.ts`), so the bytes counted are the bytes enqueued for it; the delivery counts when the source ended and exactly the expected number of bytes went out, and the record is written before the body closes. A response the client drops counts the prefix it handed over, so a download resumed from where it stopped, or parallel ranges, add up to a delivery; a read of the source still waiting when the client left adds nothing. A tail range alone and a 416 do not count. The server cannot see what the client's network stack did with the bytes after that; the grace period covers a client that lost the end.
  - **A proxy in front must not buffer file responses.** A buffering proxy takes the whole body at once, so a slow client would look delivered while it is still receiving. The download route sends `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, which nginx honours per response; any other proxy must stream `/api/storage/file/` responses unbuffered.
  - **Inputs.** An uploaded input (`uploads/...`) is held for every job or graph that reads it, taken just before the job is queued and ended when that job completes, fails for the last time (a retry that may still run keeps it) or is cancelled, or when that graph has completed, failed or been cancelled; it is deleted by the sweep `RESULT_DELIVERED_GRACE_SECONDS` after the last hold ended (each end starts the period again, but never past a day after the upload was first read), and its record is forgotten at once, so a client that uploads once and converts to several formats, one after another or at the same time, finds it for each of them, and a request for another format a moment after the last job still works. A hold on an upload ends at the latest a day after the upload was first read, however late another job reads it. An upload that no hold was ever taken on keeps its own lifetime, and one whose hold never ends is deleted after a day. Early deletion for space never deletes an upload. An output of the user chained as an input (`conversions/...`, `results/...`) is theirs and follows the rules above.
  - **One rule for every driver.** The records live in Redis when `REDIS_URL` or `REDIS_HOST` is set (keys under `easyconvert:retention:`) and in `<EASYCONVERT_STORAGE_DIR>/.retention` otherwise (`src/lib/storage/retention-ledger.ts`), shared by every web instance and worker. A change of a record is atomic: a compare-and-set script in Redis, retried after a random wait that doubles per attempt (2 ms base, 100 ms cap) so writers that raced spread out, and for the file ledger a lock file per record plus per-key ordering in the process. The lock file holds a token of its holder, which removes it only while it still holds that token; a lock older than 30 seconds is moved out of the way by an atomic rename, and put back when it turns out to be one taken just then. Every Redis command times out after 5 seconds; while Redis cannot be reached, the calls share one wait of 2 seconds for the connection and then fail at once for 5 seconds, and a sweep that is still running after 50 seconds is logged as slow and never given up, so a process has at most one sweep running and the next starts when it ends. Each web instance and each worker sweeps every minute and once at start (after the Redis connection is ready), never two sweeps at once in a process, through `IStorageBackend.deleteObject`, so `local`, `s3` and `oci` behave the same; a restart changes nothing, because a result whose time has passed is found by the next sweep, and the download route answers 410 for it before that, also when deleting it right then fails. A deletion marks the record gone in the same atomic change that checks the result may still go, and deletes the object after it, so a job that took the result in the meantime keeps it. A key due without a record is dropped from the sweep; an object whose deletion fails reopens its record, retried up to three times with a pause that doubles from 100 ms when the ledger fails too, and is tried again after five minutes, behind the keys due by then, and is not counted as deleted. A process that stops between marking the record gone and deleting the object, or a ledger that stays down through all three attempts, leaves an object that no sweep finds again; the lifetime the object was stored with (`RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS` for a result, a day for an upload) and the bucket rule below are the backstop that removes it. Deleting an object that a delivered result, an upload or an early deletion expected, and that is already gone, is logged with the key on the local drivers; an expired result's object leaves storage at the same time as its record and is not logged. An S3-compatible store answers the delete of a missing key with 204, like a delete that found the object, so on `s3` and `oci` the line does not appear. Each deletion in the store and each measurement of the disk is given up after 30 seconds and counts as failed, so one call that never answers cannot stop every later deletion of the process.
  - **A hold keeps the object, not only the record.** The object is stored with the lifetime of its record (an hour for a result, a day for an upload), and the storage removes an expired object by itself. Taking a hold therefore raises that lifetime to the end of the hold (`IStorageBackend.extendExpiry`, called by `holdResultForJob` for the storage the sweep was started with), so the storage does not remove a result or an upload under a job that still reads it, however long the job runs. On the local drivers the new expiry is written into the expiry file next to the object on the shared disk and into the copy in memory; a process whose own copy says the object expired reads that file again before it removes anything, so a worker that saved the result honours an extension made by the web server. The hold ending does not shorten it again: the record decides, and the sweep deletes the object when the record says so; the longer lifetime is only the backstop for a sweep that never ran. The object-store drivers (`s3`, `oci`) keep the expiry in the object's metadata, which cannot be changed in place without copying the object onto itself (a copy is capped at 5 GiB per request and was not checked against both providers), so there a result held past its stored lifetime is still removed by the read check; this is left for the change that moves results to an object store, and does not apply to the local driver the launch runs on.
  - **The ledger failing does not fail downloads.** A result is registered right after it is stored; when the record cannot be written, the object is deleted again and the request or job fails, so no object is left that no sweep finds. A record that cannot be read leaves the state unknown: the file is served from storage while it is there, the job record leaves `retention` out, and the account list shows the file. Keys the rule does not cover (uploads) never read the ledger.
  - **Results are deleted early when the disk runs full (local driver).** Each sweep measures, with `statfs` (use as `df` reports it), the file system of `EASYCONVERT_STORAGE_DIR`, where results live. Above `RESULT_DISK_HIGH_PERCENT` (default 85) it deletes results until the use is at or below `RESULT_DISK_LOW_PERCENT` (default 80): delivered results in their grace period first, the earliest delivery first, then undelivered results, the oldest first.
