- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the OGG row of entry 105), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: beat the reference on every conversion to Ogg Vorbis with the same audio). It changes the sentence "no patch is applied" of entry 105 to one patch.
- **Decision**:
  - **`libavcodec/libvorbisenc.c` of the pinned FFmpeg is patched** (`scripts/ffmpeg-patches/libvorbis-whole-frames.patch`, 280 lines with its commit message, one file). The encoder no longer states `frame_size` 64, it takes frames of any size (`AV_CODEC_CAP_VARIABLE_FRAME_SIZE`), and it returns its packets through `receive_packet`, so a call can return every packet the samples of a frame complete (it returned one per call, which is why frames had to be small). The packet buffer grows where it used to fail with `AVERROR_BUG`. The encoder still owns `frame_size`: init sets it to 0 where it used to set 64, so a size the caller sets (`-frame_size`, which made fftools 9.0.2 abort on the variable-size encoder in `ffmpeg_sched.c` line 1845) is cleared and the stream is the same as before. The build stops unless the encoder writes the same Ogg stream, more than 10 KB and starting with `OggS`, from a six-channel source cut into frames of 64, 7, 100 and 100,000 samples; each run must succeed, so an encoder that fails the same way for every size does not pass.
  - **The stream is the same because libvorbis is still given the same calls.** The packets libvorbis writes depend on how the samples are split across `vorbis_analysis_wrote` calls: a stream cut into calls of 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048 or 4096 samples differs from the one cut into 64 (by 3 to 30 bytes in 875,610, in packets near the start and again later). So the wrapper cuts every frame into the calls of 64 samples that the required frame size made, carries the rest of a frame to the next one (`LIBVORBIS_CHUNK_SIZE`, `libvorbis_send_frame`), writes the last short call at the end of the stream, and runs `vorbis_analysis_blockout` after each call as before. Packet timestamps come from `AudioFrameQueue` as before, which tracks samples and not frames.
  - **The install script applies the patch and checks it.** `scripts/install-ffmpeg.sh` holds the file name and SHA-256 of each patch (`FFMPEG_PATCHES`), checks the digest, applies it with `patch -p1 --forward --fuzz=0` after the archive is unpacked and before it is configured (a source that differs fails the build: the patch does not apply to 7.1.5, its dry run fails 5 of 9 hunks), and after the build fails it unless `ffmpeg -h encoder=libvorbis` lists the `variable` capability and the stream of a 3 s noise source is the same for `asetnsamples` of 64, 100 and 100,000. The patch text is installed into `/usr/share/doc/ffmpeg/patches`, and the source note and the tool-versions manifest name it. `Dockerfile.worker` copies `scripts/ffmpeg-patches` beside the script and installs `patch`.
  - **Upgrading FFmpeg** (header of the script): apply the patches to the new archive; a patch whose change the release already holds is dropped, any other is rebased and its digest changed; then run the media tests with the new build. Cost of the carry: one diff of 251 lines against one file, and a security fix upstream makes to that file is ours to merge (a release that touches the file fails the patch, which is the alarm).
- **Why**:
  - **The cause, measured.** FFmpeg 9 cuts a stream into frames of the size the encoder states in a synchronisation queue of the scheduler (`fftools/ffmpeg_mux_init.c` `setup_sync_queues`, `fftools/ffmpeg_sched.c` `enc_open` with `sq_frame_samples`) and hands each to the encoder thread through a queue of `DEFAULT_FRAME_THREAD_QUEUE_SIZE` 2 (`ffmpeg_sched.h`). `libvorbisenc.c` states 64 and has no `AV_CODEC_CAP_VARIABLE_FRAME_SIZE`, so 120 s of 44.1 kHz stereo is 82,688 frames and 234,367 futex calls (`strace -c -f`), 85,871 voluntary context switches and 0.36 s of system time next to 0.88 s of user time. A `perf record` (cpu-clock, 4 kHz, run as root because the VM sets `perf_event_paranoid` to 4) puts 72 percent of the samples in the encoder thread and 22.7 percent in the filter thread, which runs the queue. Of the encoder thread's share 46 percent of all samples is libvorbis and 14 percent is the kernel waking the thread; the filter thread is almost entirely queue and wake-up cost (12 percent kernel, 5.7 percent libc, 3.3 percent libavutil).
  - **No option of FFmpeg 9.0.2 changes it.** Measured with the product's arguments on the 120 s stereo file, the futex count of the unpatched build is 241,568 and did not move with `-threads 1` (239,787; the encoder has no threading capability), `-filter_threads 1` (240,766), `-filter_complex_threads 1` (239,073), `-thread_queue_size 512` (237,292; it sizes the muxer queue, `ffmpeg_sched.c` `sch_add_mux`), `-max_muxing_queue_size 4096` (241,821), `-frame_size 4096` (238,370; the option reaches the codec context and `libvorbis_encode_init` overwrites it, and the debug log of a 1 s run reports 690 frames of 64 samples) or `-af asetnsamples=n=4096:p=0` (238,745; the synchronisation queue cuts the frames again to the size the encoder states, `ffmpeg_sched.c` line 1850). The queue length is fixed at 2 (`queue_alloc` asserts it) and no option runs an encoder in the filter thread. Pinning the process to one CPU (`taskset -c 1`) made the run 0.90 s against 1.4 s while the context switches doubled to 171,000, which hides the cost only on a host that has nothing else to run, so it is not used.
  - **References.** FFmpeg 9.0.2 `libavcodec/libvorbisenc.c` (the required frame size and the comment "LCD of all possible frame sizes"), `libavcodec/encode.c` `encode_simple_receive_packet` and `encode_receive_packet_internal` (an encoder callback is asked for one packet and a call that returns none ends the receive loop, so a backlog stays in the encoder until the next frame, which is why large frames need `receive_packet`), `libavcodec/audio_frame_queue.c` (timestamps from samples), `libavformat/matroskaenc.c` lines 2118 to 2122 and 2895 to 2901 (the default duration and the block duration come from `frame_size`), and `libsvtav1.c` for the `ff_encode_get_frame` pattern. libvorbis 1.3.7 `lib/block.c` `vorbis_analysis_wrote` and `vorbis_analysis_blockout`. The patch is original code for the wrapper, not an optimisation of libvorbis, so no external implementation was ported; the one external fact it relies on, that libvorbis output depends on the call sizes, was measured.
- **Results** (Lima VM `default`, aarch64, 4 cores, Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8.0-147, libvorbis 1.3.7, FFmpeg configured as the install script does for the libraries involved; "base" is 9.0.2 unpatched and "head" the patched build; the product's arguments `-probesize 32 -f wav -vn -sn -dn -map 0:a:0 -c:a libvorbis -f ogg -q:a 5`; base, head, 7.1.5 and the distribution's 6.1.1 interleaved, 11 runs each, median with the range in brackets):
  - **120 s of 44.1 kHz stereo** (the corpus `music.wav` repeated 30 times): base 1.39 s [1.36 to 1.44], 11.6 ms for each second of audio; head 0.59 s [0.57 to 0.62], 4.9 ms; 7.1.5 0.76 s [0.71 to 0.79], 6.3 ms; 6.1.1 0.87 s [0.81 to 0.91]. Head is 2.36 times faster than base and 1.29 times faster than 7.1.5. User time 0.88 s to 0.60 s, system time 0.36 s to 0.03 s, voluntary context switches 85,871 to 5,626, futex calls 234,367 to 22,563.
  - **236.55 s of 16 kHz mono** (`speech.wav` repeated 30 times): base 0.82 s [0.78 to 0.85], 3.5 ms for each second; head 0.28 s [0.27 to 0.32], 1.2 ms; 7.1.5 0.37 s; 6.1.1 0.40 s. 2.9 times faster than base, 1.3 times faster than 7.1.5. Futex calls 216,673 to 46,518.
  - **Twenty-six files** (the two audio files of the corpus and 24 of the real-world cache, 1.1 to 33.8 s, among them MP3, AAC, WMA, AC-3 5.1, Opus, Vorbis, AIFF, CAF and AU), one process each, 7 rounds alternating: 2.57 s [2.51 to 2.69] for all of them on base, 1.12 s [1.10 to 1.17] on head.
  - **Why head is not twice as fast again.** A `perf record` of head puts 92.5 percent of the samples in the encoder thread and 88.5 percent in libvorbis itself (`_vp_offset_and_mix` 14.5, `_vp_tonemask` 10.5, `floor1_fit` 8.2 and `_vp_couple_quantize_normalize` 5.2 percent of all samples); the run is one thread of libvorbis analysis, wall time 0.59 s against 0.63 s of user plus system time. What is left is libvorbis, which has no SIMD path on arm64 in the distribution package; its build flags are the next lever and are not part of this entry.
  - **The same audio, checked.** The decoded samples and the packets of the stream (timestamps, durations, sizes and CRCs by `-c copy -f framecrc`) are equal on base and head for 28 inputs with the product's arguments and a random serial number. The files are byte-identical when the Ogg serial is fixed (`-fflags +bitexact`) for those 26 inputs under 8 option sets (`-q:a 5`, `-q:a -1`, `-q:a 3` with a volume change and a trim, `-q:a 10`, `-b:a 96k`, `-b:a 128k` for the 19 inputs it accepts, `-q:a 5` at 22.05 kHz mono, and `-q:a 5` with `aresample=async=1`), for 200 generated streams (mono, stereo, 3.0, 5.1 and 7.1 at 8, 22.05, 44.1 and 96 kHz, of 1, 15, 63, 64, 65, 127, 129, 1,000, 4,097 and 30,011 samples), for a 16-channel stream, for the 120 s stream cut by `asetnsamples` into frames of 1, 3, 100, 4,096, 100,000 and 1,000,000 samples, and for an input with a timestamp gap and one with an offset (the packets, with timestamps, equal in the encoder's time base). An AddressSanitizer build of the patched encoder ran five of these inputs and three frame sizes with no error; its one leak report (2,848 bytes from `vorbis_encode_setup_init`, on the AC-3 file that has a decode error) is the same in the unpatched build.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Matroska and WebM files with a Vorbis track differ in their container, not in their audio.** The Matroska muxer wrote a default duration of 64 samples (a false figure for packets of 128 to 2,048 samples) and a block duration for every packet because `frame_size` was 64; without it neither is written, and a 4 s test file is 3.8 percent smaller (35,292 bytes against 36,675). The packets and the decoded samples are equal (MD5 of the decode, framecrc at the encoder). The product writes Vorbis to `.ogg` and `.oga`, which are byte-identical, and to WebM and Matroska only when a caller asks for the codec.
  - **A patch to carry** (above). The change is written as a commit for FFmpeg and can be sent upstream; if it lands, the patch is dropped at the next bump.
  - **arm64 only.** The mechanism (a thread hand-over for each 64 samples) does not depend on the architecture, but the figures are from the arm64 VM; the amd64 image is built by CI and was not measured.
  - **Other targets are unchanged.** The other encoders state frames of 960 to 1,536 samples (Opus, AAC, MP3, AC-3), 15 to 24 times fewer hand-overs; their rows are in entry 105.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Reporting it upstream and waiting**: the report is the patch; the target is to be ahead of the reference now.
  - **A larger `frame_size` in the wrapper** (128 to 4,096): 3 to 30 bytes of the stream change (above), so the audio is not the one written before.
  - **Pinning the worker process to one CPU**: 0.90 s against 1.4 s with the same futex count, but a worker runs several jobs and the other cores would idle.
  - **A change to `fftools` (running the encoder in the filter thread, a queue longer than two)**: the scheduler is shared by every codec and the decoder code assumes the queue length (`ffmpeg_dec.c` line 1612).
  - **Giving libvorbis whole frames** (a single `vorbis_analysis_wrote` of the frame): faster still, but a different stream (above).
  - **Removing the frame cut and the carry by making the 64-sample calls inside libvorbis**: it is a library of the distribution, and the image uses the package.
- **Verified by**: `tests/worker-ffmpeg-packaging.test.ts` (the patch directory copied beside the script, `patch` installed, each patch named in the script present on disk with the digest the script states, applied once after the unpacking and before the configure with no fuzz, the patch touching one file with the receive callback, the chunk size and the variable-size capability, the build checks of the capability and of the frame-size independence, the patch named in the source note and the tool-versions manifest, installed beside the licence), the build itself (the stage fails when the patch does not apply or the checks fail), and the measurements above, taken with `scripts/install-ffmpeg.sh`'s own `patch` command and configure flags for the libraries involved on a 9.0.2 archive of the pinned digest.
- **Revisit when**: FFmpeg releases a point release or a version that changes `libvorbisenc.c` (rebase or drop the patch), upstream takes the change, an amd64 measurement is made, a Matroska consumer of the 64-sample default duration shows up, or the libvorbis build flags are looked at (the remaining 88 percent of an encode).

## 132. The grid of a format is stated once, a bare page counter dropped from a text sheet is reported, an object around a list is one record in every record format, and the scan walk of a JPEG costs at most a loop over its bytes

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #671 follow-up rows of the review of #925), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: close the review rows at their root).
- **Decision**:
  - **`gridOf(format)` (`src/lib/conversions/table-grid.ts`) is the one table of what a table holds in a spreadsheet or another target format**: columns, rows (the header row counts for a spreadsheet only), cells, and the worksheet as a refusal words it (`a worksheet`, `an .xls worksheet`), or no worksheet for a format that is not a sheet. The values are the ones that were already in force: `xls` 256 columns, 65,536 rows and 20,000,000 cells; `xlsx` 16,384, 1,048,576 and 20,000,000; `ods` 16,384, 1,048,576 and 1,000,000; `pdf` 16,384 columns and 1,000,000 cells; `parquet` 4,096, 10,000,000 and 20,000,000; every other table target 20,000,000 cells. The table of records of the data engine (`tabulate`), the ODS check (`assertSheetsWithinGrid`), the XLSX writer and the `.xls` extent check (`xls-limits.ts`) read it; the two Parquet writers read `PARQUET_MAX_ROWS`, `PARQUET_MAX_COLUMNS` and `PARQUET_MAX_CELLS` of `parquet-format.ts` directly, as the Parquet reader does, so that the format has one source for its bounds and not two, and the 10,000-sheet check of a workbook is one function (`assertSheetCount`) used by the XLSX writer and the ODS check. The messages and the error classes are those of before (`SheetLimitError` for a sheet, `PayloadLimitError` for a table that is not one, `ParquetValueError` inside the Parquet writer). The constants of each format stay in the module of that format (`office/sheet-bounds.ts` for the spreadsheets, `parquet-format.ts`, and `PDF_TABLE_MAX_CELLS` and `PDF_TABLE_MAX_COLUMNS` in `pdf-table-layout.ts`), and `table-grid.ts` only names which of them a target uses; the spreadsheet grids are typed `Record<SpreadsheetFormat, SpreadsheetGrid>`, so that the compiler checks the overload of `gridOf` that returns a worksheet name. The module of the table imports the PDF table writer for two numbers, which the XLSX writer and the `.xls` check did not load before; `data.ts` and `office.ts`, which import the writers, already load it. `XLSX_MAX_SHEETS` is gone: its one reader and its test use `WORKBOOK_MAX_SHEETS`, so there is not a second 10,000.
  - **A bare number dropped as the page counter of a text sheet is reported** (entry 127). When the text sheet of a page of a PDF without tables leaves out a line that is a bare number (`3`) because it equals the page index on every page it recurs on, the conversion carries the warning "Left out the bare number printed on pages 1, 2, 3 as a page counter: a text sheet is named after its page." (`readPdfSheets`, pages named as the other warnings of the sheets name them, `pagesPhrase`). The forms that say what they are (`Page 3`, `3 of 9`, `3 / 9`, `- 3 -`) are dropped as before and not reported, because a line in those forms is not content. A number that stays a row (the same number on every page, or one that follows no page) is not reported. The comments of `page-counters.ts` and `pdf-layout/index.ts` no longer say that a miss keeps a line: they state that a line that matches is dropped whatever it means.
  - **An object around a list is one record in every record format.** `{"items": [..]}` in JSON (to CSV, TSV and the other table targets), a line `{"items": [..]}` in NDJSON and JSON Lines, and `items: [..]` in YAML were one record whose `items` cell holds the list as JSON, while XML looked through a single wrapper element (`<root><items><item/><item/></items></root>`) and gave a row for each `item`. XML no longer looks inside: the records of an XML document are the child elements of its document element, and a wrapper element is one of them (`xmlRecords`, `data-xml.ts`). The JSON to sheet route (`parseJsonTableCells`) goes the same way: it takes an array of objects or of values as the table and refuses an object, without looking for the list inside it.
  - **A walk over the entropy-coded data of a JPEG scan costs at most a loop over its bytes.** `skipEntropyCodedData` finds the next `0xFF` with the native byte search and, after four hits in a row less than 16 bytes apart, scans 1,024 bytes with a loop before it tries the search again (`image-jpeg-stream.ts`). Plain data keeps the speed of the search; data of stuffed `FF 00` pairs runs at the speed of the loop.
- **Why**:
  - **A limit in four places is four chances to change one.** The table of records, the XLSX writer, the ODS check and the Parquet writer each held the columns and rows of their format, and `assertWorkbookSheets` held a copy of the sheet-count check of `assertSheetsWithinGrid`. A test states the values as numbers and asserts that each writer refuses with the message built from the table.
  - **The report is the cost of a rule that guesses.** A page counter is a guess about what a number means, and entry 127 says it can drop a section number. The warning names the pages so that the person who reads the sheet knows to compare it with the document, where before the loss was silent.
  - **One rule for the wrapper, the one the JSON route already has.** Looking inside an object for its list is a guess about which key holds the records. The common table reader of XML reads the children of the document element as the rows by default and does not descend further (`pandas.read_xml`, whose default `xpath` is `./*`): the JSON to sheet route of this project refuses an object root and does not look inside it (`parseJsonTableCells`, `sheet-text-tables.ts`). The three record formats that were one record keep that, and the XML reading that looked through a wrapper (added with the XML reader in #505; no test of the suite held it, the tests of XML to CSV use documents whose document element holds the records) is the one that changes. A list that is the document itself (a YAML sequence, NDJSON lines, the children of the XML document element) is still a row for each item.
  - **The cost of a search call is what bounds it.** Measured on the arm64 host over 42 MiB of scan data that ends in `FF D9`, through `walkJpegStream` before and after (median of seven runs, alternating, the range in brackets; load average 5.2 at the start, a busy host, so two runs of the same code differ by up to 1.8 times in the dense rows): no `0xFF` at all 0.8 ms before and 0.7 ms after; an `FF 00` pair every 256 bytes 3.5 and 3.7 ms; every 64 bytes 11.3 and 12.4 ms; every 16 bytes 42.4 and 45.0 ms (25.3 in the run before); every 4 bytes 196.3 (192.8 to 200.8) and 46.6 ms; every 2 bytes 339.7 (335.0 to 344.3) and 23.3 ms (20.8 to 28.5). The limiter is the call, not the bytes it skips: the search reads plain data at about 60 GB/s and a call costs about 15 ns, about 16 bytes of a loop (a plain-JavaScript model of the walk measured the loop at 38 to 45 ms and the search at 15 ns a call). The switch is at a gap of 16 bytes. Both sides were checked for the end they found (every run compares it with the length of the stream). The worst case of the walk is now a loop over every byte, 15 to 47 ms for 42 MiB, where it was 340 ms.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Only a bare number at the head of a page is reported, and only for a page that gets a text sheet.** A bare number at the foot of a page is the commonest page number and is dropped without a line in the warnings, as a counter in a form that says it is one (`Page 3`, `3 of 9`) is; a warning on those would mark nearly every paginated PDF. A run of bare numbers at the head of the pages is where a section number can be mistaken for a counter, so that is what the warning names, and a page with no other text gets no sheet and is not named.
  - **A document of tables is not reported.** The text beside the tables is left out as a whole (entry 120, the `leftOut` warning), so the counter is part of a loss that is already named.
  - **An XML export with a wrapper level is one row.** `<response><data><item/>..</data></response>` gives a single row whose cells are the list, as the same document in YAML does. A caller who needs the items as rows converts the list itself (an XML document whose children are the items) or the YAML sequence. The change is visible in a conversion that gave rows before.
  - **The byte loop spends up to 1,024 bytes on a stretch that stopped being dense.** Data built to alternate five close pairs with 1,030 plain bytes costs the loop on almost every byte: 15.2 ms (14.8 to 19.8) for 42 MiB where the search alone took 4.6 ms (same host, seven runs), three times slower than before and 22 times faster than the dense case it protects against. No file a camera or an encoder writes has that shape.
  - **The search for an end-of-image marker has the same weakness and is left.** `truncatedJpegDecodeOptions` looks for `FF D9` with `Buffer.prototype.indexOf`, which took 183 ms on 42 MiB of `FF 00` pairs and 387 ms on 42 MiB of `FF` bytes, against 33 to 38 ms for a loop (plain-JavaScript model, same host, median of five runs). It runs once for a stream, and the stream has already passed the size limits of the upload; it is a row of #671, not a finding that blocks this one.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Unwrapping the single-key list in YAML, NDJSON and JSON as XML did.** It would make the three agree with the XML reading, but it guesses which key is the list: `{"orders": [..]}` can be one record with one field, and it would become a table of the list. The JSON to sheet route would still refuse the same object.
  - **Reporting every dropped counter.** `Page 3 of 9` says what it is; a warning on every paginated PDF would be read as a fault.
  - **A cap on the hits of the native search per call.** The cost depends on how close the hits are, not on how many there are: 22 million calls at 4 bytes apart cost 187 ms and the same count 256 bytes apart would cost 3 ms.
  - **Replacing the search by a loop altogether.** It is slower on plain data by a factor of 30 or more (plain-JavaScript model: 44.1 against 0.8 ms for 42 MiB).
  - **A shared scanner for the scan walk and the end-of-image search.** A version that returned the next `0xFF` through one method took 88.6 ms on `FF 00` pairs against 38.6 ms for the loop in one function (plain-JavaScript model), and 157 ms against 33 for the all-`FF` end-marker search, because a call remained for each hit.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sheet-grid.test.ts` (the values of the table as numbers; each writer refuses past the table with the message built from it; the sheet count with one message from the XLSX and the ODS writer), `tests/data-records-sheet-bounds.test.ts` (the bounds of the table of records, unchanged), `tests/pdf-tables-to-sheets.test.ts` (a bare footer dropped from the text sheets of `1`, `2`, `3` carries the warning naming the pages, a number that stays a row and a `Page N` footer carry none), `tests/data-sources-to-sheets.test.ts` (an object around a list is one row in NDJSON, YAML, XML and JSON to CSV, and a list that is the document is a row for each item), `tests/image-jpeg-stream.test.ts` (the end of the stream is found for data of any density of `FF` and at a marker inside a dense stretch; the native search is called fewer than a hundredth of the number of pairs in `FF 00` data, counted by calls and not by time, and not more than once for each pair in sparse data).
- **Revisit when**: a caller needs the items of a wrapper as rows from YAML, NDJSON, JSON or XML (an option that names the key or the element, as a path, is the way that has a source), a nightly row shows a counter reported that is a counter, the end-of-image search of a truncated stream shows in a profile, or a format outside this list gets a grid of its own.

## 133. Follow-up rows of entries 124 to 129: a scan on a white sheet is a page of only a picture for DXF, the warning names the pages, a known refusal names its pair, and an empty input must give a book without words

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the follow-up rows that the reviews of the pull requests for entries 126, 128 and 129 added), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: close the review rows of the refusal tail).
- **Decision**:
  - **A page whose only geometry is shapes without a stroke that cover the page is a page of a picture, for DXF.** The white rectangle that an office suite or a scanner program draws under a scan has no outline; with the scan left out (entry 129) it would be written as the one polyline of the sheet and the conversion would answer a file with nothing in it but a frame. A page with at least one picture the page paints, no text written from a bitmap font, and elements that all paint no outline and reach every side of the page (within `PAGE_CLIP_TOLERANCE_PIXELS`, one point, the tolerance of a clip the size of the page) is refused as a page without geometry, with the message a scan with nothing under it already gets (`isPageBackdrop` in `src/lib/conversions/vector-dxf.ts`). A sheet with a stroke, a sheet smaller than the page, a sheet beside any other outline, and a sheet with no picture on the page are written as before.
  - **A picture that the page does not paint is not counted.** `display: none` was already skipped; a `visibility` other than `visible` (own or inherited from the group, the `<use>` or the document element, and a child can show itself again with `visible`) and a `opacity` of zero are skipped too, on the picture or on any group or `<use>` around it (opacity does not inherit, but nothing below a group at zero is painted, so the reader carries that fact down the style context as it carries visibility), and so is an `<image>` whose `width` or `height` is zero (SVG disables its rendering) or negative (an error that is not rendered) (`isDrawnPicture` in `src/lib/conversions/svg-picture.ts`). A page whose only picture is hidden converts without a warning. The collector of the pictures a page leaves out (`PicturePages`) is a required argument of the page writer (`svgPageEncoder`, `encodeSvgPageToDxfWithText`), so a caller cannot write pages and lose the warning; `withSvgPageEncoder` reports it once after the last page.
  - **The warning names the pages.** One line for the whole conversion, "Left out the pictures of pages 2, 3: a DXF holds lines and text and no bitmaps.", with the first ten page numbers and an ellipsis after them (`pagesPhrase`, the form the other page warnings use); a drawing that is not a PDF page says "the page". The pages are collected while the writer runs and reported once after the last page (`withSvgPageEncoder` in `src/worker/svg-page-encoders.ts`), so a document of hundreds of pages does not spend the 200 lines a conversion may report.
  - **`parseSvgGeometries` takes one options object**, `{ bitmapGlyphs, pens, pictures }`, in place of three positional arguments and a `leftOutPictures` field in every result. `pictures` is a collector (`LeftOutPictures`, as `bitmapGlyphs` is one); given none, a picture refuses the page. The result keeps the shape the metafile encoders read.
  - **A known refusal of the corpus run can name its pair** (`bench/realworld/known-refusals.json`, `knownRefusal` in `bench/realworld/report.ts`). `source` and `target` (one format or a list) are optional; a row without them explains the file in every pair, as before. The eleven rows of entry 129 (six PDFs, five Word documents) now name the source and the targets the nightly run asked for, so a new refusal of the same file with the same message in another pair is listed as unexplained.
  - **An input the corpus marks as empty must give a book without words.** `emptyInput` accepted any content documents of an OEB archive; now it accepts the archive only while they hold no text (`oebArchiveProblem` in `bench/realworld/output-check.ts`), so a book that carries words the input did not have is a bad output, and the structure checks (an `.opf`, a content document) apply to it as to any other.
  - **A phonetic guide is read wherever a run's content may stand.** `readRuby` in `src/lib/conversions/docx-model.ts` is called for a `ruby` inside a run, as Word writes it, and for one directly under a paragraph, hyperlink, insertion, smart tag or content control. Word writes it inside a run (ECMA-376 17.3.3.25); the other places are read because other writers put it there and dropping the base text drops words. The drawing-aware reader of documents with shapes leaves `w:rt` out before it reads the text (`withoutElements` in `src/lib/conversions/office/xml-without.ts`, also used for the phonetic runs of a workbook's strings), so it gives the base text, as the model reader does, and not the guide in front of it.
  - **One wrapper answers a legacy document the office suite could not load** (`withLegacyOfficeRecovery`, around every LibreOffice run): it runs a presentation once more with its persist id seed corrected, and gives the typed 422 for an encrypted workbook or Word document, as the two wrappers did one inside the other. One reader holds the input (`boundedInput` in `src/worker/office-input-checks.ts`): the legacy checks read a file up to `LEGACY_OFFICE_MAX_INPUT_BYTES` (256 MiB, the limit of the in-process readers) and the package checks up to the bytes a job may hold in memory. `xlsHasFilePass` now opens the compound file with `readCfbContainer`, the bounded reader of the other legacy readers, which changes two things from the walk it made before: it applies the compound file header check (`assertCfbHeader`), which the XLS reader itself does not, and it reads at most 256 MiB (`LEGACY_OFFICE_MAX_INPUT_BYTES`, the bound of the legacy readers), so a compound file past that size is answered as not encrypted (since entry 136 the bound is in `parseCfbf` itself, so the XLS and HWP readers have it too). A file the header check or the bound refuses gives `false`, as an unreadable file always did. One test of the file information block's encrypted flag serves `readFib` and `isEncryptedWordDocument`.
- **Why**:
  - **No reference was found that refuses the sheet.** The references of entry 129 leave a picture out and write the shapes they read; the sheet is a shape, so each would write its frame. The refusal is a decision of ours (the review row of entry 129 offered it or a test that pins the frame), taken because a DXF that holds only the outline of the page tells the caller nothing about the document and looks like a success; entry 129 already refuses the scan with no sheet under it, and which of the two a scanner program produced is not the caller's choice.
  - **A hidden or fully transparent picture draws nothing**, so leaving it out loses nothing and a warning about it would be untrue.
  - **A row of the corpus gate is for the file and the answer, and the pair is part of the answer**: a file refused for one target and converted for the others is the case the rows exist for; a row for any pair would also hide a regression in a pair that converted.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A page of a picture on a sheet that has a visible border is written as the border.** The stroke is geometry.
  - **A sheet that falls short of the page by more than the clip tolerance is geometry.** A page with a margin around a scan keeps the rectangle of the margin.
  - **A refusal of a whole PDF** follows from a page of only a picture, as it already did for a scan with no sheet; a PDF with one scanned page among text pages is refused, not converted without that page.
  - **`LEGACY_OFFICE_MAX_INPUT_BYTES` now bounds the encrypted check** for a workbook, where the unbounded compound-file walk of a file between 256 and 512 MiB ran before; the readers refuse such a file anyway (the Word, PowerPoint and Outlook readers did; the XLS and HWP readers since entry 136).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Writing the sheet and warning**: the reference output, but a file with a frame and nothing else.
  - **A pair written into the `detail` pattern of a known refusal**: the pattern is matched against the message, which is the same in the other pairs.
  - **A second wrapper kept apart for presentations**: the two answered the same failure of the suite, one inside the other.
- **Verified by**: `tests/dxf-pen-attributes.test.ts` (a sheet with a picture refused in four forms; a bordered, a smaller and a sheet beside an outline written; a sheet alone and a sheet under a hidden picture written without a warning; fifteen forms of a picture that is not painted and seven that are, among them a group or `<use>` at opacity zero and an image of zero width or height, red before the change for those seven), `tests/native-page-target-chains.test.ts` (a four-page document with pictures on three: one warning naming pages 1, 3 and 4; a scan on a white sheet refused; a sheet, a picture and a line written as the sheet and the line), `tests/postscript-real-file-refusals.test.ts` (the three real files: the warning names the pages on which Poppler's own SVG places a picture outside the masks, 2 and 3, 9, and 1), `tests/svg-geometry-options.test.ts`, `tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts` (a row names its source and one or several targets, a row without them still explains every pair, the list refuses a pair that is empty or not a format of the registry, the eleven rows name theirs, and every named target is advertised by the registry and planned for its file by `planJobs` with three targets a file, so a manifest change that moves the rotation fails there and not silently; red before for the names), `tests/realworld-output-check.test.ts` (a marked input is accepted with a book of no text and refused with a book of words, and its structure is still checked), `tests/media-container-named-otherwise.test.ts` (an ordinary Program Stream, `fate-pcm_aud.mpg` and `samples-eof.mpeg`, still opens as `mpeg` with `mpegts` in the list of its name), `tests/docx-model-reader.test.ts` and `tests/docx-ruby-drawing-reader.test.ts` (a guide directly under five parents, nested guides, and the drawing-aware reader's paragraphs, cells and three targets; red before), `tests/office-input-bounds.test.ts`, and the unchanged `tests/legacy-office-encrypted-answer.test.ts`, `tests/office-suite-route.test.ts` and `tests/ppt-persist-id-seed.test.ts` (whose import now names the one wrapper).
- **Revisit when**: a DXF reference writes or refuses the sheet under a picture differently, a caller needs the rectangle of the sheet, a document model gains an inline for a phonetic guide, or the nightly run lists a refusal of a pair that a row names.

## 134. DjVu documents: ddjvu of djvulibre as a separate program on a file the worker has read first, PDF and the page images as targets, and no text target

- **Status**: Implemented (the DjVu rows of issue #783: `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu`, `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu`, `tika-testdjvu.djvu`), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: draw DjVu with the program the reference engine for the format is, `ddjvu`, in the process sandbox, and offer only what the existing PDF chain handles cleanly). It ends the refusal that entries 124 and 128 left standing ("no reader yet"): until now every DjVu to PDF or text job ended in "Binary null bytes detected ... fail-closed against mojibake corruption". Superseded in part by entry 135, the only current statement of the budget of `ddjvu` (it counts 64 pixels a byte, not 16), its heaps (four), the include chains and the threads of a run (searched once, 64 tasks), and the components of 16 MiB (refused by their bytes); the bullets below on those points record what this entry decided.
- **Decision**:
  - **`ddjvu -format=pdf` (djvulibre 3.5.28, the Debian 13 package `djvulibre-bin`, GPL-2.0-or-later) draws the pages.** A `.djvu` or `.djv` source goes to PDF through it, and every other page target (PNG, JPEG, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP, TIFF, ICO, PSD, SVG, PostScript, EPS) is made from that PDF by the native PDF tools every PDF source already uses (entry 34), on the same route table as PostScript and XPS (`FIXED_PAGE_ROUTES` in `src/worker/engines.ts`, entry 95). The program decodes each page to a raster, writes it to a temporary TIFF beside the output and turns the TIFF into a PDF with the tiff2pdf code compiled into it (`tools/ddjvu.cpp`, `render` from line 235, `closefile` lines 646 to 700): a bilevel page is a CCITT G4 image, a colour page a deflate image, one image per page at the resolution of the page. It runs unmodified as a separate program (entry 11, `docs/licensing.md`) with no network, an address space of 2 GiB, an output file of at most 512 MiB, and in a directory that holds the one input file (`document.djvu`) and the output.
  - **The worker reads the bytes only, and the pages are what `djvused` says they are.** The bytes are checked in `src/lib/conversions/djvu-container.ts` from the IFF layout of `libdjvu/IFFByteStream.cpp` `get_chunk` (lines 168 to 300): the file must open with `AT&TFORM` and a `FORM` of type `DJVU` or `DJVM`, the form must end inside the file, and every chunk of a single page inside its parent (the program's own "Unexpected End Of File" and `corrupt_mangled`). Of a bundle only the header of `DIRM` is read (`DjVmDir.cpp` `decode`, lines 212 to 262): the bundle flag, a version of at most 1, and a count of 1 to 20,000 files. The offsets, the flags, the names, the pages and the files they include are not modelled. `djvused` of the same package (`tools/djvused.cpp` `command_n` and `command_size`, lines 481 to 610) runs on the same file, in the same sandbox, in the same directory and with the same options as `ddjvu`, before it: `-e n` for the page count, which prints one integer and no name of a file, then `-e size` for the size of every page. They are two runs and not one `n;size`, because the program buffers its output: a crash in `size` loses the count `n` printed (measured on an include cycle, 3.5.28 and 3.5.29), and a failure of the directory could not be told from a failure of the pages. The `n` run has a time limit of 30 s and the `size` run 120 s, each an output limit of 16 MiB and a strict parser (`src/lib/conversions/djvu-report.ts`): a line of another shape, a second line after the count, a count that disagrees with the sizes, and a size of zero end the conversion with a typed error. A page of over 100 million pixels (the pixel limit of the image paths, `EASYCONVERT_MAX_INPUT_PIXELS`) is refused before `ddjvu` starts.
  - **`djvused` judges the include structure, by what the program itself raises.** `size` opens every page and creates the files the page includes, as `ddjvu` does. A status other than zero (an offset outside the bundle or in the middle of a component, a page listed at a chunk that is no `FORM`, a file cut short inside it) or a crash signal, SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGABRT, SIGFPE or SIGILL (a stack overflow on an include cycle or a chain thousands of files deep), refuses the document with `DjvuIncludeStructureError` (HTTP 422) before `ddjvu` starts. The message says what is known and no more: "djvused crashed (SIGSEGV) under its 2048 MB memory limit while opening the pages of the DjVu document" for a crash (a fault under the address space limit can come from a stack overflow or from memory running out, which the signal does not tell apart), and "djvused could not open the pages of the DjVu document (exit status 10): ..." for a status, which says what the program did and not why (an include structure it cannot open is one cause; a component of 16 MiB or more is another, below). The sandbox reports a SIGSEGV or a SIGKILL under the memory limit as the memory limit, and now names the signal on that error (`SandboxedMemoryLimitError.signal`, also across the launcher helper and the qpdf runner), so the fault is a verdict and the kernel's out-of-memory SIGKILL is not. Every other end of the run is not a verdict on the document and keeps the error it had: a run past its own limit of 120 s or a launcher helper that went silent (both raise the sandbox's `SandboxedTimeoutError`, which the dispatcher turns into `CpuTaskTimeoutError`, HTTP 422, as it does for the `n` run), a kill from outside (SIGKILL, SIGTERM, SIGHUP), a run that ended with neither a status nor a signal (a lost launcher helper), a program that did not start (including status 126 and 127, which the shell wrapper answers when it cannot run the program, as the helper does not pass the spawn error code on), an output over its limit, and the deadline of the job. The sizes of every page are read and checked, also when a selection draws fewer: the include structure of any page is the document's.
  - **One deadline for the drawing of a document.** The two `djvused` runs, `ddjvu` and the `pdfinfo` count of the PDF it writes share one deadline, the stage limit of the job (`src/worker/djvu-render.ts` `DjvuRun`): each is given what is left of it, at most its own limit (30 s for `n`, 120 s for `size`, the budget below for `ddjvu`, 45 s for the page count), and nothing more starts once it has passed. The page count is not started with less than 2 s left (`PDF_PAGE_COUNT_FLOOR_MS`). A run the deadline cut short is the job's timeout (`CpuTaskTimeoutError`, HTTP 422) and names the stage limit of the job, not the slice the last program was given. The stage limit is 120 s by default and 600 s at most when the server sets a longer stage, so drawing one DjVu document costs at most 120 s by default, whatever its directory and its includes hold. An image target then hands the PDF to the page tools, which keep their own limits (entry 34).
  - **`ddjvu` has a budget of its own and one glibc heap.** Its time limit is `min(left of the deadline, max(15 s, 16 x t_reports) + credited pixels / 4 million a second)` (`DRAW_BUDGET_FLOOR_MS`, `DRAW_BUDGET_REPORT_FACTOR`, `DRAW_PIXELS_PER_MS`), where `t_reports` is the time since the run started, read from the clock once when `ddjvu` is about to launch, so it holds the two `djvused` runs with their launches. The credited pixels are the drawn pixels (width x height summed over the pages drawn, from the `size` output: every page for a PDF, the selected pages for page images), **at most 16 pixels for each byte of the input file** (`DRAW_PIXELS_PER_INPUT_BYTE`), because a file declares any page size for a few bytes and `djvused` accepts it: a 9 KB bundle that holds a chain of 300 shared files and one page declared 9,999 x 9,999 pixels held `ddjvu` for 40.07 s, and with six such pages until the 120 s deadline (120.02 s), with 252 of the container's 256 tasks taken meanwhile. With the cap the same files end at 15.09 s and 15.11 s (15.06 s with pages of 64 x 64 pixels). A run cut by the budget is refused with `CpuTaskTimeoutError` (HTTP 422), worded as "the .djvu document took too long to draw", and is not a verdict on its structure. `ddjvu` runs with `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1` (`DRAW_ENVIRONMENT`; the sanitized environment of a sandboxed program does not carry the worker's own setting).
  - **Only a document that holds everything in the one file is converted.** `DjVuDocument.cpp` `init_thread` (from line 307) and `request_data` (lines 1443 to 1535) show what the program reads besides the file it is given: a bundled `FORM:DJVM` reads its components from the bundle only (a URL outside it is `URL_outside`, an id not in the directory `file_outside`, lines 1485 to 1510); an indirect `FORM:DJVM` (the `DIRM` chunk has no bundle flag) and a single `FORM:DJVU` page are read together with the files they name, from the directory of the given file (`DataPool::create(url)`, line 1531). A name with a slash, a backslash or a colon is rejected (`DjVuFile.cpp` `process_incl_chunk`, line 571), so a name cannot leave the directory, but a plain name is read. So an indirect directory, a single page with an `INCL` or `NDIR` chunk, and the obsolete `DIR0` directory are refused by name before the program starts, and the program's directory holds nothing else it could read. A page of a bundled document may `INCL` shared data: those names are resolved in the bundle (measured: each of the 34 pages of `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` includes one of two shared dictionaries).
  - **Limits.** At most 10,000 pages per document, as `djvused` counts them (the page limit of the XPS reader, which also writes a PDF; the directory counts its files in 16 bits, 65,535), and at most 20,000 files in a directory: djvulibre reads a directory in time that grows with the square of its files (`djvused -e n` takes 0.6 s for 5,000 files, 2.5 s for 10,000, 9.5 s for 20,000 and 102 s for 65,535, measured with 3.5.29 on Apple silicon; 9.1 s for 20,000 with 3.5.28 on the arm64 test VM), so the count in the header is refused before any program reads it. A request for the images of more than 500 pages is refused before anything is drawn (the limit of the other page chains), and the 500 count the pages that are drawn: a selection of three pages of a document of 501 is drawn, a selection of 501 is refused. A PDF of 501 pages is written. An input over 256 MiB (the inflate budget of one document; the program keeps offsets and sizes as `int`) is refused. An image target reads the drawn PDF into memory only up to 128 MiB, as on the other two routes.
  - **A page selection is drawn alone.** For an image target `ddjvu -page=` is given the selected pages (`pages` and `page`, resolved against the count `djvused` reports, as a list of ranges such as `2-4,7`; the first selected page only when the request wants one page), so a request for one page of a long document draws one page (a page of the 34 page `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` as a PNG: 0.26 s, the whole document as PNGs 2.95 s), and the page tools are given a PDF of the selected pages with the selection removed from the request. The PDF must hold as many pages as were selected. A PDF target is every page.
  - **Two files of the program count toward the file limit.** The program limit on the size of one file is 512 MiB. `ddjvu` writes a temporary TIFF beside the output, with every page (a deflate TIFF in colour, CCITT G4 for a bilevel page), and then the PDF; each is under the limit on its own, and each is about as large as the pages' pictures together. A colour page of 2550 x 3300 pixels with photographic noise (+-12) gives a PDF of 11.06 MB (1.3 bytes a pixel) and a temporary TIFF of at most that size; the run passes under a file size limit of 10,800 KiB and fails under 10,789 KiB (measured with `ulimit -f`, 3.5.29), so the limit ends a colour document at about 47 such pages (400 million pixels), at about 20 pages (179 million pixels) for pictures that do not compress at all (3 bytes a pixel), and at 11 of them for page images, whose PDF is read up to 128 MiB. A bilevel scan is two orders of magnitude smaller: the 34 pages of `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` write 6.9 MB. The program ends with SIGXFSZ when the limit is met (status 153 under `ulimit -f`), and the job fails.
  - **A document the program could not draw is a failure.** The program stops at the first page it cannot decode, prints the reason and exits with status 10 (`tools/ddjvu.cpp` `dopage`, lines 728 to 746, unless `-skip` is given, which is not), and an exit with an error, an empty or missing output and an output over the limit each end in a typed `ConversionFailedError` that carries the first 300 characters of what it printed. The PDF must also hold as many pages as were to be drawn, counted by `pdfinfo` from the file, so a PDF with a page missing is never handed out.
  - **The registry offers PDF, ZIP and the twelve other page targets, and no text target.** `djvu` and `djv` listed `txt` (and `djv` also `epub`), which no code ever served; they are withdrawn, and `optionsSchema` of `djvu` is now `pages` and `dpi`. A DjVu file is also refused under any name but `.djvu` and `.djv`, and any other bytes under those two (`ownSignatureVerdict` in `src/lib/format-signatures.ts`).
  - **The corpus.** `tika-testdjvu.djvu` (89 bytes) is the index of an indirect document that names eight page files the corpus does not hold; it is refused by name and listed in `bench/realworld/known-refusals.json` (issue 783). No DjVu row existed in that file: the earlier refusals were never listed because the gate reads a refusal rate against a baseline.
- **Why**:
  - **References.** djvulibre 3.5.28 (the source of the Debian package, `djvulibre_3.5.28.orig.tar.xz`) for every rule above: `libdjvu/IFFByteStream.cpp`, `DjVmDir.cpp`, `DjVuInfo.cpp`, `DjVuDocument.cpp`, `DjVuFile.cpp`, `tools/djvused.cpp` and `tools/ddjvu.cpp`, read and cited by line, not copied. The reference service's listing names `ddjvu` for DjVu to PDF and offers no other target for DjVu.
  - **The program draws, and the unbounded places are closed in front of it.** `ddjvu` has no limit on the pixels of a page (`render` allocates `rowsize * rrect.h` for the whole page), on the pages of a directory or on the time; the byte checks and `djvused` decide first, and the sandbox and the deadline bound the rest. Measured with `ddjvu` 3.5.28 under an address space of 2 GiB on the 4 vCPU Linux arm64 test VM: a 100 megapixel colour page (smooth, 1.3 MB of DjVu) takes 5.6 s, 672 MB resident and writes 145 MB of PDF; a 25 megapixel colour page of noise takes 2.0 s, 222 MB and writes 61 MB; a 49 megapixel bilevel page of noise takes 1.4 s, 87 MB and writes 12.9 MB; the 34 pages of 34.8 megapixels of `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` (1.18 gigapixels of text) take 1.7 s, 50 MB, 6.9 MB of PDF. Memory is about 6.7 bytes a pixel at the limit, so 100 million pixels fits 2 GiB with margin; the ceiling of the input limit (268 million) would not, and ends in the memory-limit refusal.
  - **Why the pages come from `djvused`.** The pages of a document are what its directory flags say (`DjVmDir::File::is_page`), and the flags, the sizes and the names sit in the BZZ compressed tail of `DIRM`; a bundle of `FORM:PM44` or `FORM:BM44` pages is a document of pages, and a `FORM:DJVU` flagged as shared data is not a page. A reader of our own would decode BZZ and repeat those rules, and every difference from djvulibre is a document judged otherwise than it is drawn: taking the `FORM:DJVU` components as the pages reads a bundle that flags a 64 x 64 `FORM:DJVU` as shared data beside a 12000 x 12000 `FORM:BM44` page as one small page, which `ddjvu` draws as 144 megapixels at 1.2 GB resident. Asked of `djvused`, the count and the sizes are those `ddjvu` uses: that bundle is refused for its 144 megapixel page in 82 ms before `ddjvu` starts, and a bundle of one `FORM:PM44` page and a version 0 directory convert.
  - **Why djvulibre judges the include structure.** A page names shared files in `INCL` chunks, and the bundle finds a file by the name as an id, then as a name, then as a title (`DjVuDocument.cpp` `id_to_url`, lines 794 to 847), with the directory flags deciding which files are thumbnails. Those rules live in djvulibre, and `size` follows them as `ddjvu` does, so its verdict is the program's own, and the cost of a hostile include graph falls on a sandboxed process with a time limit, a memory limit and the deadline of the job. The worker process runs no loop that grows with the chunks of a bundle: the byte checks read the `DIRM` header of a bundle and make one pass over the chunks of a single page. The 30 s limit of `n` is six times the 4.3 s that `n;ls` took on the largest directory taken (`n` alone: 29 ms for 1,000 pages, 0.22 s for 3,000). The `size` limit was calibrated on wavelet pages, whose first chunk `size` decodes: on the test VM, 2550 x 3300 pages of scanned text (a DOGV page drawn at that size and encoded with `c44`, a first chunk of 320 KB) cost 40 ms a page as `FORM:PM44` and 37 ms as `FORM:BM44` (100 pages: 3.95 s and 3.64 s, with all chunks 4.08 s and 3.77 s), so a book of 1,000 PM44 pages takes 39.7 s (BM44 36.5 s) and of 3,000 pages 119.0 s; blank pages of the same size cost 6 ms (6.1 s for 1,000). The 1,000-page book is over a third of the earlier 30 s, so the limit is three times it, 120 s; under the default stage limit the deadline then comes first. Damaged directories, measured with 3.5.28 (test VM) and 3.5.29 (Apple silicon) alike: a page listed in the middle of a component or at an `ANTa` chunk makes `size` exit with status 10 ("IFFByteStream not ready for reading chunk") and is refused before drawing; a shared file listed so passes `size`, and `ddjvu` exits with status 10 at once (`ConversionFailedError`); a `DIRM` that counts more files than it holds makes `n` exit with status 10 ("Failed to open document"), refused before drawing. Measured with `djvused` and `ddjvu` 3.5.28 on the 4 vCPU Linux arm64 test VM (3.5.29 on Apple silicon in brackets), run directly, `n;ls`, then `size`, then `ddjvu` where `size` accepts; the result of the whole conversion through the service on the test VM follows each:
    - a chain of shared files that each include the next two (`poc_f`), 20 levels: 0.003 s, 0.002 s, 0.02 s (0.02, 0.01, 0.04 s), converted in 0.08 s; 30 levels: 0.002 s, 0.002 s, 0.43 s (0.02, 0.01, 0.51 s); 40 levels: 0.002 s, 0.003 s, 50.5 s (0.01, 0.01, 57.8 s). Under the sandbox limits with one heap, `poc_f` 30 with shared files that hold nothing but their includes converts in 1.29 s (1.4 s), 23 threads at most, and 40 levels end at the 15 s budget (38 threads);
    - a plain chain of shared files that each include the next one: 24 files convert in 0.02 s under the sandbox limits; from 32 files the program used to wait at 0 % CPU with 30 threads until killed, as each decoding thread took a glibc arena of 64 MiB of address space and the 2 GiB limit was met. With `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1`: 32 and 40 files in 0.02 s, 64 in 0.03 s (11 threads at most), 128 in 0.04 s (110), 200 in 0.06 s (199), 250 in 0.07 s (245); 300 and 500 files reach 252 threads, where the stacks of 8 MiB fill the address space, and wait until the budget ends them;
    - two shared files that include each other, and chains of 5,000 and 19,999 shared files: `n;ls` in at most 0.04 s, then `size` crashes with a segmentation fault (status 139) in 1.2 s (0.1 s); refused with `DjvuIncludeStructureError` in 0.10 to 0.14 s;
    - 19,999 entries at overlapping offsets inside one chunk followed by 500,000 empty chunks (4.5 MB): 0.04 s, 0.02 s, then `ddjvu` draws its one page in 0.02 s (0.05, 0.04, 0.04 s); converted in 0.08 s;
    - 10,000 pages: 2.3 s, 2.6 s, 12.1 s (2.4, 3.4, 6.2 s), converted in 17.7 s; 10,000 pages and 10,000 shared files, the largest directory taken: 4.3 s, 4.7 s, 11.9 s (4.4, 5.3, 6.0 s), converted in 20.9 s; 20,000 pages: `n;ls` 8.9 s (9.5 s), refused for its page count in 8.9 s.
  - **No pixel rate refuses the document; the pixels only lengthen the budget of `ddjvu`, and only as far as the file's bytes can hold them.** GhostXPS gets a rate (entry 95) because its cost per image is fixed. DjVu decodes from about 12.5 million pixels a second (noisy colour) to 700 million (text), so a refusal by rate would refuse `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu`, which is 94 s at 12.5 million and takes 1.6 s. The budget instead gives every document at least 15 s and adds the credited pixels at 4 million a second, below the slowest measured rate (12.5 million for noisy colour, 14.5 million for scanned `FORM:PM44` pages), so a document is never cut for being large, only for taking longer than its pages explain; the deadline of the job stays the outer bound, with the output limit of the file system (a file over 512 MiB ends the program with SIGXFSZ, measured with `prlimit --fsize`). The pixels are credited at most 16 for each byte of the file because the size of a page is a number in the file and costs it nothing: the first version credited the declared pixels whole, and a hostile file of 9 KB bought 25 s of a worker with it (the chain above).
  - **The budget against the measured documents** (test VM, 4 vCPU arm64, djvulibre 3.5.28, `ddjvu` with one heap under an address space of 2 GiB and an output limit of 512 MiB; the draw is the median of 3 runs, and the budget comes from the reports as measured by `djvused` alone, which the worker's launches add a few milliseconds to). The constant is 16 pixels a byte, which keeps every document below at three times its draw time or more where the deadline does not bind. The tightest row, a book of 50 `FORM:PM44` pages, needs 11.7 pixels a byte for exactly three times (146 million credited pixels on top of the 25.9 s that the reports give), and 16 leaves it 3.65 times. The pixels and bytes columns are those of the file, so pixels per byte is what the cap acts on; a document whose pixels per byte is under 16 is credited whole.
    - `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu`: 496,789 bytes, 1,182,869,724 pixels (2,381 a byte), credit 7.9 million pixels, budget 17.0 s, draws in 1.58 s (10.8 times). `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu`: 534,990 bytes, 8,415,000 pixels (15.7 a byte), credited whole, 17.1 s against 0.35 s (49 times).
    - A 100 megapixel colour page, smooth (226,497 bytes, 442 a byte): credit 3.6 million pixels, 15.9 s against 2.01 s (7.9 times); the same page flat (90,656 bytes): 15.4 s against 1.41 s (10.9 times). A 25 megapixel colour page of noise of 12 levels (1,223,580 bytes, 20 a byte): 19.9 s against 1.63 s (12.2 times). A 49 megapixel bilevel page of noise (6,450,209 bytes, 7.6 a byte): 27.3 s against 1.38 s (19.8 times).
    - 100 pages of bilevel `FORM:DJVU` text at 2331 x 3300 (3,168,365 bytes, 243 a byte, 769 million pixels): 27.7 s against 2.40 s (11.5 times).
    - `FORM:PM44` books of colour pages of 2331 x 3300 (the page of `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` drawn at that size and encoded with `c44`): 10 pages with a first chunk of 250 KB each (2,505,206 bytes, 31 a byte): 25.0 s against 4.08 s (6.1 times); 10 pages of 980 KB each (9,798,686 bytes, 7.9 a byte, credited whole): 34.2 s against 5.15 s (6.6 times); 50 pages of 250 KB: reports 1.6 s, budget 76.0 s against 20.8 s (3.65 times); 50 `FORM:BM44` grey pages of 250 KB: reports 1.5 s, 74.0 s against 19.1 s (3.87 times); 100 pages of 250 KB (25,051,540 bytes): the budget is 151.8 s and the deadline leaves 116.8 s, against 41.3 s (2.8 times; the deadline binds, not the pixels).
    - 10,000 pages of 8 x 8 pixels (`cjb2` and `djvm -c`, 526,879 bytes), whose reports take 2.3 s and 2.6 s: 78.9 s against 25.5 s (3.1 times; 24.7 to 27.2 s in three runs, so 2.9 times at the slowest). The 16 times the reports and not the pixels gives this row its time.
    - 8 pages of a 100 megapixel smooth colour page (2,859,905 bytes each, 280 pixels a byte, so the cap credits 16 of them): the budget is 26.4 s and the draw took 34.7 s on Apple silicon (djvulibre 3.5.29), and about 1.65 times the budget on the VM, so this class is refused with `CpuTaskTimeoutError` where the program would finish. The three-times claim above holds below about 70 pixels a byte for colour and does not hold above it; padding cost and this false time-out come from the one constant, so retuning it only trades one against the other. The fix is the engine memoize patch (row on #783).
    - The hostile chains: a bundle of 9 KB that holds 300 shared files that each include the next, with one page of 64 x 64 pixels, one page declared 9,999 x 9,999 or six such pages, ends at 15.06 s, 15.09 s and 15.11 s with the cap (the budget is the 15 s floor and 35 ms of credit for the 8,786 bytes), against 40.07 s for the first declared page and 120.02 s for the six when the declared pixels were credited whole.
  - **One heap does not change what is drawn.** With and without `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1`, `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` draws in 1.58 s either way (medians of 5 alternating runs, 1.581 s and 1.580 s) and the PDFs are the same 6,941,025 bytes, equal but for the creation and modification dates tiff2pdf stamps; `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu` draws in 0.35 s either way, 1,188,682 identical bytes. The real documents use at most 3 threads (DOGV 3, Hansard 2, 100 PM44 pages 2). One heap costs time where the program allocates a lot from its threads: the 10,000 pages of 8 x 8 pixels draw in 23.9 and 25.2 s with it and in 20.3 and 20.8 s without (alternating runs), 18 percent.
  - **Three builds give the same pixels.** The same two real documents drawn by `ddjvu` 3.5.28 in the Debian 13 image (`djvulibre-bin` 3.5.28-2.2 with libtiff 4.7.0-3+deb13u3), in Ubuntu 24.04 (3.5.28, libtiff 4.5) and on macOS (3.5.29): the PDFs have the same pages and sizes, and the pages render to the same pixels with `pdftoppm`. libtiff 4.7 prints "Starting directory 0 at offset 0x0 (0) might cause an IFD loop" once for each page on the error output, and the output is not changed by it.
  - **Why no text target.** The PDF holds no text layer (tiff2pdf writes one image a page), and the hidden text of a DjVu file (`TXTz`, which `djvutxt` reads) is not carried into it, by the program or by us. OCR of the PDF would be a worse source of text than the layer the file holds, and takes 80 s for the 34 pages of the DOGV file in-process. The reference service offers only PDF, and the pattern of the other two routes (PostScript offers no text target, XPS reads its text in-process) leaves the text target to a reader of the text layer.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Two more programs start for each job** (`djvused` twice; a few milliseconds each for the 34 page `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu`, and seconds for a document of 10,000 pages on the test VM, whose directory `ddjvu` reads again).
  - **A chain of shared files still costs `ddjvu` 15 s and 4 microseconds for each byte of the file.** `size` opens a chain in milliseconds and does not create the files again for each path, while `ddjvu` does, with a thread for each file it decodes at once: a plain chain of about 32 files was enough to make it wait for the deadline under the address space limit, and a chain whose files each include the next two grows by about 1.6 times a level. One heap lets plain chains of up to 250 files convert, and the budget ends what remains (deeper plain chains, `poc_f` from about 35 levels) at its floor, as `CpuTaskTimeoutError`, instead of holding a worker slot idle until the 120 s deadline. The declared page sizes add nothing to it, only the bytes do: 16 credited pixels a byte at 4 million pixels a second is 4 microseconds a byte, so a hostile file buys time by being long, 1 MB of padding 4 s and 25 MB the whole 120 s deadline, and a chain that is padded that far costs its sender the upload. The root fix is in djvulibre, which could create each included file once per document; that patch is a row on issue 783 under the engine patch rule. A real document opens one or two shared files a page.
  - **A deep chain holds one thread for each file while it lasts.** With one heap, a chain of 250 files runs 245 threads (0.07 s), and a chain of 300 or more holds 252 until the budget ends it, against a `pids_limit` of 256 for the worker container (`docker-compose.prod.yml`), whose processes and threads all count toward it. When `ddjvu` cannot start a thread it waits (measured with `prlimit --nproc` of 100 and 200: no exit until killed), so such a chain can keep the container at its task limit for 15 s, or longer when the file is padded (above), during which another job in it cannot start a program. A limit on the tasks of one program run is not part of this change (see Revisit when).
  - **A single component of 16 MiB (2^24 bytes) or more is refused, though `ddjvu` draws it.** djvulibre's directory stores the size of a component in 24 bits: `djvused -e ls` reports the size modulo 2^24 (a page of 17,898,581 bytes lists as 1,121,373), `size` exits with status 10, and `ddjvu` draws the page. The whole run fails on the one component whatever its pixels, with the exit-status refusal above (HTTP 422). Measured with 3.5.29 on Apple silicon; the boundary is to be pinned on 3.5.28 (row on #783, with a byte check in front of the program).
  - **A damaged bundle answers 422 where the byte checks answered 400**: an offset outside the bundle or in the middle of a component is found by `size` and reads as an include structure the program cannot open.
  - **A long book of large scanned pages is refused, by the output limit or by the deadline.** The `size` run, `ddjvu` and the page count share the one deadline of 120 s, and each file `ddjvu` writes is limited to 512 MiB. Colour pages of 2331 x 3300 pixels with a first chunk of 250 KB (the page of `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` drawn at that size and encoded with `c44`) cost 32 ms in `size` and 0.42 s in `ddjvu` a page and write 3.76 MB of PDF a page. A book of 100 pages converts in 45.1 s; books of 200 and 300 pages end after 66.2 s and 69.1 s with "ddjvu exceeded its output or memory limit" (`ConversionFailedError`), because the PDF passes 512 MiB at about 143 pages. Pages that write little cost only their decoding, about 0.11 s a blank page: 500 blank pages convert in 55.0 s and 1,000 in 110.4 s, so the deadline refuses a book at about 1,050 such pages, with `CpuTaskTimeoutError` (HTTP 422) naming the 120000 ms of the job. The earlier measurement of scanned `FORM:PM44` pages at 14.5 million pixels a second (0.62 s a page with `size`) reaches the deadline at about 190 pages. So a scanned book above roughly 140 to 190 pages of this size is refused whatever the budget is, and a server stage limit up to 600 s moves only the deadline, not the 512 MiB.
  - **A page of a scan is a raster in the PDF**, not text: the PDF is as large as the pictures (6.9 MB for the 34 bilevel pages, 1.2 MB for the colour page, 145 MB for 100 megapixels of colour, close to the 128 MiB limit for page images).
  - **A document that lists a page again is drawn again**, once for each entry; the bound is the deadline.
  - **An indirect document is refused though the program would draw it** when its pages sit next to it. A user who uploads one file cannot supply the pages, and `djvmcvt -b` makes a bundled document from the set.
  - **One more package in the image**: `djvulibre-bin` with `libdjvulibre21` and `libdjvulibre-text`, installed without recommends (its other dependencies, `curl`, `libtiff6` and `libjpeg62-turbo`, are already in the image), with a build check that encodes a page with `cjb2` and draws it with `ddjvu`. It carries tools the worker never starts (`djvudigital`, `djvups`, `any2djvu`); the sandbox runs `djvused` and `ddjvu` only.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A TypeScript model of the directory**: see "Why the pages come from `djvused`". A BZZ decoder in TypeScript would repeat what the program already does.
  - **A TypeScript model of the include graph**, which resolved the `INCL` names against what `ls` prints and walked the files from the bundle offsets, with limits on depth, edges and loads. It repeated djvulibre's name resolution and differed from it (the thumbnails file taken from the form type rather than the directory flag, ids split at markers they may themselves hold), and a name it could not match became no edge, so a chain it was meant to refuse passed. Its walk over the chunks of every file ran in the worker process: a bundle of 4.5 MB with 19,999 entries at overlapping offsets over 500,000 empty chunks held the event loop for 37 s, outside the sandbox and the job signal, where `djvused` reads it in 0.04 s. It was removed for the verdict of `size`.
  - **`djvudump` for the include graph**: it prints a line a chunk (80 bytes; 2 GB for the 32 million chunks of a hostile 256 MiB file), and not the names of the files.
  - **An in-process DjVu decoder** (IW44 wavelet, JB2 symbol coding, BZZ, the layer compositor): a project of its own, and its pixels would be ours to prove against the program that does it.
  - **`djvutxt` for a text target now**: it is the right source of text, and the same package carries it, but the reference offers no text for DjVu, and the decision on what a text target holds (the layer, per page, with or without layout) is QA's. The registry gets the target when it is made.
  - **Staging the files an indirect document names**: the upload is one file.
  - **Rewriting an indirect document as a bundle** (`djvmcvt -b`) before drawing: it needs the pages, which the upload lacks.
  - **A pixel rate for the whole document**: see above.
- **Verified by**: `tests/djvu-container.test.ts` (the byte checks on the real files and on built containers), `tests/djvu-report.test.ts` (the strict reading of what `djvused` prints), `tests/djvu-render.test.ts` (the real files against `ddjvu -format=pdf`, `pdftoppm`, `pdftotext` and OCR; documents built with the djvulibre encoders against the real `djvused` and `ddjvu`, including the include cycle, the deep chain, the bad offsets, an offset in the middle of a component, a directory entry that is no `FORM`, a short `DIRM`, the overlapping directory, a plain chain of 40 files (drawn; on the test VM it ends at the 15 s budget without one heap) and `poc_f` 30 (drawn); stand-in programs for the failures, the kills that are not verdicts, the limits, the heap setting, the page selection and the shared deadline), `tests/djvu-render-stubbed-launcher.test.ts` (a stand-in launcher and clock: the budget given to `ddjvu` for every page and for a selection, the pixels credited only up to 16 a byte of the file, sixteen times the work before `ddjvu`, what is left of the deadline, the budget and deadline refusals, the floor of the page count, and each way a `size` or `n` run can end, with the constants imported from the module), `tests/djvu-render.perf.test.ts` (nightly, Linux: the real chain of 300 shared files with one page of 64 x 64, one declared 9,999 x 9,999 and six such pages, each ended by the budget of `ddjvu` at its floor and not later), `tests/sandbox-signal-exit.test.ts`, `tests/sandbox-launcher.test.ts` and `tests/qpdf-runner.test.ts` (the signal named on the memory-limit error, directly, across the helper and from the qpdf runner), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts`, `tests/outlook-message.test.ts` and `tests/oracle-toolchain-preflight.test.ts`. The worker image build runs `djvused` and `ddjvu` on a page it encodes with `cjb2`.
- **Revisit when**: QA wants a text target for DjVu (then `djvutxt` reads the layer), a real indirect document with its pages is uploaded as an archive, a CVE is published for djvulibre (the program parses untrusted wavelet and symbol data and runs in the sandbox for that reason), Debian ships djvulibre 3.5.29 or later or `size` changes how it opens the files a page includes, a real document is found that `size` refuses and `ddjvu` draws, a DjVu file is found whose pages the PDF loses, djvulibre takes the patch that creates an included file once per document (then the floor of the budget can go), a real document ends at the budget of `ddjvu` (the formula leaves 3.65 times to a book of 50 PM44 pages and 3.1 times to 10,000 small pages), or the sandbox gains a limit on the tasks of one program run (then a deep chain stops at it instead of at the container's `pids_limit`).

## 135. djvulibre is built from its Debian source with two patches: a shared file is searched once for a page component or a shape dictionary, a thread that cannot start fails the drawing, a run has 64 tasks or does not start, a worker runs two at once, and the budget counts 128 pixels a byte

- **Status**: Implemented (the four DjVu engine rows of issue #783, from the review of PR #935, and the first and second reviews of PR #939), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: patch the engine under the engine patch rule of 2026-10-24 instead of bounding around it). It is the current statement of the budget of `ddjvu`, its heaps, the include chains, the threads of a run and the components of 16 MiB, which entry 134 decided first.
- **Decision**:
  - **The worker image builds djvulibre instead of installing `djvulibre-bin`.** `scripts/install-djvulibre.sh` downloads the Debian 13 source package of the version the distribution ships, `djvulibre_3.5.28.orig.tar.xz` (SHA-256 `1223b7bf…7887`) and `djvulibre_3.5.28-2.2.debian.tar.xz` (`93c56218…3ef6`), from the snapshot of the Debian archive taken when that revision entered it (`snapshot.debian.org/archive/debian/20250721T022532Z`), or, when the snapshot fails, from the pool of `deb.debian.org`, which serves the same bytes until a newer revision replaces them; either is taken only with the two digests, and the `SOURCE` note names the address that served each archive. It applies the ten patches of its `debian/patches/series` (the CVE-2021-46310 and CVE-2021-46312 fixes among them) and then ours, each with `patch --batch --fuzz=0`, builds with the compiler flags of the Debian package (`dpkg-buildflags` with `hardening=+all`: `-O2`, stack protector, stack clash protection, fortified calls, PIE, RELRO, BIND_NOW, each ELF property checked), links the library statically into `ddjvu` and `djvused`, and installs the two programs, their message catalog (`share/djvu`, what `libdjvulibre-text` holds), the Debian `copyright`, a `SOURCE` note, the patch texts, the SHA-256 of the two programs as installed (`programs.sha256`) and `tool-version.txt`, which records the source, the patches, the versions of the packages it was built with (`g++`, `libjpeg-dev`, `libtiff-dev`, `autoconf`, `automake`, `libtool`) and the reference it was checked against. The script needs the distribution's `ddjvu` of the same version as that reference (`DJVULIBRE_REFERENCE_DDJVU`, no longer optional), checks the version of its source package before it downloads anything (3.5.28 on any system, and exactly `3.5.28-2.2` on Debian, so that a Debian update of the source, such as a `+deb13u1` security fix, stops the image build until the pin moves to it, while a rebuild of the same source for a new library, `3.5.28-2.2+b1`, does not), and rebuilds into a directory that held an earlier build without nesting its catalog or keeping its patches. The image's `djvulibre` stage installs the distribution package only as the reference; the runner copies `/opt/djvulibre`, links the programs into `/usr/local/bin` (which the worker searches before `/usr/bin`, as for `gxps`), and installs no `djvulibre-bin`. CI builds the same script in a task of its own (below).
  - **Patch 1, `include-search-visit-once.patch` (SHA-256 `f5fed030…7dfe`, `libdjvu/DjVuImage.cpp`, `DjVuFile.cpp` and `DjVuFile.h`).** `DjVuImage::get_info`, `get_bg44`, `get_bgpm`, `get_fgjb`, `get_fgpm` and `get_fgbc` (lines 109 to 207 of 3.5.28) look for a page component in the page's file and then, depth first, in every file it includes, and `DjVuFile::get_fgjd` (lines 752 to 795, the recursion at line 772) looks the same way for the shape dictionary a JB2 mask (`Sjbz`) needs, each with no record of the files already searched, so a shared file reached by several paths is searched once for each path: a chain whose files each include the next two costs Fibonacci-many visits. The patch searches with a map of visited URLs, the idiom of `DjVuFile::find_ndir` and `get_merged_anno` (`DjVuFile.cpp` lines 1450 and 1567). The first file found in depth-first order is the one the recursive search found: a file is skipped only after an earlier visit searched it and all it includes without finding what is looked for. `get_fgjd` keeps its passes, which wait for the files still decoding and search again, and starts each pass with an empty map; the patch also wakes those passes only for a shape dictionary (`DjVuFile::notify_chunk_done`, line 390, now returns at once for any chunk other than `Djbz`), where they were woken for every chunk decoded below the page. Only `get_fgjd` waits on that monitor (`wait_for_chunk`, line 322, has no other caller), and the end of a file's decoding, which decides whether a pass waits again, still wakes it through `notify_file_flags_changed` (line 411). `get_info` keeps its `init_rotate` call on the information it finds.
  - **The other walks over the included files that `ddjvu` reaches already visit each file once or do not recurse**, read in 3.5.28 and listed in the header of patch 1: `DjVuFile::get_merged_anno` (the annotations of a page, through `DjVuImage::get_anno` and `merge_anno`), `find_ndir` and `decode_ndir` keep a map; `DjVuPortcaster::compute_closure` (every notification between files, `DjVuPort.cpp` line 447) keeps a set; `DjVuFile::get_anno`, `get_text` and `get_meta` read the file alone, and `wait_for_finish`, `decode_func`, `notify_file_flags_changed`, `trigger_cb` and `process_incl_chunk` look only at the files a file includes directly. `DjVuFile::stop_decode` and `stop` (lines 1378 and 1437) recurse once per path with no map, but only when a document stops its files (`~DjVuDocument`, `stop_init`, `check_unnamed_files` after a failed initialisation, and the child of a stopped file); gdb counted no call of either while the patched and the unpatched `ddjvu` drew a page over a chain of 20 such files, and `ddjvu` leaves through `exit` when a page fails. The walks of `DjVuDocEditor` (the editing commands of `djvused`, which the worker does not run) and `add_file_to_djvm` and `local_get_url_names` of `DjVuDocument` (saving, with a map) are off the drawing.
  - **Patch 2, `decode-thread-start-failure.patch` (SHA-256 `68fd3f8c…4480`, `libdjvu/DjVuFile.cpp`).** `DjVuFile::start_decode` (line 1316) sets `DECODING` and starts the decoding thread with `GThread::create` (line 1341), whose result (`pthread_create`'s, `GThreads.cpp` line 426) it ignored: when the thread cannot start, the file stays `DECODING` and every file that includes it waits in `decode_func` (`wait_for_finish`, line 487) forever, at 0 % CPU. The patch releases the life saver the thread would have released and throws `DjVuFile.decode_fail`, and leaves the thread object that never started in `decode_thread`, which the next `start_decode` and `~DjVuFile` already delete outside the `flags` monitor, as the comment above it asks (the first version deleted it under that monitor); the handler already there sets `DECODE_FAILED` and notifies, so the page fails as for an included file that cannot be decoded and `ddjvu` exits with status 10 at once. The two other threads of the library that `ddjvu` could start ignore the result too and are off the path a chain exhausts, as the patch header says: `DjVuDocument::start_init` (line 208) starts the one thread that reads the directory when the document opens, before any of its files exists, and `ddjvu_runnablejob_s::start` (`ddjvuapi.cpp` line 2695) starts the save and print jobs, which `ddjvu` does not run.
