  - **The worker runs only the patched build.** `convertDjvu` refuses a `ddjvu` whose prefix lacks the patches it relies on (`DJVULIBRE_REQUIRED_PATCHES`, the files the build installs in `<prefix>/share/doc/djvulibre/patches`, found from the real path of the program), or whose real `ddjvu` or `djvused` does not have the SHA-256 the build recorded beside them (`DJVULIBRE_DIGESTS_FILE`, `programs.sha256`), with `EngineUnavailableError` before any program starts, wherever it was found: the distribution's `/usr/bin/ddjvu`, a Homebrew build, a program changed after the build, a link to nothing, or a `DDJVU_PATH` that points elsewhere. The two programs are hashed for each document, in the slot, just before its first run (a few milliseconds against three sandboxed programs; nothing is cached, so a program replaced after an earlier document, or while this one waited for its slot, is never run); the verdict names no path (they go to the server log), and only an error of the file system (a missing file, a link to nothing, no permission) is read as an unreadable build, any other error is the worker's own. CI takes a cached build only when its programs match the same file.
  - **Each run of `djvused` and `ddjvu` is limited to 64 tasks, or does not start** (`PROGRAM_TASK_LIMIT`, RLIMIT_NPROC through `prlimit`). The kernel counts RLIMIT_NPROC over the tasks of the real uid in one user namespace (since Linux 5.14, where the count moved into the ucounts of the namespace), so the limit bounds the run alone only in a user namespace of its own (`unshare -r`). `resolveSandboxedCommand` (`src/lib/security/process-sandbox.ts`) builds the isolation arguments once, decides from those arguments whether the run has its own user namespace, and refuses a run that asks for a task limit without one, or without `prlimit`, with `SandboxUnavailableError` (HTTP 503) before it spawns anything, where it used to drop the limit. A worker on a kernel older than 5.14 counts the worker's own tasks against the limit and fails its DjVu runs; the image's hosts run Ubuntu 24.04, whose kernels are newer.
  - **A worker runs the programs of at most two DjVu documents at once** (`DJVU_CONCURRENT_RUNS`, a `Semaphore` around the three runs of a document in `convertDjvu`), so its DjVu runs hold at most 128 tasks, half the `pids_limit` of 256 of every worker container, whatever its `WORKER_CONCURRENCY` (4 at the launch, 6 in the light worker of the split profile). A third document waits for a slot for at most 20 s (`DJVU_SLOT_WAIT_MS`) and then is refused as busy with `EngineUnavailableError` for `ddjvu` (503 on the routes, and a job that is retried, on another worker when the pool has one); it also gives up when the job is cancelled, and a job whose own deadline is shorter than 20 s gets the deadline's error. The wait is bounded because two hostile files of about 3.3 MB hold both slots for their whole deadline of 120 s (the run budget of `ddjvu` is at most the deadline): with the wait counted against the deadline a waiter would hold a job slot of the worker for up to 120 s and fail as if its conversion had been slow. At 20 s a waiter costs a sixth of that; a waiter behind two of the slowest measured documents (26.5 s with four drawing at once) is refused and retried, which is the pressure valve doing its work. The slot is released when `ddjvu` has drawn, before the size check and the page count of the PDF, which are not DjVu programs, so those hold no slot and their wait does not count against the 128 tasks. The budget of `ddjvu` counts the time of the reports from the moment the document has its slot. The semaphore is its own module, `src/lib/workers/semaphore.ts` (`Semaphore`, one optional `AbortSignal` for the wait, which is how the 20 s bound and the cancellation of the job are given), which the OCR native runs and page preparations use as well, each with the saturation error at its own call site (`ocrQueue`).
  - **The budget of `ddjvu` counts at most 128 pixels for each byte of the file**: `min(left of the deadline, max(15 s, 16 x t_reports) + min(drawn pixels, 128 x bytes) / 4 million a second)` (`DRAW_PIXELS_PER_INPUT_BYTE`, 16 in entry 134 and 64 in the first version of this entry). A file buys 32 µs of drawing for each of its bytes beyond the floor: 33.6 s for a megabyte, and the 105 s left of the default deadline after the floor from 3.3 MB on.
  - **`ddjvu` runs with four glibc heaps** (`MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4`, was 1).
  - **A bundle with a component of 2^24 bytes or more is refused by its bytes** before any program starts (`DjvuComponentSizeError`, HTTP 422, in `src/lib/conversions/djvu-container.ts`): the walk reads the header of each chunk after the directory and stops at one that overruns the bundle.
  - **CI builds djvulibre in a task of its own** (`task_djvulibre` of `.github/actions/ci-setup/install-tools.sh`, limit 300 s), run after the parallel tasks because it needs the packages and the reference `ddjvu` of the apt task, and only on a miss of its cache (the runner image, the script and the patches) or when the cached programs no longer have the digests of their `programs.sha256`. `run_tasks` takes the names of the tasks it runs as its arguments.
- **Why**:
  - **The cause was not the one the row named.** The row said the program creates a shared file once per path. An instrumented build that printed each `DjVuFile::init` and `start_decode` counted 26 creations and 26 decodings for `poc_f` of 25 files, one of each per file, and 21 for 20 files. Stacks of the stalled 3.5.28 on `poc_f` 35, taken with gdb three times a second apart, were each 25 frames and more of `DjVuImage::get_bg44`, `get_fgjb` or `get_fgpm` calling itself. The search, not the creation, is per path, and that is what patch 1 changes.
  - **The same search for a shape dictionary.** The review of PR #939 reproduced it with the real `Sjbz` of a page whose mask needs an inherited dictionary, over a chain of shared files that each include the next two and none the dictionary: `djvused -e size` opens it in milliseconds, and the unpatched `ddjvu` spends its time in `get_fgjd`. Built from the first page of the reference manual (`p0001.djvu` and `dict0020.iff` after `djvmcvt -i`), the unpatched build of the same source took 0.06 s at 20 files, 1.03 s [0.96 to 1.12] at 26, 2.83 s [1.31 to 3.16] at 28 and 8.20 s at 30 (5 runs at 26 and 28, alternating with the patched one), about 1.7 times as long for each file more, and had not finished after 10 s at 40, where the rate gives about 1,000 s. gdb counted 70,845 calls of `get_fgjd` for one page over 20 files, against 196 with the patch. The patched build reports the missing dictionary ("JB2 data requires a shape dictionary", status 10) in 0.02 s at 26, 28, 40 and 60 files and 0.06 s at 100, and draws the page in 0.04 s when the first file of a chain of 20 to 100 includes the dictionary after the chain, to the pixels of the page in its own document. With entry 134's byte cap removed by the first version of this entry, an 11 KB file of that shape with a few pages declared 9,999 x 9,999 had the 120 s deadline as its budget.
  - **The plain chain waited for a different reason**, measured the same way: each file a page includes is decoded on a thread of its own, the threads of a chain stay alive until the last file is done, and when the address space or the task limit stops `pthread_create` the program waits on the file whose thread never started (patch 2). In the production-like container (Debian 13, uid 10001, the worker seccomp profile, `pids_limit` 256, `unshare -r -n`, `prlimit --as=2G`) the unpatched program on a plain chain of 300 shared files held 251 threads until killed at 20 s, and the container's other processes could not fork meanwhile ("fork: retry: Resource temporarily unavailable" in the measuring shell). Under a task limit the unpatched program also waits (32 and 64 tasks: killed at 20 s with 32 and 64 threads), so the limit needed the patch.
  - **The measurements** (production-like container on Apple silicon, Docker arm64, unless named otherwise; "before" is origin/main with Debian's `ddjvu`, "after" the patched one; the convert time through `convertDjvu` to PDF, median of the runs with the range; threads are the most any `ddjvu` or `djvused` of the run had, sampled every 2 ms):
    - `poc_f` (shared files that each include the next two) of 30 files: before 1.45 s [1.38 to 1.56], drawn; after 0.062 s [0.054 to 0.111], drawn (3 runs each). Of 40 files: before 15.02 s [15.020 to 15.028], ended by the budget (`CpuTaskTimeoutError`), 42 threads; after 0.066 s [0.056 to 0.067], drawn, 39 threads.
    - Plain chains (each file includes the next): 40 files drawn in 0.058 s before and 0.054 s after, 39 and 40 threads. 300 files: before 15.03 s [15.027 to 15.058], ended by the budget with 214 threads sampled (251 in a raw run); after 0.064 s [0.061 to 0.066], refused with "ddjvu could not draw ... Decode of an included file failed", 64 threads at most. 500 files: 15.03 s against 0.072 s, 62 threads.
    - The 9 KB chain of 300 files with one page declared 9,999 x 9,999: 15.07 s against 0.063 s; with six such pages: 15.10 s against 0.095 s, refused, 64 threads.
    - The mask of a real page over 40 and 60 shared files without its dictionary, through `convertDjvu`: 0.05 to 0.11 s after, refused; the build of the same source without patch 1, stamped so the worker takes it, was ended by the budget at 15.2 to 15.3 s, and the distribution's `ddjvu` was still searching when it was stopped after 5 s.
    - Two shared files that include each other: refused by `djvused` (SIGSEGV) in 0.062 s before and 0.066 s after; the patches do not change the stack overflow that refuses a cycle or a chain of 5,000 files (`djvused -e size` still crashes on both).
    - Real documents (5 runs each, alternating): `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` 1.365 s [1.346 to 1.374] before and 1.367 s [1.343 to 1.373] after, 3 threads; `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu` 0.383 s and 0.387 s, 2 threads; the 57-page manual 0.782 s and 0.781 s, 3 threads. No measurable difference: their time is the decoding of the pages, one page at a time, which neither patch touches, and none of them includes a shared file through more than one path.
    - 8 pages of a 100 megapixel smooth colour page (2,168,046 bytes, 369 pixels a byte): the raw patched `ddjvu` under the limits of a run draws them in 15.3 s [15.3 to 16.1] (3 runs; the two reports take 13 ms), 16.2 s on the 4 vCPU arm64 VM, and the whole conversion took 20.8 s in the nightly test; the budget was 49.7 s at 64 pixels a byte and is 84.4 s at 128 (below, under the CPU quota of a worker).
    - Blank pages declared 9,999 x 9,999 in a bundle (the raw patched `ddjvu` under the limits of a run, 1 run each; 0.46 s, 300 MB resident and 292 KB of PDF a page): 5 pages in 230 bytes, 2.41 s, 299 MB, 1.46 MB of PDF; 10 pages in 408 bytes, 4.59 s, 299 MB, 2.92 MB; 100 pages in 3,528 bytes, 45.75 s, 300 MB, 29.2 MB. Through `convertDjvu` with the cap (3 runs each): 5 pages drawn in 2.31 s [2.31 to 2.45], 10 pages in 4.60 s [4.58 to 4.61], and 100 pages ended by the budget at 15.08 s [15.07 to 15.08] (15,057 ms).
    - 10,000 pages of 8 x 8 pixels (3 runs): 30.8 s before (one heap) and 30.3 s after (four heaps), 4 to 5 threads counting the main one; no measurable difference at this run count.
  - **Why the cap is 128 pixels a byte.** A file declares any page size for a few bytes, and the patched program draws a blank page declared 9,999 x 9,999 in 0.46 s: without a cap the 3.5 KB file of 100 such pages holds a worker for 45.8 s, and 260 of them in 9 KB hold it until the deadline, as 120 s of drawing. With the cap a file's pixels earn time only in proportion to its bytes: the 100 blank pages end at 15.1 s (3,528 bytes credit 0.11 s), as 16 and 64 pixels a byte ended them. The first version of this entry set the cap from drawings on an idle machine; the production worker gives 4 jobs 2.5 CPUs, so the cap is now set from drawings under that quota (`docker run --cpus 2.5` in the production-like container, the raw patched `ddjvu` under the limits of a run, 3 runs of each document alone and 3 runs of four copies at once, alternating):

    | Document | Bytes | Pixels a byte | Alone | Four at once | Budget at 128 | Budget over the slowest |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 8 smooth colour pages of 100 megapixels | 2,168,046 | 369 | 14.9 to 15.4 s | 24.7 to 26.5 s | 84.4 s | 3.2 times |
    | 8 dense bilevel pages (a text page at 600 dpi through `cjb2`, 34.8 megapixels each) | 59,053 | 4,715 | 0.26 s | 0.39 to 0.41 s | 15.0 s (floor) | 37 times |
    | `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` (34 pages) | 496,789 | 2,381 | 1.25 to 1.26 s | 2.10 to 2.16 s | 15.0 s (floor) | 6.9 times |
    | `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu` | 534,990 | 15.7 | 0.34 to 0.35 s | 0.57 to 0.63 s | 15.0 s (floor) | 24 times |
    | the 57-page manual | 428,566 | 1,990 | 0.70 to 0.73 s | 1.18 to 1.24 s | 15.0 s (floor) | 12 times |

    Four drawings of the smooth pages take 24.9 s, 4 x 15 s of CPU over 2.5 CPUs (24 s), so the quota is what bounds them. At 64 pixels a byte their budget, 49.7 s, was 1.9 times the slowest of these runs; three times it needs 119 pixels a byte, and 128 gives 3.2 times. The documents with more pixels a byte are bilevel and draw within the floor. Through `convertDjvu`, four copies at once end at 14.7 s for the first two and 29.4 s for the two that waited for a slot (2 runs), within the deadline.
  - **Why the run is refused without a user namespace of its own.** Dropping the limit there, as the first version of this entry did, ran the program with no bound on its tasks, and the test of it passed whichever happened. Measured in the production-like container with 45 tasks of the same uid outside the run: inside its own user namespace under `prlimit --nproc=64` a shell forked 50 children and failed at 70 ("Cannot fork"); outside one, the same limit stopped its first fork, because the 45 outside tasks counted. A host that cannot give a run its own namespace cannot bound it, and DjVu refuses there as any strict sandbox does. Deciding from the isolation arguments the run actually gets, not from a second probe, keeps the decision and the command the same.
  - **Why only the stamped build.** Under the task limit an unpatched `ddjvu` waits forever on a thread that cannot start (measured at 32 and 64 tasks), and without patch 1 the budget, not the program, ends a chain, so with the old fallback to `/usr/bin/ddjvu` a host without the build was worse off than before this entry. The patches the build ships are the cheapest proof of what it is, and naming them in the worker refuses a build of the previous patch set too.
  - **Why four heaps.** Without a bound on the arenas, the patched program fails the plain chain of 40 shared files, a chain of 128 and `poc_f` 40 with status 10 in 10 to 18 ms (the Lima VM, address space 2 GiB, no task limit): each decoding thread takes an arena of 64 MiB of address space and from about 30 threads `pthread_create` finds no room for a stack. With one or four heaps all three draw (8 to 42 ms). Four arenas reserve at most 256 MiB, which leaves room for the 512 MiB of stacks of 64 tasks under the 2 GiB limit; the real documents decode on at most three threads at once (entry 134), so with four heaps none of them shares a heap. On 10,000 pages of 8 x 8 pixels, whose drawing allocates from several threads, the patched program took a median of 26.4 s with four heaps, 26.4 s unbounded and 28.8 s with one heap (19 alternating runs each on the arm64 VM, ranges 23.9 to 31.8, 23.5 to 30.9 and 25.9 to 42.0 s; the host carried a load of 5 to 10 from other work, so the ranges overlap and the 8 percent is indicative, in line with the 18 percent entry 134 measured on a quiet host).
  - **The pixels do not change.** The patched build and Debian's `djvulibre-bin` 3.5.28-2.2 draw `wc-dogv-12042005.djvu` (34 pages), `wc-hansard-1963-malaysia-bill-clause-4.djvu` and the 57-page manual of the source archive to PDFs of the same size in bytes (6,941,025, 1,188,682 and 3,276,320) whose pages `pdftoppm` renders to the same pixels, every page; the same holds for the build of the same source without our patches. Where the search order matters, a page that reaches a background through two branches sharing a file, the second branch holding a decoy background, is drawn by both builds to the same pixels (not the decoy's), and the mask over a chain whose first file includes its dictionary after the chain is drawn to the pixels of the page in its own document.
  - **Why 64 tasks.** The real documents use at most 3 decoding threads (entry 134); a chain of 40 files needs 30 to 40 (it draws at 64 and is refused at 32). At 64, the plain chains of 300 and 500 files are refused in 0.04 to 0.11 s with 64 threads at most, a quarter of the container's `pids_limit`, where the patched program alone (no task limit) reached 244 to 252 threads before the address space stopped it.
  - **The 16 MiB boundary, pinned on 3.5.28** (Debian's `djvused` and `ddjvu`, bundles built byte by byte with a second page component of the size given): `DjVmDir` stores each component's size in 24 bits (`read24`, `DjVmDir.cpp` lines 253 and 268; `write24`, line 453), so `djvused -e ls` lists 16,777,214 bytes as written, 16,777,216 as 0 and 16,777,218 as 2. 16,777,214 converts; 16,777,218 fails `djvused -e size` and `ddjvu` alike with "Unexpected End Of File" (status 10, "Cannot decode page 2"), first, middle or last in the bundle; 2^24 and 2^25 exactly are recorded as 0, which djvulibre reads as an unknown length, and convert. The byte check refuses every component of 2^24 bytes or more, the exact multiples too, because the format cannot record their size and another reader would not read them. A single-page file has no directory and is not affected. The 24-bit field is not widened: it is the layout of the `DIRM` chunk in the DjVu format (sizes in 24 bits, offsets in 32), a widened writer would make files no other reader opens, and a reader cannot recover high bits the file does not hold.
  - **Why a CI task of its own.** Inside the apt task the cold build made that task take 172 to 257 s in the first CI run of this entry and pass its limit of 300 s once (a timeout is never cached, so it would fail again), where the warm task takes 72 to 96 s. In its own task the cold build took 120 to 157 s on the x64 runners, so its limit is 300 s, about twice the slowest. Run after the parallel tasks, it adds its time to the step only on a cache miss, and the step's worst case, 360 s and then 300 s, still leaves a job of 15 minutes four.
  - **Why the thread gate accepts a crash at exit.** The gate of patch 2 demanded status 10, and two of six shards of the second CI run of the image of this entry failed it with status 139 after the decode failure: the exit-time crash recorded under the trade-offs. Run 130 times in the production-like container, the patched program ended the gate with status 10 127 times and 139 three times, each time after "Decode of an included file failed"; the distribution's program was killed at 10 s (status 137). The gate now accepts 10 or 139 only with that message on stderr, takes 124 or 137 as the missing patch, and prints stderr on any failure.
  - **Why two runs at once.** A run is bounded to 64 tasks, but the files of a chain keep their threads until their own decoding ends, so a chain whose files carry data holds its tasks for longer than an empty chain: a plain chain of 64 shared files that each carry the wavelet background of a smooth page of 4,000 x 4,000 (3,265,678 bytes) is refused at the task limit in 1.21 to 1.24 s with 64 threads, one of 400 x 400 noise (13,260,560 bytes) in 1.09 to 1.15 s, and the 40-file chains of the same files draw in 0.18 to 0.85 s with 42 threads (3 runs each through `convertDjvu` at 2.5 CPUs). The budget ends any run of such pages at its floor, 15 s. With every job of a worker drawing such a chain, 4 jobs held 256 tasks, all of the container's `pids_limit`, and the light worker's 6 jobs 384; two runs at once hold 128 in every profile, and a document waits instead.
  - **Why the search waits only for a shape dictionary.** `get_fgjd` searched every file below the page again whenever any of them decoded a chunk. Through the production-like container at 2.5 CPUs (3 runs each, alternating), the mask of DOGV's first page without its dictionary over a chain of 60 shared files that each include the next two took 2.22 to 2.34 s with 600 small chunks in each file and 8.0 to 8.6 s with 2,000, where the same chains decode in 0.77 to 0.79 s and 2.3 to 2.8 s without the mask. Keeping the finished files out of the next passes, as the review proposed, did not help (2.58 to 2.95 s and 8.6 to 8.8 s): a file of a chain finishes only after everything it includes, so nearly every file is still decoding at each wake. Waking the search only for a `Djbz` chunk brought it to 0.64 to 0.71 s and 2.2 to 2.6 s, the time of the decoding; a mask whose dictionary is the last file of such a chain is still drawn (0.23 to 0.28 s).

  - **The engine patch rule.** Reproducible build: the two source archives, fetched from a fixed snapshot or else the pool, and the two patches are pinned by digest, the flags come from `dpkg-buildflags` of the image's own Debian release, the reference must be that release's package of the pinned revision, and the stage fails unless the patches apply with no fuzz, the hardening properties hold, a page is drawn, and each check of a chain ends with the exact status only the patches give within 10 s: a chain of 40 shared files that each include the next two is drawn (status 0), the mask of the manual's first page over 40 and 60 such files without its dictionary is refused (status 10), the mask over 60 files whose first includes the dictionary is drawn to the reference's pixels of the page, and a plain chain of 100 under an address space of 512 MiB and 8 MiB stacks fails with the decode failure (status 10, or 139 when it crashes at exit after the message) instead of waiting, with the program run as `LANGUAGE=C LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` because it prints the message in the language of the environment (the package ships de, fr, ja and zh catalogues) and the gate looks for the English text; the reference is still searching the chain of 40 and the mask over 40 when it is stopped after 5 s (status 124), which shows that the checks exercise what the patches change; and the manual matches the reference's pixels on every page. Built without patch 1 the stage stops at the chain of 40 (status 124), with the first version of patch 1 (no `get_fgjd`) at the mask over 40 (status 124), and without patch 2 at the plain chain (status 137, killed). Re-applying on a bump: the header of the install script (apply to the new source; drop a patch the release holds from the script and from `DJVULIBRE_REQUIRED_PATCHES`, which names the patches, rebase any other and change its digest in the script; the build records the digests of its programs itself; run `tests/djvu-render.test.ts`). The versions of both patches before the second review applied with no fuzz to upstream 3.5.30.1 (the Djbz-only wake and the kept thread object are not rechecked there), whose `DjVuImage.cpp` and `get_fgjd` (`DjVuFile.cpp` line 755) still search per path and whose `start_decode` still ignores the result, so both can go upstream as written. CVE tracking cost: Debian's security updates of `djvulibre` no longer reach the image with the package; a new revision of the trixie source package or a djvulibre CVE is a pin bump of this script, which the version check of the stage now forces. Image: the stage takes 56 s on Apple silicon with its packages; the runner drops `djvulibre-bin`, `libdjvulibre21` and `libdjvulibre-text` (3,860 KB installed) and gains `/opt/djvulibre` (3.1 MB).
  - **References.** djvulibre 3.5.28 `libdjvu/DjVuImage.cpp`, `DjVuFile.cpp`, `DjVuFile.h`, `DjVuPort.cpp`, `GThreads.cpp`, `GContainer.h`, `DjVmDir.cpp`, `DjVuDocument.cpp` (`url_to_file`, the per-document aliases that already make each file once; `start_init`), `DjVuDocEditor.cpp`, `ddjvuapi.cpp`, `DjVuMessage.cpp` and `tools/ddjvu.cpp`, read and cited by line; the patches are ours, as no maintained fork carries them (3.5.30.1 checked). The task limit follows the RLIMIT_NPROC accounting of Linux 5.14 (`kernel/ucount.c`, `is_rlimit_overlimit` and the limit a user namespace inherits at its creation).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A build to carry** (above): two patches, one of 53 added and 72 removed lines in two function families and the wake of one of them, one of 6 added and 1 removed.
  - **A failure in many threads at once can crash at exit.** When the threads of a long chain fail together, `ddjvu` prints the error and calls `exit(10)` (`tools/ddjvu.cpp` line 746) while decoding threads still run and look up their messages in the catalog that the exit is destroying (`DjVuMessage::create_full`, `DjVuMessage.cpp` line 518): 2 of 8 runs of a plain chain of 300 without a task limit ended with SIGSEGV after the message. The document is refused either way ("ddjvu could not draw" or "ddjvu exceeded its output or memory limit"); the task limit keeps the threads that fail together to 64.
  - **A chain of more than about 60 shared files is refused** where unlimited threads would draw it; no real document has such a chain (one or two shared files a page).
  - **A document of many large blank or near-empty pages in a small file is refused at about 15 s** ("took too long to draw"), as entry 134 refused it at 16 pixels a byte, though the program would finish; 100 blank pages of 9,999 x 9,999 take 46 s.
  - **DjVu is refused on a host without unprivileged user namespaces or `prlimit`**, macOS among them: a developer without the patched build on Linux sees `EngineUnavailableError` or `SandboxUnavailableError`, and the suites that draw real files skip there, as they skip without the tools.
  - **A third DjVu document of a worker waits** for one of the two runs to end, within its own deadline: four copies of the smooth colour pages end at 14.7 s and 29.4 s instead of all at about 25 s.
  - **A file buys more time for its bytes**: 32 µs a byte at 128 pixels a byte, twice what 64 gave, so a hostile file reaches the default deadline from 3.3 MB instead of 6.6 MB.
  - **A Debian update of djvulibre stops the image build** until the pin moves, by design.
  - **A bundle with a component of exactly 2^24 or 2^25 bytes is refused** though djvulibre reads it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A per-document cache of included files** (the row's proposal): the files are already made once per document (`DjVuDocument::url_to_file` finds a file by its alias); the cost was the search.
  - **The task limit without patch 2**: the program waits at the limit (measured at 32 and 64), so the container is freed but the budget still runs.
  - **Counting every declared pixel** (the first version of this entry): the blank pages above hold a 9 KB file until the deadline, and any search the patches miss would have the same time. **Keeping 16 pixels a byte**: the smooth colour pages had 1.5 times their drawing.
  - **Dropping the task limit where the run has no user namespace of its own** (the first version of this entry): the run then had no bound, silently.
  - **Falling back to the distribution's `ddjvu`**: under the task limit it waits forever.
  - **The pool of `deb.debian.org`** as the only source: it drops the revision after the next point release. **The snapshot alone**: one address that fails stops every image build, though the pool serves the same bytes.
  - **Keeping the files that finished out of the next passes of `get_fgjd`**: measured above, no gain, as the files of a chain finish last.
  - **Comparing the binary version of the reference package**: a rebuild of the same source for a new library (`+b1`) would stop the image build.
  - **Keeping the build inside the apt task with a longer limit**: that task is the critical path of every job, and its limit would grow past what its packages need for a build that runs on a cache miss.
  - **Unbounded heaps**: chains from about 30 files fail. **One heap**: the threads of a real document share it (entry 134 measured 18 percent on 10,000 small pages).
  - **Backporting 3.5.30 from Debian forky**: it still searches per path and ignores the thread result, and moves every other part of the program.
  - **Widening the 24-bit size**: above.
- **Verified by**: `tests/worker-djvulibre-packaging.test.ts` (the stage, the reference package and its version check, the runner without `djvulibre-bin`, the snapshot and the pins, the patches applied after Debian's with no fuzz and each to its one change with the audit of the walks in its header, the patches named in the worker, the hardening checks, the gates with their exact statuses before the install, what is installed and the versions recorded, the CI task and its cache), `tests/djvulibre-gates.test.ts` (the functions of `scripts/lib/djvulibre-gates.sh` run against stand-ins for curl, pdftoppm and ddjvu: the download takes the first source with the pinned bytes, goes on after other bytes or a failed request and leaves no file when none serves them; the pixels gate names the page that differs and the PDF with the wrong page count; the thread gate accepts 10 and 139 with the decode failure, refuses them without it, refuses 124, 137, 1 and 0, and reads the message in English under `LANGUAGE=de`), `tests/djvu-render.test.ts` (on the patched build, in runs that can have their task limit: `poc_f` 40 drawn, a plain chain of 300 refused, and the mask of DOGV's first page over 40 and 60 shared files refused within the hang guard, the mask drawn through a chain to the pixels of the page; the two real files and the diamond with a decoy drawn to the distribution's pixels; four heaps), `tests/djvu-render-stubbed-launcher.test.ts` (the budget with 128 pixels a byte, including the smooth colour pages, 64 tasks for each of the three runs, two documents at once with a third that waits, is refused as busy after the wait bound or at its deadline when that is shorter, or stops when its job is cancelled, a slot freed before the page count of the PDF, a program replaced while a document waited refused when its turn comes, a build without either patch, a `ddjvu` or `djvused` that is not the program its build recorded, a build without `programs.sha256`, a program replaced after an allowed run, a link to nothing, and a `DDJVU_PATH` to an unstamped build refused before any program starts), `tests/semaphore.test.ts` (the limit, the order, the queue bound with the error it names, a wait ended by its signal, a timeout signal or a signal already aborted, with the slot handed to the next waiter and no slot lost) and `tests/ocr-cli-tsv.test.ts` (the OCR saturation error and what it names), `tests/djvu-container.test.ts` (16,777,214 accepted, 16,777,216 and 16,777,218 refused with the message, a single page of any size accepted, a walk of 500,000 chunks within the hang guard), `tests/sandbox-confinement-and-lifecycle.test.ts` (a task limit refused for a run without a user namespace of its own; with 40 sleepers of the same uid outside, a run forks 50 children and fails at 70), `tests/ci-setup-tasks.test.ts` (the limit of the CI task, the order of the steps, and the dependent task run by name without changing the job's task list), `tests/djvu-render.perf.test.ts` (nightly: the chains of 300 refused within 2.5 s whatever their pages declare, the mask over 40 and 60 files refused within 2.5 s while the distribution's `ddjvu` is still searching after 5 s, 100 blank pages declared 9,999 x 9,999 ended within twice the floor, the 8 smooth colour pages drawn within a third of the deadline, the mask over 60 files of 600 small chunks each refused in less than 1.5 times the decoding of the same chain without the mask, which the build without the Djbz-only wake fails at 2.6 s against 1.2 s, and the plain chain of 64 files with backgrounds refused within a third of the floor), the build gates, and the measurements above.
- **Revisit when**: djvulibre takes the patches (return to the distribution package), Debian publishes a new revision of 3.5.28 for trixie or the image moves to a release with 3.5.30 (rebase; the stage stops on its own), a real document needs more than 64 tasks or ends at the budget, a document with more pixels a byte than the smooth colour pages is reported (move the cap), a host runs a kernel older than 5.14, a worker's `pids_limit` or its CPU quota changes (the runs at once and the cap), or the exit-time crash is fixed upstream (the thread gate then demands status 10 again).

## 136. The compound file parser refuses a file past 256 MiB itself, storages nested past 1,000 levels and paths past 16 Mi characters, and the other limits of its references are pinned by hostile files

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the rows "one bounded input reader" and "audit `parseCfbf` against the reference readers" that the reviews of #924 and #933 left), decided 2026-10-31 (QA request: close the legacy Office bound rows in one change); reviewed in four rounds on #938, the fourth on 2026-11-01).
- **Decision**:
  - **`parseCfbf` refuses a buffer of more than `CFBF_MAX_FILE_BYTES` (256 MiB) before it reads the signature** (`CorruptStreamError`, status 400, "The compound file is larger than the 268435456-byte limit."). The constant sits in `compound-file-kind.ts` with the other limits of the parser, so the lower layer no longer imports from `office/`. `LEGACY_OFFICE_MAX_INPUT_BYTES` is gone: the RTF reader (an RTF document is held in memory whole, as a compound file is), the input readers and the check against the `.xls` sheet bounds import `CFBF_MAX_FILE_BYTES`, one number for the legacy readers. Until now only `readCfbContainer` (Word, PowerPoint, Outlook message, and the encrypted check of a workbook since entry 133) checked it; the Excel 97-2003 reader (`readCfbfWorkbookSheets`), the HWP reader (`parseHwpDocument`) and the charts embedded in a slide called `parseCfbf` with whatever a job holds in memory, up to 512 MiB. The bound now lives where the memory is spent, once: `readCfbContainer` does not test the size itself, and the refusal of the parser reaches its caller inside the message that names the label ("<label>: the compound file is malformed (The compound file is larger than the 268435456-byte limit.).", a `LegacyOfficeFormatError`). A workbook or an HWP document between 256 and 512 MiB, which the XLS and HWP readers parsed before, is refused with the 400. `isEncryptedLegacyOffice`, which reads at most the same 256 MiB from a file, and the package checks (`getMaxInMemoryBytes`) share `boundedInput` as before; the missing-file condition that two of them wrote out is one `isMissingFile`.
  - **Storages nest at most 1,000 deep** (`CFBF_MAX_STORAGE_DEPTH`). The directory walk is iterative, so no depth overflows the stack; the depth bounds the length of a path. A storage at level 1,001 is refused, with or without children.
  - **The full paths of all directory entries spell out at most 16 Mi characters together** (`CFBF_MAX_PATH_CHARS`, 16,777,216). The parser keeps a map from the full path of each stream to its bytes, and no reference builds paths. A file of 900 KiB with 1,000 storages one in another and 4,000 streams in the last held 74 MiB of path strings after the parse (measured, Apple silicon, Node 24, `process.memoryUsage().rss`); with the 65,536 entries a directory may hold that is about 1.2 GB (scaled from the 4,000, not measured), for a file of a few megabytes. 65,536 entries under four levels of names of 31 characters spell out 8.4 million characters, half the budget. The budget counts every entry, storages included, in the order the walk meets them.
  - **The directory is read through a bound, and the directory and the mini FAT are the file's structure.** The directory chain is read for at most `(CFBF_MAX_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES + 1) * 128` bytes (`CFBF_DIRECTORY_READ_BYTES`, 8,388,736), and a chain that holds more 128-byte slots than `CFBF_MAX_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES` (free slots counted, as the check of the file kind counts them) is refused, so the two readers agree on a file. Until now the whole chain was copied before any count, and the count was of named entries: a 256 MiB file whose directory chain covers every sector parsed as one entry.
  - **A destroyed structure has one typed cause, `CompoundFileStructureError`** (status 400, a `CorruptStreamError` so that every caller of the parser still sees a corrupt container). The directory, the mini FAT and the root entry's mini stream are read as *structure* chains (`ChainRole`), and a chain is refused with it when it starts at a reserved number (an empty directory, the end-of-chain, free, FAT or DIFAT marker), reaches a sector past the file or one the FAT does not cover, ends on any marker but the end of chain (a free sector or the free, FAT or DIFAT marker, which were read as the end before), returns to a sector it has read, or reads a sector of the FAT or the DIFAT; so is a directory in which no entry has a name or that holds more slots than it may, a FAT sector listed twice, a DIFAT chain that returns to a sector, a directory tree that reaches an entry twice, a stream below the cutoff when the root entry has no mini stream (it starts at a marker or holds no byte), and a chain that goes on past the last sector of a file that ends inside it. A structure chain is walked to its end whatever the bytes wanted of it, bounded by the file because each sector is claimed once: the mini FAT keeps only the entries the mini stream can address, the root entry's mini stream is copied only as far as its declared size and its tail is claimed and checked as the rest of the chain is, and the directory is copied for the slots it may hold and one more. The depth of the storages and the length of the paths stay limits, a plain `CorruptStreamError` that the suite may retry: they say the file is too large to read, not that its table of contents is wrong. A sector that a structure chain shares with any other chain is refused as the structure's damage, from whichever side it is met: a stream chain that reaches a sector of the directory or the mini FAT is told by the owner table, and the pointer that is wrong cannot be known. Before, the same damage had three outcomes depending on where the bad number landed: past the file a plain `ConversionFailedError`, on a FAT sector or another chain's sector a `CorruptStreamError` that the office suite was asked to retry, and on a free sector or a marker a directory read as far as it went. The chain of a *stream* is not read this way, and its damage stays a `CorruptStreamError` (a loop, a sector of the FAT, a sector of another stream, a chain that holds fewer bytes than the stream declares): it is cut, the stream that needed the rest is refused for its size, and the suite may still read a document whose other streams are whole. `retryRefusedLegacyDocument` does not retry a `CompoundFileStructureError`: the suite reads the same directory, and for the three real workbooks whose directory runs past the file it wrote their bytes as text. `readCfbContainer` refuses every malformed file as a `LegacyOfficeFormatError` with the label of the document in the message and the error of the parser as its `cause`, as it did before this entry, and the gate walks the `cause` chain (at most 8 errors deep, so that a chain of causes that returns ends), so a Word, PowerPoint or Outlook document is not retried either and `isEncryptedWordDocument` needs no case of its own. Both shapes reach the gate on purpose: the Excel and HWP readers call `parseCfbf` themselves, so their refusal is the bare `CompoundFileStructureError`, and the others open the file through `readCfbContainer`, whose wrapper names the document. `ConversionFailedError` takes `ErrorOptions`, so the `cause` of the wrapper is the native, non-enumerable one. POI reads these chains as streams that end only at the end of chain (`POIFSStream.java` lines 165 to 167 and 183 to 221: `hasNext` is `nextBlock != END_OF_CHAIN`, and any other number is read as a block, so a marker or a number past the file throws), and olefile with its default settings (`raise_defects=DEFECT_FATAL`, line 1048) records the same damage as a defect below that level, stops reading the chain and goes on (`olefile.py` lines 672 and 701, `_raise_defect` at 1164 to 1170); this parser follows POI, whose strictness is what a table of contents needs.
  - **The mini stream cutoff is 4096 whatever the header gives, and the header field is not read.** [MS-CFB] 2.2 requires 4096. Before, the cutoff was taken from the header: at 0xFFFFFFFF every stream is a mini stream, and one stream became a chain of millions of 64-byte mini sectors. POI never reads the field and olefile fixes it at 4096, and so does this parser (see the table), so a file reads the same whatever the field gives (0, 0x2000 and 0xFFFFFFFF are pinned by a file with a stream on each side of 4096). A writer that used another cutoff stores the streams between the two values in the other store than the one this parser reads them from, as it does for POI and olefile: the real mismatch (written with 8,192, a 5,000-byte stream in the mini stream) nearly always ends in the owner table, because the mini sector number is a sector that something else owns, and a crafted file can name unowned sectors and be given their bytes as the stream, which is no worse than the two references. An earlier round of this entry refused a file when a stream lay between the header value and 4096; it also refused valid files whose header was junk (a cutoff of 0, 0xFFFFFFFF or 0x2000 over streams placed by 4096) and is gone.
  - **The tables are no larger than the file can use.** The FAT is read from at most `ceil(sectors in the file / 128)` sectors for 512-byte sectors (as many as map every sector of the file: olefile cuts the FAT to the sectors of the file, `olefile.py` lines 1643 to 1645), where it was read from the count the header gives, so a header that names every sector of a file as a FAT sector built a FAT as large as the file; the sectors the list names beyond that are claimed as table sectors and not read. The mini FAT and the mini stream are read only when a stream below the cutoff needs them (olefile loads the mini FAT only when such a stream is opened, `olefile.py` lines 1858 to 1860), so the real workbook whose root entry points past the file and whose one stream lies in the sectors still reads, and then only the entries that the mini stream can address, `ceil(min(mini stream size, bytes in the sectors) / 64)` and at most the sectors the header counts (olefile shrinks it to the mini sectors of the root entry's size, lines 1667 and 1681; POI reads the sectors the header counts, `POIFSFileSystem.java` lines 430 to 442). The FAT and the mini FAT are filled by one loader from the sectors they lie in, a word at a time with `readUInt32LE`, so no case depends on the byte order of the host. Before, the chain was read to the end of the file whatever the mini stream held.
  - **A chain is copied into one buffer of the bytes it holds.** `ChainReader` (`cfbf-reader.ts`) lists the sectors of a chain (claiming each), and copies them into one buffer of `min(chain bytes, declared size)` with `copy`, where a buffer was made for each sector and joined with `Buffer.concat` (and copied once more for the mini stream). One list serves every chain, so a stream costs no allocation but its own bytes. The root entry's mini stream is no longer copied twice. A stream chain stops once it holds the declared size and claims no sector past it (a structure chain is walked to its end, as above), and the last sector of a file cut short counts only the bytes the file holds, so a stream is never handed bytes that are not in the file. A sector the file cuts short can only end its chain: a chain that goes on past it is refused (a `CompoundFileStructureError` for a structure chain, a `CorruptStreamError` for a stream), where the bytes of the sectors after it would have been joined to its partial bytes. The mini FAT is loaded from its chain by `ChainReader.readTable`, which reads no more whole words than the chain holds in the bytes of the file, where a chain that went through the cut sector read 128 words from it and ended in a `RangeError` with no status (found in the review of the fourth round, pinned by `tests/cfbf-structure-errors.test.ts`). One rule, `storeOf`, says where a stream lies (mini stream, sectors, or none), for the size check, the mini stream test, the copy of each stream and the position of a byte.
  - **The other limits of the parser were audited against the three references and kept** (the table below). Each is now pinned by a hostile file in `tests/cfbf-parse-limits.test.ts` that ends as the typed 400 for the reason the reference gives, inside the hang guard of `expectNoHang` (10 s, the file takes under 0.2 s).
    - A sector claimed twice by one chain, or by two chains (`ChainReader.claim`), for the FAT, the mini FAT, the directory chain and every stream. The FAT and DIFAT sectors are in the same table, owned by no chain, so a stream, the directory or the mini FAT that reads one is refused (POI claims the FAT, XFAT and property table blocks in one detector, below). POI `BlockStore.ChainLoopDetector` (`BlockStore.java` lines 85 to 117, `claim` at 99 to 115) and LibreOffice `StgStrm::scanBuildPageChainCache` (`sot/source/sdstor/stgstrms.cxx` lines 356 to 391: a set of the pages seen, `ERRCODE_IO_WRONGFORMAT` on a repeat) do the same for one chain; olefile `_check_duplicate_stream` (`olefile.py` lines 1436 to 1459, called at 853, 1403, 1406, 1409) for the first sector of every stream. Across chains it is the rule entry 88 took from olefile.
    - A FAT sector or a DIFAT sector read once, the FAT read from the count the header gives and from the sectors that map the file, every sector the list names claimed, the DIFAT chain cut at the count the header gives (`parseCfbf`, step 1). POI reads them in one `ChainLoopDetector` (`POIFSFileSystem.java` lines 389 to 442, "Each block should only ever be used by one of the FAT, XFAT or Property Table"); olefile cuts the FAT to the sectors of the file (`olefile.py` lines 1388, 1643 to 1645) and requires the DIFAT count to be the one the FAT count implies (lines 1603 to 1615). Ours ends the list at the first FAT sector past the file and stops reading FAT sectors once it holds the sectors that map every sector of the file, so the FAT never outgrows the file, as olefile's cut does; a sector listed twice, or a DIFAT chain that returns, is a `CompoundFileStructureError`.
    - The count of FAT sectors. POI refuses more than 65,535 (`POIFSFileSystem.java` lines 82 and 995 to 1007). Ours needs no constant: the FAT list ends at the file, and the file is at most 256 MiB, so 4,096 FAT sectors of 512 bytes at the most.
    - A stream that declares more bytes than the file holds. `assertStreamSizesFit` refuses the sum of the declared sizes over the sectors of the file and over the mini stream before any copy, and a chain that holds fewer bytes than its stream declares is refused. olefile refuses a stream of more sectors than the FAT (`olefile.py` lines 640 to 641) and one shorter than declared (line 724), and reads a fixed number of sectors "to avoid DoS attacks" (lines 650 to 652); POI allocates through `IOUtils.safelyAllocate` with a ceiling (`POIFSFileSystem.java` lines 64 to 67, 343). The sum is the budget of the file as a whole, which none of them keeps (entry 88).
    - A sector number past the file, or past the FAT, ends the chain of a stream (`ChainReader.walk`), and the stream that needed it is refused for its size; for the directory and the mini FAT the chain is refused where it ends there (the `structure` role). olefile raises "incorrect OLE FAT, sector index out of range" (lines 672 and 701) as a defect that it records by default.
    - A directory of 65,536 slots at the most (`CFBF_MAX_DIRECTORY_ENTRIES`), the writer's own limit (`cfbf-writer.ts`). olefile allows as many entries as the directory stream holds divided by 128 (`olefile.py` line 1787), and `PropertyTable.java` of POI sets no count. The number is ours; it counts slots, free ones included, so a directory of 8 MiB (and 128 bytes, the one slot that shows the chain is longer) is the most the parser reads.
    - A directory tree reached twice is refused as a destroyed structure (`resolveEntryPaths`). olefile refuses an entry "referenced more than once" (`olefile.py` lines 906 to 944) and POI a child added twice (`DirectoryProperty.java` line 275); LibreOffice discards a link whose leaf repeats an ancestor's or whose name is taken (`stgdir.cxx` lines 761 to 795). The walk keeps an explicit stack, as POI's `populatePropertyTree` does for the siblings.
    - The mini sector shift is 6 and the sector shifts 9 and 12 (`CFBF_SECTOR_SHIFTS` and `CFBF_MINI_SECTOR_SHIFT`). POI `HeaderBlock.java` line 166 and olefile lines 1343 to 1350.
    - The mini stream cutoff is 4096 (`CFBF_MINI_STREAM_CUTOFF`), and the header field is not read, as in POI and olefile. POI never reads the header field and compares each stream with `POIFSConstants.BIG_BLOCK_MINIMUM_DOCUMENT_SIZE` (`POIFSConstants.java` line 47; `POIFSDocument.java` lines 64 and 96); olefile notes a defect for another value and fixes it at 4096 (`olefile.py` lines 1368 to 1379); LibreOffice takes any positive value from the header (`StgHeader::Check`, `stgelem.cxx` line 205, and `stgio.cxx` line 317).
- **Why**:
  - **References.** Apache POI trunk 6327f056 of 2026-10-30 (Apache License 2.0), `poi/src/main/java/org/apache/poi/poifs/`; olefile master 7c0f1ce6 of 2024-10-28 (BSD), `olefile/olefile.py`; LibreOffice master 6e0b3914 of 2026-10-31 (MPL-2.0), `sot/source/sdstor/`. Behaviour and limits only; no code was copied.
  - **POI's depth, with its unit.** `PropertyTable.MAX_PROPERTY_DEPTH` is 1,000 (`PropertyTable.java` line 232) and `populatePropertyTree` throws when the directory it is given is deeper (lines 234 to 237); the root is depth 0 and a storage in the root is depth 1. Ours counts the same: a storage at level 1,001 is refused. olefile recurses in `append_kids` with no bound of its own, so Python's recursion limit ends a deep tree with a `RecursionError`, and LibreOffice recurses in `StgDirStrm::SetupEntry` with none, so a deep tree there is the stack. Neither is a limit to follow.
  - **Measured on the hostile files** (Apple silicon, one run each, `vitest`, a file of under 10 MiB each): a FAT chain that returns to its first sector, a FAT self loop, a directory chain that returns, a mini FAT self loop and cycle, a DIFAT chain that returns (8 MiB file with one DIFAT sector), an entry that is its own right sibling, two siblings that link to each other and a storage that is its own child each end in under 5 ms; 65,536 storages one in another end in the depth refusal in 37 ms and a directory of 65,536 entries is read in 49 ms; 1,000 storages with 600 streams end in the path refusal in 27 ms and with 500 are read; a stream of 4 GiB less one byte, a mini stream of 4,095 bytes over 960, a start sector at 0x7fffffff, a FAT entry at 0x7ffffff0, a FAT list that names a sector past the file and a version 4 entry of 2^40 bytes end under 5 ms each with less than 1 MiB of array buffers allocated; a buffer of 256 MiB and one byte is refused in 1 ms. The cases of the file pass after the change. Against the parser as it was, 5 of the first 28 were red (the two depth cases, the path budget and the two size cases) and 23 passed, because the parser already followed these references for loops and declared sizes.
  - **Memory on three hostile files, before and after the first round** (Apple silicon, Node 24, load average 8 to 9, one run each, `/usr/bin/time -l` for the peak resident set and a sampler on the `Buffer` factories for the array buffers, the file itself read in memory first and not counted in the growth). A 256 MiB version 3 file whose directory chain covers every sector: 1,050 MiB peak and 511 MiB of array buffers, parsed as one entry in 271 ms, then 414 MiB and 11 MiB, refused in 10 ms. A 255 MiB version 4 file with the cutoff at 0xFFFFFFFF and one stream over a 240 MiB mini stream: 1,669 MiB and 750 MiB in 856 ms, then refused by the cutoff in under 1 ms with nothing allocated. A 240 MiB version 4 file with a legal cutoff and 57,000 streams of 4,000 bytes in a 220 MiB mini stream: 1,839 MiB and 913 MiB in 652 ms with 3.77 million buffers, then 908 MiB and 470 MiB in 258 ms with 57,004 buffers (one per stream and three for the tables). What is left is the file, the copy of the mini stream and the copies of the streams in it, about twice the mini stream.
  - **Memory on the tables, before and after the second round** (Apple silicon, Node 24, load average 8 to 9, one run each, `/usr/bin/time -l` for the peak resident set, the file built in memory first as zeroed pages that are not resident until read, 256 MiB version 4 files of 65,535 sectors). A mini FAT chain that covers every sector after the directory, with no mini stream and the header counting 0xFFFFFFFF sectors: 988 MB peak, parsed as one entry in 150 ms (the chain copied once into a buffer and again into the table), then 93 MB in 2 ms with 0.5 MiB of array buffers (nothing is read). The same chain with a mini stream of 1 MiB: 963 MB, then 93 MB in 2 ms with 1.6 MiB of array buffers (the mini stream and 64 KiB of table). A header that names every sector but the directory and the DIFAT as a FAT sector, through 64 DIFAT sectors: 696 MB in 121 ms (a FAT as large as the file), then 94 MB in 3 ms with 0.5 MiB (a FAT of 64 sectors, the ones that map the file). The 93 MB is the resident set of the process before the parse; the same shapes at 32 MiB (8,192 sectors) are the ones `tests/cfbf-chain-bounds.test.ts` bounds at under 1 MiB of array buffers, where the parser as it was grew them by 64, 63 and 32 MiB. Third round, same host and method, the three shapes at 65,535 sectors again: 93 MB, 93 MB and 93 MB peak with 0.5 MiB of array buffers each in 2 to 3 ms, as after the second round (the FAT and the mini FAT are loaded by one function that reads the words, and the mini FAT chain is walked to its end for its rules, which lists the sectors of the chain in a 256 KB list and copies none of them). A fourth shape, a mini FAT chain over the whole file with a 1 MiB mini stream that a 100-byte stream needs, is refused for the stream's mini sector chain in 4 ms with 93 MB and 2.1 MiB of array buffers (the mini stream and the table of the addressable entries).
  - **Equivalence on real files.** The 842 compound files of the real-world sample cache and the test fixtures, against the parser of `main` before this entry: 832 give the same outcome (823 parse and give the same bytes for every stream and every path, 9 are refused with the same message), and 10 differ. Three damaged workbooks, `govdocs1-007750.xls`, `-007751.xls` and `-008063.xls`, parsed to an empty container (4, 8 and 0 entries, no stream) because their directory chain runs past the file, and the XLS reader then refused them with "Workbook stream not found"; the chain is now refused where it runs out, as a `CompoundFileStructureError` with the message of the chain, and `dispatchConversion` of each rejects with it (the explained refusals of the nightly run and `tests/xls-damaged-real-files.test.ts` name it). `govdocs1-001630.ppt`, whose directory chain returns to sector 0, was a `CorruptStreamError` that Word, PowerPoint and Outlook documents wrapped as a `LegacyOfficeFormatError`; it is the same message from a `CompoundFileStructureError`, wrapped in the same `LegacyOfficeFormatError` with that error as its `cause`, and not retried (the office suite refuses it as well, so no outcome is lost). Six POI fuzzer files were refused before and are refused now with another message: four `.ppt` files (`poihslffuzzer-4983252485210112`, `-5018229722382336`, `-6192650357112832` and `-6360479850954752`) whose mini stream chain runs to a sector the file does not hold are now a `CompoundFileStructureError` of that chain (the office suite does not load three of them, and loads the first as text), the `.ppt` with a cutoff of 318,771,200 (`-6614960949821440`) is refused for its sector 0 shared by two chains, and the `.doc` `poihwpffuzzer-5696094627495936` names a 0-byte mini stream where it named 128 bytes, because no stream of it lies below the cutoff. One POI fuzzer workbook, `poihssffuzzer-4651309315719168.xls` (an encrypted workbook that the office suite decrypts with the default password), points its root entry to a mini stream past the file while its one stream lies in the sectors; a first version of the third round read the root entry's mini stream chain always and refused it, so the mini stream and mini FAT are read only when a stream below the cutoff needs them, and it parses as it did (`dispatchConversion` to CSV gives the same empty output as `main`, and to ODS the suite's file). Against the second round of this entry, the same six files change and no other of the 842. Against the third round, none of the 842 changes outcome or message (`dispatchConversion` of the ten files that differ from `main` gives the same typed 400 as before), and the three 256 MiB shapes of the second round peak at 93 MB resident with 0.5 MiB of array buffers as before. 59 test files that read compound files (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, HWP, Outlook message, the office suite, the legacy document recovery and the compound-file kinds) pass but for four failures that `main` has too, run on the same host (LibreOffice text, the IGES writer, the synthesized-corpus reader and the pixel comparison of `document-page-images.perf.test.ts`). The parity run of the `document` family could not be made on this host: the bench has no legacy Office input in its corpus, and its strict mode needs `epubcheck`, which neither the host nor the test VM has.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A workbook or an HWP document between 256 and 512 MiB is refused where it was parsed.** Excel 97-2003 holds 65,536 rows and 256 columns, so such a file is rare; the largest compound file of the sample cache and the fixtures is 8.3 MB (`govdocs1-005540.xls`). Word, PowerPoint and Outlook messages were refused there already.
  - **The refusal of a large file by `readCfbContainer` reads "the compound file is malformed (Corrupt CFBF container: the file exceeds ...)"** where it read "the file exceeds the 268435456-byte limit" with its own label. Both are the typed 400.
  - **A directory or mini FAT chain that is damaged is refused where it was read as far as it went.** A real workbook whose directory ended at the end of a truncated file parsed to nothing and was refused by the reader; it is refused by the parser now, with the chain's message instead of "Workbook stream not found". The error is a `CompoundFileStructureError` and not a plain `CorruptStreamError` on purpose: `retryRefusedLegacyDocument` gives every file the in-process reader refuses as corrupt to the office suite, and for these three workbooks the suite imports the bytes as text and writes the binary as CSV (measured: 3.6 MB of replacement characters for `govdocs1-007750.xls`), where they were refused. A Word, PowerPoint or Outlook document goes through `readCfbContainer`, whose `LegacyOfficeFormatError` carries it as its `cause`, and the gate reads the `cause`, so it is not retried either. What is lost is a retry that might have worked on a file whose directory only this parser finds damaged; none of the 842 real files is one (`govdocs1-001630.ppt` is the only one that changed, and the suite does not load it either).
  - **A sector shared by a stream and the directory or the mini FAT is the structure's damage.** The owner table cannot tell which of the two pointers is wrong, so the file is refused as a destroyed structure; two streams that share a sector stay the streams' own corruption, which the suite is still asked to read. A file in which only a stream's start was damaged and points into the directory is therefore not retried; none of the 842 real files is one.
  - **The mini stream and mini FAT are read when a stream below the cutoff needs them.** A file whose streams all lie in the sectors reads whatever its root entry says of a mini stream and whatever its mini FAT holds, where the second round refused a destroyed mini FAT whenever the root entry named a mini stream. olefile does the same for the mini FAT (`olefile.py` lines 1858 to 1860); the cost is a destroyed mini FAT that no stream uses is no longer reported, and the sectors of an unread mini FAT and mini stream are claimed by no chain, so a large stream may lie on them (pinned in `tests/cfbf-structure-errors.test.ts`, with the same file and one small stream more refused for the shared sector). Another cost is a file that ends inside its mini stream: the root chain is a structure chain, so it is a `CompoundFileStructureError` and the office suite is not offered it, where a `CorruptStreamError` would have been retried. No file of the 842 is one.
  - **The list of FAT sectors skips a marker without counting it.** The first `fatSectorCount` sector numbers are taken, so the slots `[A, free, B]` under a count of 2 name A and B; a header whose list has a gap still reads its second FAT sector. olefile ends the list at the first free or end-of-chain marker (`olefile.py` line 1557), so a file with a gap reads a FAT of fewer sectors there and refuses the streams past them; this parser reads on, and a list of markers only names nothing (pinned in `tests/cfbf-parse-limits.test.ts`).
  - **The refusal of a large file by `readCfbContainer` reads "<label>: the compound file is malformed (The compound file is larger than the 268435456-byte limit.)"** where it read "<label>: the file exceeds the 268435456-byte limit." with its own test. Both are the typed 400 and both name the label; the RTF reader keeps the old words for its own check.
  - **The header cutoff is not read, so a stream that a writer with another cutoff placed in the other store reads the bytes of whatever lies there.** POI and olefile do the same. The alternative that the first two rounds took, refusing a file when a stream lay between the header value and 4096, turned away valid files whose header a fuzzer or a damaged writer had left behind (a cutoff of 0, 0xFFFFFFFF or 0x2000 over streams placed by 4096), and contradicted the cutoff the parser fixes. A real file written with 8,192 or 512 and holding a stream between the two is read from the wrong store and ends, nearly always, in the owner table (a refusal of the stream); none of the 842 real files carries another value but the one fuzzer file that was refused already (318,771,200), now for its sector 0 shared by two chains.
  - **The path budget is ours.** A file whose storages and names are valid and spell out more than 16 Mi characters is refused; no real file comes within a factor of two of it.
  - **The entries are counted in the order the walk meets them,** so the budget runs out at a different entry for a different tree; the file is refused either way.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Paths built on demand.** `CfbfContainer.paths` is a map that the HWP, Word, PowerPoint and Excel readers read by name; a lazy map changes the interface of four readers to save memory that the budget already bounds.
  - **A depth of 32 or 64 in place of POI's 1,000.** No real file nests more than a few levels, but the number would be ours with nothing to cite; the path budget bounds the cost either way.
  - **A cap on the FAT sector count as POI has.** The file size already bounds it by 4,096.
  - **A plain `ConversionFailedError` for a chain that runs out of the file, a `CorruptStreamError` for the rest, and the retry told apart by message.** That is what the first round did, and the same damage had three outcomes by where the bad number landed. A typed cause that every structure refusal shares is the one place the retry gate reads.
  - **Honouring the cutoff of the header, as LibreOffice does.** A header of 0xFFFFFFFF would make every stream a chain of mini sectors, and the writers of the real files all give 4096.
  - **Reading the root entry's mini stream chain as a structure chain whenever the root entry names one.** The first version of the third round did, and refused a real fuzzer workbook that the second round parsed (see the equivalence row); reading it when a stream needs it keeps that file and the rule for every file that does need it.
  - **Refusing a file whose header cutoff places a stream in the other store (`assertStreamPlacementAgrees`).** Round two did; it refused valid files with a junk cutoff and is removed. Neither reference does it.
  - **The CFB header check (`assertCfbHeader`) in `parseCfbf`.** It would change the outcome of the XLS and HWP readers for files with an odd header that parse today; entry 133 states that the XLS reader does not apply it.
- **Verified by**: `tests/cfbf-parse-limits.test.ts` (the shared sector and the sectors of the FAT and the DIFAT, the FAT sector listed twice, the FAT list that skips a marker without counting it, the FAT list that ends at a sector past the file, the directory count in slots and its agreement with the check of the file kind, a directory chain longer than the limit read for no more than the limit, directory and mini FAT chains that run out of the file or the FAT and a mini FAT chain that is not followed past what the mini stream needs, chains that return to themselves, a tree that returns to itself, storages nested deeply and the path budget at exactly 16,777,216 characters and one more, each refusal before any stream is copied, the mini stream cutoff, one buffer for a stream, sizes and sector numbers that no file can hold, and the size of the file for `parseCfbf`, `readCfbContainer` (label and message), `parseHwpDocument`, `convertXlsSource` and `xlsHasFilePass`), `tests/cfbf-structure-errors.test.ts` (each place where the bad number of a directory chain, a mini FAT chain, the tail of the root entry's chain, a stream start or a header lands, a root entry with no mini stream, a file cut inside the sector a chain goes through, the sectors of an unread mini FAT and mini stream, an empty directory and one with no named entry, the stream chains that stay `CorruptStreamError`, `readCfbContainer` keeping the type with the label, the workbook and the encrypted-Word check), `tests/cfbf-chain-bounds.test.ts` (the 32 MiB files of the second round: a mini FAT with no mini stream, with one, and a header that names every sector as FAT, each bounded in array buffers; the mini stream of exactly one mini FAT sector and of two; a file cut inside the last sector of a stream before and after the declared end; a mini FAT chain that goes through the cut last sector of the file and on, refused as a structure and as a 400 through `dispatchConversion`, and one that ends in it, read for the words that are there; a stream chain longer than its declared size beside a stream on the next sectors; a writer with another cutoff, the crafted file that would be given unowned sectors, and the sizes at each edge of both ranges), `tests/office-suite-route.test.ts` (the gate does not retry it, also under up to 8 wrappers, and ends on a chain of causes that returns), `tests/xls-damaged-real-files.test.ts` and `tests/ppt-cfb-sector-loop.test.ts` (the real files through `dispatchConversion`), `tests/office-input-bounds.test.ts`, and the test files named above. Mutations that each turned a case red: the DIFAT check removed; 2 MiB allocated before the depth and path refusals; a partial last sector counted whole (the file cut inside a stream); the byte limit `>=` made `>` (the chain longer than its stream); the FAT list not capped; the mini FAT read without a mini stream; the mini FAT not capped; the end-of-chain check removed; a shared structure sector refused only from the structure's side; the cutoff check removed; the retry gate not excluding the type; the tail of the root entry's chain not walked; the cut sector allowed inside a chain; the root entry without a mini stream left to the size check; the directory tree loop a plain corrupt-stream error.
- **Revisit when**: a real file between 256 and 512 MiB is refused by the XLS or HWP reader, a real file's paths come within a factor of two of the budget, POI or olefile adopts a limit that this table lacks, the readers of the compound file take the CFB header check, a real file written with a mini stream cutoff other than 4096 converts elsewhere and is refused here, a real file whose directory or mini FAT chain this parser refuses is read correctly by the office suite (then the refusal can be a `CorruptStreamError` that is retried), or a real workbook whose directory chain runs out of the file converts in the office suite from its sectors instead of its bytes as text.

## 137. One largest file size per plan, shown in the drop zone and enforced by every route from one table

- **Status**: Implemented (QA request of 2026-11-01: the drop zone said 2 GB while the routes refused at 50 MB, 100 MB, 500 MB, 1 GiB and 5 GiB), decided 2026-11-01. Builds on entry 16, which set 1 GB for free and anonymous callers. Extended the same day: a file over 64 MiB goes to the server in parts (lead decision). Hardened over six review rounds of the pull request (same day). Follow-ups of that review (QA request of 2026-11-01): the receipt of a completion, the release of an idempotency lock, the mapping of upload errors, the download of keys outside the stored namespaces, and the sign-in answer of the viewer.
- **Decision**:
  - **One table, `src/lib/plan-limits.ts`.** Anonymous 1 GiB, free 1 GiB, Pro 5 GiB, Enterprise 10 GiB per file, printed with IEC names (`formatBytes`) by the API, the logs and the OpenAPI document. Web pages show the same 1024 multiples as KB, MB and GB (`formatBytesForDisplay`, `useFormatBytes`): QA decision of 2026-11-08, because the reference converters write their limits that way, so a 1 GiB limit reads "1 GiB" in an API answer and "1 GB" on a page, and no server message or problem `detail` changes (`tests/format-bytes-display.test.ts`). An anonymous identity (`anon:`, built only by `src/lib/auth/anonymous-identity.ts`), a missing tier and an unknown tier get the smallest limit. While the launch is free-tier only (`PAID_PLANS_ON_SALE` false, QA decision of 2026-10-30) the 413 detail, the FAQ and the API document name only the free limit.
  - **Every route that accepts a stored file or declares a size reads the table.** `/api/queue/jobs` and `/api/v1/jobs` (the size the store reports, never the client's `fileSize`, and every `import.upload` node of a graph), `/api/v1/archives/inspect`, `/api/storage/multipart` (the declared size at `initiate`), `/api/v1/uploads` and `/api/v1/uploads/direct` answer one 413 problem ("File size 3 GiB exceeds the 1 GiB limit for the free plan.") and release their quota reservation.
  - **Transport ceilings stay and say so.** A file inside a job request is at most 32 MiB (`INLINE_JOB_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES`), a part at most 64 MiB on every route (`MULTIPART_MAX_PART_BYTES`), and `Tus-Max-Size` names the largest plan limit, since OPTIONS has no caller.
  - **One request carries at most 64 MiB of file and 65 MiB of body.** The routes that read a body whole check `Content-Length` before reading (400 when it is not a whole number, 413 naming the way in parts), and the middleware applies the same rule to every `/api` route: 65 MiB for the file routes (`/api/convert`, `/api/queue/jobs`, `/api/storage/multipart` for `chunk`, `/api/v1/archives/inspect`, `/api/v1/convert`, `/api/v1/jobs`, `/api/v1/uploads` and sub-paths), 1 MiB elsewhere. A test checks that every route wrapped in `withinSingleRequest` or `admittingNewFiles` gets one request, except `/api/fetch-url`, which takes only JSON.
  - **A body without a `Content-Length` is counted by the middleware, whatever framing it came in.** A file route refuses it with 411 at its first byte (an empty body passes), since the framework would end such a body at 65 MiB without an error; every other route takes it up to 1 MiB, then 413. nginx runs with `proxy_request_buffering off`, so it passes a chunked body on as it arrives and adds no length. The count decides the answer only: the framework keeps its own copy of what arrived, up to its body limit. Over HTTP/1.1 a body with neither header cannot exist (the server answers 400 to the stray bytes); the rule covers HTTP/2 framing.
  - **The framework body bound is 65 MiB.** Next.js 15 gives a route only the first 10 MiB of a body a middleware could read, so `experimental.middlewareClientMaxBodySize` is 65 MiB (`tests/next-config-body-limit.test.ts` holds it equal to `SINGLE_REQUEST_BODY_MAX_BYTES`). Behind the middleware the framework holds the whole body before the route runs (`finalize` in `next/dist/server/body-streams.js`).
  - **A file over 64 MiB goes up in parts and is converted by a job.** The browser opens `/api/storage/multipart` with 64 MiB parts, sends each part, completes, starts `POST /api/queue/jobs` on the stored key and links the result's own URL, so no result is held in memory. Parts and reads are sent again after a network error, 502 or 504; every request after 429 or 503 by its `Retry-After`, except refusals that last until the next day. The opening, the completion and the job start carry an `Idempotency-Key`; the job start reserves its unit only after the replay lookup.
  - **What a call made is closed by the stage it reached.** A cancellation or failure aborts an open session, asks a lost opening or completion again by its key and closes what it made, deletes a stored upload with no job (`discard`), and cancels a queued job. When the page is closed or reloaded (`pagehide`), only the closings that are one request go out with `keepalive`: abort an open session, delete a stored upload, cancel a queued job. They are sent once, and not at all for a page kept for the back button (`persisted`). Reloading the page during a conversion therefore cancels its queued job.
  - **An upload opens only when a job could start.** `initiate` answers 429 when the caller has no conversion left today or as many in flight as the plan allows.
  - **An anonymous address bucket has an upload budget** (`src/lib/api-keys/anonymous-upload-budget.ts`): at most 2 sessions open and 2 GiB per UTC day for uploads and link imports together (entry 15), an upload's declared size reserved at `initiate`, returned by `abort` or expiry, kept by `complete`; a link import holds the import limit or the bytes left when it starts, and is charged the bytes it received once it has stopped. An idle hour stops a session counting as open. The record lives in Redis under a compare-and-set (`src/lib/redis/compare-and-set.ts`) or in the process without Redis. A budget that cannot be reached refuses a new session but never a part, an abort or a completion the store took. A failed opening aborts its session and returns its bytes, each whatever the other does. An account's uploads are not metered here; its link imports have a budget of two files at its plan's limit (entry 15).
  - **Unattributed requests cannot upload anonymously.** While no proxy is declared every visitor is one identity, so an anonymous `initiate` answers 503 `client-ip-trust-unconfigured` naming `TRUSTED_PROXIES`.
  - **An anonymous session gets no signed part link** (403): the store would take whatever the link carries. Its parts go through `chunk`.
  - **`complete` assembles exactly the parts it checked, and its answer is final once the store took the session.** The parts must be 1, 2, 3 in order and hold exactly the declared size (else 400 and the session stays open). After the store consumed the session, a budget that cannot be closed still answers 200 (the reservation expires instead), and an upload that cannot be recorded is removed and answers 500 "Upload the file again" with its bytes returned. Its `Idempotency-Key` is scoped to the upload and to the caller's upload owner (the account, or one shared owner for every anonymous caller; `uploadOwnerOf`), not to the address bucket, so a visitor whose address moves still gets the first answer; a replay is authorised by the key value together with the upload id, both known only to the client that made the first request, and an upload id that is not printable ASCII within 4,096 characters never becomes a key. At completion the answer is also kept as a receipt in the retention ledger (`src/lib/storage/upload-completion.ts`), found by the upload id, with the owner the session recorded (`session.ownerUserId`), a SHA-256 digest of the part list the request sent (each entry read as the completion reads it: the number, and the ETag without quotes when it is a non-empty text, else none, in order; a request that lists none, absent or null, has its own digest) and for 24 hours. The store consumes the session, so a repeat of `complete` that finds no session is answered with the first answer while the stored file exists, with or without an `Idempotency-Key`, when it comes from the owner and lists the same parts; a repeat that lists other parts is a missing session, as an object store refuses it. The receipt is looked up only for an id of the shape a store hands out (`isUploadIdShape`). A receipt that cannot be read answers the repeat 503 with `Retry-After`, never 404, so a client does not take a stored upload for gone; only a missing receipt is 404. A receipt that cannot be written is logged and costs only that repeat. With an object store the session id is a signed token that still decodes until it expires, so a repeat finds the session open and the store answers `NoSuchUpload` to the part listing or the completion; the route answers that from the receipt too. A receipt written before the digest existed matches no repeat. An idempotency store that cannot record the answer costs the replay, not the answer. The store is asked three times (50 ms and 100 ms apart) before the answer is returned and logged, and what happens to the key depends on the action. `complete` releases it, since its repeat answers from the receipt. The opening of a session and the start of a job keep the lock, so a repeat gets the same 409 with `Retry-After: 1` as a repeat that meets a request still running. The browser sends such a repeat again at most four times, a second apart, and then reports the 409, so no second session is opened or job queued while the lock lasts. The lock bounds the repeats for the minute it lasts; a repeat sent after that runs the action again. Every call takes its lock with a random token and releases it with one compare-and-delete (a Lua script in Redis, one step in the process), so a call that outlived its lock never removes the lock of the run that took the key after it, and a recorded answer is never removed. An assembled upload whose size is not the declared one is removed (a removal that fails is logged with the key), its budget is closed, and the answer is the final 400.
  - **Parts sent at once are counted together** (`src/lib/storage/part-admission.ts`) on `chunk`, `/api/v1/uploads/direct/part` and `/api/v1/uploads` `action=part`. A part is admitted while the stored parts, the parts on the way and its own length fit the declared size, and writes at most that length (else 413 before a byte). One attempt of a part number writes at a time; a repeat meets 503 of type `part-in-flight` with `Retry-After: 5`.
