## 142. Raster pictures to SVG: the pinned vtracer release program traces a PNG the worker stages from the first frame, inside a 16 megapixel budget, 2 GiB, 120 s and a 32 MiB output bound

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-03 (lead brief from the reference converter's formats API, queried 2026-11-03; QA approved running the pinned release programs on the development Mac and in the Linux VM for the measurements). The first reference site also offers PNG to SVG; its format chips are left to the interface work.
- **Decision**:
  - **The pairs are PNG, JPG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, BMP, TIF and TIFF to SVG**, exactly the raster inputs the reference converter serves with this engine (`VECTORIZE_SOURCES` in `src/lib/conversions/raster-vectorize-options.ts`), each charged as one conversion like every other pair. No other raster input of the registry gets SVG.
  - **The engine is vtracer 1.0.0-alpha.4** (visioncortex, MIT OR Apache-2.0, tag commit `2500df76b5aea0ac22d15296b22722442f825c5b`), the project's own statically linked musl release programs: `92bcd69792d4ba981c0c37db4bb681df4e1eae6c56b0817c73164656664ec5a8` for aarch64 and `2058f611b48ed49497f78883bde47435531e9e17e3a79428432d1528bdb12e2a` for x86_64, with the licence text of the tagged commit (`81ee739f355765c110fc89feff14ffffce829901f96ba811fd0b65a41a8636c7`) and the notices of the 71 crates of the program's `Cargo.lock` dependency graph, musl libc, LLVM libunwind and the Rust standard library with the 11 crates it vendors that the programs carry (`scripts/vtracer-notices/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`, below). `scripts/install-vtracer.sh` runs on Linux only, checks the committed notices against their digest before any download, downloads over HTTPS with HTTPS-only redirects, asks curl to refuse a download announced over 16 MiB and stops reading a download at 16 MiB plus one byte whatever the server announces (`head -c` after curl, then a size check, so that no more than the bound is written before the digest is checked), and checks the three digests before anything is unpacked or copied; the `vtracer` stage of `Dockerfile.worker` and the `vtracer` task of the CI setup run it, and the runner stage traces an 8 x 8 PNG written as bytes before the image is accepted.
  - **How it runs, in the order the brief set.** A maintained build used as is was available, so it is used: the release programs above, static, with no library of the image to match. Building the CLI from the pinned source in the image (step two) would add a Rust toolchain stage for the same program the project publishes; porting (step three) is not allowed.
  - **The program is one statically linked binary, so the licences of the third-party code built into it ship with it.** `scripts/generate-vtracer-notices.ts` does what the Rust licence bundlers (cargo-about, cargo-bundle-licenses) do for the crates, without building or running anything: it takes the dependency graph of the `vtracer-cli` package from the `Cargo.lock` of the tagged commit (the workspace packages contribute their normal and build dependencies only, so `resvg` and the other development dependencies stay out), downloads each crate's crates.io archive checked against the lockfile checksum, reads only its `LICENSE*`, `COPYING*` and `NOTICE*` files, the texts of a REUSE `LICENSES` directory and the licence fields of its `Cargo.toml`, each by its exact name, writes each distinct text once with the crates that ship it, and adds the Apache-2.0 text for vtracer and `flo_curves` 0.3.1, which offer Apache-2.0 without shipping it. An empty text, a member that is not a regular file, a name tar would read as a pattern, or a crate without a text other than `flo_curves` 0.3.1 stops it. The bundlers stop at the lockfile, but the release programs are musl builds, so they also carry code no lockfile lists (both programs name rustc commit `88d9e12ae178fab0fb5cc050a94da85685d449ea` in their panic paths): musl libc (`nm` shows musl's `__libc_start_main` and `memcpy` defined in both), LLVM libunwind (both define `_Unwind_RaiseException` and `unw_init_local` and carry its `libunwind: ` messages; `strings` on the pinned x86_64 and aarch64 programs), and the Rust standard library with the crates it vendors. The source paths in the panic strings name `addr2line` 0.25.1, `gimli` 0.32.3, `hashbrown` 0.17.1, `miniz_oxide` 0.8.9 and `rustc-demangle` 0.1.27, and the symbols name `compiler_builtins`; `adler2`, `object`, `memchr`, `libc` and `cfg-if` are the other crates `std` links on a Linux target through its own dependencies (`library/std/Cargo.toml` and `library/Cargo.lock` of the component), so the generator carries these 11 crates (`STD_CRATES`). Their texts come from the official `rust-src` 1.98.0 component, which `[pkg.rust-src]` of the channel manifest ties to that commit, fetched from `static.rust-lang.org` and checked against the SHA-256 its `.sha256` file and the manifest publish (`0e977492aed5ff137815bf9b4b796e8a85b80fb2367ed64e82d5c5839870f2bf`, which pins every text in it): the `LICENSE*`, `COPYING*` and `UNLICENSE` files under `library/vendor/<crate>`, and for `compiler_builtins` the `LICENSE.txt` of `library/compiler-builtins` and of its `libm`, read by exact name with `tar` as data. The Rust project's `COPYRIGHT` leaves the holders of these crates to `COPYRIGHT-library.html`, which is not shipped, so without these files the notices would name `gimli` and the rest without carrying the copyright lines of "The Gimli Developers", "Amanieu d'Antras" and the others. LLVM libunwind's `libunwind/LICENSE.TXT` (Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exceptions, and the legacy MIT and University of Illinois terms) is fetched from a commit-pinned raw URL of `rust-lang/llvm-project` at `52ed14fcd56afc30f9cccd8ca8ce237c2eef7e04`, the revision the `src/llvm-project` submodule of the compiler commit points at (`GET /repos/rust-lang/rust/contents/src/llvm-project?ref=88d9e12a...`), and checked against its SHA-256. The generator also adds musl's `COPYRIGHT` at tag `v1.2.5` (the release `src/ci/docker/scripts/musl.sh` builds at that commit) and the Rust project's `COPYRIGHT`, `LICENSE-MIT` and `LICENSE-APACHE` at that commit, each fetched by a tag- or commit-pinned URL, checked against a pinned SHA-256 and written under its own heading. **Where a crate is offered under several licences, the notices elect one**: MIT when the crate ships an MIT text with a copyright line, Apache-2.0 otherwise (the MIT texts of `adler2`, `fdeflate`, `half`, `image`, `image-webp`, `proc-macro2`, `quote` and `syn` carry no copyright line, so those are elected under Apache-2.0, as are `moxcms` and `pxfm`, which offer BSD-3-Clause beside it), and the lists mark the election of each such crate (`; elected MIT`); an expression that offers neither stops the generator so that a person decides, and an expression that combines licences with AND (`compiler_builtins`, `unicode-ident`) elects nothing, with the texts of every part included. `.gitattributes` keeps every file of `scripts/vtracer-notices` out of line-ending conversion (`-text`): the CRLF lines some crate texts have, and the upstream manifests whose digests the tests check, so the digests hold in any checkout. The upstream manifests are kept beside the notices under their digests. The install script checks the notices against `VTRACER_NOTICES_SHA256` and installs them as `/usr/share/doc/vtracer/THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES`, which the image copies to `/licenses/vtracer.THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` (`docs/licensing.md` 2.13). The lockfile does not tell apart the procedural-macro crates used only to build the program or the crates of other platforms, so they are named too.
  - **The options are the engine's**: `vectorize.preset` (`bw`, `poster`, `photo`), `vectorize.mode` (`spline` default, `polygon`, `pixel`), `vectorize.filterSpeckle` (0 to 128, default 4), `vectorize.colorPrecision` (1 to 8, default 6) and `vectorize.simplify` (a finite tolerance above 0, off by default), with the ranges of the clap definitions of `crates/vtracer-cli/src/main.rs` and the preset values of `Config::from_preset` in `crates/vtracer/src/config.rs`. Only the values a request sets are passed, so an explicit value overrides the preset as `build_config` does. Each option is described once in `VECTORIZE_OPTIONS`, typed to the field it describes: its flag, when the engine reads it, and its kind (a choice, a whole number in a range, or a tolerance), whose constructor gives the check of its values, the rule a refused value breaks and its schema, with the ranges and defaults in the schema text taken from the same constants. The request schema's `vectorize` property, the engine's check, the command line and the queue item's sanitizing are derived from that table. The engine ignores `simplify` outside spline mode (`Config::simplify`) and the colour precision under the `bw` preset, which clusters in two colours; the dialog greys those fields out with the reason and keeps what the person typed in them, so switching back restores it, and a queue item keeps only what the engine reads.
  - **The picture is checked and staged by the worker, never by the program** (`src/lib/conversions/raster-vectorize.ts`): the program is looked up first, so a worker without it answers 503 before any decoding; the header is checked against the input pixel limit and the tracing budget before any pixel is decoded (a BMP by the project's own decoder, which checks both from its header before it allocates the index plane or the canvas, and is handed on with its embedded ICC profile like every other BMP conversion); the first frame or page is decoded with libvips, turned upright from its EXIF orientation, converted to 8-bit sRGB with alpha, and written as a stored PNG without row filters into the run's scratch directory. The program reads only that file. A cancelled conversion, or one whose job deadline passed while the picture was decoded, stops before and after staging.
  - **Limits of a run**: 16 megapixels (413 above it), 2,048 MB of address space, 120 s held to the job's remaining time, an SVG of less than 32 MiB, 64 KiB of diagnostics, no network, the scratch directory removed afterwards. The address-space and file-size limits are hard only on Linux with `prlimit`, which production has; elsewhere the memory limit is a resident-size watch every 50 ms and the output is measured after the run. A failed allocation (Rust prints `memory allocation of N bytes failed` and aborts) and the memory limit answer 413, the output bound 413 (the sandbox reports it as a `file-size` overrun, apart from the diagnostics bound), the time limit 422, a crash with SIGSEGV a typed failure naming the signal (the sandbox counts SIGSEGV under a memory limit as a memory refusal, since a C program faults on an allocation it did not check; a Rust program aborts instead, with the allocation message above or, for a stack overflow, the message of std's `stack_overflow.rs`, so a SIGSEGV of this program is most likely a fault in it, and is reported as one rather than as a memory refusal), any other failed run a typed failure without the scratch path, and a missing program 503.
  - **The jobs run on the CPU lane** (`resolveResourceClass`), whatever the file size: a compressible 16 MP PNG is small and traces for 18 s in 660 MB, and up to 120 s in 2 GB. The CPU lane gives three jobs 10 GB; the light lane puts six in 4 GB.
  - **The SVG passes the sanitizer of every SVG path** through `sanitizeGeneratedSvg`, which reads SVG that a program of the service wrote up to 32 MiB instead of the 5 MiB input cap of `sanitizeSvgDocument` (unchanged), and must still be an SVG afterwards. Sanitizing a 32 MiB SVG takes about 0.5 s of the event loop.
  - **The options dialog of these pairs shows only the tracer's options**, in English and Korean, laid out as the reference converter's dialog lays them out (preset and mode as two radio lists whose choices each have a one-line description, then an Advanced disclosure, closed at the start unless the options set one of its fields, holding filter speckle and color precision as a slider with a number field and simplify as a number field), with the preset's values for the fields a person has not changed; a number typed past a range is brought to the nearest whole number inside it on leaving the field. A queue item of these pairs keeps only those options. The pair is a section of the options capability model (`computeVisibleSections` and `sanitizeOptionsForPair` in `options-capabilities.ts`), which also leaves out the picture options and the TIFF page range.
- **Why**:
  - **Upstream sets no limit of its own**: the CLI reads any picture the `image` crate opens and traces it whole; the only bound is that crate's default allocation limit of 512 MiB for decoding. The limits above come from runs of the pinned linux/arm64 program in the Linux VM (4 cores, 6 GiB), one at a time:

    | Picture | Settings | Time | Peak RSS | SVG |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | Photograph, 0.4 MP (kodim23) | defaults / photo / poster | 0.19 / 0.71 / 0.80 s | 22 / 60 / 60 MB | 0.7 / 0.3 / 1.2 MB |
    | Photograph upscaled to 4 MP | defaults / photo / poster | 0.76 / 7.6 / 8.9 s | 99 / 284 / 285 MB | 1.7 / 1.5 / 5.7 MB |
    | Photograph upscaled to 16 MP | defaults / photo / poster | 1.6 / 16.8 / 18.0 s | 307 / 636 / 659 MB | 2.5 / 2.8 / 10.4 MB |
    | Random noise, 1 / 4 / 9 / 16 MP | defaults | 3.4 / 28.1 / 85.9 / 199.9 s | 170 / 675 / 1,516 / 2,694 MB | 9.9 / 39.9 / 90.3 / 160.6 MB |
    | Random noise, 25 MP | defaults, 4.5 GB address space | aborted after 3.6 s (failed allocation) | 2,824 MB | none |
    | Random noise, 1 MP | poster, speckle 0, pixel mode | 7.7 s | 898 MB | 58.4 MB |

    Every real picture of the set fits 16 MP, 2 GiB, 120 s and 32 MiB with room; noise, the input that gives every pixel a path, is the adversarial case, and the memory, time and output limits stop it at any size.
  - **The tracer is the same engine with the same options as the reference converter**, so the parity rows compare the product with the program given the uploaded file itself: on the generated corpus and four public samples every SSIM, path and byte row is at or within the allowance of the reference (below), and the public PNG samples give the same SVG but for the final newline.
  - **Staging keeps the program's input known**: the decoders, the pixel checks and the colour handling (the embedded profile of a BMP included) are the ones every other picture path uses, a damaged file is refused before the program starts, and the program never parses the uploaded bytes.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The picture is decoded twice** (libvips, then the program reading the staged PNG). In two speed runs on the linux/arm64 VM the rows of the generated corpus are at 0.905 and 0.916 (photograph, JPEG), 0.940 and 0.948 (GIF), 0.900 and 0.903 (16-bit line art) of the program run directly, and at 0.838 and 0.850 for the 1024 x 640 16-bit RGBA screenshot, where decoding the source (4.2 ms of a 4.7 ms staging step against a 42 ms trace) is most of the difference; the sandbox start and the sanitizer add about 1 ms each. The line art and the photograph straddle the 0.90 bar, and the screenshot is below it, so these rows will need a known-gap entry from the nightly run or the change named under Revisit. Larger pictures dilute the cost (38 ms of staging against a 714 ms trace at 4 MP).
  - **Pictures above 16 MP are refused** (a 24 MP camera photograph included), where the program alone would try them.
  - **EXIF orientation is applied**; the program alone ignores it. The reference service's own output was not compared (its API needs a key), so whether it rotates is not known.
  - **An animated GIF or WebP and a multi-page TIFF are traced from their first frame or page**, as the program reads them (the GIF row of the parity run traces the first frame of a two-frame GIF on both sides).
  - **The SVG is the engine's**: a width and a height without a viewBox, and a generator comment.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **The Python wheel or the WebAssembly package of the same engine**: a Python runtime in the worker, or a trace inside the Node process, where no per-call memory or time limit applies.
  - **Building the CLI from source in the image**: a Rust toolchain stage for the bytes the project already publishes for both architectures.
  - **Handing the uploaded file to the program** (what the reference does): faster by one decode for small pictures, but the program would parse untrusted bytes, damaged files would reach it, and the colour and orientation handling would differ from every other picture path.
  - **Staging as PNG at deflate level 1**: 15.8 ms instead of 3.7 ms for the 768 x 512 photograph, with the same SVG. A raw PAM file was as fast as the stored PNG and is not what the brief named.
  - **The 5 MiB SVG input cap of the sanitizer for this path**: the 4 MP poster trace (5.7 MB) and the 16 MP one (10.4 MB) would be refused.
- **Verified by**:
  - `tests/raster-vectorize.test.ts` (46 cases): every pair through `POST /api/v1/convert` with the pinned program, each option against what it visibly does to the SVG, the refusals before the program starts (16 MP budget, an 820 KB run-length BMP of 10000 x 10000 refused with less than 50 MB allocated where it allocated 500 MB before, a truncated PNG, eight invalid option shapes, a missing program before decoding, a cancelled job and a passed deadline), what the program reads (EXIF orientation, 16-bit, CMYK and palette input as 8-bit sRGB with alpha, the first page of a TIFF and the first frame of an animated WebP, a BMP with a Display P3 profile converted to sRGB), the CPU lane, the sandbox options the program is started with (no network, 2,048 MB, 32 MiB file size, 64 KiB diagnostics), the wrapper against stand-in programs (missing, failing, silent, not an SVG, past the output bound, a failed allocation, SIGSEGV, past its time, the scratch directory removed) and the sanitizer. It passes on macOS with the darwin arm64 release program and in the Linux VM with the linux musl one, where the output bound is enforced by the process file-size limit.
  - `tests/vectorize-options-ui.test.ts` (35 cases: the radio lists and their descriptions in both languages, the closed Advanced disclosure, open when the options set one of its fields, and what it opens to, a slider and its number field moving each other inside the range and a number past it clamped on leaving the field, the fields the engine ignores greyed out with the reason and their typed values kept across a switch, a typed 0 kept in the simplify field, the queue keeping only what the engine reads and none of the options of the hidden sections for a PNG and for a TIFF source, and the dialog driven through Apply Options to `onSave`, which receives only the values the engine reads while a value typed under a mode that ignores it stays in the dialog and comes back when the mode does), `tests/worker-vtracer-packaging.test.ts` (10 cases, the installer refusing a system other than Linux before any download among them, and a download stopped at its bound while it is read, with and without a size announced, run on the `fetch` function of the script with a stand-in for curl), `tests/vtracer-notices.test.ts` (21 cases: the notices name every crate of the `Cargo.lock` graph, the 24 crates `strings` finds in the release program and six reached only through other crates among them, each with a text but `flo_curves` 0.3.1, name the 11 standard library crates and carry the copyright line of each from the text it ships, carry the libunwind licence at its pinned commit, mark the election of every crate offered under several licences, carry the musl and Rust texts, keep their CRLF lines and the digested upstream files in any checkout, and are checked before any download; `electedLicence` on the expressions of the crates; the generator, on archives built in the test, reads root, REUSE and UNLICENSE texts and stops at an empty text, a symbolic link, a name tar reads as a pattern and a crate without a text), `tests/sandbox-launcher.test.ts`, `tests/cad-occt-wrapper.test.ts` and `tests/font-type1-wrapper.test.ts` (an output overrun and a file-size overrun told apart by their kind through the launcher, and the CAD and font wrappers answering a file-size stop as an output too large on any host; the CAD and font cases guard that behaviour and would pass on the byte comparison they replace, so the launcher case is the one that guards the move to the limit kind), and the stage lists, CI task list, registry, conformance and family-map tests.
  - The install script run in the Linux VM installs a program with the archive's digest; the runner's smoke step passes under `dash` with that program.
  - `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --family vectorize --quality-only` passes all 24 rows on macOS and in the VM. In the VM: SSIM against the source of ours / the program alone, `screenshot.png` 0.95169 / 0.95164, `lineart.png` 0.94083 / 0.94007, `photo-a.jpg` 0.72385 / 0.72522, the two-frame GIF 0.94176 / 0.94176, `wm-lineart-containers.png` 0.95769, `wm-lineart-chart.png` 0.98247, `kodim23.png` 0.86178 and `wm-alpha-graph.png` 0.95222 on both sides; paths 188 / 187, 224 / 220, 565 / 560, 225 / 225 and the same for the public samples; bytes within 3 %.
  - The speed rows above are from two runs of `npm run bench:quality -- --parity --speed-only --family vectorize` in the VM (adaptive pairs, 7 to 50 a row; the last run's intervals: screenshot [0.824, 0.872], line art [0.892, 0.903], photograph [0.898, 0.912], GIF [0.925, 0.952]), with a load average under 1 before each run. A run with the staged PNG at deflate level 1 had the photograph at 0.75.
  - The screenshot row is a tracked speed gap (issue 759, ratio 0.84) and the four vectorize speed rows are in `bench/baseline.json`. Nightly run 41570078103 (branch `fix/nightly-corpora`, workflow dispatch, x86-64 runner) failed only `vectorize/screenshot.png->svg/throughput` at 0.847 [0.826, 0.876] over 15 pairs, the staging gap named above; the previous run of that branch, 41568042194, read 0.882 [0.878, 0.888] over 15 pairs. The other three rows pass the bar in run 41570078103: line art 0.926 [0.907, 0.932] over 15 pairs, photograph 0.922 [0.908, 1.071] over 7, GIF 0.951 [0.912, 1.002] over 7. The figures quoted here are the medians of the pairs as the verdict states them. `bench/baseline.json` holds the ratio of the two throughputs in the speed report instead (screenshot 0.8484, line art 0.9248, photograph 0.9218, GIF 0.9523; the screenshot's 0.4865 / 0.5734 MB/s is 0.8484), which is why the third decimal differs. - **Revisit when**: a stable 1.0 release of the engine ships (move the pin and run the tests and the parity family again); the reference converter's own output can be fetched (compare orientation and the first-frame rule); the nightly speed rows of the screenshot stay below the bar (consider handing 8-bit PNGs to the program unchanged); or requests for pictures above 16 MP are refused often enough to matter.

## 143. Corpus files are fetched from copies that do not change, a host with a published limit is spaced, a host that refuses is held for the time it asked, and a shard that fails keeps what it fetched

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-03 (QA request: make the nightly pass again with the same coverage). The nightly run of 2026-11-02 (41424613455) and the one before it failed on files of other hosts, not on product behaviour: three real-world shards and the small quality shard. The speed failure of 2026-11-01 was a faster runner, changes nothing here, and is explained on the OCR speed issue (#644).
- **Decision**:
  - **A corpus file is read from a copy that never changes.** The two kinds of address used are a dated capture of a public web archive in its raw form (`https://web.archive.org/web/<14 digits>id_/<original address>`, which serves the original bytes) and the static storage address of the publisher where one exists. A host that rebuilds a file under the same address, or that sends a page address through a front host, is not an origin. `tests/corpus-origins.test.ts` fails for the three hosts that did this and for a capture that is not in the raw form.
  - **Eleven files moved, each to a copy whose bytes are the ones already pinned.** Seven EPUB and Kindle files of the public-domain book library (`book-pg11`, `book-pg1661`, `book-pg2701` and `book-pg345` as EPUB; `book-pg11`, `book-pg1661` and `book-pg345` as Kindle files; the three EPUB companions of the Kindle rows use the same addresses), the KF8 edition of the real-world corpus (`gutenberg-pg11-images.azw3`) and the three newspaper text layers (`chronam-*`). For each, the captures from 2026-09 on were fetched and hashed until one matched the pinned SHA-256; the address and the capture timestamp are in the manifests. No digest, size or baseline entry changes for these files.
  - **The three newspaper pages are read at the static storage address the page address redirects to** (`tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ndnp/...`), not at `chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/lccn/.../ocr.xml`. The old address answers 308, then 302, through two front hosts before the file; the final address serves the file with `cache-control: max-age=31536000` and a `last-modified` of 2009. The three digests are unchanged.
  - **`ipxe-ipxe.iso` is re-pinned** because no copy of the old bytes exists: the publisher rebuilds `ipxe.iso` in place from its rolling release (the file changed between the pinned `f0becef1…` of 2026-10-16, the `7828de07…` of the run, and `5a2a2725…` fetched later on 2026-11-03; no capture matches the first) and a capture of 2026-09-09 is the newest one the archive holds. It is now `https://web.archive.org/web/20260909011145id_/https://boot.ipxe.org/ipxe.iso`, 9,437,184 bytes, SHA-256 `97daefcbe47f5057327a4534450cae1676737cd553e7357ad8dae77f12617c3d`. It is still a bootable ISO 9660 image of the same producer, and the three jobs of the file (zip, tar, 7z) are judged ok. Entries of the reference cache of the parity benchmark are keyed by the content hash of the input file, so none of them changes; the key of the cache as a whole hashes `bench/corpus/remote-manifest.json` and does change with this edit, so the first nightly after the merge falls back to the newest earlier entry (`restore-keys`) and writes the new one.
  - **`book-pg2701.epub` keeps its pin** (837,163 bytes, `31a206f4…`): the host regenerated the file on 2026-11-02 (837,160 bytes, `8646b1f1…`), and the capture of 2026-10-16 still has the pinned bytes.
  - **Each host gets its own pacing, from a table** (`PUBLISHED_SPACING_MS`, `HostPacer` and `retryPaced` in `bench/http-retry.ts`, the one retry loop of `bench/corpora.ts` and of `fetchBytes` and `fetchSize` in `bench/realworld/http.ts`; every try goes through `HostPacer.run`, so the tests and the fetchers use one path). This is the per-domain slot of a maintained crawler: hosts are spaced only when their configuration says so, and the default spacing is none.
    - **A host that publishes a limit is spaced from its first request.** The table holds one host, the storage host of the three newspaper pages (`tile.loc.gov`), at 400 ms, its published 150 requests a minute for media under `/storage-services/`. The first request stamps the time of release, so a refusal in between never lets the next request leave early. No manifest address uses the host's JSON API, so it is not in the table.
    - **Every other host is not spaced.** A 429 or 503 holds only the host that refused, for the time it asked: the `Retry-After` it sent, else the existing 30 s for a 429, else the ordinary 2 s backoff for a 503, never less than the ordinary pause. The requests waiting for that host then all leave when the time has passed.
    - **A second refusal moves the downloads that are already waiting.** The queue of a host releases one request at a time and reads the block and the spacing again each time it wakes, so a refusal that renews the block holds the whole queue until the new time.
    - **A host that asked for longer than a download waits is a circuit breaker.** The real block is recorded (now plus the time asked, not the 120 s cap), and while more than 120 s of it remain every request to the host fails at once with `RetryAfterTooLongError`, without being sent, the requests already queued included. urllib3 does not fail: `Retry.sleep_for_retry` (`src/urllib3/util/retry.py:380-386`) sleeps for `Retry-After` clamped to `retry_after_max`, 21,600 s by default (`DEFAULT_RETRY_AFTER_MAX`, :216-220; `parse_retry_after`, :346-368). Waiting suits a client that has nothing else to do. Here the wait would be a CI shard with a time limit and a host whose block may restart at every request made during it, so the download fails with a clear message. On the real-world run that failure fails the shard (below).
    - **The wait is at the host a try reaches.** A download whose redirect the parity fetcher remembers goes straight to the storage host and waits for that host's turn (`contactedHost`). A refusal holds the host that answered, the host the try reached and the host of the address, so a later download through the front host does not reach the refusing host during its block either. The real-world fetcher lets `fetch` follow redirects, so its tries wait at the host of the address and its refusals hold the host that answered as well.
    - **Pacing is per process.** Each of the ten real-world shards runs in its own process on its own runner and paces itself; the shards do not share a pacer. The three newspaper files are in shards 1, 2 and 10, one each, so one request plus its retries reaches that host from a shard. A host that many shards read at once would need the shards limited or staggered, which no host of the corpus needs today.
    - **`fetchStream` is not paced.** It reads one gzip table for the script that builds the regression manifest (`scripts/regression-corpus-manifest.ts`), not a nightly download, and has no retry.
  - **`Retry-After` is read in the two forms RFC 9110 allows and no other.** Whole seconds, or an HTTP date in one of its three forms (IMF-fixdate, the RFC 850 form with a two-digit year, asctime) that names a real instant. The date form was treated as no time named and got the 30 s default, and the first reading with a lenient parser took `0.5`, `1,5`, `3/4` and `retry later 5` for dates in the past. A wait of zero or less (a date already past, `0`) counts as no time named: a 429 gets the 30 s default and a 503 the ordinary pause, so a refusal is never answered at once.
  - **The real-world job restores and saves its cache like the quality jobs** (`.github/workflows/nightly.yml`, job `realworld`): `actions/cache/restore` with a key that carries the run id and falls back to the newest cache of the shard, a marker file touched right after the restore, the run, then `actions/cache/save` with `if: always()` under a key of its own (run id and attempt). The save happens only when `find` finds a file in the cache directory that is newer than the marker, because the ten shards hold 214 to 453 MB each and the repository's caches share 10 GB. A file replaced by one of the same size (the re-pinned ISO's case) is newer, where a count and a total size would have seen no change and the cache would never have converged. Files are digest-checked before they are written (`ensureCached`), and a `.part` file of a killed run neither counts nor is saved, so what is saved is complete.
  - **The run stays strict, and one unreachable file costs the night's real-world verdict.** A file that cannot be fetched or whose digest differs still fails its shard. That shard writes no report, so the merge refuses the run (`got 9 of 10 shard reports`) and the night has no real-world gate result at all, not only a missing file. The job saves what the shard fetched, so the next night resumes. Reporting the file as unavailable instead (`collectFetchErrors`, which the regression corpus run uses) would hide a regression here: the real-world report has no list of unavailable files and its gate judges only the jobs it is given (fatal verdicts and refusal rates per pair), so the jobs of a missing file would drop out silently and a crash on that file would pass.
- **Why**:
  - **The failures.** Shard 1: `bench:realworld failed: ipxe-ipxe.iso: SHA-256 7828de07…, manifest says f0becef1…`. Shards 2 and 10: `failed after 7 attempts: …/ocr.xml: HTTP 429, expected 200`. Small quality shard: `book-pg2701.epub: fetched 837160 bytes with SHA-256 8646b1f1…; the manifest pins 837163 bytes with 31a206f4…`. The earlier entry 91 moved one book file for the same reason and left the others, noting that captures existed for them; the next rebuild hit another.
  - **Why the newspaper host's 429 is not fixed by waiting longer (inferred; the logs show only the status).** The host's published limits page (the path is beside the host in `PUBLISHED_SPACING_MS`) gives 20 requests a minute for its JSON API and 150 for media under `/storage-services/`, and blocks for one hour when a rate is exceeded; for one of its endpoints it adds that the countdown restarts at every request made during the block. It also says the limits fall under load and tells clients to pause on a 429. Seven attempts 30 to 64 s apart (six pauses of 216 s in all), from runners that share addresses with other clients of a public cloud, are requests made during a block. The static storage address is the endpoint with the 150-a-minute limit and skips two front hosts. Whether the runners' addresses are admitted there can only be seen on a nightly run; the fetch from a development machine returned the three files with the pinned digests.
  - **The common practice.** Test data of browser engines and PDF viewers is fetched by content digest or listed with a digest beside a link, and the link is moved to a stable copy when a host changes the file; distribution and package-manager source pins are an address plus a checksum, and an audit that finds the upstream checksum changed points the address at a versioned or archived copy, not at the new bytes. Rate limits are met by honouring `Retry-After` and spacing requests (the retry policies of maintained HTTP clients read both forms of the header; crawlers keep a delay per host).
  - **Where the pacer and the header reading come from.** Two maintained clients, read at the files and lines below and followed in behaviour (none is copied; Scrapy is BSD licensed and urllib3 MIT licensed; the line numbers are of the revisions named).
    - Scrapy at e397746c. Per-slot configuration: `DOWNLOAD_SLOTS` (`scrapy/settings/default_settings.py:334`, an empty table by default) gives a slot its own `delay`, and every other slot gets `DOWNLOAD_DELAY`, which is 0 (:315); `Downloader._get_slot` (`scrapy/core/downloader/__init__.py:317-331`) reads the table when it makes a slot. The slot is keyed by the host name of the request (`get_slot_key`, :333-343), and a redirect is resolved again for its own address (:375-378), which is why ours waits at the host a try reaches. The release loop: `_process_queue` (:397-428) releases one queued request per slot, stamps `lastseen` in the same step, and arms a later call for the remaining delay; `_latercall` (:448-450) runs it again, which reads the delay and the stamp again, so a delay raised while requests slept holds the requests already queued. Ours is that loop with the slot's delay from the table and a block that a refusal sets. Scrapy has no `Retry-After` handling; its default jitter of the delay (`DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER`, :316) is not taken, since a spacing shortened at random would cross a published rate.
    - urllib3 `src/urllib3/util/retry.py` at c5347bbd: `parse_retry_after` (346-368) accepts digits, else an HTTP date through `email.utils.parsedate_tz` (more forms than the three of the RFC, which ours is limited to), raises for anything else, clamps a past date to zero and a long wait to `retry_after_max`; `sleep_for_retry` (380-386) does not sleep for zero. The differences are deliberate: a 429 that names zero or a past time gets the 30 s default here, since an immediate retry is what the rate limit refused, and a wait above the bound fails the download (above).
    - **The three-step check for a dependency.** (1) A maintained library: neither is usable as is, since Scrapy's slot is part of its engine and urllib3 is a Python client. (2) A dependency already in use: the fetch in use (`undici`) pools connections per origin and does not queue the callers of a host that refused. (3) So a release loop of about forty lines in `bench/http-retry.ts` that follows the semantics above, with tests on a virtual clock through the same `HostPacer.run` the fetchers use.
  - **Why one pacer for both fetchers.** The parity corpus (`bench/corpora.ts`) and the real-world corpus (`bench/realworld/http.ts`) already shared `retryDelayMs`; a second policy for the host as a whole would have been another place to drift.
  - **The speed failure of 2026-11-01 (run 41294170627, row `ocr/scan.png->pdf/throughput`, ratio 0.844) was a faster runner, not a regression.** The analysis is on the OCR speed issue (#644): that night every measured row read faster for both sides, the ratio of the median row fell to 0.885 of the next night's, and the OCR row recovered the next night. The speed gate is left as it is (see the alternatives), and the report does not record the processor, so the class of the fast runner is not known.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A capture is a dependency on a public archive being reachable.** The raw capture served the same bytes on every fetch tried, the digest check refuses any other bytes, and the cache of verified samples keeps the files between runs; a failed fetch is a skipped row in the parity benchmark and a failed shard in the real-world run.
  - **The real-world ISO is no longer the publisher's newest build.** It is a dated build of the same project, which is what a fixed corpus asks for.
  - **The first nightly after the merge downloads the public samples again.** The cache of the parity benchmark's samples is named by the hash of `remote-manifest.json`, which this change edits; a rate-limited host is now met by the pause above and the failed jobs save what they fetched, so a second night finishes what the first could not.
  - **A refusal costs only the wait it asked for.** On the object-storage host, which the real-world manifest asks 838 to 840 times per shard (and the code host 176 to 180 times), one 503 without `Retry-After` costs the ordinary 2 s: 840 requests with eight workers take 10.5 s against 8.4 s with no refusal (a simulation of the real retry loop on a virtual clock). The listed host costs its spacing on every run, 400 ms a request.
  - **A `Retry-After` above 120 s is a failed shard on the real-world run**, not a long wait (above). The next night resumes from the cache of the files fetched.
  - **Superseded cache entries are not deleted.** Every save adds an entry of 200 to 450 MB, and the entries it supersedes stay until the cache evicts them. Deleting them needs `actions: write` on the job and a delete that must not fail the shard; the cache evicts entries unused for seven days and, past 10 GB, the least recently used first, and a shard saves only on a night that wrote a file, so a shard whose corpus is complete adds nothing. The newest entry is the one the restore reads, and it is used (not evicted) every night.
  - **The cache is saved only on a night that wrote a file**, so a night that wrote nothing leaves no entry for the next night to restore the newest of; the entry from the last night that wrote stays valid, and entries of other manifest digests are still found by the fallback key.
  - **Other hosts of the real-world corpus are still pinned by digest alone** (the media sample collections, the camera sample archive, the encyclopedia's media files, kernel and distribution mirrors, the free-software FTP site, the compression tools' download sites and the open preservation samples). None failed; each can be moved the same way when it does, and the new test names the hosts that did.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Changing the speed gate for the runner shift.** The shift is 12 % across rows; a normalisation would be a new gate with its own evidence, and the one row that crossed the line recovered the next night.
  - **One spacing for every host that has refused (the second and third versions of this change).** The spacing came from the newspaper host's strictest published limit, 20 a minute, and applied to any host after one 429 or 503; while workers kept the queue full it never lapsed. One 503 from the object-storage host made 840 requests take 2,498 s (178 requests to the code host 512 s) against 8.4 s, inside a 60-minute job. A host's published limit is configuration, not something a refusal reveals. An earlier version also halved the spacing at each good response, which drew 32 refusals where a fixed spacing drew 8 against a host that allows 20 a minute.
  - **Re-pin every changed file to its new bytes.** It makes the run green and the corpus unfixed again at the next rebuild; every file but the ISO had a capture with the pinned bytes.
  - **Drop the files from the corpus.** It loses a format sample (`iso`, `alto`, `epub`) and the coverage the rule of entry 37 asks for.
  - **Report an unavailable file instead of failing** (`collectFetchErrors`). The real-world gate has no notion of an unavailable file, so the jobs of the file would vanish from the verdict and a regression on it would pass (above).
  - **A copy of the files in the project's own storage.** QA decided on no new cloud storage; the licences of several sets also ask for no redistribution.
  - **More retries or a longer wait for the newspaper host.** Its block lasts an hour, and a retry inside it can only fail or restart it.
  - **Saving the real-world cache on every night.** Ten shards of 214 to 453 MB each would add about 3.5 GB of entries a night to 10.9 GB of caches in use, and push out the library and tool caches the other jobs restore.
- **Verified by**:
  - `tests/corpus-fetch-limits.test.ts` (21 cases). The pacer cases and the shard simulations go through `HostPacer.run` and `retryPaced` on a virtual clock; the cases that read a refusal over HTTP wait on the shared pacer's `run`. Failing on the version with one spacing for every host that refused: one 503 from the object-storage host costs only its wait (2,498 s before, 10.5 s after), the table spaces `tile.loc.gov` at 400 ms and no other host, a listed host is spaced from its first request (the request after a refusal left 2,205 ms after the last release, now 6,000 ms after the first at a 3,000 ms spacing), a lone download never sends to a listed host faster than its spacing, a request a millisecond after the last release waits for the rest of the spacing, a try waits at the host a remembered redirect reaches and a refusal holds both hosts, a block renewed while requests wait holds them, a block past the bound refuses the queued and the later requests at once without sending, six downloads of a host that asked for 3,600 s fail at once with one request sent in all (five requests sent into the block before, each after 120 s), and eight workers on a host that allows 20 requests a minute are never refused when it is listed (100 files in 297 s) and are refused when it is not (32 refusals). Earlier cases: the three HTTP-date forms of `Retry-After`, the junk and past values that must give a 429 its default, a leap second counted the same at any hour, a download that a front host redirected to the refusing host, and a size probe answered 429. The digest cases still fail when the check in `ensureCached` is removed. `tests/bench-corpora.test.ts` (the parity fetcher asks the pacer for the front host's turn on the first request and the storage host's on the remembered one; this failed with the front host twice), `tests/corpus-origins.test.ts` (2 cases: no address of a host that rebuilds in place, captures only in the raw form), `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts` (the order of restore, marker, run, check and save; and the check run as a script with only `PATH` from the test's environment over a cache directory: a replacement of the same size saves, files older than the marker do not, partial files are gone from the directory the save archives whole, a missing marker saves nothing and warns, a missing directory does not fail the job), and `tests/realworld-corpus.test.ts` (the retry tests, with the rate-limit case on a server of its own because the pause belongs to a host).
  - The four real-world files fetched through `ensureCached` with the manifest's addresses: `ipxe-ipxe.iso` 9,437,184 bytes `97daefcb…`, `chronam-sn83030214-1913-01-01.xml` 561,733 bytes `fb1320a8…`, `chronam-sn83045462-1913-01-01.xml` 1,307,399 bytes `eeee6f52…`, `chronam-sn84026749-1913-01-02.xml` 859,095 bytes `cf40bff7…`, and `gutenberg-pg11-images.azw3` 255,506 bytes `d8211269…`, all equal to the manifest. `npx tsx bench/corpora.ts verify --family ebook` fetched 21 samples matching the manifest. `npx tsx bench/realworld/run.ts run --shard 1/1 --sources ipxe-boot-images` judged the three jobs of the re-pinned ISO ok.
- **Revisit when**: a nightly run fails to fetch a capture or the static storage address from the runners (look at the status in the log before changing the address), a host refuses on more than one night or publishes a limit (add it to `PUBLISHED_SPACING_MS` with the page that states the limit), another host rebuilds a pinned file (add it to the test and move it), the repository gets storage of its own for the corpus, or the processor class of the runner is recorded in the speed report and the shift of 2026-11-01 repeats.

## 144. A convert route logs one line for each refusal and failure, names every download in the `filename*` form, and a conversion sent in one request shows as converting with no share

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-03 (QA report: a 54-page Korean PDF to DOCX stopped at 30 percent in production and then failed with a 400 that the server did not log).
- **Decision**:
  - **Every download is named by `attachmentContentDisposition`** (`src/lib/api/content-disposition.ts`, RFC 6266 with an RFC 5987 `filename*`): the raw-bytes answers of `/api/convert` and `/api/v1/convert?raw=true` and the answer of `/api/fetch-url`, as the storage download already was. The name is never written raw into the header.
  - **`/api/convert` builds its answer before it commits the unit**, as `/api/v1/convert` does, so an answer that cannot be built is not charged. A unit that cannot be committed is a fault of the server too.
  - **`/api/convert` reads an error by where it came from.** Only an error the conversion call threw is classified. A `TypeError` is a fault of the server (500) whatever its words. A plain `Error` is a refusal only when its message holds one of the words of `UNTYPED_INPUT_REFUSAL_WORDS` in `src/app/api/convert/route.ts`, kept for the plain errors that no class of `src/lib/types.ts` types. Everything past the conversion (building the answer, committing the unit) and every unexpected error elsewhere in the route is a fault of the server, whatever its words. The route used to match the words `Cannot convert` over the whole handler, and the Fetch API's `Cannot convert argument to a ByteString`, thrown while the answer was built, matched them.
  - **Both convert routes answer a typed error with what its class declares** (`typedFailureOf` in `src/lib/types.ts`). A typed error is one whose class declares a refusal code: `ConversionFailedError` and the classes under it, and the archive errors `MissingVolumeError` and `ArchiveEncryptedHeaderError`. It is answered with the status its class declares and its code (the `code` of `/api/convert`, and the same `code` beside the problem type of `/api/v1/convert`). A missing tool (`EngineMissingError` and the classes under it) that declares no status is a 503 with the problem type `engine-unavailable`, as `EngineUnavailableError` already was, because another worker may have the tool. Any other typed error that declares no status is a 400 refusal. A declared 5xx is a fault of the server: it is answered with that status and the route's sentence for a fault, and logged as a failure. `CpuTaskAbortedError` (a pool task cancelled by the pool, since a client that went away is answered 499 first) and `UnknownArtifactFormatError` (an artifact the registry cannot name) now declare 500, like `InvalidConversionOutputError` and `GraphStateCorruptError`. The declared 422 of `CpuTaskTimeoutError` and the declared 429 of `ImportBudgetExceededError` are kept: a task past its time limit is a verdict on that input, as the queue already records it, and the import budget is the owner's daily allowance for link imports, a 429 by meaning. `OcrTextLayerLimitError` (a page with more words or characters than a text layer may hold) is a `ConversionFailedError` of its own with the code `input_over_limit`, the status 400 and no retry: it used to sit under the missing OCR tool, so a queued job ran the OCR three times on a page that never changes and the user was told the engine was unavailable. `OcrLanguageUnavailableError` had the same two faces and is now two classes under it, so that no caller compares a status: `OcrLanguageUnknownError` (a code that names no language, joins too many, or mixes `auto` with another: 400, `option_not_supported`, final) and `OcrLanguageDataMissingError` (a language whose data is not installed on this worker: 503, `engine_unavailable`, retryable). The queue records the same status as `failedStatus` (`classifyJobFailure` reads `typedFailureOf`), so a missing tool is recorded as 503 where it was 400.
  - **A fault of the server is answered by a fixed sentence that names no path.** `/api/convert` says `The conversion failed on the server.`, `/api/v1/convert` says `Internal conversion error`, and a vanished worker output says `The conversion output is no longer available` on both. A 503 for a missing tool keeps the engine's own message, as before.
  - **Both routes read the body the same way** (`readMultipartForm` in `src/lib/api/multipart-body.ts`). A body that does not declare `multipart/form-data` is a 415 (it was a 500 on `/api/v1/convert`). A body the parser rejects (the Fetch API's `TypeError`) is a 400, with the code `multipart_required` on `/api/convert`. A client that went away while the body was read is a 499, as a client that goes away during the conversion is. Any other error of the read is a fault of the server. A `targetFormat` sent as a file part counts as missing, and a `file` field sent as text is a missing file, so both are 400s and not a 500. A field that changes the conversion or says where its result goes (`sourceFormat`, `options`, and on `/api/v1/convert` also `webhookUrl` and `webhookSecret`) sent as a file part is a 400 as well, with `invalid_options` for `options` and `unknown_format` for `sourceFormat` on `/api/convert` (`fileSentAsText` in `src/lib/api/multipart-body.ts`), and nothing is converted: read as missing, `options` would drop a `protect` or `password` request and return an unprotected file with a 200, and a webhook would be dropped without a word.
  - **What a worker thread turns into a typed error** (`rehydrate` in `src/lib/workers/cpu-pool.ts`, audited by sending each kind of error through a pool thread). The six classes the pool lists (`CorruptStreamError`, `UnsupportedOptionError`, `PayloadLimitError`, `DecompressionLimitError`, `ConversionFailedError`, `Woff2LimitError`) keep their class, status and code. Any other error becomes a `ConversionFailedError` that keeps the original `name`, the status and the refusal code the thread sent (a typed error of a class the pool does not list, `GlyphBudgetError` in its test, keeps its name and code). An error with no code of its own (a `TypeError`, a `RangeError` or a plain `Error` raised by an encoder) arrives as a `ConversionFailedError` named `TypeError`, `RangeError` or `Error` with the code `conversion_failed` and the status 500 (`SERVER_FAULT_STATUS`), so the route answers it with the fixed sentence of a fault and logs it as a failure, where it used to be a 400 that told the user the file was bad, and a queued job treats it as final. The pool's callers are the encoders of zstd, FLAC, LZMA, bzip2, PNG, WOFF2 and the 7-Zip key derivation. They are given data the server decoded itself, except the font encoder, whose tables come from an uploaded font and whose limits are typed (`Woff2LimitError`, in the list above), so an error any of them raises without a class says nothing about the upload. The one invariant a handler states itself is the `zstdJob` task, which a thread runs only for an input that `planZstdJobs` splits: asked for a job of an input that is not split, it throws a plain `Error` and arrives as a 500. The rule reads the absence of a status and of a code, because every `ConversionFailedError` carries a code.
  - **A class that names a fault of the server's own code or tools declares 500 at the throw site that proves it** (`SERVER_FAULT_STATUS` in `src/lib/types.ts`), and a class that judges the request keeps its 400. `AudioResampleFaultError` (under `AudioResampleError`) is thrown for a failed kernel and for an argument the callers validate that reached the resampler broken, while a sample rate or a ratio out of range stays an `AudioResampleError`. `OcrPreprocessFaultError` (under `OcrPreprocessError`) is thrown where a buffer, a size or a channel count disagrees with another, while the picture over the pixel limit of binarization stays an `OcrPreprocessError`. `LoudnessReportMissingError` (under `LoudnessMeasurementError`) is thrown when the measuring pass printed no report or a report that is not JSON, while a report that says the input is silent stays a `LoudnessMeasurementError`. `AvifEncoderFaultError` (under `AvifEncoderFailedError`) is an exit of `avifenc` that ended on a signal or printed neither `Invalid argument` nor `invalid dimensions` (`PICTURE_REFUSAL_DIAGNOSTIC` in `src/lib/conversions/avif-cli.ts`); an exit that prints one of them stays an `AvifEncoderFailedError` and a 400. A picture with a side over 65,536 pixels, the largest an AV1 frame holds (the frame size is written in 16 bits as the side minus one: libaom `av1/av1_cx_iface.c` lines 639 and 640 at v3.8.2, `RANGE_CHECK(cfg, g_w, 1, 65536)`; libavif `src/write.c` line 1625 at v1.4.2), is refused with the 413 `input_over_limit` before any encoder is started (`assertAv1FrameSize`, read on the resized picture), where `avifenc` answered `Invalid argument`. The writer of the OCR page image (`src/lib/conversions/pnm.ts`) refuses a side over 1,000,000 pixels as an `OcrPreprocessError` (400), and only a size that is not a positive integer is an `OcrPreprocessFaultError`. The SVG tracer stopped by SIGSEGV is a 400 failed trace, as before: the tracer always runs under the sandbox memory limit, which reports a SIGSEGV as a failed allocation or a stack overflow of a Rust program, both driven by the size of the picture, and its stderr cannot tell either from a fault in the tracer. One rule covers every signal: a SIGSEGV is a fault of the server only when the output of the program proves it, and where the input can raise it the answer is a refusal of that input. The crash of `djvused` while it opens the pages (`DjvuIncludeStructureError`) stays 422 under the same rule: the library crashes on the deep or cyclic include graph of a hostile document (entry 135), so there the document is the cause. Each of these answers with the fixed sentence of a fault and leaves a failure line that holds the message, which the user never sees.
  - **Every class that declares 500 was tried with the worst upload a person can send** (`tests/server-fault-real-input.test.ts`), and none of them is reached from a file. A PNG of 65,537 and of 70,000 pixels wide or 65,537 high to AVIF answers 413 and starts no encoder; a PNG of 1,000,001 by 8 pixels to OCR answers 400; pictures of 1 to 5,000 pixels a side with one to four channels, and a 16-bit grey one, never reach an invariant of the page preparation; every sample rate from 1 to 10,000,000 Hz and every channel count from 1 to 1,000 is refused by the resampler as a 4xx or resampled, never a fault; a WAV with no samples, three samples or one second of silence through the loudness pass never leaves it without a report; a ZIP sent as `.txt`, `.md` or `.html` is refused as `spoofed_file` before its output could be judged a container; every target of the registry is a registered format, so no artifact is stored under an unknown extension; and every input size from two blocks to forty blocks at the levels around the pool threshold is split into jobs that the thread plans again. Three classes read stored state and no field of a request: `GraphStateCorruptError` (a scheduler record read back from Redis), `WorkerOutputMissingError` (an output file the worker wrote that is gone) and `CpuTaskAbortedError` (a pool task cancelled by the abort of its caller, which both routes answer 499 first: `tests/job-deadline-sync-routes.test.ts`).
  - **`/api/convert` and `/api/v1/convert` log one line for each answer of 400 or more, and that line is the whole record** (`src/lib/api/conversion-outcome-log.ts`): `[convert] refusal {...}` with `console.warn` for a 4xx and `[convert] failure {...}` with `console.error` for a 5xx (`[v1/convert]` for the keyed route). A route does not log the error it answers with a 500 itself. The JSON holds the request id (a new UUID made before the handler runs), the status, the refusal code (the `code` field, or the name of the problem type), the source and target formats (the `extension` the registry gives the name, the same on both routes, and nothing for a name it does not know), the input size in bytes and the duration in milliseconds. When an error decided the answer it also holds the class of the error. Only a failure (5xx) also holds the error's message cut to 300 characters and its top six frames cut to 200 characters each: a refusal is named by its code and class, because the message of an engine can quote the content of the file. In a failure, the file name, its leaf after the last `/` or `\\`, the leaf without its extension, the open password, the passwords of a merge and the passwords a PDF is protected with (`PROTECT_PASSWORD_KEYS` of `src/lib/queue/option-secrets.ts`, in `protect` and directly in the options) are replaced by `[redacted]`. They are matched in one pass by one pattern of escaped literals, longest first, so the marker is never matched again and a name is cut whole before its stem. Each is matched as received and composed (NFC, and the message is composed before it is read), and percent-encoded in both forms, because a name sent decomposed and quoted percent-encoded has no composed form. The secrets are built only when the line of a failure is written, from the file name and the options as the request held them (`ConversionTrace.fileName` and `options`): a success, a refusal and a request refused before its options were validated read none of them, where the first version encoded every password of every request at once (a two-million-entry `passwords` array measured 690 ms and about 550 MB). A secret shorter than three characters is cut only where no letter, mark or digit touches it, so the stem of `a.pdf` cuts `/tmp/a.zip` and not the words of the message. The deadline helper writes one line of its own, `[deadline] Invalid deadline setting or input`, for a `JobDeadlineError`, beside the outcome line of the same 500. An error that escapes the handler (a failed read of the quota store before its own error handling) is logged the same way as a 500 and thrown again. A line that cannot be written is replaced by one short line that names the failure, and never changes the answer.
  - **Answers that turn a caller away before any work leave no line**: a 401 and a 429 that no error decided (the rate limit, the concurrency limit and the daily allowance), and the answers of the two wrappers that run before the log (`withinSingleRequest`, a 413 for a body declared too large before it is read, and `admittingNewFiles`, the 503 of a full disk). The edge already counts them by status and route, and they are the answers that grow in a flood. A 429 that a typed error decided (`ImportBudgetExceededError`) is logged. A 499 is logged as a refusal, because the client left after the server took the request and its duration says how long it waited. The 503 of a full CPU pool (`CpuPoolOverloadedError`) and the 503 of a quota store that does not answer are logged as failures: they are faults of the server's capacity, and an operator needs them in the log when they come in a flood.
  - **A conversion sent to the server in one request has no share of progress.** The row of the queue shows an indeterminate bar and `Converting...` (`변환 중...`) from the start of the request to its answer. The label covers the upload of the file as well, because the request sends the file and waits for the result in one piece and neither half can be measured apart. The client no longer reports the fixed 15, 30 and 80 percent. A file sent in parts still shows the share it reports: the bytes sent, scaled to the first 45 percent, are a measure, but the share of the job (45 to 100 percent) is the progress the worker reports, not measured work. Each new stage starts with none until it reports one. Under reduced motion the bar does not move, and its whole track is filled in the quiet accent tone (`--c-accent-edge`), so that it cannot be read as a share of the track.
- **Why**:
  - **The failure.** The production image (`sha-589db10e`) run on the same limits as the web service (0.8 CPU, 5,632 MiB, read-only root, 256 processes, the worker seccomp profile) converts the QA file to DOCX in 4.0 s when it is uploaded as `qa.pdf`, and answers `400 {"success":false,"code":"conversion_failed","error":"Cannot convert argument to a ByteString because the character at index 22 has a value of 45453 which is greater than 255."}` (176 bytes, 187 with the chunked framing the edge counts) when the same file is uploaded under a Korean name. The conversion had run, its unit had been charged, and the header of the answer failed. Nothing was logged because a refusal was not logged.
  - **The common practice.** Browsers read `filename*` first and fall back to the ASCII `filename` (RFC 6266 section 4.3); the download route of this service already wrote both. A server that answers a fault of its own as a refusal of the input tells the user the file is bad and hides the fault from the log; a request log line per refused request, keyed by an id, with the file name and the passwords cut out, is what an operator reads first.
  - **The progress.** Neither `fetch` nor the server's single answer measure how far a conversion is, and the reference converter's task API reports a status (`waiting`, `processing`, `finished`, `error`) and no percent, so its processing state can only be shown without a share. A fixed number that does not move reads as a stalled conversion.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A log line for each refusal and failure adds log volume.** The sizes were measured on the route: a refusal line of a Korean-named 1,040-byte PDF is 508 bytes, and a failure line with a 2,000-character message (cut to 300), six frames and the registry's formats is 1,164 bytes. The caps in the code bound a line to about 1.8 KB. The production logging driver is `json-file` with 5 MiB for each of 3 files for each service that uses it (`docker-compose.prod.yml` lines 32 to 36), so each file holds about 4,000 failure lines of that size before it rotates. The answers that shed load leave no line, which is what keeps a flood from rotating the log.
  - **The request id is not sent back to the client** and the edge does not log one yet. It is in the one line that holds the status and the error, so a failure is found by its time, status and route, not by an id the user can quote.
  - **A failure's message is cut and redacted, not proven free of every user text.** The file name and the passwords are removed. A message that quotes a name inside the file (an archive entry) is kept, cut to 300 characters; it is a message of the engine and the line is read only by the operator. A refusal keeps no message, so a refusal whose cause is not in its code (`conversion_failed`) is found by its class and formats.
  - **A short secret standing alone is cut wherever it stands.** A password `e` or the stem of `1.pdf` cuts the same text when a message holds it as a word of its own (`page 1 of 2` loses its `1`); the words around it stay whole.
  - **A limit that refuses every caller leaves no line.** The 401s and the 429s of the limits are counted only by the edge, so a limit set wrong is seen there, by its status and route, and not in this log.
  - **The queue's `failedStatus` changes for a missing tool**, from 400 to 503, for the jobs that fail with one after their retries. The API reads it as it is, and the interface words a failed job by its `failedRefusalCode`, which is unchanged.
  - **The reduced-motion bar is a filled track.** It looks full but is lighter than a finished bar and carries the label.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Encoding the name in the old `filename` parameter alone** (percent-encoded or replaced): browsers would show the encoded text or lose the name, and the helper that writes both forms already existed.
  - **Removing the refusal words**: plain errors that no class types still reach the route (see the Revisit row), so the words stay for them, but only for an error the conversion threw and never for a `TypeError`. The type of the error is what separates a fault from a refusal.
  - **Keeping the answer's build and the commit inside the classifier and adding `TypeError` to the exceptions**: any other error class with one of the words, thrown while the answer is built, was still a refusal of a good file, and nothing in the tests failed when the unit was committed before the answer was built.
  - **Logging the error where it is classified and the line besides**: a 500 wrote the stack, then the line, and the vanished worker output a third, so one failure was three records with no id in common.
  - **A progress estimate from the file size or the time**: it would be a guess shown as a measure.
  - **Logging the file name or the options for context**: they are user data.
  - **Skipping a secret under three characters**: a Korean name of two syllables (`보고.pdf`) would reach the log; matching it where no letter or digit touches it cuts it and leaves the words.
  - **Replacing each secret in turn**: a one-letter secret also matched the letters of the marker of an earlier replacement, and the line became unreadable (`Inv[r[redacted]dact[redacted]d]lid`).
  - **Answering a missing tool 400 as before**: it tells the user the file is bad, and a client would not retry where another worker may have the tool.
- **Verified by**: `tests/download-filename-header.test.ts` (a Korean-named PDF to DOCX on `/api/convert` answers 200 with the name in `filename*` and charges one conversion, a `TypeError` answers 500 and charges nothing, the raw answer of `/api/v1/convert` and the answer of `/api/fetch-url` carry a Korean name; all four failed before the change, the first with the production body), `tests/content-disposition-header.test.ts` (a line feed, quotes, a backslash, a percent sign, characters RFC 5987 does not allow, a Korean name and an empty name), `tests/convert-error-boundaries.test.ts` (a header helper that throws an error whose words are `Cannot convert` while the answer is built answers 500, charges nothing, leaves one line and lets the same file be converted and charged once on the next request; a unit that cannot be committed answers 500, and its reservation is given back when its lease ends; a typed refusal keeps its code; a `TypeError` is a 500; a body that is not multipart is a 400. The build test failed with 400 before this change, and fails with the quota one unit lower when the unit is committed before the answer is built), `tests/convert-outcome-log.test.ts` (the refusal line of each route with its code, formats, size, duration and id and without the file name or the password, one failure line carrying the class and a redacted message, an error that escapes the handler logged once and thrown again, a line that cannot be written leaves the answer unchanged, the target named by its registry extension on both routes, no line for a 401, a rate-limit 429, an oversize declared body or the 503 of a full disk, a line for a 429 a typed error decided, no line for a success, a refusal line with the class and no message, a message left whole for the names `a.pdf` and `1.pdf` with the password `e` (it read `Inv[r[redacted]dact[redacted]d]lid…` before), the stem of `a.pdf` cut from `/tmp/job/a.zip`, the protect passwords cut, and a Hangul name sent decomposed after a Windows path cut in its composed, decomposed and percent-encoded forms, a decomposed name quoted percent-encoded in its decomposed form, and, on both routes, no password of the options encoded for the matcher while a conversion succeeds, while the options are refused and while the conversion refuses the file, counted by the calls of `encodeURIComponent` that held a marker, and encoded for a failure; the last four, the percent-encoded name and the success and refused rows failed before the change), `tests/convert-typed-error-status.test.ts` (on both routes: `InvalidConversionOutputError`, `GraphStateCorruptError`, `CpuTaskAbortedError` and `UnknownArtifactFormatError` answer 500 and `RawEngineRequiredError` 503, each with one failure line; `AudioResampleFaultError`, `OcrPreprocessFaultError`, `LoudnessReportMissingError` and `AvifEncoderFaultError` answer 500 with one failure line and the fixed sentence of a fault, and nothing of the words of their errors; `CpuTaskTimeoutError` 422 `timeout`, `ImportBudgetExceededError` 429 `import_budget_exceeded`, `OcrLanguageUnknownError` 400 `option_not_supported` and `OcrTextLayerLimitError` 400 `input_over_limit`, each with one refusal line; a body that is not multipart 415, a broken one 400 with no error line, a client that leaves while the body is read 499, a target sent as a file 400, and `sourceFormat`, `options` (a `protect` request) and, on `/api/v1/convert`, `webhookUrl` and `webhookSecret` sent as files 400 with no conversion run. Every row failed before the change with a 400, a 200 or a 500, except the 415 and the 400 of a broken body on `/api/convert` and the file target on `/api/v1/convert`), `tests/server-fault-error-classes.test.ts` (the throw sites of the resampler, of the page preparation for OCR and of the loudness pass that prove a fault declare 500, and the sites that judge the request keep 400: a sample rate out of range, a picture over the pixel limit, a silent report, an AVIF encoder exit that blames the picture), `tests/server-fault-real-input.test.ts` (the worst uploads of the bullet above, run through `dispatchConversion`, the page preparation, the resampler, the loudness pass and the pool; the AVIF cases fail before the change with 500, the 1,000,001 by 8 pixels page with 500 where it must be 400, and the `zstdJob` case with 400 where it must be 500), `tests/queue-non-retryable-failures.test.ts` and `tests/engine-missing-errors.test.ts` (`OcrTextLayerLimitError` and `OcrLanguageUnknownError` run once and are recorded as 400, while `OcrLanguageDataMissingError` is retried and recorded as 503), `tests/cpu-pool.test.ts` (a `TypeError` of a thread arrives with the status 500), `tests/raster-vectorize.test.ts` (the SIGSEGV of the tracer is a 400 failed trace), `tests/engine-missing-errors.test.ts` (the queue records 503 for each missing tool), `tests/refusal-codes.test.ts` (the API document of `/api/convert` lists, at the status it is answered with, the code of each of sixteen typed errors, among them the 422 of `timeout`, `input_over_limit` and `conversion_failed` and the 503 of `engine_unavailable`, lists the 400 of `multipart_required`, and names no 429 for a link import, which only a queued graph raises; the problem schema of `/api/v1/convert` names `code` and its 400 covers a body that cannot be parsed), `tests/server-conversion-progress.test.ts` (the client starts the converting stage and reports no share for a request in one piece; the row shows an indeterminate bar and the label in English and Korean, and a measured share when there is one; the runner drops a share measured by the browser when the server stage starts), and the QA file (54 pages, 2.8 MB) posted to `/api/convert` under its Korean name on a production build on Linux pinned to one CPU: before the change 400 with the body above in 2.5 s and 1.5 s and no log line; after it 200 in 2.5 s, 1.6 s and 1.5 s, a 213,930-byte DOCX with the name in `filename*`, which LibreOffice opens (83 pages) and whose text holds 97.2 percent of the PDF's Hangul syllables and 6,028 of its 6,042 distinct Korean words; - **Revisit when**: the edge passes a request id to the application (log that id instead of a new one), a convert route gets a way to measure the progress of a single request (a streamed answer that reports stages), the batch route `/api/convert/batch` is used by the interface again (it has no outcome line yet), the CPU pool marks an error that arrived without a class of its own by a flag from the thread (the rule reads the absence of a status and a code, so a thread that raises an unclassified error for a bad upload would be answered 500), or the plain errors behind `UNTYPED_INPUT_REFUSAL_WORDS` are typed and the words are removed.

## 145. A path the site offers no page at is answered 404 by one rule of the slug parser, as the reference converter answers it, and a 404 page shows a thin header with the logo, a code, a heading that names the route and one sentence

- **Status**: Implemented (QA request of 2026-11-03: every page path the site does not offer answers 404, as the reference converter does, instead of a converter page with status 200), decided 2026-11-03. It supersedes the parts of entry 139 that kept the many-to-one pair pages of a category word and rendered a noindex converter page for an unregistered name.
- **Decision**:
  - **`parseConverterSlug` in `src/lib/slug-parser.ts` answers "this slug is a page" or `null`, and the slug page answers 404 for `null`** (`generateMetadata` and the page both call `notFound()`). The server page parses once and hands the result, with its canonical path (`ParsedSlug.canonicalPath`, named once for every page by `parseConverterSlug` from the page's copy, not by each constructor), to `ConverterPageView`, which therefore neither parses nor imports the job graph. It is the only place that decides, so the metadata, the page, the cross links and the tests cannot disagree.
  - **A page exists for**: the site pages (`terms`, `privacy`, `contact`, `about`, `security`, `status`, `accessibility`, `unit-converter`); `/pdf-ocr`; `<format>-converter` for a registered format; `<category>-converter` for a category of the registry (`video`, `audio`, `image`, `document`, `ebook`, `archive`, `vector`, `font`, `cad`, `spreadsheet`, `presentation`, `data`); a pair `<a>-to-<b>` of two registered formats when `FORMAT_REGISTRY[a].targetFormats` lists `b` (two names of one format that the registry lists, such as `jpeg-to-jpg`, and a format converted to itself, such as `pdf-to-pdf`, stay the page of their source, entry 139); the four unit pairs; the utility pages `merge-<format>` for the formats of a merge node (`MERGE_FORMATS`) that the registry converts to themselves (`pdf`), `compress-<format>` for the formats the job graph has an optimiser for (`OPTIMIZABLE_FORMATS`) that the registry converts to themselves (`pdf`), `save-website-as-pdf`, `website-png-screenshot` and `website-jpg-screenshot`.
  - **No page (404)**: a name the site does not know, an unregistered format on either side, `any` on either side, a category word on either side of a pair (`video-to-mp4`, `image-to-pdf`, `word-to-pdf`, `presentation-to-pdf`), a conversion the registry does not list between two registered formats (`mp3-to-pdf`, `docx-to-mp3`, `jpg-to-jpeg`, `docx-to-docx`), a pair with more or fewer than two parts (`pdf-to-docx-to-zip`, `-to-pdf`), `/ocr` and `/ocr-pdf` (the OCR page is `/pdf-ocr` alone), a utility page of a format its operation does not run (`merge-docx`, `compress-gif`, `compress-png`, `compress-jpg`), a page name with a space, a tab, a line break or a slash around it (`/pdf-to-jpg%20`, `/%09pdf-to-jpg`, `/pdf-to-jpg%0A`; the slug is read as it came, and lowercasing `A` to `Z` is the one tolerance: `/PDF-to-JPG` shows the page of `/pdf-to-jpg` and names the lowercase URL as its canonical, while a character that Unicode lowercases to a letter, the Kelvin sign for `k` in `lbs-to-Kg`, is no tolerance and the path is 404), a path of two or more segments (`/foo/bar`, `/pdf-to-jpg/extra`, `/ko/foo/bar`; `src/app/[locale]/[...rest]/page.tsx` calls `notFound()`, so it meets the same localized 404 page), a converter page of a word that is not a format or a category (`word-converter`, `photo-converter`), and a path with a dot that is not the dot of a format id (the answer entry 141 gave through `isFileSlug`, now the same rule). A name every object has (`constructor`, `__proto__`) is looked up by own keys in the info page table, the category table and the registry, and so is 404 as any other unknown name.
  - **The words that named a category the registry does not have are gone**: `word`, `excel`, `powerpoint`, `photo`, `picture` and `music` stood for the representative formats of the document, spreadsheet, presentation, image and audio categories. The category words are now the 12 categories of the registry, so the breadcrumb of every page, which links `/<category>-converter`, always leads to a page, and `CATEGORY_WORDS` is typed by `FormatCategory`.
  - **Deleted with what the parser no longer produces**: the generic fallback page and its `generic` messages, `isIndexableSlug` and the `robots` branch of `generateMetadata` (a page that exists is indexable), `isFileSlug`, `DOTTED_FORMAT_SUFFIXES`, the OCR canonical aliases, the category-pair copy (the `pair` copy holds two format ids, and the `names`, `files.category` and `tgtKind` select entries of the six removed words), the fallback target list and category of `ConverterPageView`, and the footer links `/video-to-gif`, `/video-to-mp3` and `/image-to-pdf` (`MP4 to GIF` links `/mp4-to-gif`; the other two repeated `MP4 to MP3` and `JPG to PDF`). A registered format whose id is also a category word (`presentation`) has no page of its own but the converter page of the category and no pair page, so the related lists of a page skip it (`offersConversion` and `isSelfConvertible`, with `isCategoryWord`, in `src/lib/slug-info-pages.ts` and re-exported by `src/lib/slug-parser.ts`, leaving `src/lib/format-aliases.ts` as a pure alias module with no imports). The footer link `/compress-png` ("Lossless PNG") is gone with its page; `Compress PDF` stays.
