A missing office suite is an `EngineUnavailableError` (503), as for the other `.doc` targets; there is no in-process `.doc` to fall back to.
- **Why**:
  - **The converter's own `.doc` was a Rich Text stream under the `.doc` name** (`tgt === 'doc'` in `src/lib/conversions/hwp.ts` returned the RTF with the media type `application/msword`). Word opens it, but it is not a Word 97-2003 file: since #971 (entry 157) the binary signature check for `.doc` requires the compound file header, so the output was refused by our own check when fed back as a `.doc` (the real-world output check reports it as "output bytes do not match doc"). An output must be a file of the type it is named after.
  - **The export follows the reference converters.** unoserver (MIT, `src/unoserver/converter.py`) finds the export filter of a document for its import and export type and exports with the office suite; Filee (MIT, `src/Filee.Engines/Hwp/Hwpx/HwpxConverter.cs`) reads HWPX in process and writes DOCX, HTML and the other targets from that reading, with no `.doc` of its own, which is the split used here: Hangul is read in process and Word 97 is written by the office suite. hwp.js (MIT) and pyhwp (AGPL, read for behaviour only) only read Hangul files.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A Hangul to DOC conversion starts the office suite (about 2 s) where the RTF was written in 2 ms.** The `.doc` of the other sources costs the same.
  - **The text of the `.doc` is the text of the DOCX**, which is the text of the `hwp` and `hwpx` to `txt` conversion (the test compares the words).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping the RTF and naming it by what it is (`rtf`).** The pair is offered as `.doc` and a user who asks for `.doc` gets a Word 97-2003 file.
  - **Writing the compound file in process.** There is no writer for Word 97 binary in the engine, and writing one for one source format duplicates the export the suite has.
  - **Removing the pair from the registry.** The source is well formed; the output was the fault.
- **Verified by**: `tests/hwp-doc-target.test.ts` (a real `hwpx` and a real `hwp` fixture to `doc`: the compound file header, the signature check, and the words read back by the office suite equal the words of the `txt` conversion; red before the change).
- **Revisit when**: an in-process Word 97 writer is added, or the office suite reads Hangul files itself.

## 159. Conversion-name pills and cards are removed from pair pages and the home hero, and the lists on format and category pages become small monospace chips in a dashed box

- **Status**: Implemented, QA request of 2026-11-03 (scope) and 2026-11-06 (change). Narrows the block styling of entry 139 for the blocks that hold a conversion name.
- **Decision**:
  - **Pair pages carry no list of related conversions (`src/components/pages/ConverterPageView.tsx`).** The "Convert from X" and "Convert to Y" grids of "X to Y" pills are removed from pair pages such as `/pdf-to-docx`; the page ends after the two format cards. The reference converter's pair page has no such block.
  - **The home hero carries no row of popular-conversion icon cards (`src/components/Hero.tsx`).** `src/components/workbench/PopularConversions.tsx` and the `hero.popular` messages are deleted.
  - **Frequent conversions of the home format directory are a plain list (`src/components/Features.tsx`).** Each row is the pair in monospace 12 px with a 12 px arrow, a one-line 12 px note in `ink-3` (line height 16.5 px), 8 px between rows, no border and no hover; the list heading is monospace 11 px in `ink-3`. Measured on the reference home: pair mono 12 px, note 12 px with line height 16.5 px, no visible hover.
  - **Format pages (`/pdf-converter`) list conversions as chips (`src/components/converter/FormatCrossLinks.tsx`).** Two blocks ("Convert from X", "Convert to X"), side by side from `lg` with a 40 px by 32 px gap, each with an 11 px uppercase eyebrow, a heading (`text-lg sm:text-xl`, 600), a one-line intro and a dashed 1 px `rule` box with 16 px padding and `canvas` at 30%. Chips are monospace 12 px uppercase, padding 4 px by 10 px, 1 px `rule` border, radius `xs` (2.4 px), `surface` at 80%; on hover the border is `accent` at 40%, the fill `accent` at 5% and the text `accent-ink`. Every conversion is listed (the earlier cut at 30 sources is removed). The reference uses its red primary; ours keeps the blue brand tokens.
  - **Category pages (`/video-converter`) list every format of the category (`CategoryConverters` in the same file).** One block "Converters for {category}" with the same chips, each linking its format page (`/mp4-converter`).
  - **Home format directory tabs, extension chips and list header (`src/components/Features.tsx`), added by QA on 2026-11-06.** Category tabs are text buttons with no border and no fill: 12 px text with the label at 500, a 12 px category icon, a mono 10 px count in `ink-3`, `py-1` and a 6 px gap; the active tab is `accent-ink` and has no hover, an idle tab goes from `ink-3` to `ink` on hover. Extension chips are flat mono 11 px uppercase on `surface` at 60%, padding 4 px by 8 px, 0.275 px tracking, no border and no radius; hover changes only the text colour to `accent-ink`. Above the chips a mono 11 px header row shows "{category} formats" on the left and "{n} listed" on the right, over a top rule with 16 px padding.
  - **Touch targets.** The tabs (about 20 px tall) and the extension chips (about 26 px tall) are below the 44 px target of the buttons they replace; QA chose the reference's size. The tabs sit in a wrapping row, so each stays a separate target with a 16 px gap between them.
  - **Eyebrow letter-spacing by language.** English eyebrows keep the reference's 0.18em tracking. The first reference has no Korean pages; the second reference's Korean page sets small Hangul headings at 0.05em (11 px gives 0.55 px, 14 px gives 0.7 px), so Korean eyebrows and the mono list headers of the home directory use `0.05em`. The rule is scoped by the document language (`[:lang(ko)_&]` on `<html lang>`), not by text content.
  - **Not copied:** the grid pattern inside the dashed box and the chip shadow, which are decoration; the reference's eyebrow icon.
- **Why**:
  - **QA judged the bordered conversion-name pills and cards slop, with their hover.** The reference shows each list once in a quiet form and has none on pair pages, so a smaller, flatter block matches it.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Pair pages lose their pills to the other conversions of both formats** (every target of the source and up to 30 sources of the target). Crawl paths to those pairs now run through the format pages, the category pages, the home directory and the sitemap; each pair page keeps links to its two format pages through the format cards.
  - **Chips are about 28 px tall, below the 44 px touch target** of the pills they replace. QA chose the reference's size.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping the pills on pair pages with the new chip style.** The reference has no such block on pair pages.
- **Verified by**: `tests/redesign-verification.test.ts`, `tests/internal-links.test.ts`
- **Revisit when**: search coverage of pair pages drops after launch, or a reference change adds a related-conversions block to its pair page.

## 160. Separate production keys for webhook secrets and storage credentials, JWT `kid` with `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` rotation, spoof checks on every stored input, and authenticate-before-parse on batch uploads

- **Status**: Implemented (epic #761), decided 2026-11-06.
- **Decision**:
  - **Production seals new data only under explicit keys (`src/lib/api-keys/secret-encryption.ts`, `src/lib/storage/credentials-vault.ts`).** In production `encryptSecret` seals only under `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` and `CredentialsVault.store` and `rotate` only under `STORAGE_VAULT_KEY`, each at least `32` characters after trimming. Without a valid key they refuse the write with a typed error (`SecretEncryptionKeyMissingError`, `VaultKeyMissingError`) and nothing is stored. Outside production the previous fallbacks (`KEY_HASH_PEPPER`, `JWT_SECRET`, the development salt) still seal.
  - **Reading never needs the new key.** The decryption candidates are built from every secret that is set, whatever its length: the sealing key first when it is valid, then the old chain in its old order (`KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `KEY_HASH_PEPPER`, `KEY_HASH_PEPPER_PREVIOUS`, `JWT_SECRET` for webhook secrets; `STORAGE_VAULT_KEY`, `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, `JWT_SECRET` for the vault). A value with surrounding spaces contributes its trimmed form and, when it differs, its raw form, since older releases derived keys from the raw text. A short key that is set still decrypts old data; only new writes refuse it. `reencryptSecretIfNeeded` and the API key verify path return a secret readable and unchanged when no sealing key exists, so verification never fails for a missing write key. `needsSecretReencryption` and `CredentialsVault.rotate` re-seal records that a fallback key decrypted under the sealing key.
  - **JWT `kid` and `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` (`src/lib/auth/jwt.ts`, `src/lib/config/schema.ts`).** `signJwt` adds a `kid` header derived from the signing secret (first `16` hex characters of a domain-separated SHA-256). `verifyJwt` tries the key whose `kid` matches first, then `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` (optional, at least `32` characters when set). Tokens without a `kid` still verify. Neither `JWT_SECRET` nor `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` is trimmed: both are used exactly as set.
  - **Spoof checks on every stored input (`src/app/api/queue/jobs/route.ts`, `src/app/api/v1/jobs/route.ts`, `src/lib/streaming/large-payload-streamer.ts`, `src/lib/jobs/graph.ts`).** Multipart, inline, and stored-key inputs of `/api/queue/jobs` and every `import.upload` node of a graph on `/api/v1/jobs` pass the magic-byte check against the format of their own key. Multipart uploads verify compound-file directory kinds after completion and delete a spoofed object.
  - **Authenticate before parsing (`src/app/api/convert/batch/route.ts`, `src/lib/api/multipart-body.ts`).** `/api/convert/batch` validates access, then the `multipart/form-data` content type (`415`), then parses the body (`400` on a malformed one). `/api/queue/jobs` and `/api/v1/jobs` answer a malformed body with `400`.
  - **Prototype-safe idempotency fingerprints (`src/lib/api/with-idempotency.ts`).** Form and JSON bodies are fingerprinted from null-prototype objects with sorted own keys, so `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `toString` fields change the fingerprint.
  - **`ab_base_ref` validation (`.github/workflows/nightly.yml`).** The nightly A/B job rejects a ref that starts with `-`, contains `..`, or falls outside `[0-9A-Za-z._/-]{1,256}`, and passes it to `git fetch` after `--`.
- **Why**:
  - **One leaked or rotated key must not open every secret store.** Falling back from the vault key to the webhook key to the session key in production tied three secrets to one value and made session-key rotation break stored data. Stored inputs other than the first upload, a JSON body that shadows `Object.prototype`, and a body parsed before authentication were gaps in the #761 review.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A production deployment that never set `KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY` or `STORAGE_VAULT_KEY` keeps reading but cannot write.** A new webhook secret or stored credential is refused with the typed error, API key verification and DLQ replay keep working, and existing records are re-sealed once the key is set and `rotate` has run. The keys are not required at startup because the web process may run without webhooks or storage credentials. Set them before the first write and keep the old key as a fallback until `rotate` has run.
  - **A short or space-padded key that is set stays a decryption candidate in production**, so a configuration mistake never makes stored data unreadable; it costs one extra trial decryption per read.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping the production fallback chain.** One value would still protect sessions, webhook secrets, and storage credentials.
  - **A startup-time requirement for the two keys.** It would stop deployments that use neither feature.
- **Verified by**: `tests/production-key-fallback-decrypt.test.ts` (production mode: old ciphertexts, short keys, space-padded keys, the vault with only `JWT_SECRET`, an API key with a webhook secret, `JWT_SECRET_PREVIOUS` padding), `tests/api-auth-upload-and-idempotency-hardening.test.ts`, `tests/config-schema.test.ts`, and `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: webhooks or stored storage credentials become mandatory for every deployment, at which point both keys become required at startup.

## 161. The header, footer, home hero, upload card and format cards follow the reference converter: flat sign-up button, four-column footer, no breadcrumb, trust row or format chips

- **Status**: Implemented, QA request of 2026-11-06 ("전체 레퍼 2개 기준으로 고쳐줘"). Builds on entry 159 and narrows the block styling of entry 139 (including its primary gradient) for the site chrome, the home hero and the converter pages.
- **Decision**:
  - **Header (`src/components/Header.tsx`, `src/components/UserNav.tsx`).** "Sign up" is a flat button: `ink` fill, `canvas` text, radius `xs` (2.4 px), padding 6 px by 10 px, 14 px at weight 500, hover `ink` at 90%, no gradient and no shadow. - **Status**: Implemented, QA request of 2026-11-06 ("both references decide the secondary pages"). Builds on entry 159; narrows the 404 page of entry 145 and the colour and radius values of entry 139 for these pages.

The terms checkbox of entry 146 is kept in a 16 px square with a 2.4 px radius (`.checkbox` in `globals.css`). ## 163. PDF text: a CFF composite font whose ToUnicode map lacks a code prints nothing for it, and the 22 glyph ids past 171 that pdf.js lists are read for Arial and Times New Roman

- **Status**: Implemented (the PDF text and font rows of issue #783; epic #760), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: implement conversions by following open-source source code). It extends entry 104 to CFF programs and entry 70 to the glyph ids past 171, and records which rows of the issue are settled and which stay open.
- **Decision**:
  - **A CFF composite font (CIDFontType0, a `/FontFile3` of subtype `/CIDFontType0C`, Identity-H or Identity-V) whose /ToUnicode stream lists codes gets an entry for every code its program can select that the map lacks** (`src/lib/conversions/pdf-font-tounicode.ts`, `missingCffCodes`; the codes come from `parseCff` in `font-cff.ts`). A code's text is, in the order of entry 104: the font's own map (it follows the added entries and wins), then, when the descendant's name and widths show an Arial or Times New Roman font, the glyph order of entry 70 (the CID-keyed programs of the 2002 to 2008 distillers name no glyph), and otherwise none: a run of private-use characters that the reader leaves out and counts (entry 49). The codes a program can select are the CIDs of the charset of a CID-keyed program and the glyph ids of a program that is not CID-keyed, whose CIDs are its glyph ids. The rest of entry 104 holds unchanged: a map that lists no code is no map, a `usecmap`, a named CMap and an encoding other than Identity-H and Identity-V leave the font as the file has it, a program that does not read as CFF 1 leaves it as it is, and a code that is no glyph of the program (a CID missing from the charset, or one past the highest glyph) gets no entry.
  - **Followed**: pdf.js (Apache-2.0, tag v6.3.289) `src/core/cff_parser.js` lines 274 (`isCIDFont = topDict.hasName("ROS")`), 322 to 360 (the charset of a CID-keyed font, `parseCharsets` with the glyph count of the CharStrings INDEX) and 933 to 991; Apache PDFBox (Apache-2.0, 3.0 at 649bf11a) `PDCIDFontType0.java` lines 394 to 409 (`hasGlyph`: a CID is a glyph when its charstring is not glyph 0) and 427 to 446 (`codeToGID`: the charset's `getGIDForCID` for a CID-keyed program, the CID itself "used directly as GID values" for another), with the charset formats of `fontbox/.../CFFParser.java` lines 1168 to 1260. What a code the map lacks prints is the entry 104 decision, Poppler's (`poppler/GfxFont.cc` 26.09, lines 1939 to 1948; behaviour only): the four readers differ, pdf.js and PDFBox write the code itself (`PDType0Font.toUnicode`, `PDType0Font.java` lines 589 to 595: "Use identity mapping if the given ToUnicode CMap doesn't provide any valid mapping"), pdfminer.six (MIT, a18de2a9) raises `PDFUnicodeNotDefined` (`pdfminer/pdffont.py` lines 1240 to 1246, `PDFCIDFont.to_unichr`) and prints `(cid:N)` (`pdfminer/converter.py` lines 266 to 268, `handle_undefined_char`), and pypdf (BSD, 8eeb0509) `_cmap.py` reads no CFF program at all.
  - **Bounds, kept from entries 70 and 104 and from the readers.** At most 64 composite fonts per document, 64 MiB of decoded programs, 262,144 codes of added entries and 8 MiB of copied own maps; a map that would pass a limit is not added and the later fonts are still tried. A program is parsed once however many fonts name its stream (`Known.cffCodes`), `parseCff` refuses a table past 64 MiB and checks every offset, count and range against the bytes before it follows it (a Private DICT range that overlaps the others 256 times is bounded by its own budget), a charset of repeated or backward CIDs is read as the set of CIDs it names, and an error of the parser is a font that keeps its reading. The readers' own limits are kept where they apply: a range wider than 2^24 - 1 codes is ignored (pdf.js `src/core/cmap.js` line 199, `MAX_MAP_RANGE`, used by `mapBfRange` at 235 and `mapCidRange` at 226), a `usecmap` is not followed (pdf.js adds the named CMap's codes in `extendCMap`, `cmap.js` lines 650 to 667, and PDFBox loads it in `CMapParser.parseUsecmap`, `CMapParser.java` lines 140 to 145: neither limits the depth of a chain; here the font is left as the file has it, as in entry 104).
  - **The 22 glyph ids past 171 of Arial and Times New Roman that pdf.js lists** (`src/lib/conversions/standard-font-glyph-order.ts`, `PAST_TABLE`). pdf.js's map for standard fonts written as CID fonts without a glyph mapping lists, past 171 and below the glyph ids of another version of the fonts (`getGlyphMapForStandardFonts`, `src/core/standard_fonts.js` lines 514 to 535): the four smart quotes at 179 to 182, `Aacute` 200, `Iacute` 203, `Oacute` 207, `Uacute` 210, the caron 223, `Lslash` to `zcaron` 224 to 229, `Yacute` 233, `yacute` 234, `cacute` to `ccaron` 252 to 254, `Abreve` 258 and `Aogonek` 260. They are read the way the table of entry 70 is read, against widths: the Liberation Sans fonts of pdfjs-dist through the cmap for Arial (the same files), and pdf.js's `getMetrics` widths for Times (`src/core/metrics.js` lines 1492 to 2762, by glyph name). They are added only when the base table has been read for the font; one listed CID whose width is not the reference's takes all 22 away and leaves the base table, because the order of that font past 171 is then not the one pdf.js lists. CIDs past 171 that pdf.js does not list keep the reading they had.
  - **Rows left open, each with its reason** (below).
- **Why**:
  - **Where it happens.** Of the 1,269 real-world and regression PDFs (1,267 whose structure reads), 244 composite CFF fonts with a map that lists codes are in 42 files (all Identity-H; 20 more CFF fonts have no map), and a code the map lacks is drawn once, in `govdocs1-004148.pdf`: code 12 of `TKNYRT+Universal-GreekwithMathPi`, a form feed that the text drops, so no text of the corpus changes for it. The fix is for a file that draws a printable code a map lacks, which no sample of the corpora holds; the test files are written by hand. The 22 glyph ids: `cc-4000041.pdf` draws the quotes at 179 and 180 of its Arial Bold CFF font four times, in `Logic ³1´ Switch On` and `Switch Output Logic ³1´ = Switch On`, where Poppler prints the same `³1´` and the same page sets `“Switch On”` in a font with a map.
  - **The installed fonts agree with pdf.js's 22.** The independent oracle is the installed Arial, Arial Bold, Times New Roman and Times New Roman Italic (v5.01, fontTools 4.66.1, `getBestCmap()` at glyph id = CID): all 22 ids give the character of pdf.js's list in all four, and the advance widths of the installed Arial and Times New Roman equal the references' (Liberation Sans within 0.17 thousandths of an em, the Times widths exactly). The installed fonts are the test's oracle, not data of the product (entry 70 rejected copying a table from them).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A CFF font that listed a code with no glyph in its program reads as before for that code**: a CID that is not in the charset, or one past the highest CID, still prints as itself in pdf.js (the entry 104 limit for TrueType fonts); no sample draws one.
  - **‘ and ’ of Arial are both 222 wide**, so the width check cannot tell them apart; the order of pdf.js and of the installed fonts is what decides, as for ‘ and ’ at 181 and 182.
  - **A font that is Arial by name and by the base table but has another order past 171** (an older version) and happens to give a listed CID the right width would read a wrong character; any wrong width of the 22 takes all of them away.
  - **The font pass costs more**: over the 1,196 files of both corpora that name a cross-reference to update, the pass took 164 to 165 ms in all before and 187 to 189 ms after (median of 5 per file, two runs per side, Mac), the largest file 9 ms. The conversions were not timed; the whole corpus (text) took 294 s before and 300 s after in one run each at different loads, which is noise next to OCR.
- **Rows of issue #783 left open, and why**: (the CFF rows below are reproduced against `pdftotext` and the cost of the range over the codes past the glyphs is measured in entry 175)
  - **Composite fonts without a ToUnicode map, the part still left** (`govdocs1-002701.pdf` 1,018 glyphs, `govdocs1-003638.pdf` 246: Symbol, Wingdings, MonotypeSorts, MT-Extra and AGaramond subsets whose programs keep no `cmap`, `post` or names): no reader gives them text. Poppler prints control codes; pdf.js reads a Symbol, Wingdings or ZapfDingbats font by name only when the font is not embedded (`src/core/fonts.js` lines 1257 to 1380, `fallbackToSystemFont`); PDFBox reads the embedded program's cmap (PDFBOX-5324, `PDType0Font.java` lines 609 to 640) and pdfminer.six the same through `TrueTypeFont.create_unicode_map` (`pdffont.py` lines 748 to 787 and 1152 to 1160), which entry 70 reads; pypdf reads nothing. The order of an AGaramond or Wingdings subset's glyph ids is in no source, and widths alone (entry 70) have no reference font for them.
  - **`CG.Times095` in `govdocs1-001389.pdf`**: the embedded Type 1 programs name their glyphs `G0` to `G92` with the code in the name (`dup 53 /G53 put`), and the letters are shifted by 30 from ASCII (`S` is code 53). pdf.js reads a name of `G` and two digits as hexadecimal (`src/core/evaluator.js` lines 3873 to 3877), which gives `S` for code 53 by coincidence and `9` for the code 39 of `E`, so no rule of a reader can be followed; the file stays an OCR case, as entry 49 and the issue state.
  - **Non-Identity encodings and `usecmap` with a partial map**: the corpora have one such font (a CIDFontType2 with an embedded CMap stream, `pdf-pdfjs-issue13242.pdf`, from pdf.js's own test files) and no `usecmap` map. The codes such a font can select come from its CMap's codespace and ranges, which neither the readers' limits nor this reader enumerate for the update; the font is left as the file has it.
  - **Codes past the glyph count**: no glyph of either corpus is one. One private-use gap of 65,280 codes (U+0100 to U+FFFF) costs a font about 10 ms in pdf.js (2.9 ms to 13.3 ms per conversion of a one-glyph page, median of 15, Mac) and 65,280 of the 262,144 codes of the document, so entries for the codes past the glyphs of every font would take the later fonts' real entries. The existing test `adds no entry for a CID past the glyphs of the font` pins this.
  - **The glyph ids 172 to 178 and 183 to 199 and the others past 171 that pdf.js leaves out** (the dashes at 177 and 178, `Agrave` at 172): no source gives them; 341 real-world and 229 regression glyphs were past 171 before, and the smart quotes of `cc-4000041.pdf` and the 22 are the part a source gives.
  - **The quadratic `joinContinuations` pass** is already linear since #930 and #936: 6.8, 11.5, 19.3 and 27.9 ms at 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 pages of one flowing paragraph each (the measurement of the row was 353, 971 and 2,955 ms at 200, 400 and 800).
  - **The `govdocs1-001157.pdf` to html SIGSEGV** is fixed by #907 (entry 115): the frame is V8's `Runtime_TierUpWasmToJSWrapper`; `tests/wasm-import-wrappers.test.ts` passes here, and no crash was reproduced (the original needed x64 Linux and four crashes in 103 replays). The documentation rows of entry 115 in the issue are not part of this entry.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Reading the charset names of a name-keyed CFF program as text** (the Adobe Glyph List through the standard strings): no program in either corpus has names that a font without a map needs, as entry 70 found, so the code for it would be untested against a real file.
  - **Padding every font's map to all 65,536 codes**: the cost above, and the codes of the later fonts.
  - **Pdf.js's whole standard-font map past 171** (496 ids): past 261 it follows one version of the fonts (entry 70); the 22 are the ids where the installed fonts of four styles agree with it.
  - **Taking the order past 171 from the installed fonts or from Liberation Sans** (the Mac order with `nonbreakingspace` and `apple` removed and the Euro in place of `currency` would give the dashes and the accented capitals too): that is a table derived from a font we do not ship, which entry 70 rejected, and no open-source reader has it.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-text-cff-partial-tounicode.test.ts` (CID-keyed and name-keyed CFF programs written by `tests/helpers/cff-font-builder.ts` from Adobe Technical Notes #5176 and #5177; text and Markdown against `pdftotext`; red before the change: 7 tests failed, for example `QQQRCD` where Poppler and the fix print `QQQR`; an Arial CFF font with a partial map reads `Qeport`; a map that lists every glyph, `usecmap`, a program that is not CFF, a table cut short and a font with no program leave the file as it is; 64 fonts that share a 60,000-glyph program get 4 maps; a program of 65,520 glyphs; 256 overlapping Private DICT ranges of 1 MiB; INDEX counts past the bytes; a charset of repeated and backward CIDs; the real `govdocs1-004148.pdf`), `tests/pdf-text-standard-glyph-order.test.ts` (red before the change: the 5 hand-written tests failed with `Logic ³1´ Switch On` and `it¶s ³it´`, and the real-file test's strings are absent from the base run's output; all 22 ids against the oracle's characters for Arial and Times; the smart quotes of an Arial Bold CFF font, an Arial TrueType font and a Times New Roman font; one wrong width and a font that lists only CIDs past the table leave the base table or nothing; the dashes at 177 and 178 get no text; the real `cc-4000041.pdf`), and the unchanged `tests/pdf-text-partial-tounicode.test.ts`, `tests/pdf-text-font-program-tounicode.test.ts` and `tests/pdf-text-cid-widths-bounds.test.ts`.
- **Measured**: text of the 1,261 PDFs of both corpora that read (8 more are refused as before), origin/main against the change, in-process, one pass per side: 1 file changes, `cc-4000041.pdf` (`³´³´` become `“”“”`, 4 characters; word-level F1 against `pdftotext` 26.09 0.7582 to 0.7584), and the glyphs left out are the same 51,569 in 120 files. Markdown was not compared (the map is the same layer).
- **Revisit when**: a file shows a printable code that a CFF font's map lacks, a reader or a font gives the order of Arial and Times New Roman past 171 whole, a font with a partial map and a non-Identity encoding or a `usecmap` shows glyphs with codes the map lacks, or pdf.js stops writing the code itself for a code its map lacks.

## 164. A PowerPoint presentation the office suite fails on is converted again with its embedded Excel objects kept, `dps` is read by the office suite, the archive header and volume errors are typed 422 failures, and the other office and HTML rows of issue #783 are settled by measurement

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, seven rows of the office and HTML area), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: implement conversions by following the open-source converters; measure the office suite on the worker image).
- **Decision**:
  - **A PowerPoint 97-2003 presentation that the office suite fails on is run once more with its Excel objects kept as objects** (`withEmbeddedWorkbookRetry` in `src/worker/office-suite-route.ts`, composed inside `withLegacyOfficeRecovery` in `src/worker/engines.ts`; the setting is written by `src/worker/libreoffice-profile.ts`). The first run is the default. When it ends without a verdict on the file (the stage time-out, the memory or output limit of the sandbox, a signal, or no output file; a failure to load the file and every typed failure are verdicts and are not run again), the same source is run in a profile of its own whose `registrymodifications.xcu` sets `/org.openoffice.Office.Common/Filter/Microsoft/Import` `ExcelToCalc` to `false`, and never in the pool, whose profiles other jobs share. When the second run fails too, the first failure is the answer. Only `ppt`, `pps` and `pot` are run again, once, and never after the job was cancelled.
  - **Why that setting.** On import the suite converts an embedded Excel chart or worksheet to a Calc object only when the option is on (LibreOffice core `filter/source/msfilter/msdffimp.cxx` `CheckForConvertToSOObj`, lines 7111 to 7145, the table entry `OLE_EXCEL_2_STARCALC` for `MSO_EXCEL8_CHART_CLASSID` at line 7140; the flag is read from `ExcelToCalc` in `sd/source/filter/ppt/pptin.cxx` lines 205 and 206; master `e9e154a73b3a` of 2026-11-06). A chart whose series name whole columns then gets an internal data table of 1,048,578 rows, 770 MB of `content.xml` for each of the two charts of `govdocs1-001020.ppt` (#877). With the option off the object stays an OLE object shown by the picture the presentation carries for it.
  - **The retry follows Gotenberg** (`pkg/modules/libreoffice/api/api.go` lines 684 to 698 retry a conversion that ended with `ErrCrashed`, capped at 10; `libreoffice.go` lines 534 to 554 name a LibreOffice that exited mid-conversion as that error; main of 2026-11-07): a conversion that the suite abandons is tried again. This one runs once and with the setting that removes the cause, since the same run would fail the same way. unoserver (`src/unoserver/server.py` lines 341 to 419) ends a conversion that passes `conversion_timeout` by stopping the suite and answering the error, which is what the stage time-out here already does.
  - **The suite's temporary files go into the run's own directory** (`TMPDIR` of the standalone run in `src/worker/engines.ts` and of the pool run in `src/worker/libreoffice-pool.ts`). A run that is killed left its `lu*.tmp` directory in the shared temporary directory: 2.9 GB of it after one run of `govdocs1-001020.ppt`, which filled a 2.9 GB `/tmp` and made the next conversions abort. It is removed with the run now.
  - **`dps` is a source the office suite reads** (`src/lib/conversions/office/office-suite-sources.ts`: `application: 'impress'`, interchange `pptx`, as `sxi`), and the registry offers `ppt`, `jpg` and `png` besides the targets it had (`src/lib/registry.ts`). The type table of the suite lists `dps` among the extensions of its PowerPoint 97 import (`filter/source/config/fragments/types/impress_MS_PowerPoint_97.xcu` line 21), so it opens what the extension names by its content. Before, the in-process text extractor was handed the bytes and refused them as a binary container. The reference service converts `dps` with LibreOffice to pdf, odp, html, jpg, eps and md (entry 97, check of 2026-10-25); `eps`, `md` and `swf` stay out as for the other presentation sources.
  - **`ArchiveEncryptedHeaderError` and `MissingVolumeError` extend `ArchiveInputUnprocessableError`** (`src/lib/types.ts`), so every route and a queued job treat them as the typed 422 failures they declare. They extended `Error`: `/api/convert` answered them 422 through their `status`, but `/api/convert/batch` answered 500, `classifyJobFailure` called them retryable (the queue tried the job again), and the archive readers' `instanceof ConversionFailedError` checks would have wrapped them with the file name.
  - **Rows settled with no change to the conversion.** `govdocs1-001120.html`: measured below, the loop is the office suite's and stays. In-process HTML to PDF with `<math>` and nested tables: done by entry 89 (MathML as its text, tables as wide as their content, 449 of 450 corpus pages in portrait and 450 in landscape; `tests/html-pdf-inprocess-omissions.test.ts`, `tests/html-pdf-nested-tables.test.ts` pass); the one refusal left is `govdocs1-001143` in portrait, which needs a shrink of 1.55 against the limit of 1.5 that print engines keep. `gd-579820.doc` to docx, pdf and png: converts on LibreOffice 25.2.3.2 (entry 97) and still aborts 24.2.7 with the typed refusal; the setting above does not change that (24.2.7 aborts with it too), because the crash is in the text layout and not in an Excel object. Word `w:ruby` directly under `w:p`, `w:hyperlink`, `w:ins` or `w:sdtContent`: read since #933 (`readRuby` in `src/lib/conversions/docx-model.ts` lines 597 to 604); `tests/docx-ruby-drawing-reader.test.ts` now pins the three containers for the drawing-aware reader too.
- **Measured** (Debian 13 arm64 VM, 4 cores, LibreOffice 25.2.3.2 from the archive, the package set of the worker image's office stages; the CI runner's 24.2.7 on an Ubuntu 24.04 VM; samples digest-checked from the corpus):

    | Case | Default | With the change |
    |---|---|---|
    | `govdocs1-001020.ppt` to odp, 25.2.3.2 | the ODP fails to store after 13 s (`SfxBaseModel::impl_store failed: Io Abort 27`; with scratch on a full tmpfs `double free or corruption`), 1.49 GB resident; through the worker route `SandboxedTimeoutError` at 45 s | first run fails, second run 0.6 s, an ODP of 822 KB with the 53 slides, 222 MB resident (`tests/ppt-embedded-workbook-retry.test.ts`) |
    | `govdocs1-001020.ppt` to pdf | 13.3 s, 53 pages, 3,444 words | 0.7 s, 53 pages, 3,444 words (the same text) |
    | `gd-579820.doc` to docx and pdf, 24.2.7 | abort in 1.6 to 7.9 s | the same abort with `ExcelToCalc` off |
    | `govdocs1-001120.html` to pdf, 25.2.3.2 | no end after 90 s for the page as it is and for the staged page | no change |

  - **The loop of `govdocs1-001120.html` depends on where the page breaks fall.** The page has 145 tables, nested two deep, not 145 deep (the parser of the suite limits depth to 1,024: `sw/source/filter/html/swhtml.hxx` lines 905 to 918 and `htmltab.cxx` line 4929, never reached). Of its 48 member blocks the first 47 convert in 0.3 s and the 48 end in a loop; leaving out any one of the last three also converts. Taking `width="100%"`, `nowrap` or `<pre>` out of the staged page converts it; taking out `cellspacing` or the `div` does not. No structure of the page predicts it, so no check before the run can send it elsewhere, and the 45 s stage limit and the in-process renderer (entry 90) stay the answer: the page is drawn by the in-process renderer in 18 pages (#871) with every letter and digit (`tests/html-pdf-layout-loop.test.ts`, whichever engine draws it).
  - **Opening the page as a Writer document does not help.** The default import opens an HTML page as a Writer/Web document (`filter/source/config/fragments/filters/HTML.xcu` lines 18 to 26, `DocumentService` `com.sun.star.text.WebDocument`); `--infilter="HTML (StarWriter)"` (`HTML__StarWriter_.xcu` lines 18 to 28, `TextDocument`; unoserver passes the same through `infiltername`, `converter.py` lines 236 to 250) opens it as a Writer document. On the 448 staged corpus pages, 446 convert in the Web layout (2 time-outs: `-000071`, `-001120`) and 447 in the Writer layout (1: `-000071`); of the 446 that both finish, the Writer layout loses 375,672 letters and digits against 377,892, draws 5,614 pages against 5,814, and has another page count on 101 pages. The first of two runs was implemented as a retry after the time-out and measured on `-001120`: the second run ends in 0.3 s and its PDF has 3 words past the page edge on pages 4 and 5, so entry 90 hands out the in-process PDF as before, after 46 s. A retry that changes no outcome was not kept.
- **Why**:
  - **A presentation that the suite cannot print is not damaged.** The file is intact and the suite converts it with the chart left as a picture, so a typed refusal or a time-out answers a different question from the one the file asks. The setting is the suite's own option for exactly this object, and it is used only where the default failed, so every other presentation keeps its charts as charts, as the reference service's default run converts them.
  - **A retry that cannot lose.** The second run starts only after a failure and its failure is never the answer, so a presentation that converted before converts the same, and one that failed fails with the same typed answer as before, at most one run later.
  - **The infilter and the retry of HTML stay out because they were measured not to help.** The records above are the reason, and they are listed so that the row is not opened again for the same idea.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A presentation that needs the retry loses its editable charts.** In the ODP, PPTX and PPT outputs each Excel chart stays an embedded OLE object with its picture; the PDF and the page images are the same. The alternative was a refusal.
  - **A presentation that fails for another reason costs one more run.** A corrupt `.ppt` that ends in a signal or with no output is run twice; one that times out takes up to two stage limits, which the job deadline still bounds.
  - **The first run of a presentation like `govdocs1-001020.ppt` still prints for 13 s before it fails** (21 to 29 s on 24.2.7). Looking into the embedded storages for charts of whole columns before the first run would save that time and is a design of its own; it was not done.
  - **`TMPDIR` inside the run's directory** keeps the suite's scratch on the same volume as before; a run that needs gigabytes of scratch still needs them, but they are freed when it ends.
  - **`dps` is read as what its content says.** A Kingsoft file that is not a PowerPoint 97 file fails in the suite with the typed refusal for a file it cannot load. No public `.dps` exists (entry 97); the test is a real presentation saved by the suite as PowerPoint 97 and named `.dps`.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Keeping Excel objects as objects for every presentation.** `govdocs1-001020.ppt` to pdf is 19 times faster (0.7 s against 13.3 s) and the text is the same, but every chart of every presentation would stop being editable in the ODP and PPTX the reference service writes with its default conversion.
  - **Cutting the chart data ranges inside the `.ppt` before the run.** The charts sit in zlib-compressed `ExOleObjStg` records of the binary file as Excel BIFF storages; rewriting their series formulas is a writer of the binary format for one defect, and the setting removes the cause without touching the file.
  - **Raising the stage limit for presentations.** The ODP does not fail for time on 25.2 (it fails to store), and 770 MB of table per chart is not work a longer limit should wait for.
  - **A fourth route for `dps`** (an in-process reader). No file of the format exists to write one against.
- **Verified by**: `tests/archive-refusal-answers.test.ts` (both errors through the batch route, the job classifier and the typed-failure predicate; red before), `tests/office-suite-route.test.ts` (seven `dps` rows of the source table; red before), `tests/office-suite-real-samples.test.ts` (a real presentation saved as PowerPoint 97 and named `.dps` to every target the registry lists, with the words of the suite's own PDF; on the Debian 13 VM it was refused as a binary container before), `tests/ppt-embedded-workbook-retry.test.ts` (the retry's conditions, the profile the suite is started with and its `TMPDIR`, and `govdocs1-001020.ppt` to ODP with its 53 slides, counted by the repository's PowerPoint reader, in under 64 MB and with no scratch left behind; on the VM it failed with `SandboxedTimeoutError` at 45 s before), `tests/html-pdf-layout-loop.test.ts` (`govdocs1-001120.html` with every letter and digit), `tests/docx-ruby-drawing-reader.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image's LibreOffice ends the layout loop of `govdocs1-001120.html` or the chart conversion of `govdocs1-001020.ppt` (the setting stays harmless), a second presentation fails on its charts under the same retry (a look into the embedded storages before the first run then pays), or a real Kingsoft `.dps` is published.

## 165. A compound file whose root mini stream chain is shorter than its declared size or whose tree links back to the root is a destroyed structure, and the LibRaw data-corrupted warning is accepted only for a file that carries a DNGVersion

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the rows "refuse a root mini stream chain that ends before the declared size" from the review of #938 and "accept LibRaw's `data corrupted at` warning only for files with a DNGVersion tag" from the review of #945), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: fix the open #783 rows of the document containers and vector formats from the source of the open-source readers). It extends entries 136 and 140.
- **Decision**:
  - **A root entry whose mini stream chain ends before its declared size is a `CompoundFileStructureError`** (`parseCfbf`, `src/lib/conversions/cfbf-reader.ts` step 4). The chain was already walked to its end as a structure chain and copied for `min(bytes it holds, declared size)`; when it held less, the shortfall surfaced only in the small streams that lay past it, each as a retryable `CorruptStreamError` ("declares N bytes but its sector chain holds M"), and a file whose streams all lay in the part that was there parsed. It is now one refusal of the table of contents, "its root entry declares N bytes of mini stream and its sector chain holds M", before any stream is copied, and the office suite is not offered the bytes (entry 136's retry rule for structure damage). The rule applies when a stream below the cutoff needs the mini stream, as before.
  - **The directory tree walk starts with the root entry reached,** so a left, right or child link that leads back to the root is "the directory tree reaches entry 0 twice" (`resolveEntryPaths`); before, the root was reached again as an entry named "Root Entry" with a path of its own and no refusal.
  - **LibRaw's `data corrupted at` line is accepted only when the file carries a DNGVersion** (`dngRawImageData(..., { requireDngVersion: true })`, `src/worker/raw-dng-image-data.ts`, called by `assertDecodedRawWhole`). A file whose directories carry no tag 0xC612, or only one of four zero bytes (the last four bytes read are the value, as LibRaw shifts them in), is refused with "the file cannot be shown to be whole: it carries no DNGVersion tag (or one of four zero bytes), so the decoder does not read it as a DNG". The version may sit in any directory the walk reads (LibRaw keeps `dng_version` across directories), in either byte order. The check comes after the header and the other-parsers checks and before the raw image is looked for, so the findings of entry 140 for a DNG that has the tag are unchanged.
- **Why**:
  - **References (behaviour and limits only, no code copied).** olefile 0.47 (BSD), `olefile/olefile.py`: `_open` reads the root entry's mini stream whole when the first small stream is opened (lines 1856 to 1865) and `OleStream.__init__` refuses a chain that ends before the sectors its size needs, "incomplete OLE stream" (lines 650 to 662), or holds fewer bytes than declared, "OLE stream size is less than declared" (lines 718 to 724), at defect level `DEFECT_INCORRECT`; `_load_direntry` refuses a second load of any entry, "double reference for OLE stream/storage" (line 1828), and entry 0 is loaded first. Apache POI trunk (Apache-2.0), `poifs/property/PropertyTable.java`: `populatePropertyTree` throws when the directory is deeper than `MAX_PROPERTY_DEPTH` (lines 234 to 237), which a link back to the root reaches; `poifs/filesystem/POIFSMiniStore.java` line 55 builds the mini stream from the root's start block and never compares the declared size (the shortfall shows only when a small stream is read, line 61 onwards). The decision to refuse it as structure damage and not as one stream's is ours, from the review row: olefile calls it a defect of the file, not of the stream, and POI and olefile read the same file as damaged at the first small stream.
  - **LibRaw 0.21.4 (LGPL-2.1 / CDDL, behaviour only), the release of the worker image.** `src/metadata/tiff.cpp` lines 917 to 921: tag 0xC612 shifts four bytes into `dng_version`; `apply_tiff` reads the raw image through the directory only `if (dng_version)` (line 1622) and, without it, goes through the size-derived compression guesses of lines 1853 to 1965 and the non-DNG `is_raw` rules of lines 2084 onwards; `src/metadata/identify.cpp` lines 244 (the custom camera table), 795 (`parse_smal`) and 891 and 910 (`parse_broadcom`) are the other routes that choose a decoder with no directory. `derror()` (`src/utils/utils_libraw.cpp`) prints the line from any decoder, so the `.dng` name does not say which route decoded the file, and the walk of `raw-dng-image-data.ts` models the first only.
  - **Measured on the real corpus.** The 718 compound files of the real-world manifest that fit in 4 MB (all `.doc`, `.xls` and `.ppt` rows at every third file, and every other compound format; 730 rows fetched, 718 compound), parsed by `parseCfbf` of `main` and of this change: 705 parse in both, 13 are refused with the same message in both, none differs. The real Samsung Galaxy S23 DNG carries DNGVersion 1.6.0.0 (exiftool) and develops with its warning as before; real dcraw_emu of LibRaw 0.22.2 (the Homebrew build of the host) refuses the same file with its DNGVersion cleared ("Unsupported file format or not RAW file"), so the line cannot reach the engine for it.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A compound file whose root entry declares more mini stream than its chain holds is refused as a whole even when every small stream lies in the part that is there.** olefile reads the same file as defective at its first small stream and by default (`raise_defects` is `DEFECT_FATAL`) continues; POI never looks. No file of the 718 is one. The office suite is no longer offered such a file by the in-process reader's retry.
  - **A link back to the root is refused where olefile and POI also refuse it; LibreOffice discards the leaf** (`stgdir.cxx` lines 761 to 795, entry 136). Kept as entry 136 decided for every repeated link.
  - **A `.dng` that carries no DNGVersion and printed the line is refused where it was developed after a check of a directory LibRaw may not have read.** A real DNG always carries the tag (the specification requires it, and LibRaw cannot open one without it: the S23 copy above); the refusal reaches a file that is named `.dng` and is not one.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Stating the shortfall as the stream's damage in entry 136 and changing nothing** (the other choice of the review row). It leaves the same damage with two outcomes by where the small streams lie, which entry 136's typed cause removed for the other structure chains.
  - **Putting the version check in the callers or on the file name.** The tag is the file's own statement and the walk already reads it for the private-data rule, so the check shares the walk (one read of the directories).
  - **Requiring the DNGVersion in every call of `dngRawImageData`.** The function answers whether the raw image is whole, which the cases of `tests/raw-dng-image-data.test.ts` pin on files that carry no tag; the engine asks for the version, the function does not assume it.
- **Rows of #783 that this change found already fixed, and rows left** (checked against `origin/main` 6b722371 and the Debian 13 djvulibre 3.5.28 of the Lima VM `default`):
  - **DjVu, four rows (shared included files decoded once per path, `ddjvu` threads for chains of 230 files, the 2^24 byte component, the 16 pixels per byte budget):** fixed by entry 135 (#939): the patch `include-search-visit-once.patch`, `PROGRAM_TASK_LIMIT` of 64 tasks per run, the budget of 128 pixels per input byte, and `DjvuComponentSizeError` (a `ConversionFailedError`, status 422, before any program starts). The boundary was measured again on the VM with bundles whose second page component has the given length: 16,777,214, 16,777,215 and 16,777,216 bytes draw (the last wraps to 0, which djvulibre reads as an unknown length), 16,777,217, 16,777,218 and 16,777,220 fail `djvused -e size` and `ddjvu` with "Unexpected End Of File" (`IFFByteStream.cpp` 214 and 237), 33,554,432 draws (wraps to 0) and 33,554,434 fails; the refusal at 2^24 and above keeps the two wrap-to-zero sizes out as entry 135 decided, and matches the failures. Nothing changes.
  - **DXF, three rows (a page with pictures and only incidental geometry, pictures under a transparent ancestor, a zero-size `<image>`):** fixed by #933 and #937 (`isPageBackdrop`, `PicturePages`, `isDrawnPicture` with the ancestors' opacity and `hasNoExtent`), with the cases pinned in `tests/dxf-pen-attributes.test.ts`. Nothing changes.
  - **CGM RESTRICTED TEXT with HALF alignment: left.** The fault is in LibreOffice `filter/source/graphicfilter/icgm/actimpr.cxx` `CGMImpressOutAct::DrawText` (`aTextPos.Y = ... aTextPos.X ...`, line 757 on master, read again on 2026-11-07), and the binary CGM is drawn only by the office suite's route (`src/worker/office-suite-route.ts`), which another change is editing; a workaround would rewrite the alignment of the file before the suite reads it and invent a position the importer would then have to match. The fix belongs upstream.
  - **XPS, two rows (every IFD of a JPEG XR container; nested resource uses and `xps_absolute_path`): left.** Their code is `src/lib/conversions/office/xps-image-header.ts`, `xps-resources.ts` and `xps-reader.ts`, in the directory another change is editing; they follow in their own change.
- **Verified by**: `tests/cfbf-structure-errors.test.ts` (the root chain shorter than its size with and without small streams in the missing part, the chain that holds the size exactly or more, links back to the root on both sides, and olefile 0.47 as the independent reader of the same files: "incomplete OLE stream" and "double reference for OLE stream/storage"), `tests/raw-native-decoder-warning.test.ts` (a stand-in decoder that prints the line over a whole DNG with no DNGVersion, with four zero bytes, with 1.4.0.0 and with 0.0.0.1, and exiftool reading the tag of the real S23 file), `tests/raw-dng-image-data.test.ts` (the version in IFD0, in a SubIFD, in either byte order, zeroed by a later tag, and the option off).
- **Revisit when**: a real compound file whose small streams all lie before the end of a short root chain is refused here and converts in the office suite (then the refusal can be a `CorruptStreamError` that is retried), a LibRaw release after 0.21.4 reads a file with no DNGVersion through a directory the walk models, or LibreOffice fixes `DrawText` (then the CGM row is closed).

## 166. XPS: a JPEG XR header check follows the whole directory chain, and the uses of a resource that uses another resource are multiplied

- **Status**: Implemented (the two XPS rows of issue #783 that #886 left open; epic #760), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: fix the open #783 rows by following the source of the open-source reader). It extends entry 95 (the pixel and byte budgets of the pages) and the image header read of #886.
- **Decision**:
  - **The JPEG XR container is checked as the renderer's reader reads it, every directory of the chain** (`src/lib/conversions/office/xps-image-header.ts`, `codestreamOffset`, `readDirectory`, `assertEntryReadable`). Followed: GhostPDL 10.08.0 `jpegxr/cr_parse.c` (jxrlib, BSD-2-Clause) `jxr_read_image_container` lines 185 to 199 (it reads directories until a next offset of 0, growing its table by one each time, with no test for a directory it has read already) and `read_ifd` from line 1460 (the arrays a tag keeps outside its entry are read from the offset the entry holds, a USHORT array is counted by a `uint16_t cdx` declared at line 1576 against the 32-bit count in the loop at line 1587, after a `calloc` of `count * 2` bytes at line 1581). A directory that leads back to one already read, a chain of more than 64 directories (one directory is one image; an image with its alpha plane is two), a next-directory or array offset that is odd or past the end of the file, an array whose elements do not fit in the file, and a USHORT or SSHORT array of more than 65,535 values are refused with the typed `ConversionFailedError`; the size still comes from the first image.
  - **Entries of resource dictionaries are charged for every use of the entries that use them** (`src/lib/conversions/office/xps-resources.ts`, `timesEntriesAreParsed`). Followed for behaviour only: GhostPDL `xps/xpsresource.c` `xps_find_resource` and `xps_parse_resource_reference` (AGPL, not copied): a `{StaticResource key}` is resolved while the element that holds it is parsed, so an entry that uses a key is parsed once for every parse of the entry that uses it. The times of an entry are the page's uses of its key plus, for each entry that uses it, that entry's times multiplied by its uses; the entries are taken in an order where each follows all that use it, so the work is one step for each entry and each use, with no recursion for a deep chain. A count is kept at `XPS_MAX_REPEATED_BYTES / 1,024 + 1`, the number of uses at which the existing byte budget is over whatever the part is, so a product of a fan-out is a finite number that the same two budgets (bytes, pixels) refuse. Entries that use each other in a loop are refused (`CorruptStreamError`); the number of entries a page reaches, summed over the document, may not pass `XPS_MAX_REPEATED_BYTES / 1,024` (524,288), because a long chain used by thousands of pages costs a walk each time.
  - **The names of the parts a page, a ContextColor profile, a font and a resource dictionary give are joined as `xps_absolute_path` joins them** (`src/lib/conversions/office/xps-reader.ts`, `xpsAbsolutePath`; used by `renderedXpsPageParts` and the resource reader), from `xps/xpsmem.c` lines 60 to 132 (behaviour only): not decoded, a `#` kept, `..` above the root dropped. A font name is cut at its last `#`, the number of the face (`xps/xpsglyphs.c` lines 682 to 688). Before, these four used `resolvePackagePath`, which decodes `%20`, cuts at the first `#` and refuses a name that leaves the package, so a part the renderer finds could cost nothing in the budget and one it does not find could cost something. The ContextColor profile had a second fault: its key was spread into one key for every character (`...keyOfReference(...)`), so no profile was ever charged; it is charged now, like an image, by its bytes.
- **Why**:
  - **The renderer's reading does not end on a looped container.** `gxps -sDEVICE=pdfwrite` (GhostXPS 10.07.1, the installed version; the code of the two readers is the same in 10.08.0) on a page whose brush names the sample JPEG XR file with its next-directory offset set to its own directory was still running when `timeout 20` stopped it (exit 124); the unchanged file drew in under a second (exit 0). The USHORT count past 65,535 is the same loop by `uint16_t` arithmetic in the source (lines 1576 and 1587); no sample of it was run. The process sandbox bounds the time and the address space, so before this the worker held a slot until the run limit.
  - **A used entry that uses another multiplied nothing.** The page `P` uses `B` 16 times, `B` draws 32 paths filled with `A`, `A` is a brush of a 1 MiB image: 512 decodes, 512 MiB, exactly the byte budget (hand count; `tests/xps-resources.test.ts`). The uses inside an entry were added to the uses of the page once, so this was charged one decode, and a chain of entries each using the next twice asked the renderer for 2^n decodes at the price of one.
  - **A loop of entries crashes the renderer.** GhostXPS 10.08.0 exits with 139 (segmentation fault, the stack) on a VisualBrush `A` whose Visual `V` is a canvas with a path filled with `A`; the same package without the loop drew (exit 0). Refusing it is the typed failure the worker gives for a package the renderer cannot draw.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Dictionaries are searched together, as before.** When a page names several dictionaries or repeats a key, every entry of that key is charged (the renderer uses the first only, `xps_parse_resource_dictionary` warns and ignores the rest), so the count can only be higher than the renderer's.
  - **A later page of a document with a long chain of entries costs a walk.** Over the document 524,288 entries are reached before the pages are refused; a Word print reaches a few dozen entries a page.
  - **A JPEG XR file with a malformed array in a later directory that the renderer would have skipped is refused.** Valid files keep every array inside the file at an even offset (T.832 Annex A, jxrlib `assert`s the same); the reference decoder's own demonstration program writes a container whose directory is out of place on a 64-bit machine, and the samples of the tests are put in a container written by hand for that reason.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Following the renderer's recursion with a depth limit.** A limit on depth does not bound a wide fan-out (two uses at each of 60 levels is 2^60 with a depth of 60); the product has to be taken either way, and the ordered walk needs no limit.
  - **Computing, for each entry, the images it reaches in all, and adding them for each use.** The sets grow with the square of the chain (5,000 entries, 5,000 images each).
  - **Keeping `resolvePackagePath` for the renderer's names.** It is right for the text reader, which follows the specification (a name is a URI); the renderer does not, and the budget has to count what the renderer draws.
- **Verified by**: `tests/xps-image-header.test.ts` (a directory that names itself, two that name each other, the sample's own directory named again, 64 and 65 directories, odd and out-of-file offsets, a USHORT array of 65,536, arrays that run past the file, an accepted two-directory chain; 10 of them failed before the change), `tests/xps-resources.test.ts` (hand counts of 512 decodes through two and three levels and through two entries that use one, a use deep inside an entry, a fan-out of 4^60 and one of 2^1,100 refused at once, a chain of 5,000 entries read, loops refused, an unused entry not read, 10,000 pages reaching 600,000 entries, names with `%20`, `..`, `.` and `#`; 13 of 18 failed before) and `tests/xps-reader.test.ts` (page names not decoded; 2 of 3 failed before).
- **Measured**: not timed beyond the tests (the hostile packages above are refused in under a second here); the budgets are those of entry 95 and unchanged.
- **Revisit when**: the renderer is changed to use only the first dictionary of a page, a resource entry shows an image count that the product here over-counts in a real package, or the pinned GhostPDL version changes the container reader.

## 167. The quality benchmark aligns an AAC stream by the encoder's delay, the VP9 deadline estimate follows the picture size measured on the corpus, the PDF picture check reads the object pdf.js reads, and the HEIF and Vorbis rows are settled by measurement

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the media and image rows that were left open), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: conversions follow the source of mature open-source projects). The estimate of entry 54 changes its constants; entry 131 is confirmed, not changed; entry 97 is confirmed again.
- **Decision**:
  - **HEIF to jpg, png and webp converts on Debian 13; no code changes.** Measured on a Debian 13 (trixie) root file system built in the Lima VM (arm64) with the packages of the `runner` stage at the versions of trixie, trixie-updates and trixie-security on 2026-11-07: `imagemagick-7.q16` 8:7.1.1.43+dfsg1-1+deb13u14, `libheif1` and `libheif-plugin-libde265` 1.23.6-2~deb13u1, `libde265-0` 1.0.15-1+deb13u2, Node 24.22. The seven HEIC and HEIF files of the corpus convert to all three targets through the dispatcher (21 of 21), each with the dimensions that `heif-dec` of libheif writes, and `tests/image-heif-decode.test.ts` passes there (12 passed, the two refusal tests skipped because libheif reads both files). The behaviour followed is libheif's own decoder (`examples/heif_dec.cc`, LGPL-3.0): ImageMagick calls the same library, and the rotation and cropping properties are applied once (entry 52). The libvips of the `sharp` binaries has no HEVC decoder, which is why HEIC does not go through it (entry 52).
  - **The Vorbis encoder row is the one entry 131 closed.** FFmpeg 9.0.2 `libavcodec/libvorbisenc.c` states a frame size of 64 samples (line 330; the comment "LCD of all possible frame sizes" at line 39; `AV_CODEC_CAP_SMALL_LAST_FRAME` but no variable-frame-size capability at lines 442 and 443), and the scheduler of FFmpeg 9 cuts the stream to that size and hands every frame to the encoder thread through a queue. The patch of entry 131 (`scripts/ffmpeg-patches/libvorbis-whole-frames.patch`, applied by `scripts/install-ffmpeg.sh`) takes frames of any size and writes the same stream; its measurements stay the evidence (entry 131). The issue row that still read "report upstream" is answered by that entry; the follow-ups of the review of #931 stay rows of their own.
  - **The AAC delay of a raw ADTS stream is the encoder's `initial_padding`, and the benchmark uses it instead of guessing it.** FFmpeg `libavcodec/aacenc.c` sets `avctx->frame_size = 1024` and `avctx->initial_padding = 1024` (n9.0.2 lines 1164 and 1165; n7.1.5 line 1248). An MP4 file carries that number in an edit list, so the decoder drops it; an ADTS stream has no place for it, and the decode starts 1,024 samples before the music. `bench/measure.ts` `measureAudioSnr` now takes that delay (`primingSamples`, counted at the encoded rate and moved to the source rate by `bench/families/audio.ts`) and aligns by it. The cross-correlation guess (`estimateLagSamples`) stays for streams whose delay is not known (Opus). The guess is wrong on bass-heavy music at low rates: for `music.wav` at 64 kbit/s the strongest unnormalised peak within 4,096 samples was lag 351, one period of the 65 Hz line (3.482e11 against 3.462e11 at 1,024), and at 48 and 96 kbit/s it was wrong as well (SNR 2.40 and 3.85 dB where the aligned figures are 10.84 and 27.18 dB); at 64 kbit/s the row read 2.93 dB and reads 14.03 dB. The SNR itself is `asdr`: `libavfilter/af_asdr.c` (lines 67, 68 and 228 of n9.0.2) divides the energy of its first input, the decoded output, by the error energy; the comment in `measure.ts` said "source energy" and now says what the filter does.
  - **The VP9 estimate takes the cost per pixel from the picture size.** `vp9DeadlineFor` estimated every job at 15 megapixels per CPU second on two cores, from one 1080p clip. Measured on the corpus (below), a picture's cost per pixel rises as it gets smaller, so the estimate was above the measured rate for 19 of 27 measured points. The rate is now 14 x (pixels per frame / 1920x1080)^0.4 megapixels per CPU second, flat at 14 from 1080p up, on two cores, with the same half of the stage limit as the allowance. HandBrake's VP9 presets (`libhb/encavcodec.c` 1.9.2, lines 1246 to 1318; behaviour only, GPL) use the good deadline at cpu-used 2 as their default, with row multithreading, and never the realtime deadline, so the setting for a job that fits is the same as ours; its fastest preset (good, cpu-used 5) costs 3.3 times the realtime deadline at the same speed number on the HDR clip (entry 54), which is why the switch for a job that is too big stays ours.
  - **The PDF picture check reads the definition of an object that pdf.js reads.** `PdfDocument` (`src/lib/conversions/pdf-document.ts`) scanned the file front to back and kept the last definition of every number. pdf.js (v6.3.289, `src/core/xref.js`, Apache-2.0) follows the cross-reference: `PDFDocument.startXRef` (`document.js` 1070 to 1120: the last `startxref`, with offsets counted from the `%PDF-` header found in the first kilobyte, `checkHeader`), `XRef.readXRef` (lines 535 to 615: sections from `startxref` through `/XRefStm` and `/Prev`, a cycle skipped, a damaged section skipped), `readXRefTable` and `readXRefStream` (the first entry of a number wins; a free entry is an entry; a first subsection that starts at 1 with a free first entry starts at 0; stream entries of type 0, 1 and 2, a missing type field is 1), `fetchUncompressed` (lines 725 to 775: the header at the offset must be `num gen obj`) and `fetchCompressed` (lines 777 to 858: the object at the index of the entry in its object stream). `src/lib/conversions/pdf-xref.ts` ports the section readers; `PdfDocument.followCrossReference` resolves the numbers with them and puts those definitions over the file-order ones. pdf.js reads the file by scanning only when no section is readable, the trailer's `/Root` has no `/Pages` (`XRef.parse`, lines 124 to 134), or the first or last page needs an object whose entry names another one (`checkFirstPage` and `checkLastPage`, `document.js` 1724 to 1790); the document does the same, by walking the page tree as pdf.js does (`src/lib/conversions/pdf-page-recovery.ts`: `Catalog.getPageDict` for page 0 and for page `/Count - 1`, with its skip of a node whose `/Count` ends before the page, so an empty `/Pages` node is walked past to the next kid, its fetch of a `/Count`, `/Kids` or `/Type` that is a reference, and its circular-reference error; an `XRefEntryException` from either walk is a scan, any other error from the last page's walk goes on to the walk of the whole tree, `getAllPageDicts`). The tokens of a section are the ones the lexer of pdf.js reads (`Lexer.getObj` and `getNumber`, `pdf.worker.mjs` lines 11849 to 11890 and 12096 to 12190), not the ones a writer produces: an integer is what `getNumber` returns and `Number.isInteger` accepts (`12.0`, `+12`, `12.`, `--12`, a sign and a line end before the digits), a number ends at the first character that cannot continue it (`00000n` is the number 0 and the command `n`), a lone sign or point is 0, and the same lexer reads the header of an object at an offset (a comment between its tokens, `30.0 +0 obj`, and `obj` followed by digits, which pdf.js returns as that integer). `/W` and `/Index` of an xref stream are read as the dictionary holds them (pdf.js does not follow a reference inside either array), a field is built as `(value << 8) | byte` whatever its width, and a missing `/Index` is `[0 /Size]`. Encryption and the root come from the first section's trailer, not from any `trailer` text the file holds, and the dictionary of `/Encrypt` may be a member of an object stream (pdf.js reads it before it has a cipher). An object the cross-reference does not list, or lists with an entry that names another object, keeps the definition of the scan: the reading that hides the least.
  - **The cost of following the cross-reference is bounded by the size of the file.** At most 10,000 sections are read, and the bytes they and their entries read count against twice the file plus 64 KiB (`chargeCrossReference`), whether the read succeeds or fails: a table that fails near its end has been read to there, and 200 sections that each lead to the same 400 KB table (white space in front of `xref`, or a `/XRefStm` chain) are refused at the third read; so is a search for `endstream` that runs to the end of the file for each of 20,000 entries inside one unterminated string, and 20,000 entries at fake headers (the typed structure error, a 400). The rows of the cross-reference streams of a file are bounded by their data and by two caps (`readXrefStreamRows`): the counts of the `/Index` ranges of a section add up to at most `MAX_PDF_OBJECTS` (500,000, every repeat counted, since a range over numbers that already have an entry adds nothing and no cap on objects would end it), a section whose three field widths are all 0 or less is refused (its rows take no data, so `/W [0 0 0]` with `/Index [0 400000 0 400000 ...]` repeated made 9 KB take 5.5 s, linearly in its size, and every row of it is an entry without an offset), and the decoded bytes of all the xref streams of one document share 16 MiB (`xrefStreamBudget`), so that a deflate stream that expands to that size cannot be decoded again for each of 10,000 offsets that lead to it. The three walks of the page tree that decide whether pdf.js scans (`pdf-page-recovery.ts`) are bounded as pdf.js's are not: each counts every node it pushes or pops, inline dictionaries included, and the depth of each, and a file past either limit is refused with the typed structure error (400), not read on the cross-reference's objects. The work limit is 1,000,000 per walk (`2 * MAX_PDF_OBJECTS`: pdf.js fetches a reference once, so a tree it reads costs one push and one pop for each of at most 500,000 objects, and a 50,000-page tree (`MAX_PDF_PAGES`) costs about a tenth of that in each walk), the depth limit is `MAX_PDF_PAGE_TREE_DEPTH` (64), the one `collectPages` already refuses a tree at, so a file refused here was refused later by the page list. pdf.js has neither: an inline node whose `/Kids` is a reference to an array that holds the node again is pushed for ever (321 bytes, no return in 20 s), and 16,000 inline nodes that share an array of 16,000 kids cost 256 million pushes (576 KB, 10.6 s); both are refused in about a millisecond and 43 ms. A file whose objects lie one after the other never reaches a bound.
  - **Where the check cannot tell which definition pdf.js reads, it takes the one that costs more.** The check reads the file as pdf.js does, and a reading that differs somewhere (a section the check rejects and pdf.js reads: a compressed xref stream with a filter the reader does not decode, the first page of a linearized file, which pdf.js reads from the object its linearization dictionary names, a number the lexer above does not read as pdf.js does) would leave the check on another object than the one pdf.js draws, and under-count a picture. When the check does not follow the cross-reference (pdf.js scans, or no section is readable) or rejected a section of it, and a number has more than one definition in the file, the plan is made for the file read as it is and again for the last and for the first definition of every number in file order (`PdfDocument.otherReadings`, `planPictureDecoding`), and a picture that any of them drops is dropped. A file with no duplicate number, and one whose cross-reference was read whole, is planned once. The first reading also covers the rule of `indexObjects` that a later definition with another generation does not replace an earlier one (`pdf.worker.mjs` lines 58742 to 58756).
- **Why**:
  - **Corpus measurement for the VP9 estimate.** Lima VM `default` (Ubuntu 24.04, aarch64, 4 cores, FFmpeg 6.1.1, libvpx 1.14), the product's arguments for each clip with the good deadline and cpu-used 2, the encode pinned to two cores (`taskset -c 0,1`), at most 20 s of each clip, one run at a time on an idle VM (load 0.0 before each series), 51 of the 59 video files of the corpus (the other eight gave no encode in this harness: one has no video stream, seven stopped with "received no packets" inside the 20 s cap). The slowest encode of each picture size, as megapixels per wall second on two cores (the same figures are in `tests/media-vp9-effort.test.ts`):

    | Picture | Slowest clip | Mpx/s on two cores | Mpx/CPU s |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | 320x240 | `fate-lmlm4_cifat30fps.divx` | 16.1 | 9.7 |
    | 352x288 | `ffs-encoded.m4v` | 10.4 | 5.9 |
    | 426x240 | `wc-hummingbird-hlg-05.webm` scaled | 9.8 | 5.5 |
    | 640x360 | `ffs-p6040064a.mp4` scaled | 16.7 | 9.1 |
    | 640x480 | `ffs-p6040064a.mp4` | 16.9 | 9.0 |
    | 854x480 | `ffs-p6040064a.mp4` scaled | 17.5 | 9.2 |
    | 720x1080 | `wc-urmia_lake_drought.webm` | 25.6 | 13.7 |
    | 1280x720 | `ffs-p6040064a.mp4` scaled | 22.9 | 11.8 |
    | 1920x1080 | `jellyfin-1080p-hevc-hdr10-3m.mp4` | 29.4 | 15.9 |
    | 3840x2160 | `wc-hummingbird-hlg-02.webm` | 43.5 | 22.4 |

    The scaled rows are the same footage scaled to the size, because a clip's cost per pixel falls with the picture: the urmia clip gives 15.4, 13.9, 12.1, 11.1 and 9.9 megapixels per CPU second at 1080p, 720p, 480p, 360p and 240p, the hummingbird clip 26.4, 20.0, 15.8, 11.4 and 5.5 at 4K, 1080p, 720p, 480p and 240p. The jobs on two cores use 1.85 to 1.9 of them (CPU seconds over wall seconds), so two cores stay the assumption. The flat 15 of entry 54 came from the HDR clip alone (15.4 on the first VM, 15.9 and 16.4 here) and was above the measured wall-clock rate for 19 of the 27 points that encode at least 30 megapixels (16 in CPU seconds); the new curve is under all 27 (at the closest it is 95 percent of the measured rate, the 1080p HDR10 clip), and the allowance of half the limit keeps a factor two for the rest of the conversion.
  - **`media-hdr-webm-speed.perf.test.ts` on the same VM.** The 30 s, 1080p, 60 fps HDR10 clip still takes the realtime deadline (3,726 megapixels need 133 s at the new estimate against an allowance of 75 s) and the test passes (72.7 s in all, with the lossless reference encode). The run on x86 that the issue row asks for was not made: no x86 machine was available to this change.
  - **A cross-reference is the only description of the file that its writer controls and pdf.js obeys.** The scan found the last definition of a number, so a file that ends with a definition the cross-reference does not list (bytes after `%%EOF`), keeps a different one in an object stream, or points an entry into the data of an earlier stream, showed the check a harmless picture while pdf.js decoded a large one, or the other way round. A `trailer` with an `/Encrypt` entry anywhere in the file (between two objects, where no section leads) marked the file encrypted, which turned off every check that reads picture data (JPEG 2000 and JBIG2 headers) and the incremental update that replaces a picture past a limit. The memory maximum and the deadline stay the binding bounds; this closes the gap between what the check reads and what pdf.js decodes.
  - **Measured against pdf.js itself.** On the 1,269 PDFs of the real-world corpus that the cache holds, the decision to scan instead of following the cross-reference equals the one pdf.js makes (its log line "Indexing all PDF objects", read from a pdf.js that opens each file in a process of its own) for 1,268 files (1,249 followed, 19 scanned because their cross-references are broken, as in pdf.js); the other file is refused for nesting by this reader as it is on the base commit, and pdf.js fails to open it. The plan (pictures left out, pictures painted per page, image streams, encryption) is identical to the file-order one for all 1,269; two files take the extra readings (a rejected section and a repeated number) and give the same plan. The check of the 40 largest files (169 MB) takes 1,417 ms before (median of five interleaved runs on the VM), 1,676 ms with the first cross-reference reader and 1,777 ms with the lexer, the page walk and the bounds, 9 ms a file more than before.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The AAC delay is a constant per codec.** A change of `initial_padding` in a later FFmpeg shows as a misaligned score; the test compares the benchmark with the delay found by exact comparison of the ADTS and MP4 decodes, so it fails when the number moves. The baseline row `audio/music.wav->aac/snr` (13.48 dB, recorded with FFmpeg 6.1.1 in CI) reads 14.03 dB with FFmpeg 9.0.2; its direction is "higher", so nothing fails, and the baseline is refreshed when CI moves to FFmpeg 9, as the row says.
  - **Smaller pictures reach the realtime deadline sooner.** A 3 minute 480p clip at 25 fps (1,845 megapixels) was estimated at 61 s and took the good deadline; it is now estimated at 108 s against a 90 s allowance and takes the realtime one, whose file is about a quarter larger (entry 54). Measured, the good deadline needs about 105 s for it on two cores, which is more than half of the 180 s limit once audio, muxing and other jobs are counted. A 1080p clip decides as before (a 30 s clip at 30 fps: 66.7 s against 75 s).
  - **The curve is fitted to the slowest of ten sizes among 51 clips on one architecture.** A faster host switches some jobs to realtime that would have fitted; a slower one can still time out for a job just under the line. x86 is not measured.
  - **pdf.js's linearization path is not ported.** A linearized file that was not changed since is read by pdf.js from the first-page section at the start of the file, which leads to the same entries; an updated linearized file fails pdf.js's length check and is read from the last `startxref`, as here. For the first page, pdf.js fetches the object the linearization dictionary names and walks the tree only if that fails, and it takes the page count from `/N` of that dictionary, so a linearized file with a bad entry in its page tree can differ from the walk here in whether pdf.js scans; the readings of the rule above cover the file only when the check has a reason to doubt it.
  - **A recovery the document does not model keeps the cross-reference.** pdf.js also scans the file when a later fetch throws `XRefEntryException` for an object outside the pages the two walks and the whole-tree walk reach (an annotation, a font, a picture); the document keeps the cross-reference for those, and reads the object the scan found where an entry names another one. A reference whose generation is not the entry's is not told apart either (the parsed reference carries no generation), which pdf.js fails on for the page tree and for those objects; the file does not open in pdf.js with such a page tree.
  - **The extra readings cost up to three plans, for the files that need them.** Two of the 1,269 corpus files; a file with no repeated number, or whose cross-reference was read whole, is planned once. Two readings do not cover three definitions of one number with a mixed choice (the middle one for a picture and another for its width), which an adversary needs another divergence from pdf.js to reach.
  - **Following the cross-reference costs about 9 ms a file** on the 40 largest corpus files (2.5 ms of it the page walk, the lexer and the bounds added in this amendment), and a file that needs more than twice its size of reading for its cross-reference is refused (400, a structure error), as is one whose cross-reference streams decode to more than 16 MiB together (413) and one with a section of rows that take no byte (400).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Normalised or whitened cross-correlation for the AAC delay.** Whitening (first difference) narrowed the gap between lag 1,024 and 351 to 8.480e8 against 8.474e8 on this clip: the music is one low note and its harmonics, and no correlation separates the delays reliably where the encoder states the number.
