  - **Charging every definition of an object number in the picture check.** It needs no cross-reference reader, but a replaced picture of an earlier revision would leave out the live one, and the check would still not know which definition pdf.js reads for the other readers inside `PdfDocument` (page streams, fonts). It is the rule for a file whose cross-reference the check cannot follow or reads in part, where nothing better is known.
  - **Taking the larger of the cross-reference's and the file-order definition in every file.** It would leave a picture out in a well-formed file whose live definition is small and whose earlier revision is large (the layouts of `tests/pdf-xref-resolution.test.ts` that keep the cross-reference's), for no gain where the cross-reference was read as pdf.js reads it.
  - **Refusing a file whose cross-reference the check rejects in part.** A damaged `/Prev` is common in files that open in pdf.js and in Poppler, and the check is advisory (the memory maximum binds); the plan of the worse reading costs the file at most a picture.
  - **A flat lower constant (13) for the VP9 estimate.** It fits 1080p, where the slowest clip is 29.4 megapixels per second against 26 predicted, but sends every 720p and 1080p clip of a few minutes to the realtime deadline and still leaves the small pictures above their measured rate.
  - **A longer stage limit for the good deadline.** The limit is the bound that keeps a worker free (entry 54).
  - **Dropping the first-page and last-page recovery checks.** An adversary then keeps the cross-reference valid for the page tree and gives pdf.js a reason to scan: the case the checks model.
- **Verified by**: `tests/bench-audio-lag.test.ts` (the ADTS and MP4 encodes of `music.wav` at 48, 64 and 128 kbit/s: the delay found by exact comparison of the two decodes is 1,024, and the benchmark's SNR equals the SNR summed from the aligned samples within 0.05 dB), `tests/media-vp9-effort.test.ts` (ten measured picture sizes: a job whose measured encode time is 1 percent past the allowance takes the realtime deadline; the earlier workloads and the 1080p limits), `tests/pdf-xref-resolution.test.ts` (each layout is built twice from one description, once with a raw picture that the pdf.js of the repository reads and whose width is the object in question, once with a picture past the decoder limit through the same object, so the check is compared with pdf.js and not with the code: a definition after the last section, a member of an object stream beside a later plain definition, an offset into the data of an earlier stream, bytes before the header, a first subsection that starts at 1, an incremental update, a cross-reference that leads nowhere; a stray trailer with `/Encrypt`; 20,000 entries into the same bytes and 20,000 into streams with no end; six spellings of the integers of a table entry and three of an object header, each compared with the pdf.js of the repository; an empty `/Pages` node, then a kid with a bad offset, then the page, where pdf.js scans; `/W [0 0 0]` with a range repeated 400 times; 200 sections that lead to one table that fails near its end; an `/Encrypt` dictionary that is a member of an object stream; an inline page-tree node that returns to itself through a shared array, two shared arrays that return to each other, and 16,000 inline nodes that share 16,000 kids; a hybrid section the check cannot decode beside an older definition, where it takes the larger plan), `tests/image-heif-decode.test.ts` on the Debian 13 root file system, and the existing PDF suite (the four tests it fails on macOS fail on the base commit as well).
- **Revisit when**: CI moves to FFmpeg 9 (refresh the AAC rows of `bench/baseline.json`), an x86 measurement of the VP9 curve is made, FFmpeg changes `initial_padding` of its AAC encoder, pdf.js changes `XRef` (its recovery rules or its first-entry-wins rule), or a PDF reader other than `PdfDocument` needs the same view of the file.

## 168. DXF text: the code page of the file, the `\U+XXXX` and `\M+nXXXX` escapes, the `%%` codes and the MTEXT commands are read as ezdxf reads them, and an external reference draws nothing and says so

- **Status**: Implemented (epic #760, the row "DXF text escapes such as `\U+00B0` in pre-2007 drawings render literally; external references are not resolved"), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: conversions follow the source of mature open-source projects). It extends entry 29 (the DWG reader writes `\U+XXXX` for non-ASCII text in drawings before 2007; the DXF path showed it literally).
- **Decision**:
  - **The text of a DXF file is decoded by the encoding its header names** (`src/lib/conversions/cad-dxf-text.ts`, `decodeDxfBytes`; `vector-cad.ts` calls it for every DXF that is drawn). Followed: ezdxf (MIT, github.com/mozman/ezdxf, commit c498560bb491c357deda538360ed0c8fdb11f5a7) `src/ezdxf/tools/codepage.py` `toencoding` and its table, lines 57 to 87 (a `$DWGCODEPAGE` name is matched by its ending, `ANSI_949` is Korean, `ANSI_1252` Western European; any name not in the table, such as `MAC-ROMAN`, `ASCII` or `ANSI_1361`, is Windows-1252); `src/ezdxf/filemanagement.py` `dxf_stream_info`, lines 175 to 186 (release 2007, `AC1021`, and later are always UTF-8); `src/ezdxf/lldxf/validator.py` lines 56 to 58 (`DXFInfo` starts as release 12 in Windows-1252, so a file with no `$ACADVER` or no code page is Windows-1252). The table is the Windows code pages the platform's decoders name: 874, 932 (Shift JIS), 936 (GBK), 949 (EUC-KR, which the platform defines as Windows 949), 950 (Big5) and 1250 to 1258. A file that starts with a UTF-8 byte-order mark is UTF-8. Before, every file was read as UTF-8, so a byte of a Windows-1252 file such as the degree sign `0xB0` became U+FFFD.
  - **A file that is valid UTF-8 and holds non-ASCII bytes is UTF-8 whatever the header says.** ezdxf does not do this (it decodes by the header and lets the caller override the encoding). It is kept here because the reader read every file as UTF-8 until now, and writers that never learned the rule label a UTF-8 file `ANSI_1252`; a text in a legacy code page is practically never valid UTF-8 (the lead bytes of Korean text, 0xB0 to 0xC8, can start no UTF-8 sequence at all, and a Windows-1252 letter followed by symbols that happen to form a valid sequence is not text anybody writes).
  - **`\U+XXXX` and `\M+nXXXX` become the characters they name, in TEXT and MTEXT strings.** Followed: ezdxf `lldxf/encoding.py` lines 8 and 9 (the patterns: four hex digits of either case; one digit 1 to 5 and four hex digits), `decode_dxf_unicode` lines 49 to 52 and `decode_mif_to_unicode` and `MIF_CODE_PAGE`, lines 55 to 85 (digit 1 is Shift JIS, 2 Big5, 3 Korean Wansung, 4 Johab, 5 GB 2312; a sequence the code page cannot read stays as written), applied to every string value that is not a structure tag at `src/ezdxf/recover.py` lines 871 to 877. A backslash before `\U+` does not stop it (`\\U+0391` is `\` and the letter, ezdxf's own test `tests/test_00_dxf_low_level_structs/test_056_special_string_decoding.py`). ezdxf decodes while it loads, before any other reading of the string, and so does the reader: an escape that spans two 250-character chunks of an MTEXT (group 3) is read, because the chunks are joined first. Johab (`\M+4`) stays as written, because the platform has no Johab decoder.
  - **A TEXT string is read as `plain_text` reads it** (`tools/text.py` lines 279 to 306, `caret_decode` lines 506 to 519, `lldxf/const.py` `SPECIAL_CHAR_ENCODING` lines 368 to 373): the caret notation first (`^I` is a tab, `^ ` is a caret: the next character minus 64 modulo 126), a line break and a trailing caret removed, then `%%d` a degree sign, `%%p` a plus-minus sign, `%%c` a diameter sign and `%%%` a percent sign in either case; `%%u`, `%%o` and `%%k` toggle a line and leave no character. `%%nnn` (a decimal character code, three digits) is kept as before: ezdxf has no reading of it, the AutoCAD text-code table has it. The writer of this repository writes `%` as `%%%` and `^` as `^ `, which the caret decoding now reads back.
  - **An MTEXT string is read as `MTextParser` reads it** (`tools/text.py` `MTextParser`, lines 1244 to 1670, with the lines of `plain_mtext`, lines 542 to 597): `\\`, `\{` and `\}` are the characters themselves, an unescaped brace only groups; `\P` ends a paragraph, `\~` is a space, a control character other than a tab or a line feed is a space, a tab is four spaces; the commands that set properties (`\A`, `\C`, `\c`, `\H`, `\W`, `\T`, `\Q`, `\p`, `\f`, `\F`, `\L`, `\l`, `\O`, `\o`, `\K`, `\k`, `\X`) are read through their arguments, with or without the `;` that ends them, and leave nothing; `\S` is a stack, written `numerator/denominator` whichever of `^`, `/` and `#` separated them (as before); a command that is none of these is text (`\Z` stays `\Z`). Two differences from the parser: a column break `\N` is a space, as in ezdxf's `fast_plain_mtext` (lines 423 to 503), because the columns are not laid out; and `%%u`, `%%o`, `%%k` and `%%nnn` are read as in TEXT, where the parser leaves them. The last line of an MTEXT that ends in `\P` is no longer an empty line (`plain_mtext` appends a paragraph only when it holds text).
  - **An external reference draws nothing and says so.** A block flagged 4 (external reference) or 8 (overlay) in group 70 whose definition holds no entities, when an INSERT of it is drawn, adds one warning per reference to `metadata.warnings`: `The drawing refers to the external drawing "<path>" (reference "<name>"), which is not part of the uploaded file, so it was left out.` (path from group 1, control characters replaced, 200 characters at most). A block flagged as a reference that does hold entities is drawn as any block and does not warn. Followed: ezdxf `entities/block.py` lines 60 to 76 and 104 to 111 and 182 to 189 (flag 4 is the reference, 8 the overlay, group 1 the path) and `addons/drawing/frontend.py`, which has no reading of references at all, so its drawing of a reference block is the layout of the block, empty in a single file; loading the referenced file is a separate module (`xref.py`, `load_modelspace`, line 501) that needs the file. The reference converter lists one engine for both DXF and DWG input in its formats API (queried 2026-11-07, `filter[input_format]=dxf` and `dwg`) and takes one uploaded file, so it has no companion file to read either; its output for a reference was not observable here. Entry 29 already decided that references are not resolved because the referenced file is not part of the request.
- **Why**:
  - **The nightly corpus has the cases.** `ASCII_R12.dxf` of ezdxf's integration tests (a release 12 drawing, no `$DWGCODEPAGE`) holds `ABC` followed by `0xC4 0xDC 0xD6` and `\U+03B1\U+03B2\U+03B3` in one TEXT: it was drawn as `ABC` and three replacement characters and the literal escapes, and is drawn as `ABCÄÜÖαβγ`. The 14 DXF files of the corpus (`bench/corpus/remote-manifest.json`, release 2004 to 2013; two of them, `cad-entities.dxf` and `cad-floorplan.dxf`, carry `%%` codes and `\S` stacks) were read before and after: the text of 12 of them is identical, and the two that differ differ in the two ways below.
  - **Escapes are the DWG reader's output.** Entry 29's reader writes `\U+XXXX` for the non-ASCII text of a DWG before 2007 (a degree sign is `\U+00B0`), so every dimension text and note with a symbol in such a drawing showed the escape.
  - **The two visible changes on the corpus are the ezdxf ones.** `cad-columns-r2007.dxf` has 11 of its 38 text items ending in `\P`: the empty last line is gone. 11 of the 76 text items of `cad-entities.dxf` are stacks written `\S0.01^ 0.02;`, in which the space after the caret is the caret notation's own character: the text is `0.01/0.02` now, `0.01/ 0.02` before.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A legacy code page the platform lacks is read as Windows-1252** (`ANSI_1361`, Johab; ezdxf does the same for any name not in its table).
  - **An unknown code page and a drawing with no header are Windows-1252, as in ezdxf**, so a Mac Roman drawing (`MAC-ROMAN`) shows its accented letters wrongly, as it does in ezdxf; AutoCAD itself does not write that name.
  - **The properties of MTEXT are read and dropped.** The drawing has one font, one colour and one weight; underline, overline, strike-through, colour, height, width, tracking and oblique codes change nothing in it.
  - **A text escape that decodes to a backslash starts an MTEXT command** (`\U+005C` before a letter), the order of ezdxf's loading and parsing; in TEXT it is a backslash.
  - **A reference whose file is in the same upload is not read.** A single uploaded file has no companions, and a job does not look at other files.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Resolving references from a folder or an archive.** An upload is one file; names of other files from an untrusted drawing must not reach the file system (entry 29: the referenced file is not part of the request).
  - **Refusing a drawing with an external reference.** The rest of the drawing is a correct result; the reference converter draws it. The warning names what is missing.
  - **Decoding the escapes in the stream reader for every string (layer and block names too).** Names are only compared with names, and the stream reader is the hot path of every drawing; the text of TEXT and MTEXT is the only place a person reads them.
  - **Writing `^` and `%` differently in the DXF writer.** The writer's escapes (`%%%`, `^ `) are what ezdxf reads back (its own `caret_decode` and special-character table); the reader was the half that was missing, and a test pins the pair.
  - **Taking the LibreCAD reading of `%%` codes or encodings.** It is GPL and was not needed: the open-source libraries above state the behaviour, and the rule here is to read the code only for behaviour.
- **Verified by**: `tests/cad-dxf-text-escapes.test.ts` (ezdxf's own cases of `\U+` and `\M+` including the stray backslash and the extra digits; the `%%` codes, the toggles and `%%nnn`; the caret notation; what the writer of this repository escapes; MTEXT line breaks, escapes, groups, property commands with and without `;`, stacks, unknown commands; the chunk that spans an escape; the code pages 1250, 1251, 1252, 1253, 932, 936, 949 and 950 with bytes written out, the names that fall back, release 2007 in UTF-8 whatever the page says, valid UTF-8 under an old header, a byte-order mark and CRLF; the unmodified `ASCII_R12.dxf` of ezdxf (`tests/fixtures/dxf`, MIT, digest checked); the warning once per reference, for flags 4, 8 and 4+32+64, none for a reference with entities, an empty ordinary block or a reference nothing inserts; 19 of its 25 tests failed before the change) and `tests/cad-dxf-drawing.test.ts` (its stack test now writes the caret the way a file does, `^ `).
- **Measured**: `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --quick --family cad` on the Lima VM (Ubuntu 24.04, arm64, Node 24.22.0, the pinned DWG reader built by `scripts/install-libredwg.sh`): 123 rows evaluated, 0 failing, 0 below the reference; the word F1 of the six text samples equals the baseline (`cad-entities.dxf` 0.901, `cad-floorplan.dxf` 0.951, the others 1).
- **Revisit when**: ezdxf changes its code page table or reads `%%nnn`, a user's drawing shows a code page the table lacks (add it), a reference converter output for a drawing with an external reference is observed (match its drawing of the missing file), or the platform offers a Johab decoder.

## 169. The PowerPoint reader for the XML format maps the symbol-font characters of a run as the binary reader does, and the Word text export keeps leaving footnotes out, as the reference converter's does

- **Status**: Implemented (two rows of epic #760), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: close the open rows of #760 by following the source of the open-source reader and by the reference converter). It extends entry 7, which said that presentations in the XML format map no symbol font.
- **Decision**:
  - **A `.pptx` run's symbol-font characters become the characters its font draws.** PowerPoint stores a character of Symbol, Wingdings, Wingdings 2 and 3 and Webdings at U+F000 plus its code in the font, with the font in the `a:sym` typeface of the run. `mapPptxSymbolRuns` (`src/lib/conversions/office/pptx-symbol-runs.ts`) rewrites the `a:t` text of each `a:r` run of a slide in `convertPptxSource` before any reader of the slide sees it, so the text, HTML, PDF, ODP and DOCX outputs, table cells and grouped shapes get the same characters. Only U+F020 to U+F0FF are touched, as a character, a hexadecimal reference (`&#xF0FC;`) or a decimal one (`&#61692;`); every other byte of the XML stays, and a mapped character that XML reserves (the ampersand of Symbol at 0x26, the less-than sign at 0x3C) is escaped.
  - **The font of a symbol character is the run's symbol typeface, else its Latin typeface, else its complex-script one.** LibreOffice (MPL, behaviour only) `oox/source/drawingml/textrun.cxx` (318520ca) `TextRun::insertAt` lines 99 to 126 splits the text of a run into stretches of characters whose high byte is 0xF0 and others, and sets the symbol typeface (`maSymbolFont`, the `a:sym` element) on the first kind only, so the other characters keep the run's own font; when a run has no symbol typeface its characters keep the Latin one, which is what the reader of `.ppt` files does (`symbolFontRef ?? fontRef` in `ppt-reader.ts`). The complex-script typeface is consulted last, when the run names neither. A typeface that is not a symbol font (Arial) selects no table, so its private-use characters are replaced and reported under that name, as in `.ppt`.
  - **The tables and the replacement rule are the ones of the binary readers.** `symbol-font-map.ts` is the one table; the rule moved out of `ppt-reader.ts` into `SymbolReplacements` (`src/lib/conversions/office/symbol-replacements.ts`), which both readers use: a code with no counterpart in the table, or a counterpart that a PDF cannot draw with the installed fonts (`canDrawInPdf`, for the PDF target only), becomes U+FFFD, one warning line per font and code, at most 50 listed and the rest counted. The text, HTML and other targets keep every mapped character. Before, a `.pptx` kept the private-use character in text and HTML, and the PDF writer replaced it with U+FFFD and a warning that named no font.
  - **A symbol font set by the master, the layout or the list styles (not by the run) is not followed.** Only the properties of the run itself decide; a character in such a run is replaced and reported with no font named, the same as a `.ppt` block without character formatting. Bullet characters (`a:buFont` and `a:buChar`) are not text and are not read.
  - **Word text output leaves the footnotes out, and stays so.** The reference converter's formats API (`GET /v2/convert/formats?filter[input_format]=doc&filter[output_format]=txt`, 2026-11-07) names the engine `office` for doc to txt, which is the office suite's text export. Its writer `SwASCWriter::WriteStream` (LibreOffice `sw/source/filter/ascii/wrtasc.cxx` at 63a2e191, lines 128 to 207, MPL, behaviour only) walks the text nodes of the body and the file has no footnote or endnote code; Apache POI (Apache-2.0) `WordExtractor.getText` (`poi-scratchpad/.../hwpf/extractor/WordExtractor.java` at f669cec7, lines 266 to 300) writes headers, the main text, text boxes and footers and leaves the notes to `getFootnoteText` and `getEndnoteText` (lines 137 to 152). Our `.doc` reader reads the main story only (`readMainStory`). The office suite 26.8.0.3 on `govdocs1-233541.doc` (a Word 6 file only the suite reads) writes 53,335 words to txt, with "supra note" 0 times where the printed PDF has it 60 times: the 22.7 % of #788 is the footnote story and is the reference's output too. No code changes; the 25 % allowance of that one file in `tests/doc-refusals-real-samples.test.ts` stays, and its comment now cites these sources.
- **Why**:
  - A symbol bullet or arrow in a slide (a check mark in Wingdings, alpha in Symbol) is a character in a font the viewer does not have; the same text must read as the glyph in a text file, a web page and a PDF, as it does for a `.ppt`.
  - Rewriting the slide XML once means no reader of the slide, and no later one, has to know about symbol fonts.
  - The output that the reference converter gives is the bar (policy 1); a text export with footnotes at the end would differ from its output for the same file, and no user compares a text file with the printed page.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A run that inherits a symbol font from the master or the list style gets U+FFFD and a warning, where PowerPoint draws the glyph.** The `a:sym` typeface that PowerPoint writes with every inserted symbol covers the common case; following the style chain of a presentation (master, layout, placeholder, list levels) is a larger change that no sample needed.
  - **A `.pptx` text file that held raw private-use characters now holds U+FFFD for the ones no table maps,** and its result carries warnings.
  - **The text of a `.doc` has no footnotes,** so a reader who wants "supra note 11" cannot find note 11 in the text file. The reference gives the same text file.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Copying the table or the replacement rule into the `.pptx` reader.** Two copies drift; `symbol-font-map.ts` and `SymbolReplacements` are shared.
  - **Mapping in each place that reads text (the flat text, the page drawing, tables, charts).** The slide reader has several of them; one rewrite of the XML covers them all.
  - **Writing the footnotes after the body of a `.doc` text file.** The reference does not, and the sources above do not; it would add up to a quarter of the words as text nobody asked for.
- **Verified by**: `tests/pptx-symbol-fonts.test.ts` (a slide written by hand from DrawingML: alpha, check mark and square by hexadecimal, decimal and raw character; the Latin and complex-script fallbacks; the symbol typeface over the Latin one; characters outside U+F020 to U+F0FF and a run with none left alone; the ampersand and less-than sign escaped in HTML; U+FFFD and one warning per font and code; a table cell and a grouped shape; a PDF read by a separate PDF reader; all 8 failed before the change), the `.ppt` tests that use the moved rule (`tests/ppt-text-extraction.test.ts`, `tests/ppt-corpus-symbol-fonts.test.ts`), and `tests/doc-refusals-real-samples.test.ts` for the footnote allowance.
- **Revisit when**: a real presentation shows a symbol font set only by its master or layout, the reference converter's doc to txt starts to write footnotes, or the office suite's text export changes its writer.

## 170. The output of 7-Zip reaches the worker through an anonymous file bounded by the file size limit, and the SVG tracer keeps its decoded staging

- **Status**: Implemented (rows `compression/silesia-xml.xz->tar` of #685 and `vectorize/screenshot.png->svg` of #759), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: close the last two speed rows of #759 by profiling the overhead around the pinned programs).
- **Decision**:
  - **`executeSandboxedBinary` can collect stdout through a file (`spoolStdout`)** (`src/lib/security/process-sandbox.ts`), and every 7-Zip run that prints a stream to stdout asks for it (`runSevenZipFramed` in `archive-stream.ts`). The file is made with `mkdtemp` (0700) and `open(..., 'wx+', 0600)`, then unlinked before the program starts: the program writes to the descriptor it was given, this process reads the output back by offset into one buffer of its exact size (with the head and tail room the tar writer asked for), and nothing is left on disk whatever happens to this process. The output is read before the run is settled, which closes the descriptor.
  - **The bound of the output is `RLIMIT_FSIZE` at `maxBuffer` plus one byte, and the extra byte is how a program past the bound shows.** A file longer than `maxBuffer` is a `SandboxedBufferLimitError` of kind `stdio`, the error a pipe past `maxBuffer` gives, whether the program died of SIGXFSZ, caught it and exited with a status of its own (7-Zip exits 153) or ignored the failed write and exited 0 with a cut file; an output of exactly `maxBuffer` bytes is kept. The run also gets `RLIMIT_CORE` 0 (`coreBytes` in the rlimits, `prlimit --core=0`), so that a program ended by SIGXFSZ leaves no core file in the working directory.
  - **Without Linux and `prlimit` the output goes through a pipe, as before,** and so it does when the temporary directory cannot be written to; the result is the same either way, and the callers do not tell the two apart.
  - **The SVG tracer keeps the staging of entry 142.** The picture is decoded by the worker, and the program reads only a PNG the worker wrote. The profile below shows what that costs, and the change that would remove it is left to QA.
- **Why**:
  - Profile on the Linux VM (4 cores, 7-Zip 23.01, xz 5.4.5, interleaved runs of the benchmark): `xz -d -c` of the 453 KB stream of the Silesia `xml` file (5.3 MB, a tar) takes 23.3 ms; the conversion to tar took 26.5 ms. The 7-Zip run alone costs as much as `xz` (18.9 ms against 18.3 ms to `/dev/null`), so the 3.2 ms sat in collecting the output: 82 reads of 64 KiB from the pipe, which the program waits for whenever the event loop is busy, the copy of the chunks into the frame, and a major collection started about every second conversion by the 10.6 MB of buffers it allocates. The same `xz` takes 21.5 ms when it writes to a file and 22.9 ms through a pipe, and the file is read into one buffer instead of 82 chunks and a concatenation.
  - Measured, base against head, interleaved in the benchmark's own process pairs (24 pairs): `silesia-xml.xz->tar` 1.08 to 1.11 times as fast with the row run alone, and 1.01 to 1.06 after the whole quick set had run in the same processes; `silesia-ooffice.xz->tar` (1.00 to 1.01) and `mixed.xz->tar` (0.94 to 1.03, upper bounds 1.00 to 1.10) are not slower with confidence. Against the reference tool in the benchmark's own mode (one process, 3 runs each): 0.866 [0.799, 0.894], 0.884 [0.857, 0.897], 0.880 [0.872, 0.909] before and 1.003 [0.960, 1.024], 0.999 [0.967, 1.017], 0.978 [0.947, 1.009] after. 7-Zip is the engine of this route; the native `xz` of entry 116 is not on it.
  - The vectorize row is the decode, not the process: `vectorizeRaster` of the 1024 x 640 16-bit PNG takes 44.0 ms against 38.4 ms for the program run on the file. The decode in libvips and the stored PNG take 5.2 ms (3.5 of them the decode: the 16-bit pixels inflate to 5.2 MB), the metadata check 0.2 ms, the directory and the file 0.4 ms, the sanitizer 0.3 ms, the cleanup 0.15 ms; the sandboxed run (37.6 ms) costs what the reference's run costs (the program takes 37.7 ms on the original PNG and 37.0 ms on the staged one), and the spawn through Node costs the same as `spawnSync`. The picture is decoded twice, once by the worker and once by the program in the reference, and the second decode is the 12 % of the gap. Writing the pixels as a Netpbm PAM instead of a stored PNG saves 0.4 ms and gives the same SVG byte for byte on 15 pictures (16-bit, grey with alpha, CMYK, palette, rotated, TIFF, WebP, animated GIF), which is +0.4 to +1.1 % against the base (24 pairs, upper bound 1.02 to 1.04): not enough to be worth a second staging format. Handing the program the uploaded bytes after the pixel check, as the reference converter does, was measured only to size the choice (0.84 to 0.85 before, 0.94 after, same program); it is not taken here, because it lets the tracer's PNG, JPEG, GIF, BMP, WebP and TIFF decoders read bytes of an upload, which entry 142 decided against.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - A 7-Zip run that prints a stream writes it to a temporary file, up to the in-memory budget of the request (the bound `streamToTar` passes), instead of holding it in the pipe's chunks; the file lives only until the run ends and is unlinked from the start, so a crash leaves no file.
  - A program that ignores the failed write and keeps running is not stopped at the bound as a killed process group is stopped at `maxBuffer`; it runs to its end or to the time limit. 7-Zip, `xz`, `head` and the shell stop at the first failed write.
  - The test of the decompression bomb no longer counts the wrapper that records a 7-Zip run: 7-Zip ends by the kernel's signal, so the wrapper writes its status (153) where it used to be killed first. The test asserts that no run ended with status 0.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Handing the tracer the uploaded file** (above): 0.94 against the reference, not 1.0, and a change of what the tracer parses.
  - **Starting 7-Zip from the helper process of `sandbox-launcher.ts`** to avoid the fork of a large worker: the helper copies the output once more at 2.5 ms per megabyte (its own cost model), which is more than the 5.3 MB stream gains.
  - **A pipe with a larger buffer:** Node does not expose `F_SETPIPE_SZ`, and its reads stay 64 KiB.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sandbox-stdout-spool.test.ts` (3 MiB of output equal to the pipe's, head and tail room in one buffer, an empty output, stdin and spool together, exactly `maxBuffer` bytes kept and one more refused with the limit error of kind `stdio`, no core file, a failure with what the program printed, nothing left in the temporary directory after a success, a failure, the bound and an abort, a pipe when the temporary directory is missing, `--core=0` in the prlimit arguments), `tests/archive-stream-to-tar.test.ts` (the bomb is refused with the typed ratio error and 7-Zip never returns success) and the archive, sandbox, 7-Zip and worker tests (89 files, 1,866 tests on the Linux VM).
- **Revisit when**: a program that ignores a failed write reaches a spooled run, Node exposes the size of a pipe, QA decides to let the tracer read the uploaded picture, or the worker's resident memory makes the fork of a program cost more than the helper's copy (then the launcher can take a spooled run).

## 171. The SVG tracer reads the pixels the worker decoded: vtracer's own command-line front-end, built from its pinned source for raw RGBA, replaces the PNG route of the release program, which stays as the fallback

- **Status**: Implemented (row `vectorize/screenshot.png->svg` of #759), decided 2026-11-07 (QA confirmed on 2026-11-07 that the tracer never decodes uploaded bytes, entry 142, and chose the change entry 170 left open: QA direction to take permissive open-source code as it is and improve it on top in separate steps, each measured alone).
- **Decision**:
  - **The worker hands the tracer the pixels it already decoded, and the tracer never sees upload bytes (entry 142 stands).** `scripts/vtracer-pixels` is vtracer's own command-line front-end (`crates/vtracer-cli/src/main.rs`, MIT OR Apache-2.0, tag `1.0.0-alpha.4`, commit `2500df76b5aea0ac22d15296b22722442f825c5b`, the commit entry 142 pins), copied as it is. `Args`, `build_config`, `run` and `main` are upstream's, so the `Config` is built from the same arguments by the same code as the release program builds it. The only change in the first commit is `read_image`, which reads the width and the height (two little-endian u32) and `width x height x 4` bytes of RGBA where upstream calls `image::open(path)?.to_rgba8()`; the `ColorImage` is built as upstream builds it. Upstream's `crates/vtracer-cli` at this tag has no `converter.rs` (that file belongs to the older 0.6 command line); `main.rs` holds the whole path. The library crates (`vtracer`, `visioncortex`, `flo_curves`) are not copied: they come from crates.io at the versions and checksums of `Cargo.lock`, and the `vtracer` 1.0.0-alpha.4 package there is the same source as `crates/vtracer/src` of the commit (`diff -r`, no difference). `LICENSE` is the MIT text of the commit (the digest entry 142 pins) and `SOURCE` names the copied files, the digest of the upstream `main.rs` and what differs; each addition of ours is one commit on the copy, so `git log -p scripts/vtracer-pixels` is the diff from upstream and can be applied again on a new vtracer release.
  - **The worker uses it when it is found, and the release program of entry 142 is the fallback.** `selectEngine` in `src/lib/conversions/raster-vectorize.ts` looks for `vtracer-pixels` first (`VTRACER_PIXELS_PATH`, then `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin`, then `PATH`) and for `vtracer` only without it; neither is a 503 before any decoding, as before. The picture is decoded, turned upright, converted to sRGB with alpha as before, and read out as 8-bit RGBA (`raw()`) instead of being written as a stored PNG; header and pixels are written to the run's scratch file one after the other and the program is started with the same options, in the same sandbox and with the same limits. The sandbox directory, the output file and the sanitizer stay (0.5 ms and 0.3 ms): the output bound rests on the file-size limit of the file, and the sanitizer is the gate of every SVG path.
  - **The program is built from source for the musl targets, as one static program.** `scripts/install-vtracer-pixels.sh` fetches the Rust 1.98.1 toolchain as four archives (`rustc`, `cargo` and `rust-std` for the host, `rust-std` for the musl target), each checked against a pinned SHA-256 for both architectures before anything is unpacked, and runs `cargo build --release --locked` on a copy of the source with its own `CARGO_HOME`, so the lockfile decides every crate by checksum and nothing of the host's Rust matters. The Dockerfile builds it in the `vtracer` stage next to the release program; the CI task installs it the same way. The build is repeatable: two builds in two directories give the same SHA-256 (`aba84db5b432666a5cdcc4d6daac48da24578eaf5418b7bc5ca41affbbdeeada` for aarch64 on the Linux VM, with `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=0` for the compile time that mimalloc records). The digest is written to the `SOURCE` note and printed, and it is not pinned in the script: the allocator is C, compiled by the C compiler of the host, so another compiler release can write another machine code for it.
  - **Why musl, and not the faster-looking glibc build.** The SVG must be the bytes the release program writes. A build against glibc, otherwise the same, wrote other bytes for 15 of 36 traces (6 option sets of 6 pictures): its math library rounds some results in the last bit differently from musl's, and the tracer's curve fitting shows it. The musl build was identical on all of them.
  - **Three build changes of ours, one commit each, measured alone** (Linux VM, aarch64, 1024 x 640 16-bit RGBA screenshot as raw pixels, program only, 100 interleaved rounds, speed against the build before the change, median of the rounds with the 95 % interval of the bootstrap): `panic = "abort"` 1.052 [1.048, 1.056] (no unwinding tables or landing pads in the hot loops; a panic now ends in SIGABRT, which the wrapper already reports as a failed trace with the first line of the panic message); the `mimalloc` allocator 1.166 [1.157, 1.171] (the tracer allocates a vector per cluster and path, and the allocator of musl libc is slow; mimalloc is MIT, `NOTICE-mimalloc` holds the texts of the two crates that ship it); thin LTO 1.007 [1.001, 1.010] alone and 1.026 on top of the other two (inlining across the crates). Together 1.265 [1.260, 1.271]. The check of the header size (`MAX_PIXELS`, the 16 megapixels of the worker's budget, refused before the buffer is allocated; the pixels are read once into that buffer) is a bound, not a speed: 1.268 [1.260, 1.273] with it, the same as without it, and the peak memory of a 16 megapixel trace is 300 MB either way.
  - **The SVG is byte for byte the release program's.** `tests/raster-vectorize-pixels.test.ts` compares the two programs through the product for eight kinds of picture and five option sets, and the pixels the worker gives each program (the PNG decoded, and the raw bytes) for the same eight.
- **Why**:
  - Entry 170 measured the screenshot row at 0.85 and named the staging as the cause: `vectorizeRaster` 44.0 ms against 38.4 ms for the program on the file. Not decoding the PNG again was worth little: the release program reads the stored PNG of the screenshot in less than 1 ms (`vtracer` 1.0.0-alpha.4 built with the same toolchain on the PNG, then the same code reading raw pixels: 0.998 [0.996, 1.001] and 1.018 [1.015, 1.021] against the release program). What made the row pass is the tracer itself being faster, and that is ours to do (the engine is the same; the optimisation is ours).
  - Interleaved in one process, the product on the 1024 x 640 screenshot, base (entry 142 and 170) against this change, 40 rounds: 44.26 ms against 36.19 ms, 1.229 [1.215, 1.239]; line art 1.265 [1.259, 1.271], photograph 1.273 [1.264, 1.276], two-frame GIF 1.269 [1.261, 1.276]. With `vtracer-pixels` absent the new code is the old code: 1.009 [0.992, 1.015], 0.992, 0.994 and 0.997 on the same four.
  - The benchmark's own speed rows (`npm run bench:quality -- --parity --speed-only --family vectorize`, Linux VM, ours against the release program given the uploaded file, medians and intervals as the verdict states them): base, two runs, screenshot 0.856 [0.804, 0.866] over 11 pairs and 0.855 [0.847, 0.881] over 7, line art 0.899 [0.891, 0.905] and 0.904 [0.897, 0.907] over 50 pairs (straddling the bar at the cap, a failure); change, two runs, screenshot 1.074 [1.002, 1.082] and 1.056 [1.034, 1.078], line art 1.106 [0.948, 1.674] and 1.170 [1.07, 1.182], photograph 1.161 [1.059, 1.172] and 1.139 [1.021, 1.257], GIF 1.201 [1.078, 1.236] and 1.149 [1.086, 1.211], all over 7 pairs. The screenshot row left `bench/parity-gaps.json`, as the verdict asked ("now at parity: remove ...").
  - Byte identity was checked on every vectorize picture of the benchmark, generated and public (screenshot, line art, photograph, the photograph and scan of the corpus, the two-frame GIF and the four public samples) with six option sets each: 60 SVG pairs, 0 differences.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The image and the CI job build a Rust program.** The `vtracer` stage and the CI task download about 160 MB of toolchain archives (each digest checked) and build for about 20 s; the stage needs `gcc`, `libc6-dev` and `xz-utils`. Entry 142 rejected building the CLI in the image because the project's release build existed; the release build reads only files, and the gain here needs a program that takes pixels. The release program stays installed (1.3 MB) as the fallback.
  - **Two programs trace, and the SVG is the same only while they are the same vtracer.** A vtracer upgrade moves the pin of `install-vtracer.sh` and the commit of `scripts/vtracer-pixels` together (the test compares the two pins), and the commits on the copy are applied again.
  - **The digest of the build is not pinned**, only repeated: see the decision. The inputs that decide the bytes (toolchain archives, crate checksums, source) are pinned.
  - **A panic is now an abort**; the wrapper reports it as `was stopped by SIGABRT` with the first line of the message, where it reported `exited with status 101`.
  - **x86-64 is not measured here**; the machine code differs, the rows that decide are the nightly runs on the x86-64 runner. If the screenshot row falls below 0.9 there, it goes back into the gaps file with that run as its history.
  - **`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is not edited:** it is generated from `package-lock.json` (`npm run licenses:generate`, checked by `npm run licenses:check`) and lists npm packages only. The Rust components are listed in `docs/licensing.md` (2.13) and ship in `/licenses/vtracer-pixels.copyright`, `.SOURCE`, `.THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES` (the file of the release program, a superset of what this program links) and `.NOTICE-mimalloc`.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Handing the tracer the uploaded file** (entry 142): 0.94 and the tracer would parse untrusted bytes; QA kept the rule.
  - **A glibc build**: about 1.12 times as fast as the musl build with the default allocator on the same machine (34.4 ms against 38.5 ms), and 15 of 36 traces other bytes (see above).
  - **Fat LTO with one code unit**: slower on musl in every combination tried (58 ms and 74 ms for the program against 38 ms without), and `target-cpu=neoverse-n1`: 0.3 ms of 32 on arm64 and no use on x86-64. `strip` and `opt-level` changes were not needed.
  - **Pixels on standard input**: 38.6 ms against 37.6 ms with the file in the same process, because the pipe copies the 2.6 MB through the sandbox once more. The output stays a file for the same reason as the sandbox directory.
  - **A raw PAM file for the release program** (entry 142) and **a PNG at another deflate level**: no change that matters, the release program decodes in about 1 ms.
  - **Rewriting the tracer, or linking it into the Node process**: not needed to pass the bar, and it would give up the per-run memory and time limits.
- **Verified by**:
  - `tests/raster-vectorize-pixels.test.ts` (25 cases, 9 of them need both programs): the file the stand-in program is given (little-endian width and height, the RGBA bytes, the options before `--input` and `--output`), the fallback to the release program with a PNG, 503 before decoding when neither exists, the pixels equal to the pixels of the PNG for a 16-bit RGBA PNG, a 16-bit grey PNG with alpha, a palette PNG, a CMYK JPEG, an EXIF-rotated JPEG, a lossless WebP, a GIF and a TIFF; with both programs, the same SVG bytes for those eight pictures and five option sets; the real program refusing an empty file, a short header, a zero width, pixels short of or past the header, an unaddressable size and one pixel over 16 megapixels (status 1, `Conversion failed:` and no SVG); the source note naming the pinned commit and version, the licence digest, the lockfile, the mimalloc texts, the 16 megapixel bound equal to the worker's, and the install script's eight toolchain digests and `--locked`.
  - `tests/raster-vectorize.test.ts` (46 cases) with and without `VTRACER_PIXELS_PATH` on the VM (71 and 62 passed in the two runs, the rest skipped); its stand-in cases run the wrapper of the release program with `VTRACER_PIXELS_PATH` emptied. `tests/worker-vtracer-packaging.test.ts`, `tests/vtracer-notices.test.ts` (the stage, the copies, the build-time smoke test of both programs under `dash`, the licence copies) and the CI task limit tests.
  - `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --quick --family vectorize` passes 12 rows and the full run passes all 24, in the VM with `vtracer-pixels`: SSIM against the source of ours / the release program, `screenshot.png` 0.95169 / 0.95164, `lineart.png` 0.94083 / 0.94007, `photo-a.jpg` 0.72385 / 0.72522, the two-frame GIF 0.94176 / 0.94176, the four public samples the same on both sides; paths 188 / 187, 224 / 220, 565 / 560, 225 / 225.
  - Install script run in the Linux VM twice into two directories (the same digest), the 8 x 8 smoke trace of the Dockerfile under `dash`, and `shellcheck` on the script. The Dockerfile itself was not built (no container runtime on the development machine or in the VM).
- **Revisit when**: the nightly x86-64 run reads the screenshot row below 0.9, a vtracer release changes the front-end or the library (apply the commits again and compare the SVG bytes), glibc and musl round the same (then the faster build can be taken), or a second row of the family needs the tracer faster still.

## 172. The AVIF encoder is built from pinned libavif and libaom sources at the releases of the Debian 13 package, with link-time optimisation and zlib-ng, and written files stay byte for byte the package's

- **Status**: Implemented (epic #759, rows `screenshot.png->avif`, `lineart.png->avif`, `wm-deep-dart.png->avif`, `wm-alpha-graph.png->avif`), decided 2026-11-07 (QA direction: take permissive open-source code as it is, then improve on top in separate steps, each measured alone). It follows the pattern of entry 171. Amended 2026-11-07 (epic #760 row "measure AVIF quality with the encoder the worker ships"): the quality jobs run the reference on this build too (Decision, CI; Trade-offs, first bullet). Amended again 2026-11-07 (row "Found by #998"): the VM's photograph gap was the stock libvips, not the architecture (Trade-offs, first bullet, aarch64).
- **Decision**:
  - **`avifenc` is built from pinned sources by `scripts/install-avifenc.sh`, unmodified, at the releases the Debian 13 package is built from.** libavif 1.2.1 (tag `v1.2.1`, commit `fcb084c9387e367750f5375e462005ce298f57cc`, BSD-2-Clause) with libaom 3.12.1 (BSD-2-Clause and the AOMedia patent licence), libyuv 1904 (the colour conversion libavif uses when it has it, as the package does), libpng 1.6.58, zlib-ng 2.3.3 and libjpeg-turbo 3.1.3 (libavif's applications will not build without a JPEG reader, which `avifenc` is never given), and the sources of libargparse at the commit libavif names (its configuration asks for them for `avifgainmaputil` and would fetch them with git; they come from the pinned archive and are not built, as only `avifenc` is). Every archive is pinned by SHA-256 and checked before anything in it runs, and the archives made by GitHub from a tag are also checked against the commit they record. The build tools are pinned as well: CMake 3.31.12 by the digest of its release archive for both architectures, NASM 2.16.03 (x86-64 only, for the assembly of libaom and libjpeg-turbo) by the digest of its source; the compilers are the image's. The result is one static program (libstdc++ and libgcc linked in) that needs only the C library. The Dockerfile builds it in the `avifenc` stage, copies it to `/usr/local/bin/avifenc-pinned` and encodes an 8 x 8 PNG with it during the build; its licence texts and `SOURCE` note go to `/licenses/avifenc.*`.
  - **The worker uses it first and the package second.** `AVIFENC_CANDIDATES` in `src/lib/conversions/avif-cli.ts` lists `/usr/local/bin/avifenc-pinned` before `/usr/bin/avifenc` (the package `libavif-bin`, still installed), so a machine without the pinned build (a development machine) encodes with the package as before, and a machine without either with the image library, as before. `AVIFENC_PATH` still decides when it is set.
  - **Two build changes of ours on top of the unmodified build, one commit each, measured alone** (below): link-time optimisation of the program and every library in it (`-flto`, objects with only the intermediate form, archives made with `gcc-ar`), and zlib-ng in its zlib-compatible mode instead of zlib for the PNG the encoder reads. Neither changes a byte of the output.
  - **CI**: the `avifenc` task of `install-tools.sh` builds the program (cached by the hash of the script and its note, with the program's SHA-256 beside it, limit 360 s) and links it as `avifenc-pinned`, so the unit tests and the speed rows run the worker's encoder. The quality benchmark jobs (`parity quality` of `ci.yml`, `Run the quality benchmark` and `bench-parity-quality` of `nightly.yml`) set no `AVIFENC_PATH`: the product finds `avifenc-pinned` first, and the reference side resolves `avifenc` to the same program (`NAME_ORDER_FIRST` in `bench/tools.ts` searches `avifenc-pinned` in every directory before the package's `avifenc`). Both sides of an AVIF row therefore run libavif 1.2.1 and libaom 3.12.1 and the row compares our settings, not two releases; on a machine without the pinned build both fall back to the package, as the worker does. The runner's `/usr/bin/avifenc` (libavif 1.0.4, libaom 3.8.2) still decodes (`avifdec`).
- **Why**:
  - Entry 91 measured the encoder rows with `avifenc` and ours the same binary on the same arguments, and named "a build of `avifenc` that links its libraries in" as the one way to close what was left; the package is a dynamic build at the distribution's flags (`-O2`, hardening, libraries as shared objects). The speed is ours to improve; the engine is the reference's.
  - **Speed of the program alone** (Linux VM, aarch64, 4 vCPU; `-d 8 -y 420 -q 70 --qalpha 70 -s 6 -j 4`; 80 interleaved pairs; speed against the Debian 13 package's `avifenc` 1.2.1 run from its extracted packages, median and 95 % interval of the bootstrap; the step is the ratio to the line above):
    | picture | unmodified build | + link-time optimisation | + zlib-ng |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | `screenshot.png` (1024 x 640, 16-bit RGBA) | 1.051 [1.051, 1.053] | 1.267 [1.264, 1.268] (step 1.206) | 1.317 [1.316, 1.318] (step 1.039) |
    | `lineart.png` (640 x 640, 16-bit) | 1.127 [1.123, 1.133] | 1.212 [1.207, 1.218] (1.075) | 1.261 [1.255, 1.271] (1.040) |
    | `photo-b.png` (640 x 432, 8-bit RGB) | 1.146 [1.140, 1.151] | 1.195 [1.188, 1.205] (1.043) | 1.238 [1.225, 1.247] (1.036) |
    | 8-bit RGBA made from `photo-b.png` | 1.125 [1.121, 1.129] | 1.176 [1.172, 1.180] (1.045) | 1.230 [1.220, 1.239] (1.046) |
  - The unmodified build is itself two effects (60 pairs, `screenshot`, `lineart`, `photo-b`): the same sources as a static program at `-O2`, as the package is flagged, 1.013 [1.010, 1.014], 1.043 [1.039, 1.047] and 1.084 [1.075, 1.092]; libaom's and libavif's own release flags (`-O3`) add 1.039, 1.077 and 1.065 to that. The package's libaom and this one contain the same instruction-set paths (dot-product, i8mm and SVE routines are present in both, chosen at run time): no CPU flag is left to set, and `-march=native` is not used.
  - **The product rows** (`npm run bench:quality -- --parity --speed-only --family image --base-root`, same VM, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`; base = this commit's parent with the package's program, head = this change; median of head speed over base speed in the full run and again in a `--quick` run, with the one-sided upper bound the verdict prints, then the ratio to the reference tool, which is the runner's `avifenc` 1.0.4, before and after): `screenshot.png->avif` 1.312 (upper 1.362) and 1.321 (1.336), against the reference 1.023 before and 1.347 after; `lineart.png->avif` 1.220 (1.254) and 1.216 (1.293), 1.147 before and 1.400 after; `wm-deep-dart.png->avif` 1.227 (1.259) and 1.223 (1.243), 1.058 before and 1.280 after; `wm-alpha-graph.png->avif` 1.167 (1.175) and 1.170 (1.185), 1.099 before and 1.283 after; `wm-screen-history.png->avif` 1.135 and 1.138, `wm-lineart-family-tree.png->avif` 1.109 (full run only). The rows of photographs (`photo-b.png`, `kodim23.png`, `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png`, `photo-a.jpg`) read 0.976 to 1.007: a photograph is encoded by the image library, not by this program (entries 36 and 93), so they are the control. The full run reported one failing row, `photo-a.jpg->webp` at 0.878 head against base (upper bound 0.900), a path this change does not touch; the quick run reads it 1.005, and a run of the same base against an identical copy of itself (A/A, `--quick`) reads 0.997, with `wm-alpha-graph.png->webp` at 0.927 in the A/A and 0.953 in the quick run, so the failing reading is taken as the noise of the VM (another agent's work shares it) and not as an effect of this change.
  - **The output is the package's output.** The program and the package's `avifenc` (libavif 1.2.1 and libaom 3.12.1, taken from the Debian 13 packages `libavif-bin 1.2.1-1.2` and `libaom3 3.12.1-1+deb13u1` and run in the VM) wrote byte-identical files for 56 of 56 combinations of seven pictures (8-bit and 16-bit, grey, with and without alpha, with EXIF) and eight argument sets (8, 10 and 12 bits, 4:0:0, 4:2:0 and 4:4:4, quality 40 to 100, speed 4 to 10, 1 to 8 threads, `--ignore-icc --ignore-xmp`, `-a c:tune=ssim`, `--cicp 9/16/9`), for each of the three builds in the table. Same libaom version, so the quality benchmark is not needed to bound a difference; it was run anyway (below).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The quality jobs measure the encoder the worker ships, on both sides (finding of the first measurement, resolved 2026-11-07).** The worker image has had libavif 1.2.1 and libaom 3.12.1 since it moved to Debian 13; the runner has 1.0.4 and 3.8.2, and the baseline had been recorded with the runner's encoder as the reference and as the product of the graphics. With the worker's encoder as the product and the runner's as the reference, `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --quick --family image` failed in the VM (`wm-deep-xray.png->avif` `bd_rate_ssim` 1.5087 % against the allowance of 1.5, regressions of `wm-screen-history.png->avif` and `wm-deep-xray.png->avif`). The comparison is about our settings, so the reference now runs the same program (Decision, CI) and the result is:
    - **x86-64 runner** (the authority for the baseline, the `parity quality` job of the pull request, 818 rows of every family): 0 rows failing, 0 regressed against the baseline, 22 improved. The graphics (`wm-*`, `screenshot.png`, `lineart.png`, which the program encodes) read delta 0 in every metric, the same bytes on both sides; the photographs, which the image library encodes (entries 36 and 93), read better than the old baseline (`photo-b.png` `bd_rate_ssim` 0.85 to -0.44, `kodim23.png` 0.52 to -0.22). The 103 image AVIF entries of `bench/baseline.json` whose value moved were deleted and added again from that run's report with `--baseline-from-report` (README, "Baseline"), tolerances unchanged: the numbers of the graphics follow the encoder the worker ships (`wm-alpha-banner.png->avif` 42,173 bytes with libavif 1.0.4 against 19,209 with 1.2.1, on both sides), and the photographs' deltas follow the faster-improving reference. The entries of the rows only the full nightly run measures (photographs and the class rows) were not re-recorded: they come from the first nightly after this change.
    - **aarch64 Linux VM** (`~/wavifq`, the pinned build on both sides; not a baseline source): the quick run failed 1 row (`photo-b.png->avif` `bd_rate_ssim` 1.9891) and the full image run 8 rows of 3 photographs (`photo-b.png`, `kodim10.png`, `clic-schicka-307.png`; worst `clic-schicka-307.png` `bd_rate_ssim` 2.7126 against the allowance of 1.5), with 9 regressions against the baseline. Every graphic passes at delta 0. The same code read +0.60 % mean BD-rate against the reference on the VM and -0.27 % on the runner over the 28 photograph AVIF BD-rate rows of the quick run, the worst +1.99 % and +0.09 % (`photo-b.png` 13,000 bytes there, 12,780 on x86-64, while the reference writes 12,729 and 12,734): the VM had the npm package's libvips, whose AVIF saver cuts a picture into tiles by the thread count (entry 93), and the runner has the worker's patched one; the architecture is not the cause (see the next bullet). The release of libaom is not the cause either: with a reference built on libaom 3.15.1 (the library's release, same libavif 1.2.1) the VM's full run reads `photo-b.png` 1.9166 (1.9891 with 3.12.1) and `clic-schicka-307.png` 1.7786 and 2.1118 (2.1426 and 2.7126), the photographs' mean unchanged. The photographs have no finding on the runner. The VM's reading was the library, not the architecture or our settings (found 2026-11-07, row "Found by #998" of epic #760):
    - **Cause: the VM measured the stock libvips, which tiles by the thread count.** The npm package's `libvips-cpp.so.8.18.7` (SHA-256 `97c2ae9a...bc8f`) calls libheif with `auto-tiles` true, and the worker leases 4 threads on the 4-vCPU VM, so a photograph was cut into several tiles; the worker image and the runner put the library of entry 93 over it, which is one tile. The VM's failing photographs (`photo-b.png`, `kodim10.png`, `clic-schicka-307.png`) are the ones that the "base, 4 threads" column of entry 93 lists, with its numbers (`photo-b.png` SSIM +1.99 there and here, `clic-schicka-307.png` +1.95 there and +2.71 here).
    - **Proof: the same run with that one instruction changed.** In a copy of the VM's checkout the library had `mov w2, #1` at file offset 0x16a7e8 changed to `mov w2, #0` (what `libvips-heif-auto-tiles.patch` does in the source; SHA-256 `c7794aeb...7c63`), nothing else touched: libavif 1.2.1 and libaom 3.12.1 on the reference side, the pinned `avifenc` on the product side for graphics, `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=2`, `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --family image`, aarch64, 823 rows. Stock library: FAIL, 8 rows failing and 8 regressions against the baseline (`photo-a.jpg`, `photo-b.png`, `kodim03.png`, `kodim23.png`, `clic-schicka-307.png`). Patched library: PASS, 0 failing, 0 regressions, 86 rows within the allowance (165 before). The mean BD-rate of the 72 photograph AVIF rows goes from +0.69 % to -0.28 % (the runner's 28 rows read -0.27 %). `photo-b.png` is 13,000 bytes with the stock library and 12,800 with the patched one (12,780 on x86-64; the reference writes 12,729), `clic-schicka-307.png` 13,050 and 12,704 (reference 12,664), `kodim10.png` 38,475 and 37,875 (reference 37,687). BD-rate, PSNR / SSIM: `photo-b.png` +1.20 / +1.99 to -1.58 / -0.84, `clic-schicka-307.png` +2.14 / +2.71 to -0.55 / -0.20, `kodim10.png` +1.70 / +1.56 to +0.11 / -0.04, `kodim23.png` +0.64 / +1.44 to -0.95 / +0.10. WebP and JPEG rows and the graphics' AVIF rows are identical in the two runs.
    - **Nothing in the pipeline changes.** Production runs the patched library (check-sharp.sh verifies the digest of the build), so the arm64 worker already reads as the second run; no setting, effort, chroma or tune moves and there is no speed effect. The aarch64 SIMD paths of libaom do not show up as a difference: the reference and the product are on one release and the mean is -0.28 % here and -0.27 % on the runner. A testbed that is not given the worker's libvips reads the photographs as the first run; the recipe is in the benchmark README ("Baseline and tool versions").
    - **Speed rows against the pinned reference** (VM, `--parity --speed-only --quick --family image`, ratio to the reference with the lower bound of the interval, bar 0.9): `photo-b.png` 0.988 (interval 0.918 to 1.002), `kodim23.png` 1.32, `clic-paul-itkin-46101.png` 1.146, and the graphics at 0.95 to 0.99 (the same program on both sides, so the ratio is the cost of the launcher), all passing. The reference of the speed rows is the same resolver, so it is the pinned build too; before, it was the package's, and the pinned build is faster than the package (the table above).
    - **Open**: the photograph rows of the full run on x86-64 are read by the first nightly after the merge. If one of them (`clic-schicka-307.png`, `kodim10.png`) stands above the allowance of 1.5, it needs a dated entry in `bench/parity-gaps.json` at the nightly's value, after its baseline entry is re-recorded from that nightly (a gap entry may not record a value worse than the baseline of the base by more than its allowance, `bench/parity.ts`).
  - **Two encoders in the image.** The package stays as the fallback; the stage adds a 6.7 MB program and about 2 minutes (1 min 50 s on 4 vCPU) to an image build, and the CI task builds only when its cache misses.
  - **The digest of the program is not pinned**, only repeated: the build of the same script gave the same digest twice (`6aa904...` unmodified, `22de32...` with both changes). The inputs that decide the bytes (every archive, CMake, NASM) are pinned; the compilers are the image's.
  - **x86-64 is built in CI and not measured.** The VM is aarch64. The `container` job of this pull request built the stage on x86-64 (NASM, the x86-64 CMake archive, the assembly of libaom and libjpeg-turbo) in 218 s next to the other stages and ran the smoke encode of the Dockerfile; the cold CI task (no cache) took 4 min 24 s of the setup step of the `parity quality` job on 4 vCPU, inside its limit of 360 s. The speed on x86-64 is for the nightly run to read; a failure of the build stops the image build or the CI task, never the worker.
  - **`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is not edited:** it is generated from `package-lock.json` and lists npm packages only. The components are listed in `docs/licensing.md` (2.14) and ship in `/licenses/avifenc.*`.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **libavif 1.4.2 with libaom 3.15.1** (the libaom of the sharp stage): the files change a lot (at quality 70 and speed 6, libavif 1.2.1 with libaom 3.12.1 against 1.4.2 with 3.15.1: `screenshot.png` 7,392 and 8,470 bytes, `lineart.png` 34,933 and 27,331, `photo-b.png` 12,729 and 22,017). The libavif changelog names why: 1.4.0 uses a different quality-to-quantizer mapping and the IQ tuning for the colour planes of non-RGB pictures with libaom 3.13 or newer. That is a change of the AVIF policy (entry 1), not a build.
  - **Linking the sharp stage's libaom**: it is built into `libvips-cpp.so` as a static library and is not exported; a second build of libaom 3.12.1 here keeps the package's version, which the 3.15.1 of that stage would not.
  - **zlib instead of zlib-ng** was the unmodified build's choice and stays in the first commit; zlib-ng is the second commit above.
  - **Profile-guided optimisation, `-march=native` or a fixed instruction set**: the first needs a profile and a compiler that match, the others are not portable to the worker's x86-64 baseline and arm64; libaom chooses its routines at run time.
- **Verified by**:
  - `tests/worker-avifenc-packaging.test.ts` (the stage, its base image, the copies, the smoke encode, the licence copies, the digest of every archive, the commit check, the notes naming the pins, the refusal on a system other than Linux before any download, the bound on a download) and `tests/ci-setup-tasks.test.ts` (the task list, its limit, and the cache: build and write the digest, link the cached program, rebuild when the digest differs), `tests/runtime-baseline.test.ts`, `tests/ci-install-apt-tools.test.ts`, `shellcheck` on both scripts.
  - Byte identity and the speed tables above, in the Linux VM; the install script built in the VM three times (unmodified, with link-time optimisation, with zlib-ng; 58 s, 1 min 55 s and 1 min 50 s on 4 vCPU). The Dockerfile itself was not built (no container runtime on the development machine or in the VM); the `RUN` that smoke-tests the program was run in the VM under `dash` against the extracted program.
  - `ORACLE_STRICT_MODE=1 npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --quick --family image` with the pinned build on both sides: the `parity quality` job on the x86-64 runner passes (818 rows, 0 regressed), the aarch64 VM reads the photographs as described under the first trade-off. `tests/bench-tools.test.ts` (the reference resolves to `avifenc-pinned` in a later directory over a package `avifenc`, falls back to the package, and the two workflows set no `AVIFENC_PATH`).
- **Revisit when**: the nightly x86-64 run reads the photograph AVIF rows of the full run above the allowance (a gap entry, above) or differently from the VM, a Debian point release moves libavif or libaom (then the pins and the byte comparison move together), or the AVIF policy moves to a newer libavif.

## 173. Production is watched from outside by a scheduled readiness probe every 15 minutes, and the host runs EasyConvert alone

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: the host is used for this service only, the other service on it was removed, and nothing watched production).
- **Decision**:
  - **`.github/workflows/uptime.yml` reads `https://convert.aquilaxk.site/api/health` at minutes 7, 22, 37 and 52 of every hour**, from a GitHub-hosted runner, through the same proxy and TLS a visitor goes through. The run passes on HTTP 200 with `"status":"healthy"` and otherwise tries twice more a minute apart; three failures fail the run, and GitHub mails the failure of a scheduled run to whoever last changed the schedule. It reads only the public probe (`{ status }`); the per-component view needs an administrator key and the smoke conversion under `/api/health/` is not forwarded by the proxy, so the workflow holds no secret.
  - **The host runs EasyConvert alone.** The monitoring stack, database, cluster and runners of the other service that shared it were removed; the names of the instance, of its data volume and mount (`/var/lib/easysubway-data`) and of the unit that opens ports 80 and 443 (`easysubway-open-web-ports.service`) stay, because `deploy/oci/deploy.sh` and the host's boot depend on them and renaming them changes nothing the service does.
- **Why**: a failure of production was seen only when someone opened the site. A probe from outside covers what a probe on the host cannot: the proxy, the certificate, DNS and the host itself being down.
- **Trade-offs**: a failure is noticed up to about 18 minutes late (the 15-minute schedule, which GitHub may delay under load, plus the retries), and a scheduled workflow is disabled by GitHub after 60 days without activity in the repository. The repository is public, so the runs cost no paid minutes. A one-minute outage between probes is not seen.
- **Alternatives rejected**: an uptime service with an account (a third party holding the alert and the address), the monitoring stack that was on the host (it goes down with the host it watches, and it belonged to the other service), and a probe of the smoke conversion (it is not public by design, entry on the health routes).
- **Verified by**: `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts` (the job count, a runner, a timeout, read-only permissions, actions pinned or none); the probe command was run against production on 2026-11-07 (`{"status":"healthy"}`).
- **Revisit when**: a status page or paging is wanted, the domain changes, or the health route changes its body.

## 174. A picture goes on a PDF page as its own PNG data stream, without the PDF library's byte-array reader

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the real-world file `pix-google-pixel6pro.dng` to PDF, which the corpus run listed as "job server killed (SIGKILL, memory) beside two other jobs"), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: make the file convert, or refuse it with a typed limit, and drop the known-failure row).
- **Decision**:
  - **An opaque, not interlaced grey or RGB PNG with no palette and no colour key is embedded from its chunks** (`readPlainPng` and `embeddedPicture` in `src/lib/conversions/image-pdf-pages.ts`): the IDAT chunks are joined into one buffer and become the stream of the image XObject, `/FlateDecode` with `/Predictor 15`, `/Colors` 1 or 3, the PNG's `/BitsPerComponent`, `/DeviceGray` or `/DeviceRGB`. These are the objects PDFKit 0.15.2 writes for the same PNG (its `PNGImage.embed`, direct branch), so the page and its pixels do not change; the PDF of the Pixel 6 Pro file differs from the one before in 70 bytes, the creation date and the document ID, and `pdfimages -png` extracts the same picture from both (same MD5).
  - **A palette PNG is embedded the same way** (`/Indexed /DeviceRGB` with the PLTE chunk as the lookup, the IDAT data as the stream with `/Predictor 15`, `/Colors` 1 and `/BitsPerComponent` equal to the bit depth 1, 2, 4 or 8). With a `tRNS` chunk it also gets an `/SMask` (8-bit `/DeviceGray`, `/Decode [0 1]`) built from the indices row by row; an index past the chunk's entries is opaque.
  - **A grey+alpha or RGBA PNG (8 or 16 bit)** gets the colour channels as the image and the alpha channel as its `/SMask`, as PDFKit's `splitAlphaChannel` writes them: 8 bits per component, no `/DecodeParms`, a 16-bit sample cut to its most significant byte, each plane deflated on its own at the default level. `src/lib/conversions/png-scanlines.ts` inflates the IDAT data in bounded chunks, undoes the filters 0 to 4 one row at a time and writes the planes to two streaming deflaters, so it holds two rows, a 256 KB batch per plane and the compressed output, never a value per byte.
  - **An interlaced (Adam7) PNG is written again without interlacing by sharp** (the same `sharp(png).png()` the converter already uses), which keeps its channels and depth and turns a palette or a colour key into pixels with alpha, and then takes the path of its colour type.
  - **Any other PNG still goes through PDFKit's reader**: an animation chunk (`acTL`), a `tRNS` colour key on grey or RGB, a PLTE chunk in a PNG that does not index it, a palette PNG without a palette, a chunk that runs past the end of the data or a file that is not a PNG. The pages of a multi-page document are each placed this way or that.
  - **Where the output differs from PDFKit's, the page follows the PNG**: PDFKit's reader makes palette index 255 transparent whatever the `tRNS` chunk says (it pads the alphas to 255 entries, not 256) and reads the alphas of a 1, 2 or 4-bit palette picture from packed bytes, not from pixels. The new path gives index 255 its alpha (opaque when the chunk is short) and the alpha of each pixel.
  - **No limit changes.** The file is 4080 x 3072 pixels, not 50 megapixels, and is far below the input limit (`maxInputPixels()`, 100 MP) and the RAW sensor budget (64 MP), so no refusal was due; the failure was the memory of a job the limits allow.
- **Why**: PDFKit's PNG reader (`png-js`) copies every byte of the IDAT data into a JavaScript array, one element per byte. For a developed camera picture the PNG is nearly as large as its samples (21 MB for this file, whose noise does not compress), and the heap held about 570 MB for it while the 75 MB decoded intermediate, the PNG and the PDF were also in memory. Measured on the Lima testbed (aarch64, Node 24, `/usr/bin/time -v`, three runs each, dispatcher called with the file in memory): 965,288, 966,032 and 965,416 KB resident before, 513,924, 482,372 and 480,552 KB after (the JPEG of the same file: 587,788 and 586,308 KB; the 16-bit PNG: 998,180 and 995,292 KB). The real-world run starts three job servers at once and recorded the kill as `job server died (code null, signal SIGKILL)`, the signal the kernel's out-of-memory killer sends; the file converts alone on the testbed, so the memory of the other jobs decided when it happened. A stage-by-stage run showed the whole rise at one call, `doc.image(png)`: heap 13 MB to 537 MB, 205 MB to 774 MB resident.
  - **The quality is the one of the JPEG path.** The page already took the PNG at 8 bits (`pdfimages -list`: 8 bpc, DeviceRGB), reduced by the same pipeline an 8-bit target gets for a camera file whose development curve is not sRGB (entry 25: the ICC transform to 8-bit sRGB). Against the PNG the same file develops to (16 bits, taken to 8-bit sRGB), the page picture measures 41.6 dB PSNR and the JPEG 39.8 dB, so the page is closer to the PNG than the JPEG is. The test asserts that order.
- **Trade-offs**: the PDF writer now holds a second small reader of PNG chunks (signature, IHDR, PLTE, tRNS, IDAT, and the chunk types that send a picture to PDFKit) and a row unfilter in JavaScript (an RGBA picture of 2400 x 2400 pixels takes 0.4 s, the reader took 0.7 s); a PNG that has a feature it does not know of takes PDFKit's path as before and keeps its memory use. An interlaced PNG costs one more encode by sharp. The stream is not checked for being a valid zlib stream before it is written (a PNG from the image library is), as PDFKit does not check it either.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Decoding the pixels and deflating them again for an opaque picture**: it holds the 38 MB of raw samples and the compressed copy at once, loses the PNG row filters (the PDF of this file would be larger), and writes objects PDFKit does not. The alpha planes cannot be passed through and are rebuilt row by row instead.
  - **Re-encoding an interlaced PNG with a hand-written Adam7 reader**: sharp already decodes it natively and without a value per byte.
  - **Embedding the developed picture as a JPEG**: it would change the output of every camera file and every PNG, lossy where today's page is lossless, and is a different policy from the one this entry fixes.
  - **Refusing the file with a typed limit**: the file is inside every documented limit and converts in 0.8 s.
- **Verified by**: `tests/image-pdf-plain-png-embed.test.ts` (a 2400 x 2400 picture of random pixels, RGB and RGBA, placed on a page in a process with a 96 MB V8 heap, which ran out of memory for the RGBA picture before the change and finishes after it; RGB and grey pictures extracted by `pdfimages` equal to their source samples; two pages), `tests/image-pdf-alpha-palette-png-embed.test.ts` (grey+alpha and RGBA at 8 and 16 bits, palettes of 2, 4 and 8 bits with and without `tRNS`, and an interlaced RGBA picture, each written by hand with all five row filters: the picture and its soft mask that `pdfimages -png` extracts equal PDFKit's own output for the same PNG and the PNG decoded by sharp, and PDFKit's reader is not called) and `tests/raw-dng-pdf-embed.test.ts` (the real file to PDF: `pdfinfo` page size 4080 x 3072 points, `pdfimages -list` one 4080 x 3072 8-bit RGB picture, its pixels against the PNG of the same file and the JPEG as the quality bar). `bench/realworld/known-failures.json` is empty.
- **Revisit when**: PDFKit's PNG reader stops keeping the data as an array of numbers, or a corpus file reaches the pool's memory limit on a path other than this one.


## 175. PDF text: a bullet that sits apart from its text is a list item and not two table cells, and the CFF composite-font rows that stay open are measured

- **Status**: Implemented (issue #783, the row "Found by #890"; epic #760), decided 2026-11-07 (QA request: trace the layout stage behind the three regression files, and bring the CFF composite-font rows to the rule of the other font types or say why they cannot). It supplies the trace that entry 104 says was not made (`the layout of those lines was read from the texts, not traced to the stage that changes it`) and settles which CFF rows of entry 163 stay open.
- **Decision**:
  - **A row of two segments whose first is a lone bullet glyph is a list item, one line "• text", and not two cells of a table** (`bulletItemParts` in `src/lib/conversions/pdf-layout/tables.ts`). The glyph is one the list reader takes for a bullet (`parseListMarker`) except the dash, en dash, em dash and asterisk, which a table cell holds as a placeholder or a footnote sign. A run of rows in which such items are at least half of the tabular rows is not a stream table (`buildStreamTable`); the rows are then lines, the items merged. A run in which they are fewer is a table as before: a three-column table with a bullet column, and the lines of a column of prose beside a bullet list, keep their cells.
  - **The other lines of such an item are lines of the item.** A line that starts where the text of the item's first line starts (within half an em), after the item or after lines that do, goes on with the item and does not open a paragraph with a first-line indent (`hangsUnderMarker` in `src/lib/conversions/pdf-layout/paragraphs.ts`; the line carries the start of its text as `LayoutLine.textX0`). Every other indented line opens a paragraph as before.
  - **A bullet that prints nothing leaves a plain line.** The Wingdings bullets of `gd-070040.pdf`, `gd-326174.pdf` and `gd-499819.pdf` print no text (entry 104, Poppler's reading), so their rows have one segment and are lines of text; an item is a paragraph of its own when its baseline step is more than 1.35 times the line pitch, as the other paragraphs of the flow are. Nothing marks the item as a list item: the glyph is left out, and a marker made up for it would be a character no reader prints.
  - **Followed**: Poppler 26.09 for the text (`pdftotext`, behaviour only, as entry 104): it prints the words of a bullet list line by line and no tab, and it prints the running header and footer of every page, which the layout takes out as page furniture when it recurs (`splitPageFurniture`), so a word-level comparison with it loses those words. The table rule is the layout's own: no reader the layout follows has a rule for bullets in stream tables.
  - **CFF composite fonts, the rows of entry 163 that stay open, measured and reproduced** (`tests/pdf-text-cff-partial-tounicode.test.ts`, the describe at the end; `pdftotext` and the reader on the same hand-written files, a CID font of 0x44 glyphs whose map lists codes 0x41 and 0x42 as Q and R):
    - **A code past the glyphs of the program** (code 0x50): Poppler `QQQR`, reader `QQQRP`. Closing it needs a range of the codes past the glyphs, and that range costs time in pdf.js's CMap reader: one font on one page converts in 1.2 to 1.4 ms without it and 11.3 to 12.4 ms with the range 0x44 to 0xFFFF (median of 25, Linux arm64 VM, two runs each way), so the 244 CFF fonts with a map that entry 163 counts in 42 files of the two corpora would each add about 10 ms to a file that converts in a few hundred.
    - **A map that names another CMap with `usecmap`**: Poppler `QQQR`, reader `QQQRCP`. A range written in front of the map cannot be undone by the CMap it names: pdf.js adds the codes of the named CMap only where the map has none (`extendCMap`, `src/core/cmap.js` lines 650 to 667: `if (!cMap.contains(key)) cMap.mapOne(key, value)`), so a range of "no text" in front of the map would hide the text that `/Adobe-Japan1-UCS2 usecmap` and the like give. The font stays as the file has it.
    - **An encoding other than Identity-H and Identity-V** (`/90ms-RKSJ-H`, an embedded CMap stream): Poppler `Q Q R`, reader `QQRC`. The codes the font can select are those of its CMap's codespace, which the update does not read, and a range over all of them would drop the one-byte codes of ASCII that the file's map does not list and pdf.js prints right (`C` above is the glyph of code 0x43); for a CMap of Unicode codes (`UniJIS-UCS2-H`, where Poppler also prints `QQR`) the code is the text. The font stays as the file has it.
    - **The one glyph of the corpus** (`govdocs1-004148.pdf`, code 12 of `TKNYRT+Universal-GreekwithMathPi`) is a glyph of the program (25 glyphs, CID 12 in the charset), not a code past the glyphs: entry 163's pass gives it a gap, and it is a form feed that the text drops. The row's "codes past the font's glyph count" and the corpus glyph are not the same case.
- **Why**:
  - **Where the three files change.** The row of a list item is a bullet, a gap of 14 to 18 points and the text. The gap is wider than the segment gap, so the row has two segments, and the stream-table detector reads a run of rows with two segments and a channel between them as a table (`detectStreamTables`). Before entry 104 the Wingdings bullets were control characters (U+0083, U+0099), the rows had two segments, and the lists were tables: `\x83\tMethane Sources – Overview`, a heading and its sentence in one cell (`2.2\tORGANIZATION OF REPORT The following sections provide the details of the study:`), the state names of `gd-070040.pdf` mixed into the rows of the names under them, and the running footer, one more row of the run, inside the table, so that it was not a one-line paragraph that recurs and was not taken out. With no glyph the rows have one segment, are no table, and the footer is a line again: `This document is a research report submitted to the U.S. Department of Justice ...` is out of 5 more pages of `gd-070040.pdf`, `Study of the Market Potential ...` of 1 more of `gd-326174.pdf`. That is what changed in those two files, and the footers that are now out are the 0.0001 to 0.0003 that word-level F1 against Poppler lost, because Poppler prints the footers. `gd-499819.pdf` is the other half: it has bullets that print (`•`, U+2022), and the same rows were tables there before and after entry 104 (73 lines with `•` and a tab in the text of the file before entry 104, 61 on main): the page header `Executive Summary    Why Do We Need NTCIP?` and two bullet rows made one 3 by 2 grid, and the lines that carry an item on (`exchanged (dialogs) are being added.`) stood apart from it with a blank line between.
