Redis's own persistence documentation describes this form: an RDB file is a point-in-time image produced by a fork and replaced by a rename, so copying it is safe, and a copy is the recommended backup (https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/persistence/).
  - **Six hours.** The data that changes between copies is sign-ups, new keys, quota counters and queued jobs; a free launch can lose six hours of that, and a restart loses about a second in any case. Four copies a day cost a few megabytes each.
  - **Seven days follows from the 10-day promise, not from taste.** The usual guidance on erasure (the UK data protection authority's guide to the right to erasure, section on backups) accepts a copy in a backup until the backup is overwritten, if it is not used for anything else and the erasure is applied again when the backup is restored. This design does exactly that, and makes the overwrite short enough that the promise holds in the words of the policy.
  - **The age rule runs first and without the backup.** A broken backup job must not be able to keep old accounts alive.
  - **Same disk, no off-host copy.** QA's rules are no paid service and no new billable resource, and there is no cloud storage. A copy that leaves the host would be a copy the 7-day rule cannot reach.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The loss of the data disk or the instance loses Redis.** Accounts would sign up again and API keys be issued again. Accepted for the free launch; revisit before paid plans (the same entry that lets payments exist must give the backup another place).
  - **Up to 6 hours of data are lost by a restore**, and queued jobs are lost (clients get 404 for them).
  - **The operator must meet the 2-day erasure target.** Nothing enforces it; the deletion request is a mail. A request that waits more than 2 days makes the backups outlive the promise by the excess.
  - **If runs fail for 7 days the age rule removes every backup.** No alert watches the timer yet (alerts are phase 2 of #899); the weekly check is in the runbook.
  - **A backup holds the file of an API job that was running when it was taken.** A job sent with `inputBufferBase64` (up to 32 MiB) keeps the file in its record until it ends (entry 147), and a snapshot taken at that moment holds it for 7 days, while the privacy policy said files go within minutes and that the operator makes no backup of files. The window is a few seconds a day for a small number of API jobs, but it is a copy of a user's file beyond the stated period. **Resolved (QA 2026-11-08)**: the legal texts describe the record backups instead of making the backup remove those fields (load the dump in a scratch server, delete them, dump again, which would add a step and a failure mode to every backup). Privacy section 3 has a row for the backups (every 6 hours, same server, not copied elsewhere, at most 7 days, the file of a running API job included, no backup of uploaded files and results); section 4 says deleted data cannot be restored from the system except as a copy in a backup for at most 7 days, that an account is deleted within 2 days of a verified request and its backup copies within the following 7 days and 6 hours (inside the 10 days), and that a restore deletes again every account deleted after the backup; terms section 3 and data processing terms section 7 say the same in short. The four pages move to version 2026-11-08 (`LEGAL_TEXTS_VERSION`), which makes sign-up and API key creation refuse the earlier version with `terms_outdated`. The change was read as unfavourable (a new retention of a user's file for up to 7 days), so the terms' 30-day notice (section 9, FTC article 3) is kept by not taking a backup before 2026-12-08; the sources are in `docs/legal/SOURCES.md` (key RUN).
  - **The Docker steps of the restore are not run by the drill.** The drill runs the same Redis steps with the binaries directly; the `docker run` plumbing is first exercised by a real restore or a rehearsal on a second host.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Copying the append-only directory.** It holds the history as well as the data, so a deleted account would live in it until the next rewrite, and copying a live multi-file directory needs the rewrite paused to be consistent.
  - **Erasing an account inside the backups.** Each backup would be loaded in a scratch server, edited and dumped again. The age rule gives the same promise with no editing of a backup and no new failure mode.
  - **Daily backups kept 14 or 30 days, or keeping the monthly one.** Past 8 days the promise of 10 days cannot hold with a 2-day erasure target.
  - **Cloud object storage or another host for the copies.** A new billable resource, and out of the 7-day rule's reach.
  - **No backup at all.** The audit of 2026-10-30 (#667) found none, and a damaged append-only file would end the service's accounts.
  - **An external status page service.** Even on a free plan it is a third-party account that holds the monitors and the subscribers' addresses (a processor to list in the privacy policy 30 days before use), and its custom domain and subscriber features are the paid ones.
  - **A `/status` page fed by the SLO metrics.** The metrics are internal by design (entry 179); a page served by the application is down when the application is, which is when it is needed; and the in-app page was removed in #978 because neither reference converter has one.
  - **A static page published to GitHub Pages by the Uptime workflow** is the smallest page that would work off-host, free and with no new account. It is not built: the run history already answers "is it up" for anyone who knows where to look, and a page nobody asked for is more to keep right. It is the upgrade when users ask; it needs a repository setting and, for a name under the domain, a CDN record, both QA's.
- **Verified by**: `tests/redis-backup.test.ts` (the script against a stand-in for `docker`: the sequence BGSAVE, wait, check, copy; the file, its checksum file and their modes; the password in no argument and no output; pruning by number and by age, also when the backup fails; only the script's own names are removed; each failure leaves no file; the lock; the units and the numbers 7 days, 28 files and 2 days + 7 days + 6 hours < 10 days against this entry and the runbook); `deploy/oci/redis-restore-drill.sh` (the real script against a real Redis, then the restore steps, key counts, types, values and an expiry equal before and after a restart: run 2026-11-08 on the maintainer's Mac with Redis 8.10.2 as a rehearsal, 55,052 keys, restore 0.42 s; the Linux VM run with Redis 7.4 is recorded in `docs/operations/backup-and-restore.md` when done).
- **Revisit when**: paid plans are prepared (a second place for the copies and a shorter data loss), a scraper and alerts exist (alert on the age of the newest backup), users ask for a status page (build the GitHub Pages page), or the Redis data grows past a few hundred megabytes (the copy time and the disk share).

## 187. Vector, image and CAD pairs that the office suite, Poppler, the image writers and the DXF path already serve are offered: metafile pictures, PostScript and SVG as icons, Photoshop files and drawing packages, DXF and DWG as BMP, GIF, TIFF and EPS, and Illustrator, CorelDRAW, CGM and WMF files as SVG and DXF

- **Status**: Implemented (a row of the conversion parity work, issue #783), decided 2026-11-08 (QA request: offer the vector, image and CAD pairs the reference service offers and this product does not, by wiring writers and readers it already has, keep the exclusions of entries 42 and 99 unless the reason is measured to be gone, and leave out any pair that needs a new parser or writer).
- **Decision**:
  - **The pairs, by class and route.** The reference service's formats API (read on 2026-11-08, `include=options`) lists every one of the 56 pairs this entry looks at; the engines it names are in brackets. 33 are offered.
    - **Windows metafile as a picture** `emf` to `avif`, `bmp`, `gif`, `ico`, `odd`, `psd`, `tiff` and `webp` (ImageMagick): the route of `emf` to `png`. The office suite draws the metafile into a PDF (entry 42, with the page of the header's size, entry 100), Poppler draws the page, and the shared image writer encodes it, as the same formats are written from PostScript, XPS and DjVu pages. The reference's `width`, `height` and `fit` options, and its 32 by 32 default of `ico`, are not copied: the icon is the square canvas of the shared writer (up to 256 pixels), as for the PDF pairs of entry 183.
    - **PostScript and EPS as an icon, a Photoshop file and a drawing package** `eps` and `ps` to `ico`, `odd` and `psd` (ImageMagick): Ghostscript draws the PDF of the file and the same page chain writes the picture, one picture for each page and a ZIP of them for a file of several pages, as `eps` to `gif` and `bmp` already do.
    - **SVG and SVGZ as an icon, a Photoshop file and a drawing package** `svg` and `svgz` to `ico`, `odd` and `psd` (ImageMagick): the PNG that the drawing renders to goes to the shared image writer, so that the size options, the density and the transparency of `svg` to `png` apply to the new pictures too.
    - **DXF and DWG as BMP, GIF, TIFF and EPS** `dxf` and `dwg` to `bmp`, `gif`, `tiff` and `eps` (the CAD converter): the SVG that the DXF path draws (entry 13) goes through the pipeline that writes `png`, `jpg` and `webp` and that `svg` already uses for these four targets. A DWG goes first through the pinned reader (entry 29), so the pre-R13 refusal and the release table of that entry apply to the new targets unchanged. The EPS is a picture on a page of its own size (entry 59), like `svg` to `eps`. The reference's `all_layouts` (off by default) and its `width`, `height` and `auto_zoom` are not offered; the product draws the drawing it reads, and `width` and `height` apply as for `png`.
    - **Illustrator files as SVG and DXF** `ai` to `svg` and `dxf` (Inkscape): an Illustrator file is a PDF (versions 3 to 8, a PostScript program), so it takes the PDF page chain: `pdftocairo` writes the SVG and the DXF writer of entry 99 reads that SVG, a picture being left out with a warning (entry 129).
    - **DXF of CorelDRAW, CGM and WMF files** `cdr`, `cgm` and `wmf` to `dxf` (Inkscape): the office suite draws the file (entry 42), `pdftocairo` draws each page as SVG and the DXF writer reads it, as for Visio drawings. A drawing of several pages is a ZIP with one DXF for each page. `tika-testwmf.wmf` is a bitmap and nothing else on the office suite of the Linux image (24.2.7), and a page of only a picture is refused (entry 133) with a typed answer that the real-world run explains; on the 26.8 of the development Mac the page also holds a rectangle and the picture is left out with a warning.
  - **The pairs left out, and why.** The reference lists all of them.
    - **The metafile writers still refuse what the real files hold** (entries 42 and 99): `ai`, `cdr`, `cgm`, `eps`, `ps` and `wmf` to `emf` and `wmf` (the pairs the reference lists: `ai`, `cdr`, `cgm`, `eps` and `ps` to both, `wmf` to `emf`, `emf` to `wmf`). Measured on 2026-11-08 on the real files of the corpus, converting each to EMF and to WMF through the dispatcher:
      - 82 PostScript and EPS files (79 `ps`, 3 `eps`): 19 convert and 63 are refused with a typed answer, for each of the two targets (29 files draw a character of a bitmap font as a picture, 16 hold a picture, 6 a dash array, 4 an SVG past the 5 MiB limit, 3 a stroke under a skew, 2 a mask, 1 a curved clip, and 2 are stopped by the interpreter). The reason of entry 42 holds, and entry 183 leaves out `pdf` to `emf` and `wmf` for the same pages (26 of 60 convert).
      - CorelDRAW: 1 of 2 (`office-pb-poi.cdr` holds a picture); CGM: 2 of 3 (`lo-circles.cgm` draws dashed lines whose dash array the metafile pen cannot carry); WMF to EMF: 2 of 3 (`tika-testwmf.wmf` holds a picture); EMF to WMF: 1 of 3 (`lo-computer_mail.emf` and `tika-testemf.emf` hold pictures). An Illustrator file takes the PDF chain, so it is the 26 of 60.
      - A metafile writer that carried pictures, masks and dashes would be a new writer.
    - **`emf` to `dxf`**: 1 of 3 real files converts. `tika-testemf.emf` is only a picture (the DXF writer refuses a page of only a picture, entry 133) and `lo-computer_mail.emf` has a clip whose path draws a curve (entry 99 cuts at a convex polygon only). The same pages convert to DXF from `wmf` (2 of 3 on the Linux image, 3 of 3 on the Mac; the third is a picture alone), `cgm` (3 of 3) and `cdr` (2 of 2, one picture left out with a warning), which is why those are offered and this one is not.
    - **`dxf` and `dwg` to `cgm` and `wmf`**: the SVG that a DXF is drawn as holds `<text>` for its text entities and round line caps, which the metafile writers refuse by design (entry 42). Of the 14 public drawings of the benchmark, 7 convert to WMF and 0 to CGM; both generated plates carry text and are refused. A route through the PDF of the drawing and `pdftocairo` would write the text as outlines, but it is a new route in the worker (the DXF path has none today), and the CGM it would write has no independent reader (the office suite imports the binary encoding only, and the product writes the clear-text one), so the CGM could not be checked by a program that is not the converter.
    - **`dwf` to `cgm` and `wmf`, and `sk` and `sk1` to `emf` and `wmf`**: no reader of DWF, Sketch or sK1 files is included (entry 42). The real DWF of the corpus (`tika-testdwf2010.dwf`) is refused with the reason for every target; the corpus has no Sketch or sK1 file.
    - **`gif` and `webp` to audio** (14 pairs, left out by QA as meaningless for still images): the animated paths of the product write silent video (`gif` and `webp` to `mp4`, `mkv` and the like carry no audio stream), so an audio target would be an empty file. They stay out.
  - **Every page, a ZIP for several**: the reference's `pages` has no default for a picture, so every page is converted; `emf` and the single-picture sources write one file, `eps`, `ps`, `cgm` and `ai` files of several pages write a ZIP, and `multiPageOutput: first` gives page one.
  - **The benchmark scores the geometry**: 12 new rows of the vector family (`bench/families/vector-pairs.ts`: SSIM against the analytic truth of the shapes, ours against ImageMagick (SVG, EPS), the office suite (EMF) and `pdftocairo` (Illustrator)), and 24 new rows of the CAD family (`bench/families/cad.ts`: the two generated plates to `bmp`, `gif`, `tiff` and `eps` against the office suite's export of the same DXF, ink recall, ink precision and extent error). The `odd` target has no tool that writes it and is checked by `tests/vector-pairs.test.ts` alone.
- **Why**:
  - **Each pair is the route of its sibling.** The office suite already draws metafiles and writes `emf` to `png`; the page chain already writes `ico`, `psd` and `odd` from PDF, XPS and DjVu pages; the SVG pipeline already writes `bmp`, `gif`, `tiff` and `eps` for `svg`, and the DXF path already draws `png`, `jpg` and `webp` through it; the PDF chain already writes SVG and DXF. Nothing here is a new parser or writer.
  - **DXF is offered where the reason of entry 42 is gone.** Entries 99 and 129 let the DXF writer cut a convex clip and leave a picture out with a warning, so the real files of CorelDRAW, CGM and WMF convert to DXF (2 of 2, 3 of 3 and 2 of 3 on the Linux image, beside the four Visio files of entry 42); the one that does not is a picture alone, the typed refusal of entry 133 that `pdf` to `dxf` has too. EMF and WMF still refuse the pictures, masks and dashes, and EMF to DXF still meets a page that is only a picture, so those pairs keep the withdrawal.
  - **The numbers decide, not a threshold**: a pair is offered when no real file of the source is refused for the reason that withdrew it, and a file refused for another reason is a typed refusal that the real-world run explains (`bench/realworld/known-refusals.json`).
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **The icon is not 32 by 32** (the reference default of `ico`), and the pictures do not take the reference's `width`, `height` and `fit` options of the rasters: the size options of the product apply as for every picture. The SSIM rows compare the product's icon with the reference's 32-pixel icon, so they show the product above it: 0.736 against 0.707 (SVG), 0.886 against 0.707 (EPS), 0.910 against 0.712 (EMF).
  - **The EPS of a DXF is a picture** (a raster at 300 dpi on a page of the drawing's size), not the vector page the CAD converter writes; a vector EPS needs the PDF of the drawing and `pdftops`, a route the DXF path does not have in the worker. The ink rows are at the reference on both plates (recall 1 against 1 and 0.864, precision 1 against 1 and 0.993 to 1).
  - **A DXF from a metafile or a CorelDRAW page leaves a picture out** with a warning that names the pages (`office-pb-poi.cdr`, `tika-testwmf.wmf`), as every DXF written from a page does (entry 129).
  - **DWG pairs are checked through the DXF reader's output only**: the pinned reader `dwg2dxf` is not on the Lima VM, so the 143 DWG rows of the CAD family were not evaluated (they are skipped, not failed), and `tests/vector-pairs.test.ts` writes the new targets from a DWG with a stand-in reader that writes a plate. The reader itself is judged by `tests/cad-dwg-reader.test.ts` on a machine that has it.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Offering the metafile pairs with typed refusals for the files that hold pictures, dashes or masks**: the same bar as `pdf` to `emf` and `wmf` (entry 183) leaves them out, and the product would answer with a refusal for most PostScript pages (63 of 82).
  - **A rasterising metafile writer** that carries a picture as a DIB: a new writer, and the metafile would lose its vector content next to it.
  - **A vector EPS or WMF from a DXF through its PDF** (the `pdf` to `eps` and `wmf` chain): a new route in the worker orchestration for two formats, in a file (`src/worker/engines.ts`) that is at its code-smell baseline and cannot grow.
  - **The reference's 32-pixel icon**: it is a smaller picture of the same geometry (SSIM 0.707 for the shapes against 0.736 and above for the product's).
- **Verified by**: `tests/vector-pairs.test.ts` (real EMF files, real PostScript, EPS and SVGZ files, authored SVG, the generated DXF plates and an Illustrator file written by Ghostscript, each through the dispatcher and read back by a program that is not the converter: ImageMagick, `dwebp` and `avifdec` on the rasters, Ghostscript on EPS and on PostScript, librsvg on SVG, the office suite on the drawing package and on DXF, Tesseract on the numbers of a BMP, the ink score of `bench/cad-ink.ts` read by ffmpeg on the DXF rasters; the DWG route with a stand-in reader; the registry offers the 33 pairs and none of those left out), `tests/vector-sources-real-samples.test.ts` (the DXF of the CorelDRAW, CGM and WMF files drawn again by the office suite and, where ezdxf is installed, its extents against the ink of the page; the registry targets equal the converted ones), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` (the missing-engine answer and the real conversion of every new native pair, `ai` included; the pairs left out stay withdrawn), `tests/parity-audit.test.ts`, the real-world run on the Lima VM (below), and the vector, CAD and image families of the quality benchmark (`npm run bench:quality -- --parity --quality-only --family <family>` on the Lima VM, Ubuntu 24.04, LibreOffice 24.2.7): vector (strict mode, 276 rows, 0 not evaluated, parity pass): 12 new rows, all at or above the reference: `shapes.svg->ico` 0.7361 against 0.7067, `->psd` 0.9886 against 0.9891 (within the 0.003 allowance), `shapes.eps->ico` 0.8857 against 0.7066, `->psd` 0.9969 against 0.9911, `shapes.emf->bmp|gif|tiff|psd` 0.9917 against 0.9825, `->webp` 0.8554 against 0.8259, `->avif` 0.8483 against 0.8129, `->ico` 0.9098 against 0.7117, `shapes.ai->svg` 0.9998 against 0.9998; cad (not strict, 255 rows evaluated, 0 failing): 24 new rows, all at or above the reference or inside its allowance: ink recall 1 against 1 for `plate-basic` and 1 against 0.861 to 0.864 for `plate-full`, ink precision 1 against 1 for `plate-basic` and 0.9908, 0.9969, 0.9964 and 0.9928 against 1 for `plate-full` (allowance 0.02), extent error at most 0.0024 against 0.0003 to 0.0033 (allowance 0.01); the 143 rows of the DWG samples were not evaluated because `dwg2dxf` is not installed on the VM, which stops strict mode at the first DWG sample; image (strict mode, 823 rows, parity pass, 6 not evaluated: `ssimulacra2` is not installed and five BD-rate rows where the reference curve does not gain quality): no row of this family is touched by the change, and the one row below its baseline, `wm-alpha-banner.png->avif` PSNR 54.68 against 55.03, is the arm64 AVIF encoder against the x86-64 runner's baseline (`bench/README.md`). The real-world run: the new targets rotate the plan of the real-world corpus (195 jobs are planned that were not, 189 of them `ps`, 3 `emf` and one each `cdr`, `cgm` and `wmf`, and 195 move away). The 195 new jobs ran through the judge on the Lima VM: 188 convert and 7 are typed refusals, six already explained by the rows of `govdocs1-002500.ps` and `govdocs1-006458.ps` (the interpreter stops on the file) and one new row, `tika-testwmf.wmf` to DXF (a page of only a picture); no crash, hang or bad output, the slowest job 66 s (`govdocs1-002484.ps` to AVIF). The four PostScript files that have rows were run over their planned jobs again: the rows still fit, and the row of `govdocs1-002956.ps` (a DXF whose text layer has no text) is no longer planned but stays, because `tests/postscript-real-file-refusals.test.ts` pins it. Not run: the quality benchmark with a DWG reader, `ezdxf` and Inkscape (neither is on the VM, so the ezdxf extents and the Inkscape comparisons of `tests/vector-sources-real-samples.test.ts` ran on neither machine).
- **Revisit when**: a metafile writer can carry pictures, masks and dashes (`ai`, `cdr`, `cgm`, `eps`, `ps` and the metafiles to EMF and WMF), the DXF path gets a PDF route in the worker (a vector EPS and a WMF with text), a DWF, Sketch or sK1 reader is included, the reference's 32-pixel icon is wanted, or the corpus gains real Sketch, sK1 or DWG files to measure.
## 188. Subtitle files (SubRip, WebVTT, ASS, SSA and MicroDVD) are converted by FFmpeg in the media sandbox after a text check of ours, FFmpeg's output is repaired where it loses words, and every conversion is read back by a reader that is not FFmpeg

- **Status**: Implemented (a row of the conversion parity work, issue #783), decided 2026-11-08 (QA request: offer the subtitle conversions that reference converters list and this product does not, with FFmpeg in the sandbox the media path already uses, text-only inputs with a size limit, a charset rule and a structure check, and a quality check by a reader other than FFmpeg).
- **Decision**:
  - **Five formats, eleven pairs.** `srt`, `vtt`, `ass`, `ssa` and `sub` (MicroDVD) are registry formats; `srt` goes to `vtt` and `ass`, `vtt` to `srt` and `ass`, `ass` and `ssa` to `srt` and `vtt`, and `sub` to `srt`, `vtt` and `ass`. The reference converters list `srt` to `vtt`, `vtt` to `srt`, `ass` to `srt`, `ssa` to `srt`, `sub` to `srt` and `srt` to `ass`; the other five follow from the same route. SubStation Alpha and MicroDVD are read, not written: FFmpeg writes an `.ssa` file as ASS (`ScriptType: v4.00+`), and a MicroDVD file needs a frame rate that a time-based format does not have. `ssa` to `ass` is left out because FFmpeg carries the SSA header over unchanged (a `.ass` file that still says `[V4 Styles]`), which is not a conversion. The video-extraction targets (`srt`, `vtt`, `ass` from a video with `subtitles.mode: extract`) are unchanged.
  - **Category: document** (changed to a category of its own by entry 196). A category of its own is a new tab, icon and set of Korean words in the interface (a UI change). The formats are text, and the document category holds the text formats, so they sit there, with no option sections. Their descriptions are in `messages/ko.json` like every format's.
  - **The route** (`src/worker/subtitle-route.ts`, pairs in `NATIVE_ENGINE_ONLY_PAIRS`): FFmpeg reads the first subtitle stream of one local file and writes the target with its encoder and muxer (`srt`, `webvtt`, `ass`), started by `runFfmpeg` of the media path: the namespace sandbox with no network, `-protocol_whitelist file` and the demuxer of the format fixed with `-f` (`srt`, `webvtt`, `ass` for both ASS and SSA, `microdvd`), through `openMediaInput`, which also refuses a file that opens like a playlist or a reference list. A worker without FFmpeg answers `EngineUnavailableError` (503), and the in-process engine refuses the pairs by name (`assertNotSubtitlePair`). The limit is 60 s of the job's own time, `-flags +bitexact` keeps FFmpeg's version out of an ASS header, and the output is read back (a file with no cue is `InvalidConversionOutputError`). When FFmpeg exits with an error the answer is a fixed 422 sentence, because FFmpeg's own line names the job's temporary path and memory addresses.
  - **What FFmpeg is given** (`src/lib/conversions/subtitle.ts`): text of the format named, in UTF-8, with at least one cue, within these limits (413 over, 422 for a MicroDVD frame number): 10 MiB, 100,000 cues, 500,000 lines, 20,000 characters in a line (a cue line of a film has under 100, a karaoke or drawing line of typeset ASS a few thousand; FFmpeg took over 2 minutes on one line of 3,000,000 characters after many line breaks), and 100,000 line breaks inside cue text (`\N` and `\n` of SubStation Alpha, `|` of MicroDVD). The limits are far above real files (a film's SubRip has 1,500 to 3,000 cues; typeset ASS with karaoke effects some tens of thousands) and only stop a crafted one: FFmpeg took 15.7 s on a 2 MB ASS file of 1,000,000 `\N`, and its time grows faster than the line breaks (0.2 s at 100,000, 5.6 s at 590,000). A MicroDVD frame number above 100,000,000 is refused, so the 5 seconds given to the last cue never prints in exponent form.
    - **Text only.** The first 64 KiB are read as text (UTF-16 as its byte order mark says): a NUL or another C0 control that text does not use (`libmagic`'s `text_chars` table) refuses the file, so a picture, a VobSub `.sub` (an MPEG program stream) or any binary is turned away at the upload guard (`FileExtensionSpoofError`), and binary data after a good head is refused by the whole-file check (`InvalidSubtitleInputError`, reason `not-text`, 422, code `malformed_input`).
    - **Structure.** The text must open like the format (`src/lib/subtitle-structure.ts`, no dependency, so the registry can use it): SubRip has a `hh:mm:ss,mmm --> hh:mm:ss,mmm` timing line (a time may be negative, as editors that shift a file write it) and does not open with `WEBVTT`; WebVTT opens with `WEBVTT` and has a `(hh:)mm:ss.mmm --> ...` timing line; ASS and SSA open with `[Script Info]` and have a `Dialogue:` line; MicroDVD opens with a `{start}{end}` cue. A MicroDVD file named `.srt`, a WebVTT file named `.srt` or a SubRip file named `.vtt` is a spoofed file; a file of the right opening with no cue is `no-cues`. FFmpeg alone would read a MicroDVD file as SubRip and write an empty subtitle track without an error. The checks and the repairs below take time in proportion to the file (one pass each; a pass that rescanned the lines after every empty line, or the text after every open brace, took 16 to 38 s on a 200 KB to 0.7 MB file made to trigger it, and tests hold them to a hang guard).
    - **Charset.** The text reader of the product (`decodeTextInput`, the reader of plain text input): a byte order mark makes UTF-8 or UTF-16 strict (invalid bytes are refused, `not-text`); a file without one is UTF-8 when its bytes are valid UTF-8, and otherwise legacy text, whose code page the ICU detector names (Windows-1252 when it finds none), and the conversion says which it read (`Text input is not valid UTF-8; it was read as windows-1251.`). FFmpeg gets UTF-8 and never a `-sub_charenc`, so it cannot misread a Korean, Cyrillic or Japanese file as Latin-1. UTF-32 and ISO-2022 files are not read.
  - **Repairs of FFmpeg's text** (`repairSubtitleOutput`, each found by the read-back below on a real file, and pinned by a test).
    - SubRip and WebVTT: an empty line inside a cue is removed (FFmpeg leaves one where a `{\an8}` block and a line break stood, or after two line breaks; an empty line ends a cue, so a player showed an empty cue and lost the words after it); a brace of the text FFmpeg writes as `\{{}` becomes `{`; from SSA and ASS the comments (`{words}`) and the override blocks it does not translate (`{\2c&H5D8FC3&}`) are removed, because FFmpeg writes them as text; from WebVTT `&nbsp;` (FFmpeg: the ASS hard space `\h`) is written as U+00A0.
    - ASS from SubRip and MicroDVD: a block in braces with no backslash (`{braces}`) is escaped (`\{braces}`), because ASS hides it as a comment.
    - MicroDVD: a cue with no end lasts until the next cue starts (FFmpeg works that out); the last one gets 5 seconds and the conversion says so, because FFmpeg writes no cue for it into SubRip and an end of 1193 hours into WebVTT and ASS. A file with no frame rate on its first line (`{1}{1}25.000` or `{0}{}25.000`) is read at 23.976 frames per second, FFmpeg's rate, and the conversion says so.
  - **Time.** Between SubRip and WebVTT a time is exact to the millisecond. ASS counts hundredths of a second: FFmpeg writes the start rounded to the nearest hundredth and the end as that start plus the rounded duration, so a time into ASS is within 5 ms (start) and 10 ms (end) of the source's. A cue whose text is empty after its markup is removed is not a cue to compare.
  - **Quality is read back by a reader that is not FFmpeg** (`bench/subtitle-reader.ts`): SubRip, WebVTT, SubStation Alpha and MicroDVD parsed from the format descriptions with code of its own (no subtitle library is among the project's dependencies, and none was added). It reads the source and the output, and compares the number of cues, the start and end of each (1 ms; 5 and 10 ms into ASS) and the words (markup, override blocks, entities and white space removed). 11 cases of the video family (`bench/families/video-subtitles.ts`, on the five authored files of `tests/fixtures/subtitle`) have rows for `converts`, `cue_count_mismatch`, `cue_timing_mismatches` and `cue_text_mismatches`, each compared with zero. No other tool converts these files with a fixed contract, so the source is the bar. They have no speed row.
- **Why**:
  - The reference converters offer the pairs and FFmpeg, which the worker image already runs in a sandbox for subtitles of video (entry 105), reads and writes the formats. A converter of our own in TypeScript would repeat FFmpeg's readers and add a second place to keep right.
  - FFmpeg takes almost any bytes for some subtitle format, so the checks that decide what a file is, how it is decoded and whether it has a cue have to come first. The read-back found five faults in what FFmpeg wrote on real files (the empty lines, the leaked comments and overrides, `\h`, the hidden braces and the open cue), each of which loses or garbles words.
  - The document category keeps the change out of the interface.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **Styling is not converted, only kept as far as FFmpeg keeps it.** SubRip gets `<i>`, `<b>`, `<u>` and `<font>` from ASS styles (a style with a font size other than 16 becomes a `<font size>` around every cue); WebVTT gets `<i>`, `<b>` and `<u>`; the positions (`{\an8}`, `align:`) are dropped between SubRip, WebVTT and the other formats; ASS made from SubRip or WebVTT has FFmpeg's default style (Arial 16, white, a 384 by 288 script) and no WebVTT region or cue setting. The words, order and times are the conversion.
  - A **legacy code page is a guess** by the ICU detector, as it is for text files. The conversion names the code page it read; a short file of few non-ASCII bytes is read as Windows-1252.
  - A **MicroDVD frame rate that the file does not name** is assumed (23.976), and the times are only as right as that assumption. The 5 seconds of the last open cue is a convention, not data.
  - FFmpeg's other readers of subtitles (SubViewer, SAMI, JACOsub, MPL2, PJS, RealText, STL, LRC) and the picture formats (VobSub, PGS, DVB) are not offered; `.sub` means MicroDVD, and a SubViewer or VobSub `.sub` is refused.
  - A **cue that ends before zero** (the shifted files of an editor) is dropped by FFmpeg 9; FFmpeg 6.1, which the CI runner has, reads `-0:00:06.84` as a positive time. The file converts either way, and the tests that compare cue for cue use files without negative times.
  - A file of 10 MiB is read whole in memory (twice, as bytes and as text); a subtitle file of any real film is 100 KB, and an ASS file with embedded fonts a few megabytes.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A converter in TypeScript** (parse, write, no process): the formats are small, but each has many dialects (SubRip with ASS overrides, WebVTT cue settings, SSA styles, MicroDVD codes), and FFmpeg already carries them; ours would be the second place to keep them right, and the read-back would not be independent of it.
  - **A category `subtitle`**: a UI change (tab, icon, words in two languages) for five formats; the document category has the text formats.
  - **A subtitle library for the read-back** (a Python or Node package): a new dependency of the runners and of the image for a check. The reader is 200 lines in the benchmark, written from the format descriptions, and the real files of the corpus keep it honest.
  - **Writing `ssa` and `sub` as targets**: FFmpeg's `ssa` is ASS under another name, and MicroDVD needs a frame rate the pair does not have (a 25 fps default would be a guess in the other direction).
  - **`-sub_charenc` with a guessed code page**: FFmpeg would then decode a whole file with one guess, and name nothing; the product's text reader decodes it, names the code page and refuses invalid Unicode.
- **Verified by**: `tests/subtitle-pairs.test.ts` (the eleven pairs on five authored files, each output read back and compared with the source; 11 real files of the real-world corpus (`bench/realworld/manifest.json`: FFmpeg's test suite, libass and Popcorn.js) converted to every target and compared cue for cue, and seven more that other tools wrote malformed or with times before zero, converted without a crash or an empty cue; UTF-8 with a byte order mark, UTF-16 in both byte orders, a Korean legacy code page; the refusals (a picture, a MicroDVD, WebVTT and SubRip file under another name, VobSub, binary after a good head, no cue, over the size limit, invalid UTF-16, no FFmpeg); the repairs; a file of 12,000 cues), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` (the pairs are native-engine pairs: an unavailable engine without FFmpeg, a file with it), `tests/refusal-code-inventory.test.ts` (`InvalidSubtitleInputError` answers `malformed_input`), `tests/corpus-format-coverage.test.ts` (every format has three real samples), and the 44 rows of the video family on the Lima VM.
- **Revisit when**: a subtitle format beyond these five is asked for (the text and structure checks take another format), a reader of SubStation Alpha styles is wanted for real ASS output (`ssa` to `ass`, styled SubRip), FFmpeg writes SubRip, WebVTT and ASS without the faults repaired here (each repair has a test that names it), or a QA decision gives subtitles a category of their own.


## 190. QA 2026-11-08: one-maintainer workflow

- **Status**: Implemented (QA 2026-11-08).
- **Decision**:
  - **One maintainer commits to `main`; CI runs on every push.** `ci.yml` compares a push with the commit it replaces (`github.event.before`): a docs-only push skips the heavy jobs, a push that changes a conversion family runs parity quality for it, and a push with no comparable base runs everything. The `pull_request` trigger stays for a branch someone proposes.
  - **Removed:** the issue forms, the pull request template and the release template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, `RELEASE_TEMPLATE.md`), `automerge.yml`, and `report-failure.yml` with the jobs of the nightly and regression corpus runs that called it. The `security` label exemption of the parity verdict and its `parity-gap` issues went with them (`scripts/ci-parity-policy.mjs` only decides pass or fail).
  - **A failure is visible without an issue.** A failed scheduled run shows in Actions and GitHub emails the owner; the job summaries and artifacts stay. Remaining work is listed in `TODO.md`.
  - **A release** is tagged per deploy with a short hand-written note (`docs/deploy-oci.md`, "Releases").
- **Why**: with one person there is no reviewer to hand a pull request to and no one to triage an issue for, so the templates, the label-driven merge and the auto-opened issues were ceremony. The CI gate that stops a bad change is kept.
- **Trade-offs**: a bad commit reaches `main` before CI judges it, and the owner reverts or fixes forward; a streak of nightly failures is a streak of emails, not one thread.
- **Alternatives rejected**: keeping pull requests as the gate (cost with no second reader); keeping the nightly issue (a second place to look at the same failure).
- **Verified by**: `tests/ci-workflows.test.ts`, `tests/ci-parity-workflow.test.ts`, `tests/ci-parity-policy.test.ts`, `tests/regression-corpus-workflow.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: a second maintainer joins, or a change needs a review before it lands.

## 189. JPEG XL pictures are read by libjxl's `djxl` as a separate sandboxed program, from the bare codestream and from the container, and an animation is read as a GIF or WebP is

- **Status**: Implemented (a row of the conversion parity work, issue #783), decided 2026-11-08 (QA request: accept the one input format the reference service converts and this product did not).
- **Decision**:
  - **The pairs.** `jxl` is an input with the 13 targets the reference service's formats API lists for it (read on 2026-11-08): `avif`, `bmp`, `eps`, `gif`, `ico`, `jpg`, `odd`, `pdf`, `png`, `ps`, `psd`, `tiff` and `webp`. The registry offers no `zip` for it (the reference does not), and `jxl` is not a target. HEIC reaches all 13 of these.
  - **The decoder is libjxl's `djxl`** (the Debian 13 package `libjxl-tools`, 0.11.2, BSD-3-Clause with the project's patent grant), installed through `apt` in `Dockerfile.worker` beside the other picture tools and run as the entry 38 decoders are: an unmodified separate program in the process sandbox (`executeSandboxedBinary`) with no network, a time limit (`DECODER_TIMEOUT_MS`, 120 s), a resident-memory limit (3,072 MB), an output-size limit, two threads (`--num_threads=2`), a private 0700 directory and fixed file names (`in.jxl`, `out.png`) with an argument vector that holds no request text. It writes a PNG (an APNG for an animation, 16 bits per sample for a picture of more than 8) and that file goes through the same pipeline as any PNG. The build fails if `djxl` does not start, also as the unprivileged user. `DJXL_PATH` names another executable (an absolute path; one that is not an executable file means "not installed", HTTP 503 as for the other decoders).
  - **Signatures** (`src/lib/format-signatures.ts`): the bare codestream opens with `FF 0A`, the container with the 12-byte signature box `00 00 00 0C 4A 58 4C 20 0D 0A 87 0A` (ISO/IEC 18181-2). Both sniff as `image/jxl`, a `.jxl` name takes only them, and they are refused under any other name; the ADTS and MP3 sniffers (`FF F?`, `FF E?`) and the ISO base media sniffer are untouched (`FF 0A` is neither, and the signature box is not an `ftyp` box).
  - **Limits before the decoder starts.** The size comes from the SizeHeader at the start of the codestream (ISO/IEC 18181-1), read in the application without decoding: from a bare codestream, from the `jxlc` box, or from the `jxlp` boxes in order. The pixel limit of every still reader applies (`assertInputPixels`, 100 megapixels by default, 413 with `input_over_limit`), so a few bytes that declare 30,000 x 30,000 pixels are refused unread. A header that cannot be read is `Invalid image: the JPEG XL header could not be decoded` (422), a picture the decoder refuses `Invalid image: the JPEG XL picture could not be decoded`; its own words go to the log. The size of the PNG the sandbox lets the decoder write is 8 bytes a pixel of the declared size, and at least the 512 MiB that bounds any decoded animation (the header does not count frames).
  - **An animation** is read as an APNG is: still targets take frame 1 (`sourceFrameCount` and `frameUsed` report it, `page` selects another frame), `gif` and `webp` keep every frame with its delay and the loop count, and the budgets of any decoded animation (4,096 frames, 512 MiB of decoded frames) apply. This is the rule the pipeline has for GIF, WebP and APNG, because the decoder's APNG is what the pipeline reads.
  - **Metadata.** The orientation of the codestream header is applied by the decoder (a picture stated as 500 x 606 with orientation 5 is 606 x 500). The colour description the decoder writes (an ICC profile, or the sRGB, gamma and chromaticity chunks, and `cICP` in 0.7) is kept, and the pipeline treats it as it does for HEIC: converted to sRGB for PNG and TIFF, attached for JPEG. The EXIF block, which the decoder writes into a text chunk (`Raw profile type exif`) that the image library ignores, is copied into the `eXIf` chunk (`src/lib/conversions/image-jxl-exif.ts`) with its Orientation set to 1, so it reaches JPEG, WebP and PNG outputs and a viewer never turns the picture twice: libjxl 0.7 leaves the tag of the Exif box in the block, and writes the offset field of the box (4 bytes, 0) in front of the TIFF header, libjxl 0.11 writes an `Exif\0\0` prefix and Orientation 1. A text chunk that is not a well-formed profile is left alone.
- **Why**:
  - **It is the reference implementation, from the distribution.** `djxl` is what the format's authors ship; Debian patches it for security, so the image takes fixes with `apt-get upgrade`. Neither the libvips of the prebuilt `sharp` binaries, nor Debian's ImageMagick (7.1.1.43, no JPEG XL coder and no dependency on libjxl), nor the pinned FFmpeg 9.0.2 (built without libjxl) reads the format, and a decoder in a separate process keeps a parser of untrusted input out of the application's address space, as for HEIC and JPEG 2000.
  - **The image grows by little.** Estimated from the Debian 13 package index for the whole install list of the runner stage (dependencies resolved by their first alternative; no image was built, there is no Docker here): `libjxl-tools` adds 923 KiB (amd64) or 939 KiB (arm64) installed and `libtcmalloc-minimal4t64` 374 or 414 KiB, 1.3 MB in all, because `libjxl0.11` and `libhwy1t64` (with `libavcodec61`), `libopenexr-3-1-30` (with `libfreeimage3`) and `libgif7` (with FontForge) are in the image already. On a bare Debian 13 base the same package would bring 11 packages and 18.8 MB (amd64). The first build confirms the figure in `/licenses/tool-versions.txt`.
  - **The pairs are the reference's, and the writers are the ones the sources of entry 38 use**, so a JPEG XL picture needs no new encoder.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - One more process per conversion (measured on the arm64 Lima VM with the Debian 13 build of `djxl` 0.11.2, unpacked there: a 24-megapixel picture decodes in 1.09 s with 226 MB resident, a 100-megapixel one in 4.60 s with 900 MB, and the product converts that picture to JPEG in 6.4 s; the memory limit of 3,072 MB is three times the largest picture the pixel limit lets in).
  - The PNG between decoder and encoder costs a write and a read (a 1-megapixel photograph: 1 MB). The AVIF row of `jxl-bicycles.jxl` measured 0.869 of the reference's speed (confidence interval 0.843 to 0.880 over 7 pairs; WebP 1.02, JPEG 0.97), the reference being `djxl` and `avifenc` as two commands; ours adds the sandbox start and the PNG read. Not changed here.
  - `djxl` 0.7.0 (Ubuntu 24.04, the CI runner) cannot write a picture whose alpha is deeper than its colour (`alpha_premultiplied`: 12-bit colour, 16-bit alpha) and answers with the typed 422; 0.11 converts it. A 16-bit picture of 0.7 carries an sRGB profile and `cICP` where 0.11 writes `sRGB`, so the profile's transform rounds a sample by up to 0.4 percent of the range (the tests allow 512 of 65,535).
  - The PNG that the product writes for an 8-bit picture is larger than the reference's (zlib level 8 and no adaptive row filter; the page pictures of entry 34 use one, and that entry measured a photograph 75 percent larger without it). Adaptive filtering with level 6 writes the decoded `jxl-bicycles.jxl` as 1,000,922 bytes in 43 ms, against 1,564,524 bytes in 29 ms as the product writes it (one encode each, on an Apple silicon host): the PNG target of `jxl-bicycles.jxl` is 1,523,900 bytes against 973,150, `jxl-delta-palette.jxl` 1,058,400 against 523,480 and `jxl-noise.jxl` 857,370 against 815,970. This is the encoder's existing choice for every source; the rows are in the benchmark and fail the parity gate until it is revisited (see the open items).
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **A libvips build with libjxl** (a rebuild of the `sharp` binaries, `docker/sharp-libvips`): the product would own the build and the ship of an LGPL library for one format, and the decoder would be inside the application's process. The application does not use the distribution's libvips either.
  - **The upstream static build of libjxl's tools** (the project's release archives): x86-64 only, so not for the arm64 OCI Ampere A1 host, and outside the distribution's security updates.
  - **A WebAssembly decoder in the application**: slower than native code with SIMD, bounded by the WebAssembly memory, a new npm dependency and licence to track, and again the parser of untrusted input inside the process.
  - **ImageMagick or FFmpeg**: neither of the image's builds has the codec (above).
  - **One frame only for an animation**: loses what GIF and WebP targets can carry, and the pipeline's rule for animations is the product's choice for the other animated sources.
- **Verified by**: `tests/image-jxl-header.test.ts` (the SizeHeader of every length form and aspect ratio, the container's box forms, the signatures and the spoof check), `tests/image-jxl-exif.test.ts` (the EXIF chunk from the layouts of both libjxl generations and the cases it leaves alone), `tests/image-jxl-decode.test.ts` (lossless files written by `cjxl` from known pixels as codestreams and containers at 8 and 16 bits and to all 13 targets read back by ImageMagick; eight conformance files of the libjxl project, `bench/realworld/manifest.json`, against a reference decode by `djxl`; the orientation, the profile, the animation, the limits and the stand-in decoder), `tests/registry-engine-conformance.test.ts` (the 13 pairs with `tests/fixtures/images/probe.jxl`), the real-world judge (104 jobs, the eight files to all 13 targets, and the nightly plan of 24: all ok, none refused, on the Lima VM with `djxl` 0.11.2) and the image parity rows (`jxl-bicycles.jxl`, `jxl-noise.jxl` and `jxl-delta-palette.jxl` to PNG, JPEG, WebP and AVIF, `bench/families/image.ts` and `image-jxl.ts`). The tests ran on the Lima VM with `djxl` 0.7.0 (Ubuntu 24.04, the CI toolchain) and 0.11.2 (the Debian 13 build). Not run: a build of `Dockerfile.worker` (no Docker here), so the size above is an estimate from the package index.
- **Revisit when**: the CI runner gets a libjxl newer than 0.7, the 8-bit PNG encoder gets adaptive row filtering (the `png` rows of the JPEG XL samples are then at the reference), the JPEG encoder is brought to the reference on noisy pictures (`jxl-noise.jxl` to JPEG measured +5.2 percent BD-rate in PSNR, the same bytes as the PNG of the same pixels), the AVIF path avoids the PNG between decoder and encoder, or JPEG XL is wanted as a target.

## 191. A Sigma SD15 X3F is read with its Sunlight calibration when the header says Daylight, a developed RAW picture is rewritten in the buffer it was read into, and a Nikon high-efficiency NEF stays refused until a released LibRaw reads it

- **Status**: Implemented for the first two points, decided 2026-11-08 (QA request: the three RAW rows of `TODO.md`: the Samsung Galaxy S23 DNG, the Nikon Z f NEF and Sigma SD15 X3F, and the Pixel 6 Pro DNG to PDF memory). The third point records what was found and changes nothing. Entry 195 acts on the Nikon finding.
- **Decision**:
  - **A Sigma X3F whose header names "Daylight" and whose calibration has no Daylight entry is read with the "Sunlight" entries** (`findWhiteBalanceEntry` in `src/lib/conversions/raw-x3f.ts`). The SD15 sample (`_SDI5651.X3F`, 2640 x 1760 sensor layers, TRUE-coded sensor data) lists `SunlightWBGain`, `SunlightCCMatrix` and the other white balances of the camera, and no `DaylightWBGain`, so the decoder refused it with `no WBGain calibration for the "Daylight" white balance`. The x3f tools (BSD-licensed, `src/x3f_meta.c`, `x3f_get_camf_matrix_for_wb`: "Workaround for bug in SD1") make the same exchange when a "Daylight" finds no entry. A header that names any other white balance is looked up as before, and a Daylight entry, when the file has one, is used first.
  - **The developed picture of a camera file is rewritten in place** (`readDecodedRawImage` in `src/worker/raw-decoded-tiff.ts`, `withoutAbsoluteResolution(..., { inPlace: true })`). The decoder's TIFF is read into a buffer that only the conversion holds, and the resolution unit was changed in a copy of it, so a 12.5 megapixel picture (75 MB of 16-bit samples) was held twice for the rest of the conversion. The bytes written are the same: the PNG, JPEG and TIFF of the Pixel 6 Pro file have the same SHA-256 before and after.
  - **The Samsung Galaxy S23 DNG already converts; nothing was changed for it.** Entry 140 (#945) accepts LibRaw's `data corrupted at` line for a DNG that holds every strip of its raw image. On the CI image's LibRaw (0.21.2, Ubuntu 24.04, measured on the Lima testbed) `tests/raw-native-decoder-warning.test.ts` passes: the file is developed to JPEG and PNG at 4000 x 2252 with the warning. The `TODO.md` line described the state before that entry.
  - **A Nikon NEF with high-efficiency compression (HE, HE*) stays refused**, and this is the finding for the Nikon Z f sample (`DSC_0043.NEF`, `NEFCompression` "High Efficiency" in the maker note, 14 bit, 6064 x 4040). The CI runner and the worker image carry the distribution's LibRaw (0.21.2 on Ubuntu 24.04, 0.21.4 on Debian 13), which has no decoder for it: it prints `data corrupted at 4275203` for the sample, and the engine refuses any stderr line from a NEF (entry 140). LibRaw 0.22.2 refuses the same file with `Unsupported file format or not RAW file`. The decoder exists only in the development branch of LibRaw: `src/decoders/nikonhe.cpp` (3,013 lines, LGPL-2.1 or CDDL-1.0) came with "LibRaw snapshot 202611" of 2026-11-05, whose changelog lists "Nikon HE/HE* format (Z6-III, Z8, Z9, Zf cameras)"; the file is absent from the tags 0.21.2, 0.21.4 and 0.22.3 (released 2026-10-26, a bug-fix release). Not run: a build of that snapshot, which is code from outside the repository.
- **Why**: the SD15 file is a real camera file that was refused for a name, and the exchange is the one the reference implementation has. The extra copy was the avoidable part of the peak of the DNG-to-PDF row; the rest of the peak is the developed picture itself and the page that is built from it.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - The SD15 read relies on the colour matrix and gains of the Sunlight entries being the camera's "Daylight" ones, as the x3f tools assume; the picture was checked against the full-size picture the camera embedded in the file (luma correlation above 0.95 on a 64 x 44 grid, same 2640 x 1760 size), not against another decoder's output.
  - Memory of the Pixel 6 Pro DNG to PDF (Lima testbed, aarch64, Node 24, the dispatcher called with the file in memory, resident size of the Node process sampled every 10 ms, `dcraw_emu` the same 151 MB in both): 469, 493, 469, 493 and 498 MB before, 438 (first run, which also filled the TypeScript cache), 420, 424, 426 and 401 MB after, so the median falls from 493 to 424 MB. About 235 MB of both is the loaded program before the conversion starts. The row still holds the TIFF (75 MB), the page PNG (21 MB) and the PDF chunks at the end, so three of these jobs side by side need about 1.3 GB of the Node processes alone.
  - A Nikon HE NEF is refused with the decoder's own words, not a message that names the codec. `NEFCompression` could be read from the maker note before the decoder runs, which would also make the answer the same for every LibRaw version; it is not done here.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Building the LibRaw snapshot into the worker image and the CI runner**: it would read the Z f file, but it is an unreleased snapshot of a library that every other RAW row uses, with a decoder that holds about 8 bytes per sensor pixel in 3 passes (the changelog's estimate: 400 MB for a 45 megapixel Z 9), needs a pinned build in two places, and every other RAW row would move to the new library. It needs a decision on the build and a new RAW family check; it was not started.
  - **A TypeScript port of `nikonhe.cpp`**: 3,000 lines of LGPL/CDDL code, copy-left, not the permissive source the RAW work copies, and a second maintained decoder for one codec.
  - **Falling back to the preview in the file**: the engine does that only for a file the decoder does not recognise and only when the request allows it; a developed picture at 24 megapixels and a preview of a few are different conversions.
- **Verified by**: `tests/raw-x3f-sunlight-white-balance.test.ts` (the header and calibration names of the real SD15 file, and its conversion to PNG and JPEG against the picture the camera embedded), `tests/image-print-density-reader.test.ts` (the in-place rewrite changes the one byte and returns the same object), `tests/raw-native-decoder-warning.test.ts` (the S23 file on LibRaw 0.21.2), `tests/raw-dng-pdf-embed.test.ts` (the Pixel 6 Pro file to PDF).
- **Revisit when**: a LibRaw release (or the distribution's package) contains the Nikon HE decoder, the worker image builds LibRaw from source for another reason, a Sigma file shows another white balance name that the calibration spells differently, or the developed picture is handed to the encoder from its file instead of a buffer.

## 192. An OpenXML workbook that holds one part name twice is refused as a typed error, and the empty files the real-world corpus expects are marked

- **Status**: Implemented (QA 2026-11-08, TODO item "empty or wrong-format output").
- **Decision**:
  - **A workbook (XLSX, XLSM) whose ZIP holds one part name twice is a typed 400 error to CSV, TSV and every other target** (`openOpcPackage`): "The XLSX package holds the part … more than once, so it has no single content to read." The ZIP reader kept the last of the two entries and the cells of the first were dropped, so `duplicate-filename.xlsx` of the Apache POI test data (a sheet part twice, `v1` as a shared string and `v2` as an inline string with no `<is>`) was returned as an empty file, a success with an `emptyOutput` warning, for a workbook that does hold a cell.
  - **The other pairs of the TODO item were checked on the real files and stay as entry 8 has them.** All 450 saved pages of the govdocs1 sample to TXT and Markdown, the 352 XLSX and 14 XLSM workbooks to CSV and TSV and the 4 DOTX templates to TXT of the real-world corpus give either text, an empty file with the `emptyOutput` warning for an input with nothing to write, or a typed refusal. The empty files not yet marked in the corpus manifest were two frameset-only pages, `govdocs1-001422.html` and `govdocs1-001781.html` (the same three frames as `govdocs1-001421.html`, which was marked); both now carry `emptyInput` with the reason, which makes 52 marked files. A workbook of CSV and TSV is written with every sheet, each under a `### Sheet:` line, so an empty first sheet does not hide a later one.
  - **PDF/A-1b rule 6.7.3-1 already holds on the current code (entry 149); no code changed.** veraPDF 1.30.2 (`--flavour 1b`) failed the 9 LibreOffice 24.2.7 exports of Word documents it was given (created and modified dates with a `Z`, a fraction, an offset, a date only, the year 1601, a modified date before the created date, and no dates) on rule 6.7.3-1; after `normalisePdfADates` none fails 6.7.3-1 or 6.7.3-8, and neither do 40 corpus PDFs read by the Draw filter on the same LibreOffice, nor 18 hand-written `/Info` and XMP date pairs (a missing side, no time zone, no seconds, a fraction, a date cut after the year, an attribute form, the `xap` prefix). `tests/pdfa-1b-dates.test.ts` gained eight cases of the same kind.
- **Why**: a package that names a part twice is not valid under OPC (ECMA-376 Part 2, 10.1.2.1), and which of the two a reader sees is the reader's accident; the Apache POI reader refuses such a file for the same reason. A refusal tells the sender the file is broken, where an empty CSV says the sheet is.
- **Trade-offs**: a workbook that Excel opens (it takes one of the entries) is refused here. Only XLSX and XLSM use the check; the other packages (DOCX, PPTX, ODF, EPUB, CBZ) read as before.
- **Alternatives rejected**: reading the first entry instead of the last (equally arbitrary); checking every package kind (a comic archive with a repeated page name is a file people have, and the page order is the order of the entries).
- **Verified by**: `tests/empty-output-pairs.test.ts` (HTML, XLSX, XLSM and DOTX to the text targets: empty with a warning, content written, a duplicated part refused), `tests/conversion-output-check.test.ts`, and the 450 pages, 366 workbooks and 4 templates of the corpus converted before and after (the only change is `duplicate-filename.xlsx`).
- **Revisit when**: a real workbook that Excel opens carries a repeated part name, or the other OOXML readers are found to read one wrongly.

## 194. The web container's health check asks a liveness route that touches no dependency; `/api/health` stays the readiness probe

- **Status**: Implemented (QA 2026-11-08, TODO item "split a liveness route from /api/health").
- **Decision**:
  - **`GET /api/health/live` answers 200 `{"status":"alive"}` while the process serves requests.** It imports nothing but the framework and reads nothing of the request, so Redis, storage and the worker cannot turn it red. `GET /api/health` keeps its readiness meaning (Redis PING, storage, advisory tools; 503 when a required dependency is down) and is what the Uptime workflow and `deploy/oci/deploy.sh` still ask.
  - **The `HEALTHCHECK` of `Dockerfile.web` asks the liveness route.** `deploy.sh` still waits for the readiness answer of `/api/health` for up to 150 seconds before it calls a release started, so a release whose Redis or storage is down is still rolled back.
  - **The edge middleware treats both paths as health probes:** `GET` and `HEAD` are exempt from the shared bucket of unattributed clients and stay up while the client-IP trust mode is undeclared. A client that is attributable is limited per client as before.
  - **The route sits under `/api/health/`, so the host proxy's 404 for that prefix already keeps it on the loopback port**; `nginx-easyconvert.conf` is unchanged.
- **Why**: a container health check is a restart signal, and restarting the web process does not repair Redis or storage; a readiness check there makes a dependency outage look like a dead web container (and, with `up --wait`, delays or fails a start for a reason that is not the web process). Separate liveness and readiness probes are the usual practice for container platforms.
- **Trade-offs**: `docker ps` no longer shows a web container as unhealthy while Redis is down; the Uptime workflow and `deploy.sh` are where that shows. The liveness route proves the HTTP server answers, not that the event loop is free of long synchronous work beyond the check's 8 second timeout.
- **Alternatives rejected**: `/api/livez` (a second prefix to block at the proxy); keeping one route with a query switch (a probe URL that changes meaning by query is easy to misconfigure).
- **Verified by**: `tests/health-live-route.test.ts` (200 with the readiness probes and the key guard replaced by modules that fail when loaded, and the route's imports), `tests/middleware-client-ip-rate-limit.test.ts` (the exemptions of the two paths), `tests/oci-deploy.test.ts` (the `HEALTHCHECK` asks `/api/health/live`).
- **Revisit when**: the platform restarts containers on an unhealthy status and a stuck event loop needs to be caught, which would call for a probe that checks event-loop lag.

## 195. A Nikon NEF with High Efficiency compression is developed by a pinned LibRaw development snapshot run as a separate program, and every other camera file keeps the distribution's LibRaw

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA approved fetching the LibRaw development source pinned to an exact commit and building and running it on the Lima testbed to verify; no deploy is approved, nothing is deployed). It replaces the third point of entry 191, which recorded that such a NEF stays refused.
- **Decision**:
  - **The compression is read from the maker note before any decoder runs** (`src/worker/raw-nef-compression.ts`): tag 0x0051 of the Nikon maker note (a 24-byte block whose SHORT at offset 10 is the compression) in the Z 6III, Z 8, Z 9 and Z f, tag 0x0093 (a SHORT) in older bodies, 13 for "High Efficiency" and 14 for "High Efficiency*" (the tables of ExifTool's Nikon module). Only a file of a Nikon maker note of the layout with a TIFF header of its own that records 13 or 14 is a High Efficiency file; a file that is not a TIFF, has no Exif directory or maker note, or is cut inside them reads as "not High Efficiency" and goes to the distribution's decoder as before. At most a few hundred bytes are read.
  - **Such a NEF is developed by a second `dcraw_emu`** (`convertWithNativeRaw`, `rawDecoderFor` in `src/worker/raw-decode-settings.ts`): the one named by `DCRAW_EMU_HE_PATH`, or found at `/usr/local/bin/dcraw_emu_he` or `/opt/libraw-he/bin/dcraw_emu`. It runs with the same flags and in the same sandbox as the distribution's (`-T -6 -w -o 1`, no network, 4 GB address space), and its stderr and the developed TIFF go through the same checks. Every other camera file, NEF files of other compressions and every other format included, runs the distribution's `dcraw_emu` as before, so no existing output changes. Where the second program is not installed, the distribution's runs and refuses the file with its own words (`data corrupted at 4275203` for the Z f sample), as it did before this entry; where the distribution's is missing the engine is unavailable as before.
  - **The program is built from one commit of the LibRaw development branch** (`scripts/install-libraw-he.sh`): `a9a14b1970d188c25dade81f8326ff00a6e33649`, the head of `master` on 2026-11-08 when it was chosen (the snapshot commit `4d9bd21acdf3` of 2026-11-04, which brought `src/decoders/nikonhe.cpp`, and the fixes after it; the library reports itself as 0.23.0 snapshot 202611). The script fetches that commit by its hash, stops unless the fetched commit is exactly it, exports the tree (no patch), and builds `lib/libraw.a` and `bin/dcraw_emu` with the project's `Makefile.dist` and `-O3 -fopenmp -D_FORTIFY_SOURCE=2 -fstack-protector-strong`, without the optional zlib, JPEG and LCMS support (this program is run on NEF files only and writes the built-in sRGB). The result is one program that needs only the C, C++ and OpenMP libraries the image already has (the distribution's `libraw-bin` pulls in the same `libgomp1`).
  - **Two places build it.** `Dockerfile.worker` has a `librawhe` stage (`build-essential`, `git`) and the runner copies `bin/dcraw_emu` to `/usr/local/bin/dcraw_emu_he` with its licence texts and a `SOURCE` note naming the commit (`/licenses/libraw-he.copyright`, `/licenses/libraw-he.SOURCE`), and checks that it starts. The CI setup (`.github/actions/ci-setup`) builds it as the `libraw` task, caches `/opt/libraw-he` by the hash of the script and links it as `/usr/local/bin/dcraw_emu_he`. The licensing notes are section 2.16 of `docs/licensing.md` (`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is generated from the npm lock file and holds no system tool).
  - **The reference of the RAW family decodes such a NEF with the same build** (`bench/families/raw.ts`): without it the Z 9 sample is a `converts` row against a reference that cannot develop the file and no quality row; with it the row is scored like every other sample (the product against the same development plus the reference encoder).
- **Why**: a Nikon Z f or Z 9 file is a current camera's file, and High Efficiency is a setting people use to save card space; the only decoder for it is in the LibRaw development branch, and a release is not scheduled. A separate program built from a fixed commit gives the files a decoder without moving any other RAW row to an unreleased library, and without linking anything: the application sees a file in and a TIFF out, as with the distribution's program.
- **Measured** (Lima testbed, aarch64, 4 CPUs, the pinned build, `-T -6 -w -o 1`; `/usr/bin/time -v`, three runs each):
  - Nikon Z f `DSC_0043.NEF` (13,462,016 bytes, 6064 x 4040): TIFF of 146,993,232 bytes, 0.53 to 0.69 s, peak resident size 279,340 KiB (286 MB). Nikon Z 9 `Nikon_-_NIKON_Z_9_-_14bit_compressed_(Lossy_High_Efficiency).NEF` (24,839,168 bytes, 8280 x 5520): TIFF of 274,235,472 bytes, 0.98 to 1.45 s, peak 504,164 KiB (516 MB), 11.3 bytes per sensor pixel (the changelog estimates 400 MB for a 45-megapixel Z 9). Neither prints a line on stderr.
  - The developed pictures are the sensor frame LibRaw reports, 6064 x 4040 and 8280 x 5520, 16 x 8 and 24 x 16 pixels larger than the 6048 x 4032 and 8256 x 5504 pictures the cameras embedded; the margin holds picture content (the mean of the outermost 8 columns of the Z f picture is 0.386 against 0.387 for the next 8), not black. Against the full-size JPEG each camera embedded (`exiftool -b -JpgFromRaw`), the luma of a 64 x 44 grid correlates at 0.980 (Z f) and 0.977 (Z 9), above the 0.95 bar of the SD15 check; the Z f picture was also looked at beside the camera's, and the Z 9 picture alone (a street scene with a yellow sculpture, no visible block or colour fault).
  - Through the product (`dispatchConversion`, the pinned build selected by the maker note), both files convert to JPEG and PNG at those sizes with no warning and the same correlation test (`tests/raw-nikon-he-decode.test.ts`: the PNG of the Z f took 2.7 s and of the Z 9 8.5 s, correlation test included).
  - The `raw` family on the Lima testbed with the pinned build (strict mode, 381 rows): 0 failing and no gate regression. The Z 9 sample, a `converts` row against a reference that could not develop it before, now measures 41.844 dB PSNR and SSIM 0.9689 against the reference's 42.137 dB and 0.96943 at quality 70 (within the allowance of 0.3 dB and 0.003), 3,764,400 bytes against 4,269,600, BD-rate -5.3 % (PSNR) and -9.7 % (SSIM); its PNG has SSIM 0.99996 and 226.2 MB against 225.1 MB. A run that shares the testbed's disk with another run failed the PNG of this sample, and of the Canon R5 CR3 files, with `ENOSPC`: the family keeps about 11 GB of scratch files in `/tmp` until it ends, and a 30 GB testbed with another run's files has less than that free.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - A snapshot of an unreleased library parses the JPEG XS stream of a file from outside, in C++, and nothing was fuzzed here. The exposure is the one the distribution's program has (a separate process, no network, a private directory, an address-space limit, and only for files whose maker note says High Efficiency), but this code has had less use. The decoder holds about 11 bytes per sensor pixel (516 MB for the 45-megapixel Z 9) against the 4 GB limit, and the product then reads the 274 MB TIFF.
  - The pin is moved by hand and the build exists in two places (the image and the CI setup), at about 26 CPU seconds each time the CI cache misses. A camera body added to LibRaw's High Efficiency list after the pin reads only after the pin is moved (the decoder is chosen by LibRaw from the model name and the stream header, not by this code).
  - The developed colour is LibRaw's for the model and not the camera's: the luma matches the embedded picture at 0.98, not pixel for pixel, as for every other RAW row.
  - A High Efficiency NEF is still refused where the program is absent, with the distribution's words; the refusal does not name the codec.
- **Alternatives rejected**:
  - **Waiting for a release**: the snapshot's changelog lists the Z 6III, Z 8, Z 9 and Z f, and the distribution's package of a release that has the decoder (0.23) is further away still; QA approved the pinned build.
  - **Replacing the distribution's LibRaw with the snapshot for every RAW file**: it would move every other RAW row (and the memory of every decode) to an unreleased library for one codec.
  - **A tarball with a SHA-256**, as the other pinned tools use: the archive GitHub makes for a commit is not a promised byte-for-byte file, while the commit hash names the content; the script fetches by hash and compares.
  - **Linking LibRaw into the application, or a TypeScript port of the 3,000-line decoder**: copy-left code inside our own, and a second maintained decoder (entry 191).
  - **Falling back to the embedded preview**: a 24-megapixel developed picture and a preview of a few are different conversions (entry 191).
- **Verified by**: `tests/raw-nef-compression.test.ts` (byte-built maker notes in both layouts, both byte orders, every value 0 to 19, damaged and cut files, wild offsets, and the real Z f, Z 9 and scanner NEF), `tests/raw-nikon-he-decode.test.ts` (stand-in decoders show which program runs for which file, the distribution's words where the pinned build is absent, and the real Z f and Z 9 files to JPEG and PNG against the camera's picture where the build is installed; a strict run fails where it is not), `tests/worker-libraw-he-packaging.test.ts` (the stage, the copy, the pin and its check, the CI task and cache key, the licensing note), the stage and task lists in `tests/runtime-baseline.test.ts`, `tests/phase-4-security-and-sandbox-hardening.test.ts`, `tests/ci-setup-tasks.test.ts` and `tests/ci-install-apt-tools.test.ts`, and the `raw` family above. The image itself was not built here: no container runtime is installed on the testbed, so the `librawhe` stage and its start check run first in the CI image build; the script ran on the testbed (Ubuntu 24.04, GCC 13.3, aarch64).
- **Revisit when**: a LibRaw release with the Nikon decoder reaches the distribution's package (drop the stage, the script and the CI task), the pin needs to move (a new body, a decoder fix), a fuzz run or a report finds a fault in the decoder, or a High Efficiency file shows a maker note this reader does not recognise.

## 196. Subtitle formats are a catalogue category of their own, and the home format tiles start on DOCX to PDF

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA approved the screen fixes from the review against the two reference converters, item 8 and item 3). It replaces the category point of entry 188.
- **Decision**:
  - **`subtitle` is a registry category** holding `srt`, `vtt`, `ass`, `ssa` and `sub`. The format catalogue on the home page and the format picker show it as a tab of its own (Korean 자막, English Subtitles) after Audio, with the captions glyph and three common pairs (`srt` to `vtt`, `vtt` to `srt`, `ass` to `srt`).
  - **No URL changes.** Every page of a subtitle pair keeps its slug. The category has no `/subtitle-converter` page: `CategoryWord` leaves it out, so the sitemap and the category pages are as before. The page copy of a subtitle format names it by `files.kind.subtitle` ("자막" in place of "문서").
  - **Routing and limits are untouched.** The route is chosen by format id, not by category (`src/worker/subtitle-route.ts`); a subtitle source stays in the `document` deadline family (`DOCUMENT_CATEGORIES` names `subtitle`), so its deadline is what it was. The metric `family` label gains `subtitle`.
  - **The home format tiles start on DOCX to PDF** (the reference converters start on a pair, not on two empty tiles). Changing a tile opens the page of the pair as before; changing the source to the format the target already shows opens nothing.
- **Why**: The reference converters group formats by the media they belong to, and a subtitle file is not a document a person edits in a word processor. A person looking for SRT or VTT under Documents does not find it. A starting pair shows at once what the tiles do.
- **Trade-offs**: The format count per category moves (Documents loses five formats, Subtitles has five), and a Prometheus series for the new `family` value appears. A person who searched Documents for subtitles now finds them one tab over.
- **Verified by**: `tests/home-format-picker.test.ts`, the registry, catalogue and message tests, and `tests/job-deadline-*.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: more subtitle formats arrive (SubViewer, SAMI, LRC), or a category page for subtitles is wanted for search.

## 197. Every sandboxed program runs in a PID namespace of its own, started by pid-init so that it is PID 2; office input is opened with a fixed LibreOffice profile, the declared import filter, and without macros found by content; ffprobe and the qpdf steps of the compression keep the limits and the signal of the job

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA request: the TODO lines of the sandbox and the office suite); nothing is deployed. It extends entries 60 and 119.
- **Decision**:
  - **Every run of a native program gets a PID namespace of its own** (`resolveSandboxedCommand` in `src/lib/security/process-sandbox.ts`), on top of the user and network namespaces of `unshare -r -n`. A run could signal another one before: `kill(sibling, 0)` succeeded, because the runs of a worker share one user ID, and so did a SIGKILL or a SIGSTOP. The command line is now `unshare -r -n -- pid-init -- [prlimit ...] <program>`. `pid-init` (`native/pid-init`, about 120 lines of C, built next to `qpdf-runner`) makes the namespace and forks PID 1 of it; PID 1 forks the program, which is PID 2, reaps what is left without a parent and reports the wait status of the program through a pipe; the process outside ends in the same way the program did (the same exit status, or the same signal re-raised on itself).
  - **Why the program is not PID 1** (`unshare -p --fork -- <program>`, which `sandboxOptions.pidNamespace: true` still means): the kernel does not deliver to PID 1 of a namespace a signal it has no handler for, unless the sender is outside the namespace. Measured on the Lima testbed with the program as PID 1: `kill -9 $$` and `kill -11 $$` from a shell do nothing and the run ends with status 0, and a signal the program sends itself (SIGABRT, SIGTERM) does not end it either. Tests failed on that first version (the signal-exit tests of `tests/sandbox-signal-exit.test.ts`, the SIGXFSZ file size limit test, and the SIGABRT and SIGTERM cases of `tests/archive-xz-sandbox.test.ts`, and the memory-limit tests that name SIGSEGV and SIGKILL). With the program as PID 2 they pass unchanged.
  - **What the namespace ends**: when the program ends PID 1 leaves and the kernel kills everything the program started that is still running (the process group kill of the old code missed a descendant that made a group of its own). PID 1 dies with the process outside (`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`), so killing that process, or its group, takes the whole tree. The memory watcher reads the program, two levels below the process it started (`memoryWatchPid`).
  - **The namespace is on by default; `SANDBOX_PID_NAMESPACE=false` turns it off** (`probePidInit`). It was off from 2026-11-08 to 2026-11-09 while aborted runs and calibre were fixed (entry 203); calibre is the one program that runs outside it.
  - **A host that cannot make the namespace, or has no `pid-init`, runs programs as before** (user and network namespaces only), and says so once in the log (`[sandbox] Programs run without a PID namespace of their own: ...`). `getUnshareCapability` runs `unshare -r -n -- pid-init -- /bin/true` (2 seconds allowed) to find out, so a seccomp profile that lets `clone` make the first two and not the third degrades instead of refusing every conversion; a host that degraded is tried again every 60 seconds, because a probe that failed on a cold start or under load is not a fact about the host. `PID_INIT_PATH` names the program; `/usr/local/bin/pid-init` and `/usr/bin/pid-init` are searched otherwise. `scripts/verify-worker-container.sh` (check 10) fails the container job when the image has none or the profile does not allow the namespace, and the worker image build runs `pid-init` once.
  - **`qpdf-runner` does the same for its jobs**: `unshare(CLONE_NEWUSER | CLONE_NEWNET | CLONE_NEWPID)`, then the child forks PID 1 of the namespace, which forks the job (PID 2); the child stays outside, is the process the runner waits for and kills with its group, and ends like the job. What the job started ends with the job, so the runner no longer waits `EXIT_GRACE_MS` for a descendant that holds the streams of a job (four tests of the runner were rewritten to say so: the job ends at once with the result of its first process).
  - **The qpdf steps of the compression keep the signal and the deadline of the job** (`src/lib/conversions/pdf-postprocess/compress.ts`): the first lossless rewrite, the question whether qpdf lists the pages, the repair of the page tree, the `qpdf --check` that decides whether the input is already clean, and the lossless rewrite after a failed check each run under the job's signal and with the time left to the deadline as their limit (at most the 60 s of a qpdf run). A program is not started once the job was stopped or its deadline passed. Before, the check and the last rewrite had no signal at all, and the others had the signal but a fixed 60 s: a cancelled job left qpdf running, and a job at its deadline started the next step. A check that ends because the job was stopped is no longer read as a damaged input.
  - **Every office suite run starts from a fixed profile** (`writeOfficeProfile` in `src/worker/libreoffice-profile.ts`), written into `user/registrymodifications.xcu` before the suite starts, for the standalone run, the profile of each pool slot (before its pre-warm run), the readiness probe and the PDF/A conversion: `Common/Security/Scripting` `MacroSecurityLevel` 3 (very high), `DisableMacrosExecution`, `DisableActiveContent` and `BlockUntrustedRefererLinks` true, and `Calc/Content/Update` `Link` 2 and `Writer/Content/Update` `Link` 2 ("never" update links when loading). The names and types are read from the schema of the installed suite by `tests/office-import-filters.test.ts`. The profile of a run that keeps the Excel objects (`keepEmbeddedExcelObjects`) holds that setting beside these, not instead of them. The suite has no setting that restricts `file:` reads as such: a document's links are what it reads through, and with them never updated the suite does not open the file or the address a link, an external reference or a linked section names.
