Measured on the Lima testbed (LibreOffice 24.2.7), a Writer section linked to a local text file and a Calc cell referencing another workbook convert to their stored text (`PLACEHOLDER-TEXT`, `CACHED-VALUE`) under the default profile, under a profile that updates links always, and under the fixed profile, so the headless suite did not update them in any of the three and the setting pins what the default happens to do; a positive control that leaks was not found.
  - **The office suite opens a declared format with its import filter** (`soffice --infilter=<name>`, `OFFICE_IMPORT_FILTERS` in `src/lib/conversions/office/office-suite-sources.ts`), for the Office Open XML, OpenDocument, StarOffice, WordPerfect, Lotus, AbiWord, iWork, Visio, CorelDRAW, Publisher and Sony formats, RTF, and PDF in the PDF/A conversion. A file that is not what it was declared as is refused by the importer instead of being read by the one the suite picks from its bytes. Not named: the legacy binary Word, Excel and PowerPoint formats and their templates, Works, the Palm databases, the text formats and the metafiles. The suite has one filter per generation behind each of those extensions and refuses a file of an older generation with the newest one, so naming one would turn today's conversions into failures; they are opened by the suite's own detection as before. The names are checked against the filter registry of the installed suite.
  - **Macros are removed from a package by what it holds, not by its name** (`stripOfficeMacros` in `src/lib/conversions/office-macro-strip.ts`, called by `officeInputWithoutMacros` for every ZIP package that reaches the suite): the VBA project parts of an Office Open XML package (found by content type, by relationship and by name, with their relationships and content-type entries), the Excel 4.0 macro sheets (`macrosheet` content types and relationships, with their `sheet` entry in `xl/workbook.xml` and the sheet scope of the defined names that followed them), the macro-enabled main content type made the plain one, and the `Basic/`, `Dialogs/` and `Scripts/` libraries of an OpenDocument package and of its embedded objects (`Object 1/Basic/`, matched by path segment, with their manifest entries; the `mimetype` entry stays stored and first). The content types and the relationships are read with the scanner the Office readers share (`safeExtractXmlElements`), so the open-and-close form of an element, single quotes, any attribute order and a `>` in a value are read as XML has them; every pass over the entries or elements is one pass, and a package with more than 100,000 entries or a content types part with more than 100,000 elements is refused as a typed 400 error (a first version scanned every entry for each `Default` element and took 33 seconds on 10,000 of them and 20,000 entries; the same package now takes a fraction of a second, `tests/office-macro-strip.test.ts`). Before, only a file declared `docm`, `xlsm`, `pptm` and the like lost its macros, so a `.docx` with a `vbaProject.bin` reached the suite with it. A package without any is handed over as the very buffer. The legacy binary formats (`doc`, `xls`, `ppt`) keep their VBA storages and rely on the profile above; a package larger than the in-memory limit is not read for this (the suite runs it with macros disabled).
  - **The profile of a pool slot is written again before every job**, so a setting that one job (or a document) left in the shared profile does not reach the next.
  - **ffprobe keeps limits and no longer holds the event loop for the probe of an input**: every ffprobe run (`runFfprobe`, `runFfprobeAsync` in `src/lib/conversions/media-process.ts`) is in the namespace sandbox with 2 GB of address space, 1 MB of file size, CPU time of the run's time limit plus 2 seconds, and no core file (FFmpeg runs keep their own limits). It already ran in the sandbox, but as `spawnSync` with only a time and an output limit. The probe of the whole input (the stream list, the timeline and the duration, with the check for undecodable audio) and the duration check that opens every media conversion now run asynchronously (`probeInputAsync`, `probeMediaDurationAsync`), under the signal of the job; the answer is remembered, so the argument builders that ask for it afterwards run no process, and a probe that failed is handed once to the next `probeInput` of the same input (within 10 seconds) instead of being run again on the event loop. The other probes still run synchronously, with the same limits: the audio channel, sample rate and stream count questions of the argument builders, the HDR and empty-output probes, and the run that explains a failed probe (TODO.md).
- **Why**: a sandboxed program parses an upload and is the part of the system most likely to be hostile; it should not be able to touch the other uploads being converted beside it. The user and network namespaces keep it off the network and off the host's files by permission; the PID namespace keeps it from the other runs' processes.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **`/proc` is not remounted**: the sandbox cannot mount (`deny mount` in the AppArmor profile, `mount` denied by the seccomp profile, and a container's `/proc` has masked paths that make a new mount fail), so the program still sees the container's `/proc/<pid>` entries by their numbers in the outer namespace. It can no longer signal them or name them in a system call, and `ptrace` is denied by the profile. Measured on the Lima testbed (`ptrace_scope` 0, so Yama does not help there): a run reading the entries of a sibling run gets the command line (`cmdline`, which holds the paths of the sibling's files) and `status`, and `EACCES` for `environ`, `maps`, `mem`, `root` and `cwd`, because a process that entered a user namespace and executed a program is not dumpable. So the command line of a sibling was still readable (entry 208 refuses it with a Landlock ruleset).
  - Two more processes stand between the worker and each program: 0.10 to 0.24 ms more per start (`unshare -r -n -- /bin/true` 0.54 and 0.64 ms, with pid-init 0.75 and 0.79 ms, mean of 300 starts, twice, on the testbed) and about 1.3 MB resident (1,008 kB and 340 kB). `RLIMIT_NPROC` counts them.
  - A program's orphaned children are reparented to PID 1 of its namespace, not to the host's init, and are killed with it.
- **Alternatives rejected**: `unshare -p --fork` alone (the program as PID 1, above); a distinct user ID per run (needs `newuidmap` and a range of subordinate IDs in the container, which the worker does not have and the seccomp profile does not allow); `bwrap --unshare-pid` (another dependency with its own mount setup, which the profile denies); a Node helper as PID 1 (a runtime started for every program).
- **Verified by**: `tests/sandbox-isolation.test.ts` (a run cannot find or signal a sibling run, with an opt-out run as the control; what a run left running ends with it; the memory is read from the program), `tests/pid-init.test.ts` (the program is PID 2, exit statuses, SIGKILL/SIGSEGV/SIGXFSZ re-raised, 126/127, the tree ends with the process outside), `tests/qpdf-runner.test.ts`, `tests/pdf-compress-qpdf-limits.test.ts`, and the container check 10 of `scripts/verify-worker-container.sh`.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image gets a way to mount `/proc` in a namespace of its own, or a program of the sandbox needs to run as PID 1.

## 198. PNG and JPG have compress pages that re-encode the file in its own format, and the Tools menu lists them with PDF/A

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA approved adding the tool pages the two reference converters have and the server already supports). It replaces the 404 that entries 139 and 145 gave `/compress-png` and `/compress-jpg`.
- **Decision**:
  - **`/compress-png` and `/compress-jpg` are pages**, the compress page of `/compress-pdf` for two more formats (`COMPRESSED_IMAGE_FORMATS` in `src/lib/image-compression.ts`, read by `parseUtilitySlug`). Each names itself as its canonical, in both languages. `/compress-gif`, `/compress-webp` and the rest stay 404.
  - **The page converts the file to its own format on the server encoders.** JPG to JPG re-encodes at the quality of the slider (85 by default). PNG has no quality, so the quality of a PNG compression becomes the size of its palette (`paletteColorsForQuality`): 256 colours from quality 80 up, then 256 times the square of quality over 80, at least 2 (40 gives 64, 20 gives 16). The request carries `palette: true` and `colors`, which the image engine already honours. The tier router sends a same-format PNG or JPG to the server when no filter is asked for, since the browser canvas cannot shrink a PNG.
  - **The Tools menu** lists Compress PNG, Compress JPG and Convert to PDF/A. PDF/A is the existing `/pdfa-converter`; no `/pdf-a` page is added, so one URL holds that content.
- **Why**: The reference converters have both pages and the engine already writes smaller PNG and JPG files; only the pages and the PNG palette request were missing. The 256-colour default is the lossy palette the reference tools of this kind use for PNG.
- **Trade-offs**: A PNG compressed at the default quality is lossy (256 colours). A compression never makes a file larger (QA 2026-11-08): when the options ask for nothing but quality and the server's result is not smaller than the input, the page gives the input back unchanged under its own name and the row says "already optimised" (`answerOfCompression` in `src/lib/client-converter.ts`); the run is still charged, as the server converted the file. A size, a filter or stripping the metadata asks for a change in the content, so the result is given as it is: the input would keep the metadata asked to go. Archive create and extract and PDF split and rotate are pages too, by entry 200.
- **Verified by**: `tests/image-compression.test.ts`, `tests/unknown-path-404.test.ts`, `tests/internal-links.test.ts`, `tests/site-review-copy.test.ts`, `tests/subpages-routes.test.ts`, `tests/i18n-routing.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: a run that comes back unchanged should not be charged.

## 199. A converter page shows its title alone, and the sign-up prompt sits under the login button

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA approval of visitor feedback).
- **Decision**:
  - **A pair page and a format page show their title with no sentence under it** (`ConverterPageView`, `PairHero`). The sentence "converts X to Y online, also to A, B and C" stays the page's meta description for search results. Tool pages (merge, compress, OCR) keep their sentence, since it says what the tool does with the files.
  - **No small "also to HTML, MD, EPUB" line either**: the target tile lists every target of the source, and the format card links to the format page that lists them all.
  - **The "no account? sign up" prompt (and "have an account? log in") sits under the submit button** of the auth card (`AuthPageView`).
- **Why**: Visitors read the sentence under "DOCX → PDF converter" as the title said again. Both reference converters do put a sentence there, but it repeats the title (one has a typo in it), and neither lists other targets near the title; one places the sign-up prompt under the button, the other under the title.
- **Trade-offs**: The hero is shorter and says less on a pair whose name a visitor may not know; the format cards below still describe both formats.
- **Alternatives rejected**: a small grey line naming other targets (repeats what the target tile offers); keeping the reference sentence (visitor feedback).
- **Verified by**: `tests/slug-copy.test.ts`, `tests/pair-page-tiles.test.ts`, the auth page tests, and before/after screenshots QA approved.
- **Revisit when**: search traffic to pair pages drops after the change, or visitors ask which other formats a page converts to.

## 200. Merge, archive and PDF page tools run on one web route, one conversion for each run, for visitors without an account

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-08 (QA: the reference converters let visitors without an account merge PDFs, create and extract archives and split and rotate PDFs under the same daily limit). It fixes `/merge-pdf`, which until now only reworded the converter page: each PDF was converted alone and no merged file came out.
- **Decision**:
  - **One route for each tool, `POST /api/tools/<tool>`**, for `merge`, `archive-create`, `archive-extract`, `split` and `rotate` (`src/app/api/tools/<tool>/route.ts` over the shared `handler.ts`, and `src/lib/tools/web-tools.ts`). It takes `files` and a JSON `options` field as a multipart form and calls the code of the job graph nodes `merge`, `archive.create`, `archive.extract`, `pdf.split-pages` and `pdf.rotate-pages` (no engine is rewritten; `extractGraphArchiveEntries` is exported for it). `/api/v1/jobs` stays closed to anonymous callers.
  - **Access is the access of `/api/convert`**: `validateApiAccess` with `allowAnonymous` before the body is read (the anonymous rate limit, the unattributed-visitor rule, the daily allowance), the same concurrency slot, `withinSingleRequest` and the file routes of the middleware (`/api/tools` in `FILE_ROUTES`, one request of at most 64 MiB), the plan limit on each file, and the synchronous deadline.
  - **One run is one conversion**, whatever the number of files: the unit is reserved before the run and committed after the answer is built, so a refusal or a failure gives it back (`withReservedUnit`).
  - **Limits**: a merge and an archive take 2 or 1 to 50 files (`MAX_TOOL_FILES`), the other tools one; the files together may not exceed one request; a merge and the PDF tools take PDFs and extract takes an archive, each checked against its signature. The `options` field is at most 8,192 characters and only the keys of the tool are copied (a format for an archive; `ranges` or `everyNPages` for a split; one `rotation` of 90, 180 or 270 and its `pages` for a rotate, never a list of rotations), so nothing else a body names reaches an engine. An archive is unpacked under caps of its own (`WEB_EXTRACTION_LIMITS`: 1,000 files and 32 MiB, `MAX_EXTRACTED_BYTES`, as the listing travels as base64 and costs about four times that in memory) that every reader takes as an optional `limits` argument in place of `ARCHIVE_SECURITY_LIMITS`, whose 500 MiB stay the default of the job graph and the API: the ZIP reader sums the declared sizes before it inflates and stops each entry at the size it declares, the gzip stream and the TAR reader count the bytes they produce, the 7Z reader caps each folder's output, and the RAR step reads the size of an unpacked file before it reads the file. A listing past a cap is a 413 (`input_over_limit`) in every format, and the unpacked files are checked once more before they are listed. The file a tool answers is at most 64 MiB (`MAX_TOOL_OUTPUT_BYTES`), a split included. RAR cannot be written. A split writes at most the parts the engine allows. An entry is listed by the leaf of its name, as the job graph names its outputs, with a number added to a name that repeats, so no name leaves a folder.
  - **A stopped run keeps its slot**: the deadline and the disconnect give the signal to the engines that take one (the qpdf steps of a split and a rotate, 7-Zip, a merge between two inputs); the others finish what they began, so the route holds the concurrency slot until the work has settled and gives the conversion back at once. A caller cannot stack work behind its five slots.
  - **Answers**: merge, archive and rotate answer the file, split answers a ZIP of its parts, extract answers JSON with each file's name, size, type and base64 bytes. The route is documented in the OpenAPI document as an internal route (`/api/tools/<tool>`).
  - **Pages**: `/merge-pdf`, `/create-zip-archive`, `/extract-zip-archive`, `/split-pdf` and `/rotate-pdf`, each canonical to itself, in the Tools menu. The upload card is the converter's, then the files in a list (merge and archive can be ordered with arrows), the options in a dialog (archive format ZIP, 7Z or TAR.GZ; every page or ranges for a split; 90, 180 or 270 degrees and pages for a rotate), one action, one result. An unpacked archive lists its files with a download each and "download all" as a ZIP built in the browser.
- **Why**: The reference converters offer these tools to visitors without an account, and the server already runs them. Opening the job graph to anonymous callers would also open its webhooks, uploads and storage; one route that does one run keeps the surface as small as `/api/convert/batch`.
- **Trade-offs**: A listed archive travels as base64 in JSON (a third larger) and is held in memory, so it is capped at 32 MiB; a larger archive goes through the API. The rotation takes one angle for one set of pages; several angles in one run go through the job graph. A PDF that needs a password is refused (the tools take no password yet). A run of the daily allowance is spent on a run that returns a file, not on each file in it.
- **Verified by**: `tests/web-tools-route.test.ts` (the charge and the refund of every tool, file count, total size, a decompression bomb, an archive over the listing limits, traversal names, page ranges, the options field and its keys, the anonymous allowance, the concurrency limit), `tests/web-tools-slot.test.ts` (a stopped run keeps its slot until its work settles), `tests/web-tools-extract-limits.test.ts` (a ZIP whose headers understate its data, a gzip bomb, a TAR and a 7Z past the cap), `tests/openapi-web-tools-contract.test.ts`, `tests/request-body-limit.test.ts`, `tests/tool-pages.test.ts` and the page tests of the slugs.
- **Revisit when**: a tool needs a password for a PDF or an archive, or listed archives need to be larger than 32 MiB.

## 201. Every run of the office suite opens a file called `input.<format>` without the macros found by content, and a ZIP package past the in-memory limit is refused

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: an external code review of the office route); nothing is deployed. It extends entry 197.
- **Decision**:
  - **The office suite is given its input under the name `input.<format>`, in a folder of its own** (`resolveOfficeInputContext` in `src/worker/worker-output.ts`), for the pool and for the standalone run. The suite names its output after the file it is given and the run looks for `input.*` in the run's directory, so a file of the store (`<digest>.bin` under local storage, `<uuid>.staged` under remote storage, which the queue workers pass as `{ inputPath }`) produced `<digest>.pdf` and the run ended with "completed without producing expected output file", which became a 400 or 422 "corrupt document" and kept the in-process engine from taking over. The stored file is now linked (not copied) as `source/input.<format>`, so its extension is the real one for the suite's choice of filter, its lock file lands in the run's folder and not in the store, and an output in the format of the source (`input.odd` of `input.odd`) is no longer taken for the input.
  - **Macros are removed in the one place every run of the office suite starts** (`runHeadlessOffice` in `src/worker/engines.ts`), not in the image session only. The interchange route (a presentation to Markdown through a PDF, a Calc file to `.xls` through an XLSX workbook, the retry of a legacy document) called the suite with the macros in place. `officeInputWithoutMacros` now returns a payload that keeps its `outputPath` when it has to hand over stripped bytes, and returns a file that is no ZIP package (an encrypted package in its compound file, a legacy binary document) as it is, so an encrypted `.docm` is answered by the spoof check with the 422 of an encrypted document and not refused as a damaged package.
  - **A macro-enabled template or slide show stays a template or slide show** for the suite (only the macro-enabled part of the main content type goes: `...template.macroEnabledTemplate.main+xml` becomes `...template.main+xml`); the write of a variant as its plain format (`ooxmlVariantToPlainFormat`, in-process) runs the same removal (`stripOfficeMacros`) first and then gives the main part the content type of the plain family. Before, it used a second, narrower scanner (double-quoted attributes, self-closing elements, `vbaProject` relationships of the main part only), which left single-quoted or open-and-close markup, `vbaData.xml`, macro sheets and macros attached to other parts in the output, and for an absolute target (`/word/macros.bin`, `./macros.bin`) it removed the relationship and then failed to remove the part.
  - **Package paths are normalised whether or not they start at the root** (`resolveZipPath`): `/word/./vbaProject.bin`, `/word/sub/../macros.bin` and `/word//macros.bin` name `word/vbaProject.bin` and `word/macros.bin`. A macro part reached only by such a relationship was left in the package.
  - **An OpenDocument package is recognised by its manifest**, with or without a `mimetype` entry (the suite loads both), and a macro library is a `Basic`, `Dialogs` or `Scripts` directory at any depth (`subdoc/Basic/...`), not only at the root and in `Object N/`.
  - **A ZIP package larger than `MAX_IN_MEMORY_BYTES` (512 MiB unless set) is refused with HTTP 413** (`PayloadLimitError`) before the suite opens it. The removal and the check of the embedded pictures' pixel counts read a package whole, and a file past the limit skipped both and went to the suite unchecked.
- **Why**: The stored-file naming defect made every queued office conversion from a stored file fail, and the gaps in the removal left macros in the input of routes the first version did not cover. Refusing a package that cannot be checked is the choice that keeps the removal and the picture limit true for every input; the profile of entry 197 (macros disabled) stays the second lock.
- **Trade-offs**: An office package of more than 512 MiB (a document of mostly pictures) is refused instead of converted. The limit is an environment setting a larger worker may raise; no measurement of how many uploads sit past it was made. A stored file is linked, so a file system without symbolic links would need a copy; the worker's temporary directory and its store are on the same kind of file system.
- **Alternatives rejected**: matching the output by the parsed base name of the stored file (the suite would also pick its filter from `.bin`, and the lock file would stay in the store); copying the stored file (a second copy of every upload, and a hard link does not cross the temporary directory and the store); stripping from the file with bounded reads (needs a file-backed ZIP rewriter the repository does not have, and a rewrite of the package needs it whole anyway); handing a package past the limit over unchecked (macros and a picture past the pixel limit reach the suite).
- **Verified by**: `tests/office-file-input.test.ts` (the pool and the standalone run with a real file `<digest>.bin` and `<digest>.staged`, a .docx and a .doc, through the real office suite and through a runner that names its output like the suite), `tests/office-macro-strip-coverage.test.ts` (absolute and unnormalised targets, the plain-format write, ODF without `mimetype`, macros removed on the interchange routes, the 413 past the limit, encrypted packages), `tests/office-macro-strip.test.ts`, `tests/ooxml-variants.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: a job holds documents past 512 MiB in memory by design, or the repository gets a ZIP reader that works on a file with bounded reads.

## 202. A request body is held to what its call carries, an Idempotency-Key keeps only an answer that cannot change, and deleting a converted file deletes the stored file

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: an external code review of the API and storage routes); nothing is deployed. It refines entry 137 (the size a body may have) and the `Idempotency-Key` rule of the job and conversion routes.
- **Decision**:
  - **A body is classed by the call, not by the route** (`bodyKindOf` in `src/lib/api/request-body-limit.ts`, read by the edge middleware). A JSON control call takes at most 1 MiB and needs no `Content-Length`: `POST /api/v1/uploads?action=initiate|complete|abort`, `POST /api/v1/uploads/direct`, and `POST /api/v1/uploads/direct/complete`. A body sent without a length (chunked, or framed by HTTP/2 alone) is counted as it arrives and refused with 413 past 1 MiB. A part (`PUT /api/v1/uploads/direct/part`, `POST /api/v1/uploads?action=part`) takes at most `UPLOAD_PART_MAX_BYTES` and must declare its length (411 otherwise). A file in one request takes one request as before, and must declare its length: the tus creation and chunks, a multipart form to either job route, and every other route entry 137 lists. A JSON call to `/api/v1/jobs` or `/api/queue/jobs` may carry its file inline (`inputBufferBase64`, up to `INLINE_JOB_PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES` of file), so it takes one request too, but needs no length: a body sent without one is counted as it arrives and refused with 413 past one request. A content type of `multipart/form-data` (in any letter case) marks a job call as a form with a file.
  - **Deleting a converted file in the account deletes the stored file** (`DELETE /api/account/files/<id>`): the object first, then its retention record, then the history record. The download answers 404 afterwards, as for a file that never was, not 410. A store that fails answers 503 and leaves the history record, so the same request can be sent again; an object already gone is not an error. Only the owner's record is found, and only a key under `conversions/<that user>/` is deleted.
  - **Every completion of an upload records it** (`registerCompletedUpload`): the direct completion, `?action=complete` against local storage and against an object store, and the last chunk of a tus upload (the creation with a body as well). An account's file under `conversions/<userId>/` is therefore an upload and not a result that its first download registers and the sweep deletes a minute later, and a job that reads it holds it. A completion whose record cannot be written deletes the file again and answers 500 without an internal message (a tus chunk, which the client sends again, answers 503 with `Retry-After`). The staged tus file stays until the upload is recorded, so that chunk sent again is appended to the whole file, and a staged file that is not the declared length is refused before anything is stored from it (the client continues from what the file holds). An object-store completion checks the first bytes against the declared format, as the local store and the direct route do, and deletes a file that does not match (422).
  - **`POST /api/v1/archives/inspect` answers 400 for a malformed multipart form or JSON body** and a fixed 500 for anything unexpected; the parser's message and the error text stay in the server log.
  - **A link import keeps a remote file name that is not valid percent-encoding** (`filename="100%.pdf"`) as written; the name is read before the import is charged.
  - **An `Idempotency-Key` on `/api/v1/jobs` and `/api/v1/convert` keeps a success and the refusals that only the request causes**: 400, 413, 415 and 422. Every other answer releases the key, so the same request may be sent again: a 429 (quota, rate, slot or budget), a 404 (a file not stored yet), and every 5xx. The store is guarded: an answer it cannot record is returned all the same, with the lock kept for a success (a repeat would create and charge again), and a release that fails is logged.
  - **A graph's `export.url` node checks the destination before it opens the artifact**, closes the artifact whatever the request does, and refuses a destination that redirects (`OutboundRequestBlockedError`, from `safeFetch`, which follows a redirect only for GET and HEAD): the body is a stream that cannot be sent again.
  - **A job or graph that inherited its API key's webhook names the key** (`webhookKeyId`), so the key's rotated secret signs the delivery and the previous one signs it too during the grace period. A job queued before the rotation, which carries the secret rotated away, is signed with the current one. A webhook the request brought is signed with the secret it carries.
  - **The job lists leave out the node jobs of a graph** (`listVisibleJobs`): the graph is the job a client runs, charges and cancels, by its own id. The queues are read once per list request (up to 1,000 jobs of the caller), then filtered.
- **Why**: The size classes followed the route, so a JSON call to a route that also takes files needed a length that HTTP/2 does not send (411), the control calls of an upload could claim a whole file's size, and a part was held to a request instead of a part. A deleted file that stays downloadable is not deleted; an upload that its first download turns into a result is deleted a minute later; and a refusal that depends on the day or on a file not yet stored must not be replayed for 24 hours to a client that did nothing wrong. The stable refusals are replayed because the answer to the same bytes cannot change, and the existing replay tests hold them.
- **Trade-offs**: The control calls of an upload are held to 1 MiB where they could declare up to a request before; none of them carries a file. A JSON job call is not held to 1 MiB, because the inline file it may carry is the reason it exists. A client that is refused a 429 under a key and sends it again runs the request again instead of getting the first 429 back. The history of converted files is still kept by one process (the sync conversion route writes it, the queue does not), so a deletion is exact for the process that holds the record; `TODO.md` lists the shared store.
- **Alternatives rejected**: Keeping every 4xx under the key, as the first version did (a transient 429 or 404 replayed for a day); keeping only 2xx (a malformed body is cheap to refuse again, but the replay tests of 400 and 422 set the other rule); a 410 after a deletion by the owner (the file is not "expired", it was removed, and a 410 would keep its retention record for a day); re-opening the artifact stream for each hop of a redirect (a destination that redirects a PUT to another address is not a destination the export can trust with the body).
- **Verified by**: `tests/request-body-limit.test.ts` (each call class, the middleware with and without a length, the parts at the largest part), `tests/account-file-delete.test.ts` (end to end through the download route), `tests/upload-completion-registers.test.ts`, `tests/tus-remote-record-retry.test.ts` and `tests/remote-storage-upload-actions.test.ts` (the record of every completion, the spoofed object-store upload, the unwritable record), `tests/archive-inspect-malformed-input.test.ts`, `tests/download-filename-header.test.ts`, `tests/idempotency-refusals-not-cached.test.ts` and `tests/idempotency-concurrency.test.ts`, `tests/graph-export-url-stream.test.ts`, `tests/webhook-rotated-secret-jobs.test.ts`, `tests/graph-node-jobs-hidden-from-lists.test.ts`; each was red before the change.
- **Revisit when**: the history of converted files moves to the shared store (the delete then covers a record held by another process), a client needs a JSON job call larger than 1 MiB, or a 413 or 415 under a key turns out to be state-dependent.

## 203. calibre runs outside the PID namespace, the PID namespace is on by default again, and pid-init ends a PID 1 whose parent died during the start

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: the TODO line that turned the namespace off after CI run 42489934607). It refines entry 197; nothing is deployed.
- **Decision**:
  - **`SANDBOX_PID_NAMESPACE` is on unless it is `false`** (it was off by default since 2026-11-08). A host without `pid-init`, or one that cannot make the namespace, still degrades with one warning, as entry 197 says.
  - **calibre's `ebook-convert` runs without a PID namespace of its own** (`runCalibre` in `src/worker/ebook-calibre.ts` passes `sandboxOptions: { pidNamespace: false }`, which also goes through the launcher helper). It keeps the user and network namespaces, the resource limits, the memory watch and the process group kill. veraPDF (`runVerapdf` in `src/lib/conversions/pdf-postprocess/pdfa.ts`) runs the same way: with the namespace on, CI run of d9b99b3f saw it answer with something other than its JSON report twice, and a JVM reads `/proc/self` for its container and thread setup; the start of such an answer is now logged.
  - **pid-init closes the window in which its PID 1 could outlive its parent** (`native/pid-init/pid-init.c`): the process outside holds the write end of a pipe for as long as it lives, PID 1 looks at the other end right after it has asked for `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, and ends when the end is closed. Before, a process killed between the fork and that request left PID 1 and the program running with nobody to report to.
  - **The tests find a program of the sandbox by what it was started with, not by the id it reads for itself** (`processesWithArgument`, `uniqueSleepInterval`, `ancestorsOf` in `tests/helpers/process-state.ts`; `runningWrappers` of the 7-Zip spy). No product code changed for the aborted-run failures: the kill already reached the program. The same holds for the qpdf stand-in of `tests/pdf-password-argv.test.ts`, the AVIF stand-ins of `tests/image-avif-direct-handoff.test.ts`, the concurrency count of the pdftoppm stand-in in `tests/poppler-ppm-png.test.ts` (one marker file per run, made by `mktemp`, instead of one named by `$$`), and the parent check of `tests/image-avif-launcher.test.ts`, which now reads the host's process tree for every process that has the wrapper's path in its command line (the version probe, run by the worker itself, has it too, so the check starts after the wrapper's record exists).
- **Why**: The CI failures had two causes, neither of them a run left behind. (1) The stand-in tools of the abort and timeout tests (lbzip2, libdeflate, avifenc, OCR, the 7-Zip spy) wrote `$$` to a file and the test asked whether that process was still running. In the namespace `$$` is 2 and the host's process 2 is `kthreadd`, which never ends, so the test reported a left-over program that was gone (`/proc/<host id>/status` of the program shows `NSpid: 3925976 2`, and the tests pass once they look for the program by its arguments). The OCR concurrency test named its marker files by `$$` too, so every run wrote the same file and the count never passed 1; the launcher test read `$PPID` (1 in the namespace) and compared it with the helper. (2) calibre's launcher calls `getpid()` and reads `/proc/<that id>/exe` (`strace` on arm64 calibre 9.15.0: `getpid() = 5`, then `readlinkat("/proc/5/exe") = -1 EACCES`; on a runner the host's process of that number is another process or none), which fails with "Failed to read exe path from:". `/proc` can only show the namespace's processes when it is mounted again inside it, and the worker profile has no `mount` (`docker/seccomp-worker.json`) and AppArmor denies it, so no setting can make calibre read its path there. Any program that reads `/proc/<own id>/` needs the same exemption; calibre is the only one found, in a run of the whole suite on CI.
- **Trade-offs**: A calibre run can see and signal the other runs of its worker, as every run could before entry 197 (they share one user ID). Its input is a book it was handed by the job, it has no network, and it runs under the same limits and in a directory of its own; the PID namespace was the one layer it could not have. `ebook-convert` starts Python workers of its own; with no namespace they end with the process group kill, and one that makes a group of its own (it does not) would outlive the run. The pipe check adds two descriptors and a `poll` to the start of every program.
- **Alternatives rejected**: remounting `/proc` in the namespace (needs `mount`, denied by the profile); running calibre as PID 1 with `unshare -p --fork` (its id is then 1 and `/proc/1/exe` is the host's init); a wrapper that rewrites the path calibre reads (it is read by a library inside the release build); forwarding SIGTERM and SIGKILL from pid-init to its child (the process group kill and the death signal of PID 1 already end the whole namespace, measured by the abort tests); polling the parent's id in PID 1 (the parent is outside the namespace, so `getppid()` is 0 there).
- **Verified by**: on the Lima testbed (Ubuntu 24.04) with the namespace on: `tests/archive-native-bzip2.test.ts`, `tests/archive-native-deflate.test.ts`, `tests/archive-stream-to-tar.test.ts`, `tests/image-avif-library-encoder.test.ts`, `tests/image-avif-launcher.test.ts`, `tests/ocr-cli-tsv.test.ts`, and with calibre 9.15.0 `tests/ebook-calibre-writers.test.ts`, `tests/azw4-and-cbc.test.ts`, `tests/ebook-added-pairs-real-samples.test.ts` (failed with the namespace before the exemption, passed after); `tests/pdf-password-argv.test.ts`, `tests/poppler-ppm-png.test.ts` and `tests/image-avif-direct-handoff.test.ts` (failed on CI with the namespace on at the first merge, and on the testbed once `pid-init` was installed in `/usr/local/bin` so that the launcher helper, whose environment does not carry `PID_INIT_PATH`, used it too); `tests/ebook-calibre-route.test.ts` (a stand-in that reads `/proc/<own id>/exe` fails in the namespace and runs under the calibre route); `tests/pid-init.test.ts` (400 starts killed at random moments leave nothing: before the fix 2 of 3 runs of the test failed, and 4 processes were left by 300 starts; after it none of 800 starts in a separate harness left anything, and 7 runs of the test passed); `tests/sandbox-pid-init-probe.test.ts` (on unless `false`).
- **Revisit when**: the worker image can mount `/proc` in a namespace of its own (calibre then joins the others), another program is found that reads `/proc/<own id>/`, or calibre is replaced by an engine that does not.

## 204. The history of converted files lives in Redis and takes the results of queue jobs, the job lists name a user's graphs from a per-user index, and the first rotation of a key's webhook secret keeps the old one

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: three TODO lines of Operations and security); nothing is deployed. It carries out the "revisit" of entry 202 (the history of converted files moves to the shared store) and refines entry 202's rule that the job lists leave out the node jobs of a graph.
- **Decision**:
  - **The history of converted files is kept in Redis** (`RedisUserFileHistory`, used by `RedisKeyStore` whenever it has a Redis client): each record is a JSON value `user_file:{<userId>}:<fileId>` that expires with the result it names (`PX` = the time left to `expiresAt`, RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS from the end of the conversion), and `user_files:{<userId>}` is a sorted set of the ids scored by `expiresAt`. A record is written by one script that also drops expired ids and keeps at most 500 records a user (the one that expires first goes, with its key). Every key has the `{<userId>}` tag, like the day's count and the reservations, so a script stays in one cluster slot and `scripts/erase-account.ts` lists and deletes them with the rest of the account's keys. Reading a record names the caller in the key, so a user cannot reach another's record by id. Without Redis the history stays in the process and `user-files.json`, as before; with Redis, a record that could not be written (Redis did not answer) is kept in the process and listed with the others, because the conversion it records has already succeeded.
  - **A queue job's result is recorded when the job completes** (`recordJobResultInHistory`, in the `completed` listener that every worker has): under the job id, so a completion reported twice records it once; for a signed-in owner only (a visitor without an account reaches the result by its link, and a graph's node jobs are answered for by the graph); a history that cannot be written is logged and never fails the job. The delete in the account (`DELETE /api/account/files/<id>`) deletes the stored result of such a record too (`job-result` keys, besides the owner's `conversions/<userId>/` keys), because the record is the owner's and was made by the job's own completion; a record whose key is not `results/<record id>/…` is refused (404) and nothing is deleted. A record in both Redis and this process (kept here during an outage, then recorded again into Redis) is listed once and deleted from both.
  - **`forgetUsage` is asynchronous and removes the records in Redis too**; `scripts/erase-account.ts` awaits it, and the keys tagged with the account id are swept as before.
  - **No migration of `user-files.json` into Redis.** A record lives at most RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS (default 1 hour, at most 24 hours) and nothing is deployed, so a file left on a host holds only records that expired by the time the new version starts. If one holds a live record, the process still reads it (`RedisKeyStore` lists the records of Redis and those it holds), so it stays visible and deletable until it expires, and no copy needs to be made.
  - **The job lists name a user's graphs.** `GET /api/queue/jobs` and `GET /api/v1/jobs` merge the caller's queue jobs and graphs by creation time and return the newest `limit`. A graph has the fields of a job under its own id (`name` is `graph` in the web list; no `fileSize`, no `result`: its nodes hold the outputs, read through `GET /api/v1/jobs/<id>`). A running graph is `active` in both lists (the job vocabulary of their filters and schemas; `GET /api/v1/jobs/<id>` keeps saying `running`) and answers to the `waiting` and `active` filters; `delayed` matches no graph.
  - **The graphs of a user are indexed** (`RedisGraphScheduler`): `user_graphs:{<userId>}` is a sorted set of graph ids scored by creation time, added to after the graph's state is stored (so an indexed graph always has a state; a start that failed in between is indexed again when it is recovered), kept at most `MAX_INDEXED_GRAPHS_PER_USER` (1,000) long, with the graphs older than a state can live (the deadline ceiling plus the retention of an ended job) dropped when a graph is added, and expiring that long after the last graph. A list reads the index once and then the graphs it names, a page at a time, until the page is full (a status filter can thin a page); a graph whose state expired leaves the index when it is met, and one whose record is damaged is logged and left out of the list. No list scans the keys; `graphsOfUser` still does, and only the erase script calls it.
  - **The first rotation of a key's webhook secret keeps the secret the key signs with** (`POST /api/v1/webhooks/secrets/rotate` with `apiKeyId` and no `endpointId`): when the key has a webhook secret and no rotation record, that secret is stored as the record's primary secret first (`seedPrimarySecretIfAbsent`, `SET ... NX` in Redis, so a rotation that wrote a record in the meantime is never replaced), and the rotation then moves it to the previous secret for the grace period. A rotation of an endpoint (`endpointId`) never takes the key's secret.
- **Why**: Only the synchronous conversion wrote the history, in the memory of one process and a file, so the results a worker made were not listed, and a delete was exact only in the process that held the record. Redis is the store of the other account data, and its expiry follows the result, so nothing outlives what it names. A client that starts a graph and cannot list it by anything but its id cannot find it again after a restart; the nodes cannot stand for it (the owner cannot cancel them). The first rotation had no previous secret, so a receiver that had not yet taken the new secret failed every delivery in the grace period; the second rotation already kept one.
- **Trade-offs**: The names of a user's converted files stay in Redis, and in its backups, for at most the result's retention (24 hours at most) and the backup's own 7 days, which the privacy text already says of records. A user who converts more than 500 files within the retention sees the newest 500. A queue job's result is listed from the time the worker's `completed` event is handled, so a job whose process dies in between is not listed (the result is still reachable by its job). A list that filters by status reads up to 1,000 graphs of the index in the worst case, a page at a time, where an unfiltered list reads one page. The graphs of a user are not listed while the scheduler is the in-memory one with several processes (it is for development only).
- **Alternatives rejected**: Importing `user-files.json` at start (a copy of records that expire within hours, and a second idempotence rule to test); a hash per user with a field for each record (Redis cannot expire a field before 7.4, and the expiry is the retention rule); a status index beside the creation index (a second sorted set to keep in step with every graph transition, to save reading a page of states); scanning the graph keys per request (the full scan a reviewer already blocked once); listing the graph's node jobs (they cannot be cancelled by the owner); a `running` status in the lists (not in the status enum of their schemas, and not a filter value).
- **Verified by**: `tests/account-file-history-redis.test.ts` (two processes on one Redis, delete for all, expiry, the cap, forget, the fallback), `tests/job-result-history.test.ts` (a real worker, the same result twice, no owner / anonymous / graph node, the delete of the stored result), `tests/erase-account.test.ts` (the tagged keys include the history), `tests/graph-user-lists.test.ts` (both lists, merge order, filters, one read per list), `tests/graph-user-index-redis.test.ts` (the index, its cap and retention, no key scan, expired graphs, recovery), `tests/webhook-first-rotation-keeps-secret.test.ts`.
- **Revisit when**: the history needs more than 500 records a user or a retention longer than a day, a client needs to filter the graph list by something the index does not hold (then a second index), or the in-memory scheduler is used by more than one process.

## 205. The PDF guard reads resources through /Parent, counts every draw and covers encrypted files, and a node job of a graph that has ended is not run

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: the two TODO lines of the operations list on the PDF guard and on the start of a graph); nothing is deployed. It refines entries 101 (the checks before pdf.js reads a document), 44 (the page limit) and 15 (the start of a graph).
- **Decision**:
  - **A page's resources are those of its own `/Parent` chain** (`PdfDocument.inheritedEntry`, ISO 32000-1 section 7.7.3.4; pdf.js reads `Resources`, `Annots` and the page boxes through `getInheritableProperty`): the page's own entry, else the nearest ancestor's, stopping at a node seen twice and at 64 levels (a PDF structure error). The `/Kids` path the tree is walked by gives the resources only when the chain gives none. Before, the check took the resources met on the way down the `/Kids` lists, so a page whose `/Parent` names a node that is not the one listing it, or a page found by its `/Type` because the tree lists none, was read with no XObjects, and the pictures and forms it draws were neither counted nor decoded under the budgets.
  - **Every draw counts, per page and per document** (`DrawLedger`, `src/lib/conversions/pdf-draw-count.ts`): each `Do` that leads to an image or form XObject, and each inline image (an `ID` operator outside strings, names, comments and image data), a form's own draws again on every invocation. A page may draw 100,000 times and a document 500,000 times; one more is a 400 (`PdfStructureError`), checked as the count grows so that a stream of a million draws is stopped at the limit. The picture check counted each image once per page (a set), so a page that drew one picture a million times passed.
  - **An encrypted file is checked after it is decrypted, or refused.** `runPdfTextJob` (the way every text reader reaches the thread) opens the file with `openPdfForReading` first, with the empty password that pdf.js would have tried (converters that hold a password open the file with it before, as they did), so the thread checks the plain bytes; a file that needs another password is a `PdfPasswordRequiredError` (422), and one with qpdf missing an `EngineUnavailableError`. The stream guard itself (`assertPdfStreamsWithinLimits`, `assertPdfAnnotationStreamsWithinLimits`) refuses bytes that are still encrypted with an `EncryptedOfficeDocumentError` instead of passing them to pdf.js unread, which decrypts with the empty password. The page and pixel budget of a render opens the file the same way (`checkOpenedPdfRasterPageBudget` in `pdf-access.ts`, used by the OCR renderer and the Poppler page outputs; it decrypts and then calls `checkPdfRasterPageBudget`, which stays free of server-only imports because the browser OCR bundle reaches `pdf-page-geometry.ts`): pdf-lib cannot open an encrypted file, and the fallback scan of the raw bytes found no pages when the page tree is in an encrypted object stream, so such a file was not held to the page limit.
  - **A node job of a graph that has ended is not run, whatever became of its cancel.** The queue's processor asks the scheduler first (`processGraphNodeJobIfAlive`, `IGraphScheduler.onNodeStarted`, now a boolean): the answer is the store's (the Lua script of the Redis scheduler, which already refused a node of a graph that is not running or a node that is not waiting or active), true for a node of a running graph that has not ended, a retry of its job included, and false for a graph that was cancelled or failed, a node that completed, was skipped or cancelled, and a graph or node the store does not hold. A job that is refused is logged, ends as completed with no result and reads, holds and writes nothing. Nothing is remembered in the process that cancels, so the rule holds after that process died between ending the graph and cancelling the jobs.
  - **The cancel of a node job is tried again** (`cancelGraphNodeJobOrLog`): up to 3 tries, 100 ms and 200 ms apart, as the cancel of a graph whose start failed already was. A job whose every try fails is logged and left to the rule above; the graph is ended and its reservation settled all the same.
- **Why**: The measured costs are small and the gaps were real. On the 1,312 PDFs of the real-world corpus cache, `bench/corpus` and `tests/fixtures`, the page that draws most draws 23,958 times (a map of small pictures; over the files, the busiest page draws 1 time at the median and 2,636 at the 99th percentile) and 31,854 after qpdf decrypts the 66 encrypted files (all open with the empty password); the most a document draws is 123,697 (20 pages). The caps are three to four times that, so no file of the corpus is refused, and a 12 KB file whose page draws one picture a million times is refused in 67 ms (pdf.js reads it as 1,001,002 operators in 0.3 s and keeps them all). A `/Parent` chain is what pdf.js follows, so the check now looks at the resources that will be drawn. Encrypted files were the way round every limit: the cipher text of their streams cannot be decoded here, and 66 of the 1,312 PDFs are encrypted. For the graph, the cancel of a node job is a call that can fail on its own (a connection that drops for a moment); a cancel that lands after the graph ended has nothing left to protect, and only the store survives a crash, so the worker asks it. The earlier code ran the job of a cancelled graph to its end (it read its inputs, held units and wrote outputs) and only the final report to the scheduler was ignored.
- **Trade-offs**: A page that draws more than 100,000 times, or a document more than 500,000 times, is refused; no document of the corpus comes within a factor of three, and a map or a chart that draws that many small pictures is not a document a text or page-image conversion can serve in a job deadline. An encrypted file now costs a qpdf run before the thread reads it, where pdf.js decrypted it in the thread; every converter that held a password already paid it. A refused node job ends as completed with an empty result, so it counts in the completed jobs of the metrics; it has no reservation, webhook or input hold of its own, and the graph carries them. The cancel retries add up to 300 ms per node job that cannot be cancelled, one node at a time, when the queue cannot be reached.
- **Alternatives rejected**: Marking the queued jobs in the process that ended the graph (a set of job ids the worker consults): lost with the process, and no better than the store the worker can ask. Failing the job of an ended graph with an error: a failure is retried up to 3 times and counted as a failed job in the metrics and reported to the scheduler again. Walking the `/Parent` chain only when the `/Kids` path gives nothing: the two disagree in the files that matter, and pdf.js follows `/Parent`. Counting only the image draws of the picture decoders: an inline or plain image that is drawn a million times costs the page reader the same. A cap that scales with the file size: the file does not show the draws (12 KB for a million).
- **Verified by**: `tests/pdf-guard-resources-draws-encrypted.test.ts` (18 tests, red before the change: resources on the page, on its `/Pages` node, on the node its `/Parent` names while another lists it, on the node of a page found by `/Type`, the nearest resources winning, a chain that returns to itself; the limits at 100,000 and one more, inline images and the text that spells `BI ID`, a form's draws on each invocation, the document limit with every page under its own; the guard refusing encrypted bytes and, through `runPdfTextJob`, the limits applied to an encrypted file with no open password, a file that needs one answering `PdfPasswordRequiredError`, and a 501-page encrypted file with its page tree in an object stream refused by the render budget), `tests/graph-ended-node-jobs.test.ts` and, on a real Redis server, `tests/graph-ended-node-jobs-redis.test.ts` (listed in `test:redis`; shared cases in `tests/helpers/graph-ended-node-cases.ts`: a start that failed after one node job was stored, every cancel retried once, every cancel failing for 3 tries and the graph still ended, the worker leaving the job alone and touching no storage or scheduler state, `onNodeStarted` for a live graph, a retry, a node that completed, a cancelled and a failed graph, and a graph the store never held), mutations that each turned cases red (the `/Parent` chain removed, the limits raised, the encrypted checks removed, the worker's question removed, the retry set to one try), `tests/quota-graph-charge.test.ts` and `tests/quota-accounting-redis.test.ts` (a cancel that fails is tried 3 times and its job is not reported cancelled), and `tests/pdf-xref-resolution.test.ts` (the `/Encrypt` dictionary in an object stream is refused for its password). The families `pdf-ops` and `document` (`--parity --quality-only --quick`, on the development Mac, base and head) evaluate 184 rows with none failing on either, and no row moves beyond the one-byte run-to-run noise of `pdf-ops/watermark.pdf->pdf/bytes` and `compress.pdf->pdf/bytes`. Over the 1,312 PDFs of the corpus cache, `bench/corpus` and `tests/fixtures`, none is refused by a draw limit; the 66 encrypted ones read through qpdf with the empty password. The suites of `test:redis` pass on a local Redis server.
- **Revisit when**: a real document draws within a factor of two of a limit (the cap then moves with the measurement), the text thread learns to take a password (the empty-password decryption then moves into the thread's input), or a job's report needs to tell a node that did not run from one that completed.

## 206. The first real-browser accessibility pass: standalone links are 24 px tall, text fields have a 3:1 border, focus is never lost or hidden

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: finish WCAG 2.1 AA in a real browser); nothing is deployed. It closes the open rows of entry 178 for contrast, target size, focus order, focus visibility, reflow and zoom.
- **Decision**:
  - **The audit** ran axe-core's colour-contrast and target-size rules in Chrome on the home page, a converter pair page, a format page, the tool pages, pricing, the sign-in, register and password pages, the dashboard, the API documentation, the legal pages and the 404 page, in light and dark, at 390, 640 (200 % zoom of 1280) and 1440 px, and at 320 px for reflow, plus a keyboard walk of the converter flow. Text contrast and axe's target-size rule found nothing in either theme.
  - **A standalone link or control is at least 24 px tall** (`min-h-6`): the footer links, the home page's API link, the format-card links, the links of the password pages and the "show sub-properties" summary. Links inside a sentence keep their line height, which WCAG 2.5.8 exempts.
  - **A text field's border is the `rule-strong` token** on the sign-in, register and password-reset forms (4.97:1 on the light card; the options and API-key fields already used it). The default `rule` border was 1.21:1, below the 3:1 of WCAG 1.4.11.
  - **The visually hidden file input is not a Tab stop** (`tabIndex={-1}`); the visible "Choose file" button opens it. The input took focus with nothing to show for it (WCAG 2.4.7).
  - **When the queue settles and the Convert button leaves, keyboard focus moves to the first download** if it was lost to the page (WCAG 2.4.3).
  - **The format picker's search, category list and format grid show the global 2 px focus outline**, inset so the popover does not clip it. The category list showed only a background change, which the selected category already had, and the format grid used the accent ring that is 2.88:1 on the dark card.
  - **The three format-tile row shrinks its connector lines below 360 px** so the row fits a 320 px window beside a classic scrollbar (WCAG 1.4.10).
- **Why**: The review counted 13 targets under 24 px on a phone, and an automated check in jsdom cannot see contrast, size or focus. A browser walk found two failures axe does not report: the invisible focus stop and the lost focus after a conversion.
- **Trade-offs**: The footer link rows grow by 4 px each. The sign-in and register tab-switch sentence links stay at their line height as in-sentence links.
- **Alternatives rejected**: Making every inline link 24 px tall (it breaks the line spacing of the legal text for no gain under the exception); a darker `rule` token for the whole site (it would darken every card edge, which has no 1.4.11 duty).
- **Verified by**: `tests/a11y-axe.test.ts` (the file input is out of the Tab order, the footer links carry `min-h-6`, focus reaches the download when the queue settles) and the browser pass recorded in `.cache/a11y-review/`.
- **Revisit when**: the 2.2 AA row set is adopted as the target (focus not obscured by the sticky queue bar, 2.4.11) or a page adds a custom widget.

## 207. The legacy binary Office files and the Palm databases are opened with the import filter of the generation found in the file

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: the open row of entry 201 for the declared `--infilter`); nothing is deployed.
- **Decision**:
  - **The office suite is told the filter of the generation of the file** (`officeInputFilterArgs` in `src/lib/conversions/office/legacy-import-filter.ts`) for `doc`, `dot`, `xls`, `xlt`, `ppt`, `pps`, `pot`, `wps` and `pdb`, as it is told the filter of every other declared format (entry 201). The generation is read from the file, with bounded reads of its compound file directory and header: the class ID of a Word file or the `nFib` of its `WordDocument` stream (`MS Word 97` for 193 and later, `MS Word 95` for 104, `MS WinWord 6.0` for 101), the stream name of a workbook (`Workbook` is `MS Excel 97`, `Book` is `MS Excel 5.0/95`), the `PowerPoint Document` stream (`MS PowerPoint 97`), and the database type and creator of a Palm file (`TEXtREAd` is `Palm_Text_Document`, `DataPlkr` is `Plucker eBook`). A template or slide show takes the template or `AutoPlay` filter of its generation where the suite has one (`MS Word 97 Vorlage`, `MS Word 95 Vorlage`, the two Excel `Vorlage/Template` filters, `MS PowerPoint 97 Vorlage`, `MS PowerPoint 97 AutoPlay`); a Word 6.0 template has none and is opened with `MS WinWord 6.0`. A `.wps` that is a Word compound file is read as Word.
  - **A file whose generation is not recognised gets no filter** and is opened by the suite's type detection as before, so no refusal and no error mapping changes: a Works `.wps`, a raw Excel 2 to 4 sheet, a `BOOKMOBI` database, an HTML or XML file named `.xls`, and a compound file that no reader can open.
- **Why**: The suite has one filter for each generation behind one extension (`registry/*.xcd`), and the filter of the newest refuses a file of an older one, so one fixed name was not possible. Naming the generation the file has makes the suite open it with the importer of the format it was declared as and never with one its own detection picks from the bytes.
- **Trade-offs**: Each such run reads the directory of the compound file once more, and a Word 6.0 or 95 file (class ID `00020900`) reads the file in full to find its `nFib`. A Works `.wps` and the raw Excel 2 to 4 sheets still depend on the suite's detection because their signatures are not a sure sign of one filter.
- **Alternatives rejected**: One fixed filter per extension (refuses older files); trying the filters in turn on failure (hides the refusal of a file that is not what it was declared as and costs a run per attempt).
- **Verified by**: `tests/office-legacy-import-filters.test.ts` (the filter named per generation, none for an unrecognised file, every name present in the registry of the installed suite, and the Word, Excel, PowerPoint and Palm files made or built there opened with the filter named); the Word 6.0, Word 95 and Excel 5.0/95 generations are checked by name only because the suite cannot write them.
- **Revisit when**: a real Works, Excel 4 or Plucker file is among the corpus samples, or the suite adds a filter for another generation.

## 208. A sandboxed program cannot read the command line or the status of another run in /proc: pid-init and the qpdf runner start it under a Landlock ruleset

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: the TODO line on the `/proc` entries of other runs); nothing is deployed. It refines entries 197 and 203.
- **Decision**:
  - **The program is started under a Landlock ruleset** (`make_ruleset` and `enforce_ruleset` in `native/pid-init/pid-init.c`, applied by the program's own process just before `exec`, and the same code in `native/qpdf-runner/qpdf-runner.c` for the job process). The ruleset handles reading and writing files (`LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_READ_FILE`, `LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_WRITE_FILE`) and moving them between directories (`LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REFER`, on directories), and allows these below every entry of `/` except `/proc`, and below every entry of `/proc` except the directories whose names are numbers. `/proc/self` and `/proc/thread-self` are among the entries it allows, and they name the directory of the program itself (the number it has outside its PID namespace), so the program keeps its own `/proc` and every system-wide file (`/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/sys/...`, `/proc/cpuinfo`). What is left outside is `/proc/<number>` of every other process: the command line, the status and the rest of another run, the runner and the worker are refused with `EACCES`, and so is writing the OOM score of another process (the runs share one user ID, so that write was allowed before). Landlock needs no mount and no capability beyond the ones `unshare -r` gives; `landlock_restrict_self` is irrevocable, so a program that holds every capability of its user namespace cannot lift it.
  - **Every `/proc` entry a rule names is kept open for as long as the program runs.** A rule belongs to the inode it was made for, and `/proc` makes a new inode for an entry whenever the kernel has dropped its cached entry; the rule then matches nothing and the program loses that file. Measured on the testbed with `drop_caches` written twice while a program waited: with the entries closed, `/proc/self/status`, `/proc/thread-self/stat`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/net/dev`, `/proc/mounts` and `/proc/uptime` all answered `EACCES` afterwards, in a PID namespace and without one; with them kept open all answer. In the PID namespace the program sends the descriptors to PID 1 over a socket before it executes (PID 1 keeps them until it ends, which is when the program has), so the program carries none; with `--no-pid-namespace`, where nothing stays behind the program, they are descriptors of the program itself, numbered 200 and up (about 60). The qpdf job keeps them in the job process. Nothing is put in force unless the entries are kept first. The entries of `/` need no keeping: they are the roots of file systems or files of a disk, whose inodes Landlock itself keeps alive.
  - **Moves between directories are handled.** A ruleset that does not handle `LANDLOCK_ACCESS_FS_REFER` refuses every `rename` and `link` between two directories with `EXDEV` (measured: `os.rename("a2/f", "b2/f")` and `ln` failed, a `mv` only seemed to work because it copies instead). The ruleset asks the kernel for its Landlock version and handles the right from version 2 (Linux 5.19). **On version 1 (Linux 5.13 to 5.18) no ruleset is made** and the program runs with the notice below: the conversions rename and link between directories, and a hiding that breaks them is worse than none. `pid-init --check` exits 3 there.
  - **A program that opts out of the PID namespace is still started through pid-init**: `pid-init --no-pid-namespace -- <program>` applies the ruleset and runs the program in place (no fork, no PID 1, `levelsAboveProgram` stays 0). calibre and veraPDF (entry 203) are in this case and keep working: they read `/proc/<their own id>/...`, which the ruleset allows.
  - **Operator switch and exemption.** `SANDBOX_HIDE_PROC=false` (trimmed, any case, as `SANDBOX_PID_NAMESPACE` is read) starts every program with `pid-init --keep-proc` and the qpdf runner with `--keep-proc`: the PID namespace stays, only the hiding goes, and the probe does not ask about it. A single call opts out with `sandboxOptions.hideProc: false` (a qpdf call with sandbox options already goes the usual way, through pid-init). `SANDBOX_PID_NAMESPACE=false` turns off pid-init, so both. Nothing uses the per-call option today.
  - **`pid-init --check`** exits 0 when the ruleset can be made and in force and 3 when it cannot. The probe of `getUnshareCapability` runs it after the PID namespace probe; a host that cannot says once `[sandbox] Programs can read the command line and the status of the other runs of this worker in /proc: ...`, and runs programs without the ruleset (as a host without a PID namespace runs them without one). **A run that could not be put under the ruleset after a good probe says so too**: pid-init and the runner print `pid-init: /proc not hidden: <reason>` as the first line of the standard error of the program, and the worker takes that line off the output (`withoutProcHideNotice` in `executeSandboxedBinary` and in the reader of the runner's results) and logs it once. Check 10 of `scripts/verify-worker-container.sh` fails the container job when the program reads the command line of a sibling (Landlock off in the kernel, or the seccomp profile denying `landlock_create_ruleset`), or cannot link a file between directories.
  - **A ruleset that is not whole is not put in force**: if a rule cannot be added for a reason other than a missing entry (out of descriptors, a refused rule), or the open entries cannot be kept, `pid-init` runs the program without it and says so, because a missing rule would take a whole directory away from the program.
- **Why**: entry 197 left the command line of a sibling readable (it holds the paths of the sibling's files, which the runs of a worker can read, as they share a user ID). `/proc` cannot be hidden by a mount here: the worker's seccomp profile has no `mount`, `pivot_root` or `chroot`, AppArmor denies `mount`, and a container's `/proc` has masked paths, which make the kernel refuse a new procfs in a user namespace. The Landlock calls are in the allow list of `docker/seccomp-worker.json` already (Docker's default set), AppArmor does not mediate them, and the kernel of the testbed and of current Ubuntu has Landlock in its LSM list. Measured on the Lima testbed (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 6.8, Landlock ABI 4, under the `flatpak` AppArmor profile that allows `unshare -r`): before the change a sandboxed run read `cmdline` and `status` of a sibling and wrote its `oom_score_adj`; after it each fails with `EACCES`, in a PID namespace and without one, and the run still reads its own entries, the threads of its own, `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/sys/kernel/pid_max`. Reading the links and descriptors of another run (`/proc/<n>/fd`, `cwd`, `root`, `environ`) is refused by Landlock's own ptrace rule, not by the path rules: a process under a ruleset cannot be given ptrace access to a process outside its domain.
- **Trade-offs**:
  - **A process the program forks has a `/proc/<number>` of its own that no rule can name beforehand**, so a descendant that reads its own `/proc/self/status` or `maps`, and a parent that reads the `/proc/<child>/stat` of its child, get `EACCES` (measured: `python3` running `cat /proc/self/status`). Threads are not affected (their entries are below the directory of the program). Checked against what the worker runs: the office suite (oosplash and its `soffice.bin` child: the Word to PDF conversion gives the same PDF text and size with and without the ruleset, and the real-sample suites pass), ffmpeg, the PDF and image tools, the archive tools, OCR, a JVM, and calibre. For calibre the image installs the Debian package (8.5.0) and the worker uses `ebook-convert` for the five Palm, Kindle, Sony and Open eBook targets only; its PDF output (Qt WebEngine, which reads `/proc/self` in its child processes) is not used. It was checked anyway with the 9.15.0 release on the testbed: epub to PDF (59,715 bytes) and mobi to PDF (15,456 bytes) are byte-for-byte the same size with and without the ruleset, and docx to epub has the same XHTML (the file size varies from run to run with the generated cover, in both modes); the four calibre suites (96 tests) pass with the ruleset and without it. Under `strace` every process of calibre is a child, and 26 reads of `/proc/<own id>` answered `EACCES` while the PDF came out the same. So calibre and veraPDF stay under the ruleset; a program that needs the files of its own children is exempted with `hideProc: false`, and none was found.
  - **The list of `/proc` still names the other processes** (`readdir` is not handled by the ruleset, so a program can still list which process numbers exist); what is refused is the content of every file below them. The files that only a process allowed to trace another can read (`environ`, `maps`, `mem`, `cwd`, `root`) were refused before.
  - **About 95 rules and about 60 kept descriptors** per start: 0.18 ms more per start (`unshare -r -n -- pid-init -- /bin/true` 0.61 ms before and 0.79 ms after, mean of 400 starts, 7 steady rounds of 8, interleaved, on the testbed; through `executeSandboxedBinary` 0.88 ms and 1.08 ms, 300 starts, 6 rounds); a program that stood outside pid-init before (calibre, veraPDF) goes from 0.41 ms to 0.63 ms; the self-test job of `qpdf-runner` goes from 1.95 ms to 2.09 ms. The entries of `/` are read when the program starts: a top-level directory made later is not allowed to it (the image's root file system is read-only). A program started with `--no-pid-namespace` sees about 60 more open descriptors, numbered 200 and up, and passes them to the programs it starts (they are `O_PATH` descriptors of `/proc` entries and harmless); one that closes every descriptor loses the rules for the entries it closed when the kernel drops them.
  - **Landlock must be enabled in the kernel of the host** (`cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm` lists `landlock`; Linux 5.19 or later for the moves). Without it the worker says so once and runs as before.
- **Alternatives rejected**: a new procfs mount with `hidepid=2` and `subset=pid` (what a bubblewrap `--proc`, a systemd `ProtectProc=invisible` or a minijail/nsjail mount does) and a tmpfs bound over `/proc`: both need `mount`, and widening the profile for it (a `mount` call, an AppArmor rule, `systempaths=unconfined` to lift the masks) opens the container's own kernel surface for every program of the worker; `chroot` or `pivot_root` into an empty tree: not in the profile; a distinct user ID per run so that the permission bits of `/proc/<number>` refuse it: `hidepid` is a mount option of the host's procfs, which the container does not control, and the directory of a process is world-readable whatever its owner (measured: a process that is not dumpable still shows `cmdline` and `status`); `newuidmap` ranges are not in the image (entry 197); a seccomp filter on `openat`: a filter cannot read the path; Yama and `ptrace_scope`: they guard `ptrace` and the files that need it, not `cmdline` and `status`; a helper process that stays beside a program in place to hold the descriptors: it would be a child the program did not make, counted by `RLIMIT_NPROC` and seen by a program that waits for any child.
- **Verified by**: `tests/sandbox-isolation.test.ts` (a sandboxed run, in a PID namespace and without one, cannot read `cmdline` or `status` of a sibling or write its OOM score, and reads its own and the system-wide entries; the controls outside the sandbox and with `hideProc: false` read them; two tests failed before the change), `tests/pid-init.test.ts` (the same through pid-init with `--keep-proc` as the control, `--no-pid-namespace` running in place, `/proc/self`, `--check` exiting 3 and the program running without the ruleset and with the notice when `landlock_create_ruleset` is denied by a seccomp filter, links and renames between directories, the kept descriptors in PID 1 and in the program, and the reads of `/proc` after `drop_caches` where `sudo` allows it; six of these failed against the first version of the ruleset), `tests/qpdf-runner.test.ts` (a job cannot read the runner's or the test's `/proc` entries and holds only the kept entries as descriptors; it failed against the first runner), `tests/sandbox-pid-init-probe.test.ts` (the warning once, the wrapper of a program that opts out, `SANDBOX_HIDE_PROC` and `hideProc`, the notice taken off the output), `tests/seccomp-worker-profile.test.ts` (the three Landlock calls are allowed), and on the testbed with the ruleset on: the office suites (`office-suite-real-samples`, `office-conversions`, `office-suite-route`, `office-advertised-pairs-conversion`, `libreoffice-*`), the media suites (`media-conversions`, `media-audio-targets`, `edge-media-*`, `media-hls-dash-packaging`), `poppler-ppm-png`, `pdf-password-argv`, `ocr-cli-tsv`, `image-avif-*`, `archive-native-*`, the `qpdf-runner*` suites and the calibre suites (`ebook-calibre-writers`, `azw4-and-cbc`, `ebook-added-pairs-real-samples`, `ebook-calibre-route`) with calibre 9.15.0, all passing.
- **Revisit when**: the worker image can mount `/proc` in a namespace of its own (the PID namespace then hides the entries and the ruleset can go), a program is found whose children read their own `/proc/<number>`, or Landlock is missing from the kernel of the host the worker is deployed on.

## 209. The final outputs of a completed graph are recorded in the history of converted files of its owner, and the account deletes them with the graph's own keys only

- **Status**: Implemented, decided 2026-11-09 (QA request: the TODO line on the graph outputs in the file history); nothing is deployed. It refines entry 204, whose history took the results of queue jobs and left a graph's nodes out.
- **Decision**:
  - **When a graph completes, the files of its `export.internal` nodes are recorded** (`recordGraphOutputsInHistory`, called by `finishGraph` after the state is read and before the webhook is told), for a signed-in owner only. These are the outputs the graph returns (`results/<graphId>/<nodeId>/<index>/<name>`); the intermediate files of the other nodes, removed when the graph ends, and the outputs of an `export.url` node, which are sent elsewhere, are not. A node that did not complete (a `continue` graph that skipped or failed one) records nothing.
  - **Each record has a stable id** `<graphId>:<nodeId>:<index>`, so a completion reported twice replaces the record (the same rule as the job id of a queue job), the storage key the file lives at, its stored name and size, the source format of the graph, the extension as the target format, the download URL of the key, a new field `graphId`, and the retention of a job's result (RESULT_UNDELIVERED_TTL_SECONDS from the end).
  - **The delete in the account checks the key against the graph.** For a record that names a graph, a `results/<id>/` key must be the one of that graph (`record.graphId`), as a job's record must be under its own id; any other key is refused (404) and nothing is deleted. The owner's request deletes the stored file, then the record. A record is found by the caller's id in its key, so another account cannot reach it.
  - **Account erasure needed no new code:** the records are the user's history records, which `forgetUsage` removes (in Redis and in this process), and `erase-account` already deletes `results/<graphId>/` for each graph of the user.
  - **The step is bounded, because the webhook and the cleanup of the graph wait for it:** at most `MAX_RECORDED_OUTPUTS_PER_GRAPH` = 100 outputs of a graph are recorded (a fifth of the 500 records a user keeps, so one graph, such as an archive with thousands of entries, cannot push the rest of the history out; the count left out is logged), 8 at a time (`RECORD_BATCH_SIZE`), and the whole step stops waiting after `RECORD_STEP_TIMEOUT_MS` = 5 s (what is recorded stays, the timeout is logged, and the end of the graph goes on to its webhook and cleanup). A Redis or a store that does not answer therefore delays the webhook by 5 s at most.
  - **A failure to record is logged and never fails the graph:** the end of the graph is already recorded and its reservation settled; one output that cannot be recorded does not stop the others.
- **Why**: A client that converts through a graph (every web conversion with tasks) saw the file in the download link but not in the list of its converted files, while the same conversion as a plain job or a synchronous call was listed. The record must name the graph because the key of a graph output is under the graph id and not under the record id, which the delete check for job results compared.
- **Trade-offs**: A graph whose state cannot be read at its end (read twice before the end goes on) records nothing, and nothing records it later; its outputs are still reachable by the graph. The graph's outputs are listed when the graph ends, not when each export node completes. A graph of more than 500 outputs within the retention pushes the oldest records out, as the cap of entry 204 does for any user.
- **Alternatives rejected**: Recording from the export node's job (the node does not know the graph completed, and a failed graph would list outputs of a graph that rolled back its reservation); a second delete route for graph outputs (the account list shows one kind of record); deriving the graph from the record id by splitting it (node ids may contain the separator).
